effective mixing rate and the available boundary states. That relation
remains open.

For other partitions, however, C2 and C3 can be tuned independently. In
biological systems (Chapter 13), the protein conformational landscape
has a hidden sector substantially smaller than cosmological
(\(N_H \sim 10^{10}\) conformational states), with slow dynamics set by
folding-landscape physics rather than horizon thermodynamics. Each
condition has a different source: C3 from the configurational entropy of
the conformational space; C2 from the kinetic barriers separating
metastable conformations. In engineered quantum systems (Chapter 15), C2
and C3 can be tuned independently by choosing the substrate material
(which controls \(N_H\) through the TLS bath density) and the operating
temperature (which controls \(\tau_B\) through bath equilibration
rates). The BEC analogue-gravity experimental program (Chapter 15 §15.8)
specifically tests the framework's predictions in the regime where C3 is
marginal while C2 remains satisfied --- an experimental design that
depends on the independence of the two conditions.

The conditions have distinct roles in the history-memory result of
{[}Main §3.4{]}. A C4 witness implies hidden influence in every faithful
realization, C3 bounds capacity for each supplied law, and C2-slow has
the stated conditional mixing scope. The framework's empirical content
(Chapters 13, 15) and forward predictions (Chapter 18) rely on the
separate physical sources to make distinct quantitative claims about
regimes where one condition is marginal and others are satisfied.

The finite-law representation and the history-memory characterization
use separate hypotheses. The remainder of the chapter develops the proof
in the stages identified in §1.1: partition-relativity (§1.4),
P-indivisibility (§1.5), the two routes to unitary quantum mechanics
(§1.6), Bell-inequality violations (§1.7), the characterization theorem
in its current per-horizon form (§1.8), and the algorithmic reading of
what the theorem establishes (§1.9).

\hypertarget{partition-relativity}{%
\subsection{1.4 Partition-relativity}\label{partition-relativity}}

The marginalized transition probabilities of the previous section depend
on three inputs: the dynamics, the partition, and the measure. The
framework's lemmas fix the dynamics. The measure is fixed only by adding
a selection principle: Lemma 3 takes the invariant measure of maximal
entropy as the canonical one. Under the canonical measure only the
partition remains as a free input, and the following result establishes
that this is the entire freedom: the emergent description is determined
by the partition alone.

\textbf{Lemma.} \emph{Under the canonical measure of Lemma 3, the
emergent description is uniquely determined by the partition.}

\emph{Proof.} By Lemma 3 the Hamiltonian flow \(\phi_t\) is unique. By
Lemma 2 the partition is fixed. An embedded observer with incomplete
knowledge of the total energy averages over energies with a smooth
prior, recovering the Liouville measure \(\mu\) on a phase-space band
--- the continuum form of Lemma 3's maximal-entropy selection. Letting
\(\pi_V\) project onto the visible sector, the marginalized transition
probabilities are
\[T_{ij}(t_2, t_1) = \int_{\Gamma_H} \delta_{x_j}\!\bigl[\pi_V\bigl(\phi_{t_2-t_1}(x_i, h)\bigr)\bigr] \, d\mu(h),\]
determined by dynamics, partition, and measure. With the dynamics fixed
and the measure set to the canonical one, only the partition remains as
input. \(\square\)

Three statements about the measure are distinct, and the lemma above is
stated under the second. \emph{Invariance.} Invariance alone does not
single out a measure: on each orbit the invariant measure is unique and
uniform, but a bijection with two or more cycles carries distinct
invariant measures, the uniform measure on each cycle (kernel:
\texttt{invariance\_does\_not\_select} in
\texttt{OIBridge/CanonicalMeasure.lean}), so the deterministic evolution
by itself does not fix the measure. \emph{Canonical selection.} Among
the invariant measures, Lemma 3 selects the counting measure as the one
of maximal entropy compatible with the observer's records; its continuum
form is the Liouville measure. The selection is a principle the
framework adopts for constructed realizations --- a standard but
substantive epistemic postulate, carried in the posit ledger of {[}Main
§4.5{]} --- not a consequence of invariance. \emph{Realization datum.}
The canonical measure is the default, not a constraint on
representations. A particular realization may carry its own fixed hidden
prior \(\mu_H\) as part of the realization datum --- a structured
preparation --- and the emergent law is then a function of the dynamics,
the partition and \(\mu_H\). The same bijection and partition under
different priors generally give different visible laws; the two-state
swap under a uniform and under a point-mass hidden prior is the simplest
case ({[}Main §1.2{]}). Partition-relativity is therefore relative to
the declared measure, and the framework's baseline transition matrices
use the canonical one.

Different partitions of the same \((S,\varphi)\) can give different
reduced laws for a common preparation. Chapter 7 relates \(\hbar\) to
the counting scale under H-slope, H-count and the stated horizon
conditions. The \(1/4\) entropy coefficient is a consistency relation of
that calibration. The September 2025 analysis of GW250114, observed on
January 14, used inferred Kerr horizon areas to test the classical area
theorem. The entropy coefficient itself has no direct test.

Partition-relativity establishes that the emergent description is
well-defined. The next question is what kind of description it is ---
whether the marginalization produces a Markovian process, a generic
non-Markovian one, or something more specific. The result of this
section is that, in the recurrence and non-permutation regimes
established there, the process satisfies a precise structural property
with a name in the open-systems literature --- P-indivisibility ---
while C1--C4 by themselves deliver accessible non-Markovianity ({[}Main
§3.4{]}). The two sections following establish how the imported
correspondence supplies the quantum representation across its class,
under the translation hypothesis (T) --- with P-indivisibility governing
whether that representation is nontrivial ({[}Main §3.1{]}), which is a
claim about the two-time marginal family and does not transport the
multi-time content of (C4).

\hypertarget{p-indivisibility}{%
\subsection{1.5 P-indivisibility}\label{p-indivisibility}}

The central technical result of the chapter is that, on a finite
reversible representative, the marginalized process is P-indivisible
across the recurrence cycle whenever, under the uniform hidden prior,
its one-step visible matrix is not a permutation, as non-trivial
coupling acting at the first step makes it. On accessible windows the
proved statement is conditional memory: a (C4) readback gap forces
\(I(X_{<k}; X_{k+1} \mid X_k) > 0\), which does not by itself make the
process P-indivisible there ({[}Main §2.3{]}).

\textbf{Theorem (P-indivisibility).} \emph{Let \(\mathcal{C}_V\) and
\(\mathcal{C}_H\) be finite sets with \(|\mathcal{C}_V| \geq 2\), and
let
\(\varphi: \mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H \to \mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H\)
be a bijection with}
\[T_{ij} = \frac{|\{h \in \mathcal{C}_H : \pi_V(\varphi(x_i, h)) = x_j\}|}{|\mathcal{C}_H|}.\]
\emph{With the common uniform hidden prior, if \(T\) is not a
permutation matrix, the rooted family fails P-divisibility by the
return.}

P-indivisibility is a precise property of stochastic processes that
requires unpacking. For a fixed preparation at the root time \(t_1\),
the family is \emph{P-divisible} when every pair \(t_1 < t_2 < t_3\)
admits the row-kernel factorization
\[T(t_3, t_1) = T(t_2, t_1) \cdot \Lambda(t_3, t_2),\] where
\(\Lambda(t_3, t_2)\) is a valid stochastic matrix --- non-negative
entries, rows summing to one. P-divisibility expresses the natural
intuition that probabilistic dynamics should compose: the probability of
going from \(x_i\) to \(x_k\) over the long interval \([t_1, t_3]\)
should be obtainable by chaining the probability of going from \(x_i\)
to some intermediate state \(x_j\) over \([t_1, t_2]\) with the
probability of continuing from \(x_j\) to \(x_k\) over \([t_2, t_3]\).
Classical Markov processes satisfy this property trivially because the
future depends only on the present state, not on history.
P-indivisibility means some such pair has no row-stochastic divisor.
When the earlier matrix is invertible, a negative entry of the unique
candidate proves the failure.

Breuer, Laine, and Piilo (2009) introduced a more directly interpretable
signature of non-Markovian dynamics: \emph{information backflow}. In a
P-divisible process, the distinguishability of any two initial
conditions can only decrease over time --- the future loses information
about the past monotonically, as in any classical Markov chain reaching
equilibrium. In a P-indivisible process, distinguishability can rebound:
information about the initial condition that appeared lost can return to
the visible sector at a later time. A revival concerns the rooted
transition matrices. The link between the finite-return criterion and
history memory within the recurrence cycle uses a full-support visible
prior ({[}Main §2.3{]}). In the coin--die example below, conditioning on
the history reveals information about a preloaded hidden selector. The
signature runs one way: a rebound certifies P-indivisibility, but a
P-indivisible process need not produce one --- some keep the
distinguishability of every pair of initial distributions non-increasing
({[}Main §2.3{]}) --- so the absence of backflow does not establish
P-divisibility.

The proof of the theorem uses the total variation distance between
probability distributions,
\[d(p, q) = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_k |p_k - q_k|.\] This quantity ranges from
\(0\) (identical distributions) to \(1\) (distributions with disjoint
support) and measures how distinguishable two probability distributions
are by any measurement. For a P-divisible process, \(d\) is
non-increasing along trajectories: starting from \(\delta_i\) (the point
mass at \(x_i\)) and \(\delta_j\) (the point mass at \(x_j\)), the
quantity \(d(\delta_i T^{(t)}, \delta_j T^{(t)})\) --- where \(T^{(t)}\)
denotes \(t\) steps of the dynamics --- cannot grow with \(t\).
P-indivisibility is therefore established by demonstrating non-monotonic
behavior of \(d\) along some trajectory.

\emph{Proof of P-indivisibility.} The proof exhibits non-monotonicity
through a three-step construction.

\emph{Step 1 (Recurrence to maximal distinguishability).} The dynamics
\(\varphi\) is a bijection on the finite total set
\(\mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H\). Every bijection on a finite set
is a permutation, and every permutation generates a finite cyclic group:
there exists an integer \(N\) (the least common multiple of the cycle
lengths in \(\varphi\)'s cycle decomposition) such that
\(\varphi^N = \mathrm{id}\). Applied to the marginalized dynamics, this
means \(T^{(N)}\) equals the identity matrix \(I\). Starting from
\(\delta_i\) and applying \(T^{(N)}\) returns \(\delta_i\) unchanged;
starting from \(\delta_j\) returns \(\delta_j\). The distinguishability
is \(d(\delta_i T^{(N)}, \delta_j T^{(N)}) = d(\delta_i, \delta_j) = 1\)
for any \(i \neq j\). After \(N\) steps, the two initial conditions are
again perfectly distinguishable.

\emph{Step 2 (Strict contraction at intermediate times).} If \(T\) is
not a permutation matrix, then there must exist visible states \(x_i\),
\(x_j\), and \(x_l\) with both \(T_{il} > 0\) and \(T_{jl} > 0\). (If no
such triple existed, each row of \(T\) would have a single nonzero entry
equal to one, making \(T\) a permutation.) The existence of \(x_l\) as a
common destination from both \(x_i\) and \(x_j\) means the post-step
distributions \(\delta_i T\) and \(\delta_j T\) both assign positive
weight to \(x_l\) --- they overlap. For overlapping distributions
\(p, q\) with \(p_l \wedge q_l > 0\), the total variation distance
satisfies \[d(p, q) = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_k |p_k - q_k| < 1,\] the
inequality strict because of the overlap. So
\(d(\delta_i T, \delta_j T) < 1\).

\emph{Step 3 (Non-monotonicity).} Combining the previous two steps: at
\(t = 0\), \(d(\delta_i, \delta_j) = 1\). At \(t = 1\),
\(d(\delta_i T, \delta_j T) < 1\). At \(t = N\),
\(d(\delta_i T^{(N)}, \delta_j T^{(N)}) = 1\). The trajectory of
distinguishability is therefore
\(1 \to (\text{something less than } 1) \to 1\) --- non-monotonic. A
P-divisible process cannot produce this trajectory because \(d\) would
be non-increasing throughout. The process is P-indivisible. \(\square\)

The proof uses the finite bijection, the common hidden prior and the
non-permutation first-step matrix that gives overlap. C1 can be
witnessed later than the first step. The general overlap-and-return
criterion in {[}Main §2.3{]} permits such later witnesses. In continuous
time, for a Hamiltonian flow on compact energy surfaces, the same
argument needs the flow to return near-totally at a common time after
the rooted maps have left the permutation class --- the counterpart of
\(\varphi^N = \mathrm{id}\). Poincaré recurrence does not supply this
for a general flow: it returns almost every state at its own time, and a
mixing flow never again returns a whole visible cell at once at late
times. The extension therefore holds for flows with such a common return
and is open for general Hamiltonian flows ({[}Main §2.3{]}).

\textbf{The accessible-timescale lemma.} A potential objection to the
proof as stated is that the recurrence time \(N\) can be astronomically
large. \(N\) is the order of \(\varphi\) as a permutation of the
\(n = |\mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H|\) total configurations. For
any bijection it is at most Landau's function \(g(n)\), the largest
order of a permutation of \(n\) points, with
\(\ln g(n) \sim \sqrt{n \ln n}\), and it divides
\(\mathrm{lcm}(1, \ldots, n) = e^{(1 + o(1))\,n}\); under the exactly
linear update rule (A5) it is below \(n\) (Chapter 18 §18.7). The
framework bounds \(N\) but does not compute it, and \(n\) is not fixed
by visible data. For \(N\) of astronomical size the distinguishability
restoration at \(t = N\) is not directly observable. What an observer
can measure is memory on \emph{accessible} timescales --- times short
compared to \(\tau_B\), the hidden sector's intrinsic memory time ---
not at recurrence. The accessible-timescale lemma supplies that memory,
as conditional mutual information, wherever the stored record is read
back (C4). It does not supply P-indivisibility on those windows: a
readback gap is compatible with a population law that is divisible on
every window short of recurrence ({[}Main §2.3{]}).

For an illustration of retention, suppose that uniform exponential
erosion in the iterated coarse channel gives a per-step retained
fraction \(r=e^{-\tau_S/\tau_B}\). A record that undergoes \(k\) such
steps retains the fraction \(r^k\approx 1-k\tau_S/\tau_B\) when
\(k\tau_S\ll\tau_B\). This is a model estimate for retention of the
record.

The quantitative observable bound uses readback. If two histories with
the same present state each have probability at least \(p_0\) and
next-step laws separated by total variation at least \(\delta\), then
\(I(X_{<k};X_{k+1}\mid X_k)\ge p_0\delta^2/\ln 2\) ({[}Main §2.3{]}).
The probabilities and gap depend on the history pair and its readout.

For illustration, inserting \(\tau_B\sim H^{-1}\sim 10^{17}\) s and
\(\tau_S\sim 10^{-15}\) s into the retention model gives
\(k\tau_S/\tau_B\sim 10^{-12}\) at \(k=10^{20}\). The calculation
assumes the proposed cosmological retention time applies to the
laboratory coupling. The physical preparation, rate and readout needed
to test that assumption remain open. In the separate horizon count,
\(e^{S_{\text{dS}}}\) modeled boundary states would have capacity
\(S_{\text{dS}}/\ln 2\) bits.

The witnessed readback gap gives conditional memory inside its
accessible window. A non-permutation rooted map followed by the finite
return gives P-indivisibility across the recurrence cycle.

\textbf{A worked six-hidden-state model.} A concrete example makes the
mechanism tangible. Take a two-state visible sector
\(\mathcal{C}_V = \{0, 1\}\) --- call it a coin with states Heads and
Tails --- and a six-state hidden sector
\(\mathcal{C}_H = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\) --- call it a die. The dynamics
is the permutation
\[\sigma = (0{,}1 \leftrightarrow 1{,}1)\,(0{,}2 \leftrightarrow 1{,}2)\,(0{,}3 \leftrightarrow 0{,}4)\,(0{,}5 \leftrightarrow 0{,}6)\,(1{,}3 \leftrightarrow 1{,}4)\,(1{,}5 \leftrightarrow 1{,}6).\]
Each pair \((\cdot \leftrightarrow \cdot)\) is a transposition that
swaps two total states; all six swaps together are independent (act on
distinct states), so the full dynamics is a product of disjoint
transpositions and satisfies \(\sigma^2 = \mathrm{id}\).

The die is a preloaded selector. C1 holds because the coin flips for
\(h=1,2\) and stays for \(h=3,4,5,6\). The die's successor is the same
at a matched hidden seed whichever initial coin value is used. The
selector survives the update and the uniform preparation gives differing
next-step laws for histories that meet at the same coin value, a C4
witness. The six hidden states satisfy the capacity bound for this law.

Compute the one-step transition matrix starting from \(x = 0\) (Heads)
with the die uniformly distributed. The dynamics sends
\((0, 1) \to (1, 1)\) and \((0, 2) \to (1, 2)\) --- Heads becomes Tails
for these die values. It sends \((0, 3) \to (0, 4)\),
\((0, 4) \to (0, 3)\), \((0, 5) \to (0, 6)\), \((0, 6) \to (0, 5)\) ---
Heads stays Heads for these die values, though the die value changes
within the hidden sector. So \(P(0 \to 0) = 4/6 = 2/3\) and
\(P(0 \to 1) = 2/6 = 1/3\). Symmetric reasoning for \(x = 1\) gives
\[T(1, 0) = \begin{pmatrix} 2/3 & 1/3 \\ 1/3 & 2/3 \end{pmatrix}.\] The
distinguishability after one step is
\(d(\delta_0 T, \delta_1 T) = \tfrac{1}{2}(|2/3 - 1/3| + |1/3 - 2/3|) = 1/3\).
The two initial conditions, perfectly distinguishable at \(t = 0\) with
\(d = 1\), have become much less distinguishable: \(d\) has dropped to
\(1/3\).

A time-homogeneous Markov chain with this one-step matrix would have
\(T(2, 0) = T(1, 0)^2\). Computing,
\[T(1,0)^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 5/9 & 4/9 \\ 4/9 & 5/9 \end{pmatrix},\]
with distinguishability \(1/9\) in that homogeneous example. But the
actual second-step matrix is \(T(2, 0) = I\) because
\(\sigma^2 = \mathrm{id}\) sends every total state back to itself, so
the visible-sector marginals are unchanged from the starting point. The
distinguishability at \(t = 2\) has returned to \(1\). The two initial
conditions are perfectly distinguishable again. Complete un-mixing ---
impossible for any Markov process.

The signature of P-indivisibility shows up as negative entries in the
would-be intermediate propagator. Invertibility of \(T(1,0)\) makes the
right divisor in \(T(2, 0) = T(1, 0) \cdot \Lambda(2, 1)\) unique. It is
\[\Lambda(2, 1) = T(1, 0)^{-1} \cdot T(2, 0) = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \cdot I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.\]
The off-diagonal entries are \(-1\). No valid stochastic matrix has
negative entries --- the factorization through \(t = 1\) fails by direct
computation. The process is P-indivisible.

Starting with a uniform die, observing the coin flip tells the observer
that the seed was in \(\{1,2\}\). Observing it stay tells the observer
that the seed was in \(\{3,4,5,6\}\). Two such histories may end at the
same present coin value, yet one predicts a flip and the other predicts
a stay. This is posterior learning about the hidden selector. The second
step returns the initial coin with certainty.

A causal write has an extra requirement: varying the visible input at a
fixed hidden seed must change the later hidden state ({[}Main §2.3{]}).
The two-card SWAP in §1.11 supplies that witness. The coin--die example
supplies history readback from a preloaded selector. The next section
takes up how these finite records are represented.

\hypertarget{the-two-routes-to-quantum-mechanics}{%
\subsection{1.6 The two routes to quantum
mechanics}\label{the-two-routes-to-quantum-mechanics}}

There are two complementary routes from the observer's stochastic law to
quantum form.

The first is internal and elementary. A finite reversible realization
lifts to a permutation unitary on the Hilbert space spanned by the total
configurations. With the hidden register prepared in the corresponding
prior, fixed-basis Born readout reproduces the visible stochastic law
exactly, including its finite multi-time trajectory statistics. Combined
with the finite process-dilation theorem in the reverse direction, this
yields, for a supplied law on a finite alphabet through a finite
horizon, the exact equivalence \(S\iff D\iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\).

The second route is the stochastic--quantum correspondence of Barandes.
It supplies a compressed quantum representation and the associated
interpretive dictionary for the source's finite-configuration class. The
important logical point is that the existence of a Hilbert/unitary/Born
representation does not require P-indivisibility --- every finite
stochastic law has such a representation. Accessible conditional memory
instead identifies the memory-bearing sector; indivisibility across the
recurrence cycle is a separate property, present wherever a rooted
visible map is not a permutation.

The Born rule in the fixed-basis representation is therefore part of the
representation dictionary, not a selector derived uniquely from C1--C4.
The full operational problem is narrower, and it is answered as a
classification rather than a derivation ({[}GR §3.3{]}): with operations
taken to act on the complex matrices indexed by the configurations of
the system and of its composites --- a kinematics the classification
assumes and does not derive --- the coherent preparations,
transformations, and measurements of one OI system and its composites
form one standard quantum instrument algebra exactly when five
operational conditions hold --- valid probabilities, consistency under a
trivial one-state ancilla, inert spectators, full reversible control,
and iterated composition --- and each is independent of the others and
of the observation process, so embedded observation alone does not
select quantum mechanics; the selection principles are named. Finite
classical action-labelled controls are already jointly dilatable; the
genuinely coherent/noncommuting and compositional structure is what
those conditions supply. The same classification has a layered form,
quantum-complete OI (OI⁺): the unchanged OI core with well-formedness,
observational independence, reversible richness, and observer recursion,
equivalent on every nonempty finite carrier to exact finite endomorphic
operational quantum mechanics, each added principle independent of the
core, well-formedness, and the other two, and none of them entailed by
bare OI ({[}GR §3.3{]}). A primitive-source refinement restates those
three principles at the level of physical implementations and embedded
observers --- implementation locality, phase-free richness --- one
continuously driven transition and the exchanges of distinguishable
states, with no phase operation --- and embedded observation, with no
closure of the implementations under the adjoint and no inverse
accessibility assumed --- equivalent to the same operational quantum
mechanics on every nonempty finite carrier ({[}GR §3.3{]}). A
substratum-source form completes that refinement: the concrete OI
substratum, in its finite model (ledger item (ii)), supplies the
structural architecture --- closure under composition and
coarse-graining, stability under an uncoupled spectator, relabelling
invariance, reversibility, the exchanges of distinguishable states, and,
as a stated intervention principle rather than a consequence of its
finite states and bijective dynamics, the phases --- but, under finite
bijective read-write dynamics, as represented by the specified monomial
implementation class, elementary drivability fails, and the generated
theory on the two-state carrier lacks composite unitary control. A
structurally closed extension of this class that supplies elementary
drivability, including continuously tunable state mixing, generates
exact finite endomorphic operational quantum mechanics on every nonempty
finite carrier. Conversely, that quantum theory is generated by a
structurally closed extension supplying elementary drivability. In the
memory-swap example, a nontrivial exchange of the selected states has a
monomial operator ({[}GR §3.3{]}). Its typed form removes the
endomorphic qualifier: under the carrier-general typed operational
interface --- identity, composition, coarse-graining, relabelling,
uniform finite attachment, discard, and factor readout, an interface
that itself carries no quantum content --- the same equivalence holds
with exact finite-dimensional typed operational quantum mechanics,
operations between any two nonempty finite carriers included, so the
remaining qualifier is finite-dimensional rather than endomorphic ({[}GR
§3.3{]}). The finite theory admits a canonical infinite-region
completion without a continuum limit: the finite regions of the
fixed-spacing lattice carry full matrix algebras joined by compatible
injective unital embeddings with observables of disjoint regions
commuting, the norm completion of their union is a quasilocal
\(C^{*}\)-algebra on which every consistent family of finite-region
density matrices is a state and the reversible finite-range substratum
update is an isometric \(*\)-automorphism, and any system carrying the
same local stages is canonically and uniquely \(*\)-isomorphic to it,
intertwining the dynamics; this removes the finite-region cutoff for the
algebra, the state space, and the OI-induced discrete dynamics rather
than characterizing all infinite-dimensional quantum instruments or all
locality-preserving quantum dynamics; the lattice spacing stays
fundamental, no Hilbert-space representation and no superselection
sector is selected at the level of the laws, the restriction to the
substratum-induced dynamics is a theorem rather than a convention --- a
phase automorphism at one site preserves locality without arising from
any reversible finite-range bijection --- and, while the update is
joined to the identity by an exact strongly continuous path of
\(*\)-automorphisms of that algebra, with no one-parameter-group law
established and no generator exhibited, a continuous-time Hamiltonian
law remains additional structure ({[}GR §3.3{]}). Within the structural
architecture the substratum supplies, with the phase intervention
stated, exact finite endomorphic operational quantum mechanics holds
exactly when one continuous layer flow of an involution of the
configuration space moving some configuration is an available operation
at every level and every intermediate time, the executability of that
flow being an assumption not derived by configuration-level generation,
as the phase intervention is an assumption on the substratum class and
not a consequence of the finite states with the bijective dynamics
({[}GR §3.3{]}). The stated substratum dynamics with the observer's read
and write access do not source that executability, the layers being
available at time one and not at intermediate times, and the
observer-level lift, in every formulation stated that lands in the
operational interface, derives neither a non-monomial admissible
operator nor the layer flow, the site-space wave-operator formulation
being unresolved rather than excluded ({[}GR §3.3{]}).

\hypertarget{bell-inequality-violations}{%
\subsection{1.7 Bell-inequality
violations}\label{bell-inequality-violations}}

The Bell claim must separate the deterministic completion from the
reduced stochastic description. For a Bell-relevant substratum whose
coupling range does not connect the wings before readout, the dependency
graph gives exact pointwise separation. If each setting intervention,
applied at one step, also reads and writes only its own wing, every run
records a \(\pm1\) outcome at each wing, and the response-complete
pre-setting ensemble is independent of the settings, determinism yields
an ordinary Bell-local hidden-variable model and \(|S_{\rm CHSH}|\le2\).
Hidden memory and indivisibility do not alter that ceiling.

The framework therefore declines the
measurement-dependent/superdeterministic horn and takes \textbf{ontic
parameter dependence}. In the specific SM/GR realization the target
mechanism is preparation-indexed adjacency in the already
state-dependent graph \(G(x)\) (or an equivalent ontically nonlocal
response): the vacuum/uniform reference graph remains geometric and
bounded-range, while an entangling preparation may supply Bell-relevant
long adjacency so a microstate response at one wing can depend on the
remote setting. H-Bell is the open requirement that those prepared
graphs preserve operational no-signaling and the metric/Ollivier--Ricci
continuum limit. The curvature condition is downstream of a harder one.
The cited convergence theorem is arbitrary-dimensional only for the
manifold-distance-weighted graph metric, and for the degree-\(6\) cubic
reference graph the intrinsic hop metric is exactly \(\ell_1\) --- a
\(\sqrt2\) diagonal stretch that does not decay at any scale --- so the
hop-metric curvature route fails for the reference family, before any
Bell edge is added, and no \(D=3\) extension of that theorem would
rescue it. The emergent geometry itself is not in question: the
substratum's dispersion relation is isotropic at leading order. What
must be re-founded is the curvature functional, on the
propagation/Laplacian geometry rather than on shortest-path counts {[}SM
§3.2{]}. The setting-dependent alternative is recorded but not adopted;
Main §3.3 gives the model-independent necessary lower bound
\(I_{\rm ont}\ge0.0309\) bits for the quantum value. Hall--Branciard's
optimized causal CHSH model uses about \(0.080\) bits, while the smaller
\(\sim0.046\)-bit benchmark is retrocausal.

The cited causal-local indivisible \textbf{stochastic} construction
separately obeys Tsirelson's bound because its causal-independence
notion is weaker than Bell factorization. That theorem is not the
hidden-variable locality structure of the deterministic completion. If
the spatial/intervention restriction is removed, the general finite OI
response construction can realize PR-box behavior, showing that
representability, no-signaling, hidden memory, and indivisibility do not
by themselves select the quantum Bell set.

\hypertarget{the-characterization-theorem}{%
\subsection{1.8 The characterization
theorem}\label{the-characterization-theorem}}

The characterization is best read as a layered biconditional rather than
a single slogan.

\textbf{Finite representation theorem.} On any finite horizon,
\(S\iff D\iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\). Every finite stochastic process has a
finite deterministic reversible realization, and every such realization
has an exact fixed-basis unitary/Born representation. This supplies both
directions of the finite observable-law equivalence.

\textbf{Readback theorem.} C4 is the condition that makes the OI sector
memory-bearing. It forces different hidden posteriors for visible
histories that share a current state but have different future laws, a
persistence/readback requirement, and the capacity lower bound of C3.
Because the physical representative is, under A1, finite and reversible,
it also recurs: its rooted visible maps, defined for every root under
one hidden prior, return to the identity, and a non-permutation
stochastic matrix has no stochastic inverse, so any non-permutation
rooted map makes the rooted law indivisible somewhere in the recurrence
cycle. A C4 gap supplies such a map, and so does every non-deterministic
visible step, including in laws that are Markov on every accessible
window. With a full-support visible prior, that indivisibility is
equivalent to memory at some order below the recurrence time; an
observer sees the memory only when it appears at an accessible order,
which is what C4 asserts.

\textbf{Spatial extension.} The dependency graph supplies finite causal
cones exactly for finite-range substrata. Bell adds a separate
constraint: for a response-complete deterministic completion that
records a \(\pm1\) outcome in every run, measurement independence plus
parameter independence would imply \(|S_{\rm CHSH}|\le2\). Section §1.7
therefore takes the measurement-independent, ontically
parameter-dependent branch for Bell-violating substrata and keeps
operational no-signaling separate.

\textbf{Operational boundary.} These theorems do not prove that the
entire family of coherent instruments and composites equals the standard
quantum operational theory. On a finite carrier, within complex matrix
kinematics taken as given, that equality holds exactly under the five
completion conditions of {[}GR §3.3{]}. The substratum's stated
interventions do not supply one of them, full reversible control;
whether an extended OI mechanism can supply it, and which of the others
the substratum supplies, are open; this is not a qualification on the
exact finite stochastic/representation equivalence itself.

A second boundary sits alongside it, and it concerns which unitary
evolution relates two times. The equivalence says which visible laws
admit a fixed-basis unitary representation; it does not single out the
evolution connecting one time to the next. For dilated processes one
visible family can admit distinct coherent unitary lifts --- each
reproducing the visible law at every time, each composing exactly across
times --- whose relating evolutions differ, because a lift may be
deformed by a time-dependent right action that preserves everything the
visible law sees. A deformation constant in time cancels from every
relating evolution, so time dependence is what the nonuniqueness needs.
Making the relating evolution unique therefore requires a selection
condition beyond visible-law representability and ordinary coherence,
and this book does not supply one or say what form one must take. The
invisible freedom itself has two sides --- a right action by the
anchored class and a left action within each visible output's hidden
fibre, each maximal among uniform actions of its kind --- and it does
not exhaust the freedom: two lifts can fail to be related by any
uniformly invisible right deformation and still agree on every relating
evolution, and a pair outside that right class can differ in relating
evolution while being related by a left in-fibre move. At one time, what
the visible law leaves free after both actions is known exactly: it is
the off-diagonal part of the fibre-Gram data --- for each visible
output, the overlaps among the hidden states into which the lift sends
the visible inputs --- modulo phases, with the visible law as its
diagonal; and that residue is not inert, since two lifts of one visible
law can differ in it and differ in relating evolution. That residue does
not reach the fixed-basis layer. With a trivial ancilla, the fixed-basis
datum built from a lift's unitary at one time, with uniform initial law
and identity readout, has finite-horizon trajectory laws fixed by the
visible law alone, also after contractively scaled partial permutations
on either side, and two such data have equal laws exactly when their
visible laws are equal; the fixed-basis correspondence acts on the
quotient by visible equality. The trivial ancilla is part of that
statement: an ancilla attached as a tensor factor with its own unitary
leaves the rooted family unchanged, while an ancilla carried between
steps as hidden basis states can separate two lifts that share every
column entering the visible law, already in the two-step law. What
remains open is two-part: what selects the trajectory of that data
through time, and what fixes the relating evolution within a trajectory
--- the latter not fixed even by the complete trajectory. No selection
principle is named or excluded. None of this weakens the finite
observable-law equivalence, and none of it makes embedded observation
and quantum mechanics inequivalent.

\hypertarget{what-the-theorem-says}{%
\subsection{1.9 What the theorem says}\label{what-the-theorem-says}}

The theorem says something stronger than ``quantum mechanics can be
simulated by a classical hidden model'' and something more precise than
``C1--C4 uniquely force all of quantum mechanics.''

It says that, for finite observable laws, the stochastic,
reversible-deterministic, and fixed-basis quantum descriptions are
mathematically intertranslatable. A finite embedded observer therefore
does not need quantum mechanics added as a separate microscopic
postulate in order for a Hilbert-space/unitary/Born description to
exist. History readback then supplies the physical distinction between a
trivial Markov member of that representation class and the
memory-bearing sector characteristic of OI.

The converse is equally important: every finite quantum record has a
finite reversible OI realization. Given the quantum conditional
probabilities for a fixed preparation and finite instrument menu, one
finite response table serves all protocols through the chosen horizon.
The exact continuum operational theory is a mathematical idealization
rather than a requirement that the physical carrier itself be infinite.

The remaining qualification is localized. To identify the complete local
operational theory of complex quantum mechanics, rather than its exact
stochastic representation, one must lift the whole coherent intervention
and composite hierarchy into one compatible quantum instrument theory,
which on a finite carrier, within complex matrix kinematics taken as
given, happens exactly under the five completion conditions of {[}GR
§3.3{]}. The Bell fork is logically separate: §1.7 specifies the adopted
measurement-independent, ontically parameter-dependent completion and
its no-signaling requirement rather than treating Bell screening as one
of those completion conditions. The book keeps both boundaries explicit
rather than weakening what is already exact.

\hypertarget{the-four-structural-limits}{%
\subsection{1.10 The four structural
limits}\label{the-four-structural-limits}}

The exact equivalence \(S \iff D \iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\) applies to
supplied laws on finite alphabets through finite horizons. On a horizon
containing a C4 witness, every faithful deterministic realization has
hidden influence (C1) and obeys the quantitative capacity bound (C3).
Reversibility retains the record in exact realizations, including
realizations of memoryless laws. A physical mixing-time bound for
C2-slow uses the conditional-mixing hypothesis ({[}Main §3.4{]}). The
following limits illustrate particular mechanisms and preparations.

\textbf{The C1 limit: the isolated observer.}

C1 requires non-trivial coupling between visible and hidden sectors. In
the limit of complete failure --- no coupling at all --- the visible
sector evolves as a \emph{closed} deterministic system. The bijection
\(\varphi\) restricted to \(\mathcal{C}_V\) is a permutation; the
dynamics on \(V\) is just the corresponding classical evolution. No
information ever crosses the partition boundary. The hidden sector
exists but is causally disconnected from the visible sector for all
purposes.

The dynamics in this regime is fully classical in character: memoryless.
The reduced description still admits the fixed-basis quantum
representation --- every finite law does, trivially here ({[}Main
§3.4{]}) --- but there is nothing memory-bearing in it: no
coupling-induced non-Markovianity for a nontrivial representation to
encode, hence none of the interference phenomenology the framework
attributes to hidden-sector memory. No P-indivisibility arises from a
partition with no coupling, since the visible sector then evolves
autonomously by a permutation; Bell violation is a separate question,
governed by ontic parameter dependence (§1.7), not by P-indivisibility.
The observer sees a classical Newtonian world with deterministic
trajectories and well-defined values of every observable at every time.

This is the regime closest to the historical picture of classical
mechanics: a clockwork universe where every particle has a definite
position and momentum and the equations of motion fully determine the
future from the present. The framework's content is that this picture is
correct for the limit \(C1 \to 0\) --- but no laboratory observer
occupies this limit. Gravitational coupling between visible and hidden
sectors is unavoidable in our universe; stress-energy conservation
forces correlations across any horizon; the cosmological horizon is not
an impermeable wall. Real observers are coupled, and what coupling
produces is the memory-bearing quantum phenomenology --- the
representation itself is universal; coupling supplies the nontrivial
sector.

The C1 limit therefore illuminates a structural point: classical
mechanics is what \emph{uncoupled} systems do. The framework's proposal
is that the apparent quantumness of the world is a signature not of
intrinsic randomness in the underlying reality but of our
\emph{non-isolation}. Quantumness here means the phenomenology, not the
bare representation, which the uncoupled limit keeps; what is proved is
that memory in the observer's record cannot arise without the coupling.
The substratum is deterministic; what makes physics look probabilistic
is that the observer is coupled to something they cannot directly see.
An observer who could isolate themselves completely from everything
outside their measurement apparatus would see classical mechanics. No
such observer exists in our universe, and the framework's content is
that no such observer can exist --- gravitational coupling is universal.

The proposal has a striking consequence: the project of ``explaining
quantum mechanics'' by finding the right deterministic substructure is
well-defined within the framework, but the dynamics an uncoupled
observer would see in that substructure is memoryless classical
mechanics. Quantum mechanics, on this proposal, is the dynamics that
\emph{embedded} observers see when they are coupled to the substructure;
the substructure itself, viewed from a hypothetical uncoupled vantage
point, would be classical. The framework's reframing is that the
persistent intuition ``there must be a deterministic story underneath''
is correct, and the deterministic story is classical, but it is
structurally inaccessible to any actual observer.

\textbf{The C2 limit: the thermalized observer.}

C2 requires persistence of the record used at readback. The slow-bath
mechanism uses \(\tau_S / \tau_B \ll 1\) with \(\tau_B\) an effective
mixing time ({[}Main §1.3{]}). In the limit of complete failure --- the
record is erased instantly, \(\tau_B \to 0\) --- the hidden sector
equilibrates between every visible-sector measurement. No correlation
written into the hidden sector during one measurement persists to
influence the next. History readback cannot occur because there is no
memory in the bath for the visible sector to read back.

The dynamics in this regime is \emph{fully Markovian}. The reduced
description on the visible sector is a classical stochastic process with
transition probabilities depending only on the current state. The
observer sees probabilistic dynamics, but the probabilities are
memoryless: the memory-bearing/interference mechanism is absent, while
the fixed-basis representation survives, trivially diagonal-preserving
({[}Main §3.4{]}). This temporal statement must not be turned into a
Bell claim: Bell violation in the deterministic completion is governed
separately by ontic parameter dependence (§1.7), not by
P-indivisibility. The Born rule reduces to the classical probability
assignment for transitions between well-defined states. A
Schrödinger-form unitary representation still exists ---
\(Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\) supplies one for every finite law --- but here it
encodes no temporal correlations: what the regime lacks is the
memory-bearing content, not the equation's existence ({[}Main §3.4{]}).

This regime corresponds to what physics calls the \emph{thermal limit}
--- systems in contact with a fast equilibrating bath, where the bath's
state at any moment is independent of the system's history. The
classical statistical mechanics of thermal systems is exactly this
limit. Brownian motion, chemical reaction kinetics in well-stirred
solutions, ordinary diffusion processes --- these are all Markovian
dynamics described by classical stochastic processes, and the
framework's content is that this is what C2 failure looks like.

A cosmological estimate uses the proposed time \(\tau_B \sim H^{-1}\).
Applying it to laboratory records requires the effective-channel and
preparation link described in §1.3. Under effective mixing and uniform
erosion, the coarse-grained dynamics generated by iterating the one-step
channel suppresses the readback gap when \(\tau_{\rm mix}\ll\tau_S\)
({[}Main §§2.3, 4.6{]}).

The C2 limit therefore illuminates a different structural point:
classical stochastic mechanics is what \emph{thermalized} systems do.
The framework gives a structural account of why decoherence and the
classical limit emerge in systems coupled to fast environments --- a
familiar phenomenon in quantum mechanics. Decoherence theory describes
how quantum coherences are destroyed by coupling to a fast bath; the
framework's reading is that decoherence is the transition from the
memory-bearing regime back toward the C2 failure limit. Systems with
engineered fast baths approach classical stochastic behavior; systems
isolated from fast baths retain quantum coherence. The conventional
thermal-classical-limit story is the framework's C2 limit told from
inside quantum mechanics.

A corollary, stated carefully: what the framework requires is a hidden
sector that RETAINS the record across the window, which is not the same
as a frozen one. Fast hidden dynamics that conserve and route the record
satisfy the condition --- a shift-register bath rotating five cells per
visible step supports a maximal readback gap
(\texttt{fastbath\_probes.py}) --- so persistence, not slowness, is
doing the structural work beyond merely providing some unobserved
degrees of freedom. An observer whose fast hidden bath scrambles the
record sees statistics with suppressed readback; one whose fast bath
conserves and routes it retains the full memory-bearing description
(\texttt{fastbath\_probes.py}). Small \(\tau_S/\tau_B\) is a proposed
mechanism for persistence in the cosmological model and a parameter of
the conditional channel approximation. The finite-law and history-memory
theorems use their own premises ({[}Main §3.4{]}).

\textbf{The C3 limit: the universe-sized observer.}

C3 requires sufficient hidden memory capacity ---
\(\log_2|\mathcal{C}_H| \geq I^*\), with \(N_H \gg N_V\) the comfortable
realization regime. A capacity shortfall caps the amount of memory that
can be represented. The extreme case considered here is a trivial hidden
configuration space, where the visible sector \(V\) covers the total
system \(S\). There is no trace-out because there is nothing to trace
over. The observer is \emph{coextensive} with the universe.

The dynamics in this limit is fully deterministic and fully classical.
The bijection \(\varphi\) on the full system \(S\) is just a permutation
of classical states; the observer who is all of \(S\) sees its complete
deterministic evolution. No memory-bearing sector --- the fixed-basis
representation survives, trivially, as always ({[}Main §3.4{]}) --- and
no interference phenomenology, but for a different reason than in the C1
case. In the C1 limit, the visible sector is closed but the framework
still applies to it as a system; in the C3 limit, the framework's
content has no purchase because there is no embedded observation taking
place. The ``observer'' is not observing anything; they are the system
being observed, with no separation between knower and known.

This is the regime that superficially resembles a \emph{God's-eye view}.
The traditional theological framing imagines an observer who stands
outside the universe and sees everything at once with no uncertainty.
The framework's C3 limit is similar in eliminating quantum
indeterminism, but it differs structurally: there is no ``outside'' in a
deterministic universe. Such an observer would be coextensive with the
universe, not transcendent of it. They would not be viewing the
universe; they would be the universe describing itself.

Three structural features of this regime are worth noting.

\emph{Observation breaks down entirely.} In the framework's account,
observation is a \emph{partition-relative} concept. The observer reads
the visible sector through measurements that depend on the partition's
coupling. Without a partition --- without anything in the hidden sector
to be coupled to --- measurement has no meaning. The observer cannot
perform observation in the framework's sense. The God's-eye view is
therefore not a limit case of observation but a category outside it.

\emph{Limits of prediction from a record.} A proper observer may
identify the state, or its visible future, on some supported records.
Where compatible hidden states lead to different visible futures, the
available record does not fix which future occurs. Substratum
Proposition 24.5 gives the corresponding reversible examples.

Gödel's, Turing's and Wolpert's results concern specified formal,
computational and inference-device tasks (Chapter 12 §12.8). They
illustrate the limits of universal inference. Which states or futures a
particular observer can identify depends on the support and dynamics of
their model.

The coextensive case lies outside the definition of a proper observer.
Within a proper partition, predictive limits depend on the available
records and the dynamics.

\textbf{The three limits together.}

The three failure modes are structurally distinct.

In these limit models, zero hidden influence gives autonomous visible
evolution and full erasure gives a Markov law for the stated
preparation. A hidden-sector capacity shortfall bounds accessible
memory. A coextensive description is the extreme case of zero hidden
capacity.

Together the limits illustrate different roles for C1--C4. A physical
model of a laboratory observer must specify its preparation, hidden
coupling, retention and readout. The proposed cosmological application
has yet to provide that link.

The finite-law representation applies across these regimes. The
distinctive history-memory result concerns observations with differing
next-step conditionals from the same present value. The physical
conjecture is that the relevant hidden processes of our world generate
the observed quantum statistics under a common operational interface.
The named control and readout questions in {[}Main §3.4{]} remain open.

This reframing has consequences for the framework's empirical content
beyond what is already developed in Chapters 5 through 19. Each of the
four conditions is independently testable through the restricted
quantum-statistical regime --- engineered systems approaching the
marginal-failure boundary. Chapter 15 §15.7 develops the restricted
quantum-statistical regime in engineered quantum systems with the BEC
analogue-gravity test as the framework's cleanest experimental probe of
marginal hidden capacity. Chapter 13 §13.7 develops the proposal's
conjecture for biological systems. Chapter 18 §18.3 develops the
restricted quantum-statistical regime as a forward prediction of the
mechanism proposal. The four structural limits are therefore not just
conceptual content but a framework of empirically accessible regimes,
with current experiments now beginning to probe the marginal-failure
boundaries.

\hypertarget{the-card-table-and-the-chessboard}{%
\subsection{1.11 The card table and the
chessboard}\label{the-card-table-and-the-chessboard}}

Chess is a game of complete information: every piece stands in the open,
and in principle the game is exhaustively analyzable --- a sufficiently
large lookup table settles every position. Poker is a game of incomplete
information, and that difference is not cosmetic. When von Neumann
founded game theory he took poker, not chess, as the interesting case,
precisely because hidden cards force probability into rational play even
though nothing in the rules is random. The mixed strategy is not
ignorance dressed up; it is the correct mathematical form of play from
inside an information set. The framework's claim can be stated in
exactly these terms: the substratum is a chess game, and physics is the
rulebook a piece would rationally write from inside it. What this
section shows is that ordinary poker is not a rich enough interior view
--- and that the specific way it falls short, and the specific
modification that repairs it, together reproduce the anatomy of Chapter
1 in miniature.

The comparison game uses a static hidden deal. For a visible record that
screens earlier play from the future, its odds factor through the
intermediate record. The modified table below gives a finite example in
which the observed record fails that screening condition.

Three modifications close the gap, and they are conditions C1--C4 of
§1.3 in card form. First, the shuffle between streets is a
deterministic, reversible permutation of the deck --- a faro shuffle,
say --- rather than a randomization: bijective dynamics on the full
state. Second, each street deals burn cards, face down and never shown,
which the shuffle correlates with the live cards: a hidden sector
coupled to the visible one (C1), whose configuration persists between
streets (C2), with capacity to store a record of the visible play (C3).
Third, revealing a card is an intervention, not a passive glance: a
revealed card is burned and replaced under a fixed rule, so revelation
physically breaks the card's correlation with the rest of the deck.

A small such game gives a causal write and readback through a burn card.
The finite return illustrates the same kind of revival as the coin--die
example of §1.5. The player holds one hole card, red or black --- the
coin. One burn card, red or black, lies face down --- the memory
register the die provided. The shuffle between streets is the simplest
reversible move available: hole card and burn card trade places. Then,
writing the odds that the hole card at showdown matches the hole card as
dealt:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
protocol & matching odds \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
one shuffle, then showdown & 1/2 \\
two shuffles, then showdown & 1 (certain) \\
two shuffles, odds chained through the unobserved middle & 1/2 \\
two shuffles with a peek (and forced re-burn) in the middle & 1/2 \\
\end{longtable}

Each line is checkable by hand --- there are sixteen cases in the
longest protocol. A single shuffle randomizes the visible card
completely. Two shuffles return it with certainty: the first swap writes
the hole card into the burn pile, the second reads it back --- the same
write-then-read information backflow that §1.5 exhibited in the would-be
intermediate propagator with negative entries. Chaining the one-street
odds through the unobserved middle street predicts even money and is
simply wrong: the process is P-indivisible, and the two-shuffle odds
differ from the odds obtained by chaining one-shuffle kernels. And
peeking at the middle street, which forces the re-burn, makes the
divisible answer correct again: a division event in the sense of §1.5,
enacted with cardboard.

The game isolates a rooted revival through a hidden record. Peeking
causes the prescribed re-burn and changes the odds by removing the
correlation that the undisturbed swap would use. The calculation
exhibits indivisibility in this finite law. General quantum interference
and phase require their own mathematical description.

A linear shuffle on ranks modulo \(q\) extends the finite analogy. Its
card-table constraints come from the chosen permutations and hidden
preparations. Unistochasticity concerns squared moduli of a unitary on
the visible space itself, a separate constraint from marginalizing a
permutation over hidden cards ({[}Main §3.1{]}). For the
nearest-neighbor second-order update on \(\mathbb Z^d\) over a prime
field with nonzero coupling, NR-1 Theorem 3.3 gives rooted
P-divisibility and no rooted revival for a common Haar product exterior
prior and a finite nonempty two-register lattice-convex window. The
proved comparison with the corresponding finite torus applies before
wraparound, when \(\operatorname{ext}_j(W)+2t<L\) in every coordinate.
Multi-time history memory is a separate question.
\href{../verification/audits/foundations/nr1-near-return-20261116/NR-1.md}{NR-1}
One boundary must be stated as plainly as the successes: a card
mechanism played under the restrictions below is a local classical toy.
It exhibits a rooted revival, P-indivisibility and an intervention that
removes the selected correlation. It obeys the Bell bound when, once the
deal is down, every operation --- each shuffle the rules prescribe, each
move and each setting choice --- reads and writes one player's own cards
only; which operation is applied to a player's cards, and how that
player's \(\pm1\) outcome is read from them, depends only on those
cards, that player's own setting and on chance that, taken together with
the deal, is independent of the settings; an outcome is recorded in
every run and no run is set aside; and the settings are chosen
independently of the deal: such a game is a local hidden-variable model
(Main §3.3). The Bell-type correlations of §1.7 belong to the full
construction, through the level-identification analysis taken up in
Chapter 3 (§§3.7--3.7.1, where the boundary drawn here becomes the
diagnosis), not to the toy. An illustration that claimed otherwise would
be teaching a falsehood, and the analogy earns its keep precisely by
knowing where it ends.

What remains is the pair of views. Turn the deck face up and track every
permutation, and the game is chess: complete information, deterministic,
exhaustively analyzable. Sit in the player's seat and the same game is
poker --- and not the poker of static ignorance, but the modified game
whose rational odds sheet carries interference terms. Nothing changed
but the seat. That is the framework's thesis in one gesture: observation
is what the rest of the board looks like from inside a piece.

\textbf{Schrödinger's cat, played as cards.} Every reader arrives
carrying one thought experiment, and the game just built is the right
table to play it on. Schrödinger (1935), in the same paper that coined
\emph{entanglement}, sealed a cat in a chamber with a radioactive atom,
a Geiger counter, a hammer, and a flask of poison: within the hour, the
formalism's entanglement chain has amplified one atom's superposition,
link by link, into a description assigning the cat itself equal parts
alive and dead until the box is opened. He offered it as a ``quite
ridiculous case'' --- a reductio, not a report. If the wavefunction is a
complete description and ``measurement'' an undefined primitive, nothing
in the theory says where along the chain atom → counter → hammer → cat a
definite fact appears. Ninety years of interpretation dispute is the
residue of that question.

Played on this table, the paradox takes four sentences. The sealed hour
is an unobserved middle street. ``Alive \(+\) dead'' is not a state of
the cat but a line on the odds sheet --- the indivisible pricing any
player must use for a hand whose history routes through the burn pile.
Opening the box is the peek with its forced re-burn: an intervention
that severs a correlation, not the creation of a fact. And the deal was
definite throughout --- the substratum holds exactly one configuration
at every moment; the superposition is bookkeeping for where the record
resides, in cards the observer has not turned. What dissolves the
\emph{cat} specifically is a further observation: a cat's middle street
is never unobserved. In the analogy, forcing a re-burn removes a
particular correlation. Environmental interactions in a physical cat
experiment can degrade coherence, with the extent and recoverability
depending on the interaction and preparation (§1.6).

Schrödinger's instinct was therefore sound --- no cat is ever
alive-and-dead --- but the framework's repair is subtraction where the
objective-collapse programs (GRW/CSL, Diósi--Penrose) offer addition.
They make the cat definite by appending a stochastic law; the framework
makes it definite by deleting a premise --- the superposition was the
observer's ledger, not the chamber's state, so there was never anything
to collapse (and Chapter 18 records that additions of the Penrose type
are structurally forbidden here). The two repairs part company at
exactly the frontier of §1.6: engineered ``cat states,'' superpositions
of macroscopically distinct configurations held genuinely unobserved,
for which the laboratory tests concern specific physical models and
their predicted decoherence or collapse rates (Chapter 4 §4.5). The
finite-record theorem gives an exact representation of the supplied
records. The deterministic model, under its stated hypotheses, has no
intrinsic collapse mechanism. The boundary drawn above remains
load-bearing: a cat in one box is a single-system story, the toy's home
turf; it is Bell's two boxes, not Schrödinger's one, where the cards
must be surrendered to the full construction.

The substratum that the framework's algorithm operates on is constructed
concretely in Chapter 2 --- a three-dimensional cubic lattice with
bilinear, block-diagonal dynamics whose structural constraints fix the
framework's empirical content. Chapter 3 takes up the framework's full
philosophical positioning, including its relationship to the structural
realism program, its relation to Bell, Kochen-Specker and PBR-type no-go
theorems through separate checks of their local-response,
operational-algebra and preparation premises, and its parallels to the
broader intellectual landscape of incompleteness results from Gödel
through Wolpert. Chapter 4 develops the methodological posture --- the
single-foundational-commitment derivation pattern, the
architecture-level engagement with the no-go results, the classification
of claims by derivational rigor --- that organizes the framework's
program as a whole. The remaining chapters trace the framework's
predictions through particle physics, gravity, cosmology, the structural
cascade from atoms to intelligence, and the framework's reach into
chemistry, biology, medicine, and quantum engineering.

The remainder of this part of the book develops the substratum, the
structural realism, and the methodology in detail. Part II turns to the
framework's quantitative physics. Part III traces the cascade from
substratum to chemistry, biology, and intelligence. Part IV develops the
framework's reach into working scientific fields.

\hypertarget{chapter-2}{%
\section{Chapter 2}\label{chapter-2}}

\hypertarget{the-substratum}{%
\section{The Substratum}\label{the-substratum}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-constructs}{%
\subsection{2.1 What this chapter
constructs}\label{what-this-chapter-constructs}}

Chapter 1 established the exact finite observable-law equivalence
between stochastic processes, finite reversible deterministic
realizations, and fixed-basis unitary/Born representations. It also
showed that genuine history readback forces hidden predictive memory in
every faithful completion. This chapter now asks the inverse structural
question: what is the finite reversible object \((S,\varphi)\) whose
observer-level projection has that description?

Three questions need separation. First, which \textbf{local propagating
lattice/gauge residue} is fixed by the framework's empirical and
structural inputs? Second, which changes of a representative leave that
local observable content unchanged? Third, can the Bell-violating
preparation/composite structure be embedded in the same deterministic
ontology, and if so is it unique? The reconstruction theorem answers the
first, the substratum gauge group addresses the second for the
reconstructed dilation/local data, and H-Bell addresses only the
existence/compatibility part of the third; Bell-inclusive uniqueness
remains open.

The quantum input to this reconstruction should be read in the scoped
sense established in Chapter 1. The visible law has an exact quantum
representation, spatial OI provides graph causal cones, and finite
quantum records have finite reversible realizations. The operational
completion for arbitrary coherent instruments/composites, which holds,
within complex matrix kinematics taken as given, only under the five
completion conditions of {[}GR §3.3{]}, is not silently consumed as
though the substratum had been shown to supply them; where the
reconstruction uses stronger standard-QM structure, that structure is an
empirical input or a named modeling premise.

\hypertarget{the-finite-representative-as-a-lossless-memory}{%
\subsection{2.2 The finite representative as a lossless
memory}\label{the-finite-representative-as-a-lossless-memory}}

The framework's central object is a triple. \(S\) is the set of total
configurations, finite in the representative specified under the open
hypothesis A1 (§2.4). \(\varphi: S \to S\) is a bijection --- a
deterministic, reversible transition rule that maps each state to its
unique successor. \(V \subsetneq S\) is the visible sector, the
observer's window into \(S\); the complement \(H = S \setminus V\) is
the hidden sector. The triple \((S, \varphi, V)\) specifies the dynamics
and the observer's access. The marginalized description also uses the
preparation, including the hidden law conditional on the visible start.

The most useful physical interpretation is in terms of memory. In the
finite representative, \(|S|\) is the number of distinguishable total
configurations that the system can occupy, a finite storage capacity.
\(\varphi\) is a bijection, so information is never created or
destroyed; the substratum is a \emph{lossless} memory in the precise
information-theoretic sense. The partition \(V\) defines the observer's
access to this memory, both read and write. The observer reads the
visible sector by measuring \(x\). In a causal write, changing the
visible input while holding the hidden seed fixed changes the later
hidden state. History readback can also arise by learning about a
preloaded hidden selector.

On a finite alphabet and horizon, a supplied observer-level law has an
exact fixed-basis quantum representation. The structural form of C2
requires the hidden record to persist until the readback that uses it. A
slow bath under the stated mixing and erosion assumptions gives one
retention mechanism. C4 is what makes the stored information
operationally matter. Chapter 1 proves that such readback forces hidden
predictive memory in every faithful completion. Interference and
entanglement are represented quantum-mechanically in the corresponding
observer-level description; identifying every possible coherent
intervention with the standard quantum instrument algebra holds there,
within complex matrix kinematics taken as given, exactly under the five
completion conditions, with physical sourcing of full reversible control
and a common operational interface still open.

This memory interpretation makes several of the framework's structural
quantities concrete. The \(10^{122}\) vacuum-energy discrepancy of
Chapter 1 is the compression ratio between total storage and readable
storage --- between the full configuration space \(S\) and the visible
sector \(V\). The dark sector of cosmological observation is the
gravitational effect of the unreadable storage in \(H\). The
Bekenstein-Hawking entropy is the storage capacity of the partition
boundary, the number of independent modes crossing \(\partial V\) times
the entropy \(\sigma\) of one mode. The action scale \(\hbar\) is the
conversion factor between storage geometry (boundary area) and
read-write statistics (the unitary group's parameter). Chapter 7
develops each of these under the conditions it names; for the present
chapter they motivate the interpretation.

The substratum dynamics is defined on the full configuration space, not
on the visible sector alone. The wave equation that selects \(\varphi\)
among second-order reversible nearest-neighbor dynamics --- developed in
detail in Chapter 5 --- operates on both \(V\) and \(H\). The partition
imposes an observer-access structure on this common dynamics but does
not change the dynamics itself. Both sectors are governed by the same
underlying rule; the only difference is which states the observer can
read.

\hypertarget{what-the-substratum-is-and-is-not}{%
\subsection{2.3 What the substratum is and is
not}\label{what-the-substratum-is-and-is-not}}

The substrate objection asks an obvious question: what is the memory
made of? What physical stuff implements the configuration
\((S, \varphi)\)? The framework proposes a structural description of
dynamics and observation rather than specifying an underlying material.
Two implementations that give identical data at a specified observation
interface cannot be distinguished by a decision based only on those
data. An independently prepared, normalized, exactly decoupled finite
ancillary factor is one such redundancy: tracing it out leaves the
original observed channel unchanged {[}Substratum Theorem 24(iii){]}.
This does not show that every proposed implementation has identical
data, that a sector which later couples to the observer is redundant, or
that the explanatory regress has been terminated. A complete
observable-to-substratum classification remains open. The physical
implementation question is therefore separate from the exact invariances
that have been established.

A closer analog than physical substance is the abstract structure of a
computation. A Turing machine has three components: a tape (the storage
medium), a head (the read-write access window), and a transition
function (the update rule). The mapping to the substratum is direct:
\(S\) corresponds to the tape, \(V\) to the head's access window,
\(\varphi\) to the transition function. But three differences are
physically significant.

First, a Turing machine's tape is potentially unbounded while the exact
OI model here has finite \(S\). Finiteness of the total carrier gives
the exact return used by Chapter 1's recurrence argument. The
holographic bound instead concerns the observed sector under its stated
interpretation; it does not establish total-carrier finiteness. An
infinite extension requires its own normalized state or measure and
well-defined dynamics.

Second, a Turing machine is generally irreversible --- it can erase,
overwrite, and halt. The substratum bijection \(\varphi\) is reversible
by Lemma 3 of Chapter 1: nothing is erased, nothing is created, there is
no halting state. Reversible Turing machines (Bennett, Fredkin--Toffoli)
are a well-studied subclass; the substratum sits in this class.

Third, a Turing machine computes an \emph{extrinsic} function --- input
from an external user, output to an external observer. The substratum
computes no extrinsic function. It is a closed permutation that cycles
through its states; no input, no output, no halting condition. The
appearance of dynamics, probability, particles, and forces is entirely
the observer's perspective --- what the permutation looks like through
the partial window \(V\).

The third difference is the load-bearing one. The framework extends
Turing's question. Where Turing asked what computation a machine can
perform for an external observer, the framework asks what computation
looks like to a \emph{component of the machine} --- a subsystem with
bounded access to the machine's own state. Chapter 1 gives an exact
quantum representation of the supplied finite records and separates the
problem of physical operational recovery.

This extension places the framework in a specific intellectual lineage.
Three foundational results form what can be called the incompleteness
family. Gödel: a formal system rich enough to encode arithmetic cannot
prove all true statements about itself; the unprovable truths have rigid
structure. Turing: a computer cannot decide all questions about its own
behavior; the undecidable problems have rigid structure. Observational
Incompleteness studies an embedded observer's limited access to a
deterministic system. Its exact theorem represents supplied finite
records in fixed-basis quantum form. The three comparisons concern
different tasks and have their respective hypotheses.

Hidden-state identification is a record question in a specified model,
not the Turing halting problem. The hidden state has a definite value,
but whether an observer can determine it depends on the model and
retained observations. In a known finite model, a quantity is determined
by a nonempty record fibre exactly when it is constant on that fibre
{[}Substratum Proposition 24.5{]}; two readouts of a visible/hidden
swap, for example, identify the initial hidden coordinate.
Independently, every finite observable law admits the exact fixed-basis
unitary/Born representation of Chapter 1. This representation theorem
does not rest on a blanket impossibility of hidden-state identification.

Two further comparisons deserve separation from unresolved hidden-state
facts. An independently prepared finite factor evolving exactly
independently of the observed system changes the deep-sector cardinality
while preserving the original fixed-interface coherent channel
{[}Substratum Theorem 24(iii){]}. A deep sector coupled to the boundary
layer under the posited influence bound H-BD of {[}GR §3.2{]} preserves
only the leading-order accessible-time law, with the stated correction.
Infinite extensions require specified normalized states or measures and
dynamics. Alphabet change preserves observables only under the
alphabet-size hypothesis of Chapter 5. These are redundancies relative
to particular data; they do not show that all inaccessible
cardinalities, coupling structures or physical implementations lack
determinate or observable consequences.

The reconstruction theorem developed in the next section fixes the
\textbf{local lattice/gauge residue} --- under its stated conditions ---
from observed physics plus structural assumptions. It does not uniquely
determine a Bell-inclusive full substratum; H-Bell conditions the
existence of that completion and its preparation-indexed Bell rule
remains underdetermined.

\hypertarget{the-reconstruction-theorem}{%
\subsection{2.4 The reconstruction
theorem}\label{the-reconstruction-theorem}}

Chapter 1 took a substratum \((S, \varphi)\) as input and developed the
emergent quantum description from it. The converse direction is
necessarily scoped: the reconstruction theorem asks which \textbf{local
propagating lattice/gauge data} observed physics fixes. It establishes
uniqueness of that local residue's Stage-2 invariants under its stated
conditions. Bell-inclusive completion data are separate: their existence
is conditional on H-Bell and their uniqueness is not established.

The theorem takes two kinds of input. The first is \emph{empirical}:
structural facts about the observed universe. The second is
\emph{structural}: assumptions about the class of candidate substrates
the reconstruction is permitted to consider. Both are necessary, and
both must be stated explicitly. A reconstruction theorem that did not
specify its structural assumptions would either claim too much
(uniqueness without restriction) or claim too little (uniqueness only
within an undefined class).

\textbf{Empirical inputs.} The reconstruction draws on seven structural
inputs about observed physics, six established by experiment and one
(E3) a theoretical bound:

\emph{(E1) Unitary quantum mechanics.} The observed microscopic physics
is described by states in a complex Hilbert space evolving unitarily,
with observables as self-adjoint operators and measurement outcomes
following the Born rule. This is Chapter 1's framework input.

\emph{(E2) Bell violations.} Observed correlations between spatially
separated measurements violate Bell-type inequalities, ruling out local
hidden-variable theories satisfying factorizability. Confirmed
experimentally since Aspect's 1982 measurements and refined in
loophole-free tests since 2015.

\emph{(E3) Finite boundary entropy.} The entropy of any bounded region
of spacetime is finite and scales as the boundary area rather than the
volume. This is the holographic bound --- a theoretical bound rather
than a direct observation --- supported by black-hole thermodynamics and
applied to the cosmological horizon.

\emph{(E4) Spatial isotropy.} Observed physics is rotationally
invariant; no spatial direction is preferred. Confirmed across
observations from the CMB to laboratory tests of fundamental constants.

\emph{(E5) Propagating gravity.} Gravitational degrees of freedom
propagate as waves with the observed signature of two transverse
polarization states, directly detected since LIGO 2015.

\emph{(E6) Stable matter.} Atoms, planets, and bound states exist on
observed timescales. This requires both gravitational and atomic-scale
stability against the dynamics.

\emph{(E7) Boundary-entropy concordance.} Near spatial flatness in the
standard cosmological model constrains the total gravitating density
relative to the critical density. The stated horizon calculation gives a
Hubble-volume average with \(\rho_s / \rho_{\text{crit}} = 2/(d-1)\),
which equals unity at \(d=3\). Comparing this average to the gravitating
density requires a separate physical identification (Chapter 7 §7.9).

Within A4's periodic-lattice class and the continuum conditions of SM
§3.1--§3.2, E5--E7 enter the dimensional selection. The first two
constraints already intersect at \(d=3\); the third is a consistency
check. Propagating gravity (E5) requires \(d \geq 3\), since the Weyl
tensor governing gravitational-wave propagation vanishes in
\(d \leq 2\). Stable matter (E6) requires \(d \leq 3\), since the
Coulomb potential gives unstable atoms in \(d \geq 4\) (Ehrenfest's
theorem) and gravitational orbits are unstable in \(d \geq 4\)
(Tangherlini's result). Boundary-entropy concordance (E7) checks \(d=3\)
conditional on the physical identification in E7. Within A4's
periodic-lattice class, integer rank \(d\) is already an input. The
filters select its value \(3\) on the stated continuum branch, subject
to the continuum conditions of SM §3.1--§3.2.

The convergence has an external echo. A literature independent of this
framework reaches the same selection from different starting points:
Ehrenfest's stability analysis (atoms and planetary orbits are stable
only for \(d = 3\)), the sharp-propagation property of the wave equation
(Huygens' principle holds cleanly only in odd spatial dimensions, and
distortion-free signal propagation singles out \(d = 3\), as Hadamard's
analysis of the wave equation shows), and Tegmark's predictability
argument (field equations well-posed enough for observers to process
information select \(3+1\)). These are convergent arguments rather than
theorems, and they are not an independent axiom base in the sense of the
reconstruction theorems of Chapter 1: like the framework's own three
