filters, they condition on the existence of stable structure and
embedded observers. Their force is corroborative texture --- several
instruments, pointed from different premises within the same
observer-admitting family, land on the same integer.

\textbf{Structural assumptions.} The reconstruction restricts attention
to candidate substrates satisfying six properties:

\emph{(A1) Finiteness.} The configuration space \(S\) is finite. Lemma 1
of Chapter 1 delivers finiteness of the observer's distinguishable
states; the extension to all of \(S\) is an open hypothesis, not
adopted, read as the choice of the minimal finite representative and
motivated by E3 (the holographic bound read as a dimension cutoff). Its
scope, and which results use it, are stated in {[}Main §1.2{]}, Remark
(status of the early commitments).

\emph{(A2) Determinism.} The dynamics \(\varphi: S \to S\) is a
bijection --- deterministic and reversible. Its status is two-part
(Chapter 1, Lemma 3): the bijective substratum is a representation
choice --- the minimal recurrent bijective representative of the hidden
dynamics, which for a finite system is the dynamics restricted to its
eventual image, the states lying on its cycles --- and injectivity is
anchored by a dilemma argument with one structural prong (finiteness,
for registered states in the eventual image) and one empirical prong
(the observed statistics).

\emph{(A3) Bounded coupling degree.} Each site of the substratum is
coupled to a bounded number of neighbors through \(\varphi\). This is
required for the emergence of a coupling graph with well-defined
dimensional structure and underlies locality in the emergent
description.

\emph{(A4) Center independence.} The dynamics does not depend on a
choice of preferred site or origin: \(\varphi\) commutes with lattice
translations up to gauge (the coupling graph is a finite periodic
lattice, the quotient of a rank-\(d\) lattice by a finite-index
sublattice, \(d\) being its dimension), and the update at a site
contains no explicit copy of that site's present value. The second
property is what the derivation of the wave equation in Stage 2 below
uses.

\emph{(A5) Linearity.} The wave equation governing \(\varphi\) is
linear. The affine characterization uses the stipulated
base-point-independent first differences. Linearity is a further
restriction. Covariance under affine relabelling also permits nonlinear
rules (SM §2.7).

\emph{(A6) Background independence.} The dynamics is covariant under
spatially varying internal-index transformations: a site-dependent
transformation of the internal index is a symmetry provided the coupling
data carried on the links are transformed with it. The content of the
assumption is this covariant interface --- the coupling is link-valued
data on which the transformations act --- and once it is in place the
local transformation law imposes no further condition on the rule. It is
not the stronger fixed-background condition that the same
transformations leave the dynamics invariant with the coupling held
fixed, which for an invertible constant coupling forces the
transformation to agree across every coupled pair of sites and fails at
the symmetric point of the coupling matrix for every transformation that
differs across a coupled pair; the global commutant symmetry --- the
transformations constant across the lattice that leave the coupling
unchanged --- is the specialization from which the local gauge reading
of Chapter 5 proceeds. The state-dependent coupling graph, under which
the graph itself evolves with the state, is a separate principle that
shares the name.

The reconstruction theorem's claim is that, under E1--E7 and A1--A6 with
M1-T, C2-mixing and the nearest-neighbor restriction, the \textbf{local
propagating lattice/gauge residue} is fixed, including the listed
Standard-Model/discrete outputs and \(\hbar = c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\)
with their stated qualifications. Bell violation is handled
independently by M1-B: a common measurement-independent deterministic
completion exists only conditional on H-Bell, and the theorem does not
make that Bell-inclusive completion unique.

\textbf{Stage 1: A deterministic embedding of supplied records.} The
inputs are the quantum-mechanical content E1, the Bell-violation content
E2, the boundary-entropy bound E3, the finiteness and determinism
assumptions A1, A2, and the two-clause modeling premise M1 --- M1-T puts
the temporal data used in Stage 1 in the history-readback sector, while
M1-B puts Bell-violating composites on the measurement-independent,
ontically parameter-dependent branch. For a supplied law on a finite
observable alphabet through a finite horizon, Chapter 1 §1.8 gives a
finite reversible realization and its fixed-basis quantum
representation. When the law has an accessible history-memory witness,
the characterization gives C1, C3 and C4 in a corresponding realization.
C2 is treated separately ({[}Main §3.4{]}). M1-T's observed temporal
memory structure certifies the C1/C3/C4 history-readback sector, while
M1-B's Bell violation independently requires Bell-relevant cross-wing
coupling/ontic parameter dependence; the observed memory-bearing
phenomenology --- not quantum representability, which is universal ---
grounds C2 and C3, with C2's slow-bath necessity conditional on the
hidden-sector mixing hypothesis (ETH its physical motivation) and its
persistence form holding without it. The output of Stage 1 is a triple
\((S, \varphi, V)\) with \(S\) finite, \(\varphi\) a bijection, and
\(V \subset S\) the visible-sector partition, with the supplied finite
observable law reproduced by marginalizing the evolution over the hidden
sector \(H = S \setminus V\) under the specified preparation.

At Stage 1, the Stinespring theorem controls only the \textbf{finite
channel/dilation datum used by the temporal reconstruction}: its
familiar dilation freedom lies in hidden-sector/gauge directions. It
does not make the full triple \((S,\varphi,V)\) unique across coherent
composites, does not select a preparation-indexed Bell graph, and does
not discharge the separate finite-predictive-dimension, local-tomography
or operational-purification requirements of the full lift.

\textbf{Stage 2: From deterministic embedding to specific lattice and
gauge structure.} Stage 2 combines Stage 1's output with the remaining
empirical and structural inputs E4--E7 and A3--A6. Within A4's assumed
periodic-lattice class, E5--E7 select \(d = 3\) subject to the continuum
conditions of SM §3.1--§3.2. The wave equation, internal-index
structure, gauge construction, matter interpretation and discrete
symmetries have their further hypotheses stated at the corresponding
steps.

The dimension argument follows the three-filter convergence described
above. Under A4 the coupling graph is a finite periodic lattice of some
integer dimension \(d\), an input of the assumption; statistical
isotropy (E4) alone would not supply it. The filters E5--E7 then select
\(d = 3\) on the stated continuum branch; they do not supply the
integer-rank lattice assumption itself.

The wave equation follows from center independence (A4), isotropy (E4),
and linearity (A5), together with the nearest-neighbor restriction (an
assumption beyond A3's bounded coupling degree). The unique second-order
reversible nearest-neighbor dynamics compatible with these constraints
has the form \(f = \alpha(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_{2d}) \bmod q\), with
coupling coefficient \(\alpha\). The coefficient is not the propagation
speed: causal support travels at most one lattice edge per update
whatever its value, and on the observer-level normalized branch it
equals \(1/d\).

The number of internal components per lattice site follows from the link
count under H-link. It gives \(K = 2dm\), with the single-copy clause
\(m=1\) and \(d=3\) giving \(K=6\). This count uses the specified link
carrier. This locks the candidate-sector count at three --- read as
three physical generations only under H-spin' (SM §4.7) --- since three
spin-\(1/2\) staggered tastes emerge from the \(K = 6\) minimum (Chapter
6 develops this).

The six-link representation has the geometric decomposition
\(T_1\oplus E\oplus A_1\) of dimensions \(3,2,1\). The unitary commutant
of the cubic action on this multiplicity-free carrier is
\(\mathrm{U}(1)^3\). Its bicommutant is the full block algebra. A
distinct-block equivariant condensate has stabilizer
\(\mathrm{U}(3)\times\mathrm{U}(2)\times\mathrm{U}(1)\) under H-cust.
The specified charged matter action and anomaly constraints select the
local Standard Model gauge algebra on the physical H-link branch. A6
imposes covariance with transformed link data. The global gauge action
and its identifications require separate data (Chapter 5 §§5.5--5.6).

The staggered-fermion reduction supplies three candidate sectors on the
single-copy H-link branch. Their interpretation as three chiral
generations uses H-spin', H-χ' and light-spectrum selection. The singlet
taste accommodates the supplied Higgs doublet. Checkerboard parity
grades spin and taste together, with both spin chiralities in each
grade. Physical chirality requires H-χ'. Chapters 5 and 6 develop each
step in detail; the chain ends with hypercharges
\((Y_Q, Y_u, Y_d, Y_L, Y_e) = (1/6, 2/3, -1/3, -1/2, -1)\) uniquely
determined on the nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch, up to normalization.

T-invariance of the bijection \(\varphi\) combined with detailed balance
gives reciprocal visible transition counts and narrows the QCD angle to
\(\theta\in\{0,\pi\}\); it does not fix \(\bar\theta\), which is open
(SM §5).

Uniqueness at Stage 2 follows from the uniqueness-given-inputs character
of each step. Each derivation is the unique consistent choice given its
inputs, the wave-equation step within the nearest-neighbor class and the
hypercharge step apart from its exceptional branch; the chain is a
composition of unique selections, and the output is unique within those
qualifications.

\textbf{Stage 3: From dynamics to emergent constants.} Stage 3 takes
Stage 2's output and derives the emergent action-scale relation. The
argument is that thermal self-consistency at the partition boundary ---
established in Chapter 7 from the boundary layer's emergent
thermodynamics, conditional on H-slope and the further conditions of
{[}GR §8.5(b){]} --- forces the relation
\[\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2 / (4G\sigma),\] with the discreteness scale
\(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\,\ell_P\) (twice the Planck length at
\(\sigma = 1\), one nat per boundary mode) as the unique simultaneous
solution, which fixes only the ratio
\(\epsilon/\sqrt{\sigma} = 2\,\ell_P\). With this calibration the
boundary-mode count reproduces the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy
\(S = A/(4 \ell_P^2)\), the \(1/4\) coefficient being the ratio
\(2\pi/8\pi\) of the KMS period to the first-law prefactor that the
calibration matches.

Uniqueness at Stage 3 follows from the unique solvability of the
boundary gap equation, which Chapter 7 develops.

\textbf{The composite theorem.} Composing the three stages yields the
chapter's central result.

\textbf{Reconstruction Theorem.} \emph{Let E1--E7, M1-T and M1-B, and
A1--A6 hold, with the hidden-sector mixing hypothesis for the slow-bath
form of the C2 necessity direction and, additionally, the
nearest-neighbor restriction of Stage 2. Then the \textbf{local
propagating lattice/gauge residue} is fixed: \(d=3\), \(K=6\), block
multiplicities \((3,2,1)\), the stated local gauge algebra,
matter/representation content and discrete-symmetry outputs, conditional
on single-copy H-link, H-cust, the specified charged action and the
matter premises H-spin', H-χ', light-spectrum selection and the supplied
Higgs representation where applicable (Chapter 5 §§5.4--5.6) --- and
\(\hbar=c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\) with the qualifications carried by
the cited derivations. A single measurement-independent deterministic
completion also realizing the Bell-violating M1-B composites exists only
conditional on H-Bell. Bell-inclusive full-substratum uniqueness is not
established.} \(\square\)

The theorem's content is striking. From the empirical inputs of observed
physics --- quantum mechanics, Bell violations, finite boundary entropy,
spatial isotropy, propagating gravity, stable matter, spatial flatness
--- together with six structural assumptions and the nearest-neighbor
restriction, the substratum is forced to be a specific kind of object
with specific properties. The single-copy H-link hypothesis fixes the
physical carrier in this construction. With H-cust, a distinct-block
equivariant condensate and the specified charged action, the result
selects the local Standard Model gauge algebra. Global identifications
require separate data. The three candidate staggered sectors have their
physical interpretation under the stated matter premises (Chapters
5--6). The Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) factor is not a postulate; it is
fixed by the horizon calibration under the conditions Chapter 7 names.
The cosmological constant problem is not resolved by tuning; the
framework's structure makes \(\hbar\) and \(G\) commensurable through
the boundary thermodynamics, and the apparent \(10^{122}\) discrepancy
is the compression ratio Chapter 7 develops.

\textbf{Two scope remarks.} First, uniqueness is within the structural
class A1--A6 with the nearest-neighbor restriction. The theorem does not
exclude alternative substrates outside this class: intrinsically
continuum theories (violating A1), intrinsically stochastic theories
(violating A2), theories with unbounded coupling (violating A3), or
theories violating center independence, linearity, or background
independence (violating A4--A6). The framework's defense of A1--A6 is
that they are the natural assumptions given the empirical inputs, but
this defense is an argument rather than a theorem. A separate analysis
would be needed to rule out alternatives violating any \(A_i\).

Second, the empirical inputs E1--E7 are stated as structural facts
rather than as specific measurement outcomes. Operationally, no finite
measurement set establishes any of them; finite data is consistent with
them but does not uniquely require them. The reconstruction theorem
holds for the inputs as stated --- the idealized infinite-data regime
--- and proves \textbf{local-residue uniqueness} in that regime. The
operational discrimination available against finite data comes from the
cumulative weight of the framework's quantitative Standard-Model record
(Chapter 6). This finite-data issue is distinct from Bell-composite
underdetermination: Bell-inclusive uniqueness is open even in the
idealized-input formulation.

The reconstruction theorem identifies the equivalence class
\([(S, \varphi)] / \mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) as the framework's central
object. The next section makes the gauge group
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) explicit by identifying its generators;
whether they exhaust the freedom in the reconstruction is open.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-substratum-gauge-group}{%
\subsection{2.5 The substratum gauge
group}\label{the-substratum-gauge-group}}

The reconstruction theorem identifies
\([(S, \varphi)] / \mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) as the framework's central
object. This section makes \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) explicit by
exhibiting three families of generators; whether they exhaust the group
is open.

For the reconstructed dilation/local datum, observational equivalence is
relative to a specified visible/hidden interface, preparations and
readouts. Equality of the coherent channel family is stronger than
equality of its rooted population transition probabilities. The
representative freedoms denoted by \(\mathcal G_{\text{sub}}\) preserve
the particular data stated in Substratum Theorem 24: uniform
hidden-coordinate relabelling and independently prepared finite
decoupled enlargement preserve the coherent family; alphabet change
retains its separate hypothesis. This is not a classification over all
partitions of a structural class.

The gauge group is not a symmetry of a Lagrangian or an action. There is
no Lagrangian at the substratum level; the substratum is a set (finite
under A1) with a bijection on it. \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) is a
symmetry of the \emph{equivalence class of substrata} defined by the
observability condition. The emergent gauge symmetries (the Standard
Model gauge group, the diagonal phase ambiguity in the emergent
Hamiltonian) are Lagrangian symmetries in the standard sense, derived
from the substratum through the trace-out.

\textbf{Theorem (Generators).} \emph{\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\)
contains the independent families of transformations (i) and (iii)
below, and, under the alphabet-size hypothesis of Chapter 5, the family
(ii); (iv) is a structural graph comparison, not a family of
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\):}

\emph{(i) Hidden-state relabeling.} For any bijection \(\sigma\) of the
hidden configurations \(\mathcal{C}_H\), applied in every visible fibre
as \(\pi(v,h) = (v, \sigma(h))\), the substratum
\((S, \pi \circ \varphi \circ \pi^{-1})\) produces the same emergent
physics as \((S, \varphi)\). The transition probabilities depend on the
coupling structure of \(\varphi\) --- which states are sent to which ---
but not on which labels are attached to which hidden states; a
relabeling \((v,h) \mapsto (v, \sigma_v(h))\) that differs between
visible fibres preserves the transition probabilities \(T_{ij}(t)\) but
not, in general, the coherent channels. This is an
\(|\mathcal{C}_H|!\)-element subgroup, vastly larger than any gauge
group appearing in the Standard Model.

\emph{(ii) Alphabet change (under the alphabet-size hypothesis).} The
local state space at each lattice site can be replaced by
\(\mathbb{Z}/q'\mathbb{Z}\) for any integer \(q' \geq 2\), while
preserving the coupling graph and the dynamics class, without changing
any observable if the alphabet-size hypothesis of Chapter 5 holds. The
internal alphabet at a lattice site is the number of distinguishable
local states; some results hold for every \(q \geq 2\) and others carry
\(q\) (Chapter 5). This family is parametrized by the integers
\(q \geq 2\).

\emph{(iii) Finite decoupled ancillary enlargement.} Adjoin a finite
factor to the deep hidden sector, prepare it independently in a
normalized density matrix, and keep its dynamics exactly decoupled from
the original system. At the fixed visible/hidden interface, tracing out
the factor preserves the full original coherent-channel family and
therefore every rooted population law {[}Substratum Theorem 24(iii){]}.
This is stronger than a population-only assertion. Infinite factors
require a separately specified normalized state or measure and
well-defined dynamics; finite uniform counting does not supply that
extension. Enlargements coupled under the influence bound H-BD instead
change the law by the correction stated in Chapter 7 and preserve only
its leading-order accessible-time description.

\emph{(iv) Graph isomorphism (up to statistical isotropy), with a
gauge-sector qualification.} Two coupling graphs \(G_\varphi\) and
\(G_{\varphi'}\) that are quasi-isometric, with the same polynomial
growth exponent \(d\), the same spectral mode count, and the same
statistical isotropy at large scales, each admit a finite-law
representation and share the growth exponent \(d\), but need not give
the same transition probabilities \(T_{ij}(t)\) at a fixed observer
interface, and the continuum-curvature step of the gravitational
construction has its own conditions (§3.1 of the SM paper); in that
sense the regular cubic lattice \(\mathbb{Z}^3\) and a bounded-degree
random graph with \(d = 3\) polynomial growth and statistical isotropy
are structurally comparable, not observationally equivalent. The
\emph{Standard Model gauge group} is where this crystallography is read
out: its multiplicities \((3,2,1)\) come from the octahedral point group
on the six link directions, which is not a quasi-isometry invariant, so
only the spectral mode count \(2d_s = 6\) transfers to a generic
isotropic graph --- not the cubic decomposition. For the gauge sector,
therefore, comparison (iv) is restricted to orientation- and
octahedral-structure-preserving isomorphisms, and the simple-cubic
Bravais type is an empirically-selected input rather than a gauge
choice. The gauge group itself is a universality-class invariant, shared
with any Standard-Model-reproducing class through different machinery
({[}Structure §2.3, §14.4{]}); within OI's class it is realized through
the cubic-group commutant.

\emph{Proof for the specified data under the stated hypotheses.}
Generator (i): conjugation by the hidden permutation leaves the uniform
hidden prior invariant and cancels under the partial trace, so every
visible channel is unchanged; a fibre-dependent relabeling fixes the
visible coordinate and permutes each fibre's uniform hidden prior
bijectively, so every transition probability is unchanged. Generator
(ii): this is the alphabet-size hypothesis of Chapter 5, under which the
family is stated. Generator (iii): the product dynamics sends the
independent ancillary state \(\sigma_A\) to
\(W^t\sigma_AW^{\dagger t}\). Its trace remains one, so the partial
trace over it returns the original reduced channel exactly, as in
{[}Substratum Theorem 24(iii){]}. Comparison (iv): the finite-law
representation holds for any finite bijection and the growth exponent is
shared by hypothesis; the transition probabilities depend on the
specific graph. \(\square\)

\textbf{Completeness.} For the reconstructed dilation/local datum, it is
open whether families (i)--(iii) exhaust \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\)
--- whether any observables-preserving transformation of that scoped
datum decomposes as a composition of generators (i)--(iii). This
completeness question does not extend to preparation-indexed Bell
adjacency or other Bell-composite data.

Three candidate further generators are compared with the three already
listed:

\emph{Time reversal} (\(\varphi \to \varphi^{-1}\)). The wave equation
that selects \(\varphi\) is T-invariant, giving
\(\varphi^{-1} = T \circ \varphi \circ T^{-1}\) where \(T\) is the
phase-space layer swap exchanging successive timesteps. Since \(T\) acts
on the visible layers, this is not generator (i).

\emph{Hidden-sector dynamical reparametrization} beyond enlargement.
Equality of the visible channel family does not force a hidden-sector
unitary relating two dilations of equal hidden-sector dimension: two
permutation systems on \(\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_3\) have equal
visible channels at every time without being unitarily conjugate
(Substratum §4). Whether such reparametrizations reduce to generator (i)
is the open completeness question.

\emph{Visible-sector emergent global phase} (\(U \to e^{i\theta} U\)).
At the substratum level, \(S\) is a finite set with no complex
structure; the emergent phase corresponds to no substratum-level
transformation. It is the identity on \((S, \varphi)\).

\textbf{The three-level gauge hierarchy.} The framework has three
distinct gauge symmetries, each appearing at a different level of the
derivation, with its own equivalence notion:

\emph{Level 3 --- reconstructed-datum substratum gauge.}
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) acts on the reconstructed dilation/local
representative \((S, \varphi)\) before any marginalization. Within that
scoped reconstruction it includes transformations with no analog at
lower levels (deep-sector enlargement, and alphabet change under the
alphabet-size hypothesis). Bell-composite preparation rules are outside
its scope.

\emph{Level 2 --- emergent quantum field theory gauge.} The Standard
Model gauge group
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\) acts on
the emergent fields after Stage 2 of the reconstruction has produced
them. It follows from the substratum construction (Stage 2) and acts on
internal components within the blocks of the equivariant condensate
\(\Sigma\).

\emph{Level 1 --- emergent Hamiltonian gauge.} A residual
diagonal-unitary freedom \(H \to D H D^\dagger\) (where \(D\) is a
diagonal unitary on the emergent Hilbert space) remains after all
transition-probability data has been extracted. It corresponds to the
rephasing of basis states in the emergent quantum description.

The levels carry distinct equivalence notions; inclusions between them
and a map from \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) onto the Standard Model
gauge group are not established.

The substratum construction provides a structural account of why the
Standard Model gauge group is what it is. The conventional puzzle is:
why \(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\) rather
than some other group? Standard Grand Unified Theories address this by
embedding the Standard Model in a larger simple group at high energy and
then breaking it; the framework here answers differently. The Standard
Model gauge group follows from the substratum construction (Stage 2)
once the cubic lattice is selected from observation and conditionally on
the carrier bridges H-link and H-cust (Chapter 5 §§5.4--5.5). Within
that class the Standard Model gauge group is fixed by the structure of
the substratum, not chosen from a landscape.

\textbf{Substrate freedom and the realism question.} A uniform
hidden-coordinate relabelling, with the uniform hidden prior, and an
independently prepared finite exactly decoupled ancillary factor
preserve the coherent channel at the fixed visible interface. Alphabet
change carries its stated alphabet-size hypothesis. Decisions based only
on the preserved data cannot distinguish the corresponding descriptions.
A different permitted interface, preparation or coupling may ask a
different observational question. Realism about the reconstructed local
invariants therefore does not amount to a proof that every possible
implementation or measurement belongs to one equivalence class.

This is what makes the framework's scoped structural realism
non-trivial. The invariants of the \textbf{reconstructed local
lattice/gauge residue} are uniquely determined --- under the
reconstruction theorem's stated conditions --- by observation plus
structural assumptions. Individual representatives of that local residue
related by the generators of \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) are gauge
expressions of the same reconstructed physical content, like coordinate
choices on a manifold or specific representatives of a homotopy class.
Bell-composite preparation data lie outside this uniqueness statement:
H-Bell conditions compatibility/existence, and no result here selects a
unique Bell-inclusive full representative.

The reconstruction theorem identifies the \textbf{local lattice/gauge
residue}; the gauge group identifies what within that scoped
reconstruction has no observable content. With both in place, observed
physics fixes that local residue under the theorem's stated conditions.
H-Bell separately conditions Bell-inclusive existence, and
Bell-inclusive uniqueness is not established. The next section turns to
the synthesis: how quantum mechanics and general relativity relate to
the substratum as projections of the same construction, and what a third
projection establishes about the arrow of time.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-three-projections}{%
\subsection{2.6 The three projections}\label{the-three-projections}}

The reconstruction theorem and the substratum gauge group have
established what \((S, \varphi)\) is and what equivalences leave its
observables unchanged. The question taken up in this section is what
relationship \((S, \varphi)\) bears to the framework's three large
emergent structures: quantum mechanics, general relativity, and the
arrow of time.

The framework's claim is that quantum mechanics and general relativity
are not two independent theories. Conditional on H-Bell at the
Bell/local-lattice interface, they are projections of the same
deterministic construction, and a third projection bears on the arrow of
time. Each projection applies the same trace-out machinery to the same
\((S, \varphi)\) along a different axis, and each produces a distinct
emergent structure as the observer sees the substratum from inside.

\textbf{The visible-sector projection: quantum mechanics.} Chapter 1
developed this projection in detail. For a supplied law on a finite
alphabet through a finite horizon, the stochastic, finite reversible and
fixed-basis unitary/Born representations are exactly equivalent:
\(S\iff D\iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\). C4 readback then identifies the
memory-bearing sector by forcing hidden predictive memory. In the
spatial construction the coupling graph supplies exact causal cones for
finite-range substrata. Bell is separate from the full-QM lift: a
measurement-independent response-complete deterministic completion with
parameter independence and a \(\pm1\) outcome in every run would obey
\(|S_{\rm CHSH}|\le2\), so the framework's Bell-violating branch is
ontically parameter-dependent with operational no-signaling required.
Two independent qualifications remain beyond the finite-law equivalence:
the simultaneous coherent instrument/composite lift ({[}Main §3.4{]})
and H-Bell, the compatibility of the local lattice sector with the
ontically parameter-dependent Bell completion. On the stated \(d=3\),
single-copy H-link lattice branch, the six-link decomposition fixes the
carrier blocks. The Standard Model reading uses H-cust, the
distinct-block condensate and the specified charged action for the local
gauge algebra, with separate premises for the physical matter and global
gauge data (Chapters 5--6). Chapter 8 gives the leading solar angle with
Cond 2, \(b_{23}=1\) and the stated Cabibbo and flavor inputs. Its
retrodictive comparisons are \(0.14\sigma\) to the direct estimate and
\(0.07\sigma\) to the global fit including the direct data. The local
nearest-neighbor sector cannot itself supply Bell parameter dependence
for wings with one-step own-wing setting interventions outside each
other's graph cone under measurement independence; identifying it with
one Bell-violating total completion is the open H-Bell compatibility
hypothesis.

\textbf{The boundary-thermodynamic projection: general relativity.} A
second projection takes the same substratum but applies the trace-out
machinery to the partition boundary rather than to the bulk. The
boundary of the visible sector --- the surface across which the coupling
\(H_{\text{int}}\) acts --- carries its own thermodynamic structure: a
temperature set by the boundary's classical surface gravity, an entropy
set by the number of boundary modes, and a dynamical evolution set by
the coupling between boundary and bulk. Jacobson's thermodynamic
argument applied to local causal horizons yields Einstein's equations as
the Clausius relation \(dE = T \, dS\) at the boundary.

Applied to the cosmological horizon as a causal partition, the
boundary-thermodynamic projection produces, conditionally on the open
covariant rung G3 (Chapter 19 §19.2.1), general relativity with
quantitative predictions. The emergent action scale
\(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2 / (4G\sigma)\), with
\(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\,\ell_P\), follows from thermal
self-consistency at the boundary layer under the infrared
detailed-balance condition H-slope. The boundary-mode count reproduces
the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy \(S = A/(4 \ell_P^2)\), the \(1/4\)
coefficient being the ratio \(2\pi/8\pi\) that the calibration matches
and conditional on H-count and the horizon conditions of Chapter 7; the
September 2025 analysis of GW250114, observed on January 14, supports
the classical area theorem from inferred Kerr areas --- the \(1/4\)
coefficient itself has no direct empirical test. The cosmological
constant problem receives a conditional treatment: the quantum vacuum
energy and the effective \(\Lambda\) are properties of logically
distinct levels of description rather than commensurable quantities
whose \(10^{122}\) ratio requires cancellation; the dissolution is
conditional on the covariant coupling step (Chapter 7). The
boundary-entropy proposal gives the MOND scale
\(a_0 = cH/6 \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-10}\) m/s² on the de Sitter branch
with the specified heat input, using the numerical factor from
Verlinde's emergent-gravity analysis. Chapter 7 develops each of these.

\textbf{The horizon-clock projection: the arrow of time.} A third
projection applies the trace-out machinery to the horizon-growth
parameter along an observer worldline. The substratum is time-symmetric:
\(\varphi\) and \(\varphi^{-1}\) are equally valid as forward-time maps,
and there is no preferred direction at the substratum level. Condition
C2 --- persistence, in its slow-bath realization --- is a retention
condition: it requires the hidden sector's correlations with the visible
sector's past to persist to readback, and the coarse-grained mixing time
it constrains is the same in the two directions; the direction in which
records are written and read is fixed by a preparation and the
observer's orientation convention. The structural observer-selection
theorem developed in Chapter 1's appendix material for a finite
bijective model --- under the effective-mixing hypothesis, for
sufficiently fast-mixing equilibria (\(\tau_{\rm mix} \ll \tau_S\)), and
in the coarse-grained description generated by iterating the one-step
effective channel ({[}Main §4.6{]}) --- restricts observers satisfying
C1--C4, with C2 read in its timescale form (record persistence and
readback there being suppressed, not excluded), to the non-equilibrium
phase of \((S, \varphi)\); the restriction is time-symmetric and selects
where observers can exist, not a direction. On an expanding cosmological
background satisfying the null energy condition --- inputs, not derived
--- the area \(A(t)\) of the apparent horizon, and the horizon entropy
\(S_{\text{dS}}(t) = A(t)/(4\ell_P^2)\) assigned to it at the de Sitter
calibration, is non-decreasing, strictly increasing while
\(\rho + p/c^2 > 0\) and constant in exact de Sitter. That the selected
non-equilibrium phase is ordered by this growth is not established.

The apparent-horizon area provides a structural clock on that
background. Every comoving observer of an expanding homogeneous
general-relativistic background satisfying the null energy condition
agrees that it does not decrease --- standard background kinematics, not
a prediction derived from the substratum --- and the criterion is
expansion with the null energy condition, not acceleration: in exact de
Sitter the area is constant. Whether the other arrows of time align with
this clock is not established. Jacobson's coupling relates the boundary
energy density to the expansion rate, not matter entropy to horizon
area, so the direction of the thermodynamic arrow rests on a low-entropy
or product boundary condition, and the generalized second law is open.
C2 concerns record persistence, and the slow-bath model treats retention
in either direction under its coarse-channel assumptions; the direction
of the memory arrow comes from a preparation and the observer's
orientation convention. The measurement arrow --- the observer records
past outcomes and prepares future states --- inherits the memory arrow's
direction. The chain uses one input (horizon growth on the expanding
branch) and one structural constraint (C1--C4 observer selection,
conditional on the effective-mixing hypothesis of {[}Main §4.6{]} and
stated for the coarse-grained description generated by iterating the
one-step effective channel), which excludes C2-slow for bounded-diameter
partitions in sufficiently fast-mixing equilibria of that coarse model.
The exclusion uses the stated preparation and rate hypotheses. Applying
it to a physical observer's records requires a link from the iterated
channel to those records.

The framework's content here is precise: on the expanding branch it
establishes a non-decreasing horizon parameter along observer
worldlines, and it does not establish that the four arrows of time
align. Nor does it derive the convention of which direction along the
horizon-clock parameter to call ``future.'' The two directions are
related by the layer swap at the substrate level
(\(\varphi \leftrightarrow \varphi^{-1}\)), and the observer's choice of
convention is residual freedom. The parameter is conditional on the
expanding branch; the labeling is an observer-imposed convention. There
is one further qualification worth stating: a monotonic parameter is
monotonic with respect to an \emph{ordering} of the worldline's moments,
and the framework's foundational treatment axiomatizes that there is
more than one moment while leaving the ordering of moments as a
separate, open question. The result here is therefore conditional on
that ordering as well --- it establishes that ordered moments on the
expanding branch yield a non-decreasing parameter, not that directedness
arises from the substratum with no assumption about ordering at all. CP
violation in CKM and kaon/B systems is a flavor-basis feature of the
specific bijection \(\varphi\) rather than a consequence of the
time-arrow cascade --- the framework treats flavor-sector CP phases as
solution-specific inputs that do not affect the cascade's structural
content.

\textbf{The common structure.} The local and Bell-composite sectors
require H-Bell to coexist in one common full substratum \((S,\varphi)\).
The visible-sector reduction uses the update, partition and preparation
to obtain the finite records. The local Standard Model sector also uses
its carrier and charged-action inputs. The boundary-thermodynamic
calculation uses the horizon and counting hypotheses, with native
covariant closure G3 open. The horizon clock uses the background and its
ordering premises, with alignment of the other arrows still open.

The shared structure is not metaphor or analogy. The same local lattice
sector that gives the Standard Model gauge group from the stabilizer of
the equivariant condensate gives the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy as the
boundary mode count. H-Bell is required only for identifying that local
sector with the Bell-violating total completion. The conditions C1--C4
that characterize the memory-bearing sector --- whose conditional memory
readback makes measurable --- for the visible-sector projection produce
the persistence-based observer selection for the horizon-clock
projection. The substratum gauge group \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\)
controls the gauge equivalences of the \textbf{locally reconstructed
residue} across the three projections; it does not classify all
preparation-indexed Bell-composite rules. The framework's claim is that
the three projections are co-derived from a single construction, not
three separate applications of similar machinery.

\hypertarget{the-qm-gr-incompatibility-as-a-category-error}{%
\subsection{2.7 The QM-GR incompatibility as a category
error}\label{the-qm-gr-incompatibility-as-a-category-error}}

The conventional formulation of the QM-GR unification problem treats
quantum mechanics and general relativity as two competing theories in
the same logical category --- two attempts to describe the same regime,
awaiting reconciliation in a deeper unified theory. Every program of
unification proceeds from this assumption. Quantum gravity programs
treat the metric as a quantum field to be quantized. Geometric programs
treat the wave function as a structure on the spacetime manifold.
Emergent programs treat one of the two as derived from a deeper
substrate that recovers the other. The persistent failure of all three
approaches to produce a quantitatively confirmed unification --- half a
century of intensive work without an empirical test of the unification
regime --- suggests that the underlying assumption may be wrong.

The framework's claim is that quantum mechanics and general relativity
are not two theories of the same regime at all. They are two projections
of the same construction, viewed at different levels and through
different machinery. The visible-sector projection that produces the
memory-bearing dynamics quantum mechanics represents and the
boundary-thermodynamic projection that produces general relativity refer
to \emph{different objects} in the construction. The wave function is a
property of the embedded observer's compressed description of the
visible sector --- the bookkeeping device that tracks what the observer
knows and does not know about a system. The metric is a property of the
classical thermodynamics of the partition boundary --- the geometric
content of the surface across which the trace-out is performed. These
are not two descriptions of the same physical system at different levels
of approximation. They are descriptions of two different substructures
of the same total object \((S, \varphi)\), derived by different
projection maps from a single source.

The structural analogy that captures the relationship most clearly is
the relationship between thermodynamics and statistical mechanics.
Thermodynamics deals with pressure, temperature, and entropy.
Statistical mechanics deals with particle positions, momenta, and
microstate counting. These are not two competing theories of the same
gas, and the question ``how do we unify thermodynamics and statistical
mechanics?'' is not a coherent question. They describe different things
about the same system. The relationship between them is one of
projection --- statistical mechanics produces thermodynamic quantities
by averaging over microstates --- rather than unification. Asking how to
unify thermodynamics and statistical mechanics into a deeper theory
mistakes the structure of their relationship.

The relationship between quantum mechanics and general relativity in the
framework is structurally identical. General relativity describes the
thermodynamic projection of \((S, \varphi)\): the boundary geometry, the
surface gravity, the entropy, the dynamical evolution of the partition
under coupling to the bulk. The quantum representation describes the
statistical projection: the visible-sector dynamics under
marginalization over the hidden sector --- universal over finite laws,
with nonzero conditional memory marking the memory-bearing sector and
the unitary evolution capturing its non-Markovian structure. The two are
related by a definite procedure (the trace-out, with C1/C3/C4 diagnosing
where the memory sector is nontrivial), with the substratum gauge group
controlling the equivalences. The question ``how do we unify them?'' is
recast as a category error rather than answered, conditionally on the
open covariant rung G3 (Chapter 7 §7.7; Chapter 19 §19.2.1).

This is not the same as saying that quantum mechanics is more
fundamental than general relativity, or vice versa. Both are emergent.
Both depend on the trace-out and the partition. Both are derived
structures rather than features of the underlying reality. The
fundamental object is \((S, \varphi)\) --- a set (finite under A1) with
a deterministic bijection on it --- and neither quantum mechanics nor
general relativity is a feature of \((S, \varphi)\) itself. They are
features of how an embedded observer or a horizon-bounded thermodynamic
regime sees \((S, \varphi)\) from inside. (Nor is the ranking question
recoverable from inside: by the factoring argument of Chapter 7, no
criterion grounded in the accessible observations can separate two
descriptions faithful to the same data --- the fundamentality question
is answered at the level of \((S, \varphi)\), not adjudicated between
its projections.)

The recasting of the unification problem has two consequences worth
marking explicitly. First, it recasts the QM-GR unification problem as a
category error between two projections of one object, conditionally on
the open covariant rung G3 (Chapter 7 §7.7; Chapter 19 §19.2.1). The
persistent failure of unification programs is no longer puzzling ---
they were trying to merge two descriptions of different things, which
cannot be done. Second, it provides an explanation for why the Standard
Model has the gauge group it does. The Standard Model gauge group
follows from the substratum construction (Stage 2) conditionally on the
carrier bridges H-link and H-cust (Chapter 5 §§5.4--5.5). The gauge
group is not chosen from a landscape of alternatives; it is obtained
from the stabilizer of the cubic-equivariant condensate, given the
reconstruction theorem's structural inputs and the cubic lattice
selected from observation.

The framework's synthesis claim is structural and architectural, not
predictive in the conventional sense. It does not claim to produce
gravitational phenomena that conventional quantum field theory plus
general relativity cannot reproduce. The framework's empirical content
is concentrated elsewhere: in the Standard Model derivation (twenty-two
quantitative retrodictions, Chapters 5 and 6), the JUNO neutrino
prediction (Chapter 8), and the dark-sector predictions specific to the
boundary-thermodynamic projection (Chapter 7). What the synthesis claim
establishes is that these predictions are not independent. The same
construction that produces the Standard Model produces the gravitational
sector. The same trace-out that gives the Standard Model gauge group
from the stabilizer of the equivariant condensate gives the
Bekenstein-Hawking entropy as the boundary mode count. The framework's
derivations across Chapters 5, 6, and 7 are not separate applications of
similar machinery; they are co-derived consequences of a single
construction.

\hypertarget{what-follows}{%
\subsection{2.8 What follows}\label{what-follows}}

The reconstruction theorem and the substratum gauge group establish the
substratum side of the framework. The three projections establish its
relationship to quantum mechanics and general relativity, and what it
establishes about the arrow of time. With both in place, the technical
core of Part I is complete; the chapters that follow develop its
consequences in three directions.

Chapter 3 develops the framework's philosophical positioning. The
substratum's ontological status --- what it means to commit to the
equivalence class \([(S, \varphi)] / \mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) as the
framework's metaphysical object --- is articulated in its full
hierarchical form, with realism operating at multiple levels of the
observation hierarchy and the gauge hierarchy. The framework's relation
to Bell, Kochen-Specker and PBR-type no-go theorems is developed through
separate checks of their local-response, operational-algebra and
preparation premises, with the stated unresolved obligations retained.
The framework's intellectual position is located against the
contemporary observer-dependence programs (QBism, relational quantum
mechanics, the recent CLPW and Maldacena work on observer-incorporated
entropy) and against the older philosophical lineage (Cusa's docta
ignorantia, Spinoza's attribute theory, Worrall's epistemic structural
realism). The relationship to Hofstadter's strange-loop framework is
developed in detail.

Chapter 4 articulates the framework's methodological discipline. The
methodological account takes the occurrence and recurrence of registered
differentiation as its two starting axioms and identifies the further
premises used in the derivations. The architecture-level engagement with
the no-go results is developed: the substratum, observable law and
trace-out identify the objects constrained by Bell, Kochen-Specker, PBR
and Frauchiger-Renner, while each theorem retains its own premise
checks, including the open H-Bell realization and the stated operational
and preparation assumptions. The classification of claims by
derivational rigor --- theorems, derivations, structural retrodictions,
and informed speculation --- organizes the framework's program by
epistemic status. The framework's pre-registration of falsification
conditions is discussed as a methodological commitment.

Parts II and III then develop the framework's quantitative consequences.
Chapter 5 develops the Standard Model gauge group from the cubic-lattice
substratum: the wave equation, the link count under H-link, the
cubic-group commutant decomposition, checkerboard trace-out with the
additional H-χ' premise for physical chirality, and anomaly-free
hypercharges. Chapter 6 develops the matter content and quantitative
predictions: three generations (physical reading conditional on H-spin',
SM §4.7; chirality on H-χ', SM §4.8), the composite Higgs, gauge
couplings, and the twenty-two classified quantitative retrodictions (two
parameter-free structural and five conditional structural; Appendix A).
Chapter 7 develops the gravitational sector: the boundary
thermodynamics, the calibration \(\hbar = c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\),
the Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) factor, the conditional dissolution of
the cosmological constant problem, the dark sector predictions. Chapter
8 develops the JUNO neutrino prediction in detail. Chapter 9 takes up
universality and the framework's empirical scope.

The cascade through chemistry, biology, evolution, and intelligence in
Chapters 10--12 takes the structural results of Parts I and II as
derived inputs and develops their consequences for the structural
conditions under which complex matter, life, and intelligence become
possible. The applications in Chapters 13--17 develop the framework's
reach into working scientific fields: quantum biology, quantum computing
and engineering, medicine, bioinformatics.

The two observation axioms and the finite-capacity definition set the
starting point. The specified local lattice and gauge inputs give the
forward local reconstruction. The finite-record quantum representation
is exact within its scope, and the matter, gravitational and
cosmological derivations use the separate hypotheses stated in their
chapters. The book's role is to make this chain of derivations available
for evaluation against the experimental record now being assembled and
forthcoming.

\hypertarget{chapter-3}{%
\section{Chapter 3}\label{chapter-3}}

\hypertarget{hierarchical-structural-realism}{%
\section{Hierarchical Structural
Realism}\label{hierarchical-structural-realism}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops}{%
\subsection{3.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops}}

Chapter 2 established the framework's metaphysical commitment as ontic
structural realism on the equivalence class
\([(S, \varphi)] / \mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\). What is real at the
substratum level is the class's reconstructed local residue (§3.5), not
any specific bijection within it. The chapter argued for this commitment
in its own terms: stronger claims commit to features the gauge group
identifies as unobservable, weaker claims undersell the reconstruction
theorem's uniqueness, and the class's local invariants are what
observation plus structural assumptions, under Theorem 23's stated
conditions, force.

That argument is correct but incomplete. The framework's
structural-realism position has more structure than the single
commitment Chapter 2 articulated. Different parts of the framework's
content live at different levels of generality, with different empirical
predictions, different falsifiability conditions, and different
philosophical commitments at each level. The framework's twenty-two
Standard Model retrodictions live at one level; the central claim that
embedded observers' statistics universally admit the quantum
decompression --- a representation, explicitly non-unique --- lives at a
broader level; the foundational fact that observation occurs lives at
the broadest level. A single structural-realism commitment that applied
to all of these uniformly would either claim too much at the
foundational level or too little at the specific predictive level.

This chapter develops the framework's structural realism in its full
hierarchical form. The structural-realism position operates on a
two-dimensional hierarchy: an \emph{observation axis} running from the
framework's foundational commitment to its specific predictive content,
and an orthogonal \emph{gauge axis} running from narrow gauge
equivalences within the emergent quantum mechanics to broad equivalences
across structural classes of embedded observers. Different empirical
predictions live at different intersections of these axes;
falsifiability is stratified accordingly; and the framework's strongest
realism claim --- the Chapter 2 commitment to
\([(S, \varphi)] / \mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) --- is what the hierarchy
locates at a specific intersection.

The chapter has four pieces of work. §§3.2--3.3 develop the observation
axis and the observer-admission distinction that the framework's third
level introduces. §§3.4--3.5 develop the gauge axis, its orthogonality
with the observation axis, and the resulting multi-level structural
realism with its stratified predictions. §3.6 identifies gauge freedom
with observational incompleteness on a precisely delimited part of its
range, distinguishing the two species of incompleteness this produces.
§§3.7--3.8 develop the framework's relationship to the contemporary
no-go theorem literature and to the older philosophical lineage of
incompleteness-and-perspective accounts. §3.9 closes the chapter and
points forward to Chapter 4's methodology and to Chapter 8's
universality and cross-framework analysis.

\hypertarget{the-observation-axis}{%
\subsection{3.2 The observation axis}\label{the-observation-axis}}

The framework's content nests in four levels of increasing specificity
along an axis I will call the \emph{observation axis}. Each deeper level
is a more specific commitment about what the framework asserts. At the
broadest level, the framework posits that registered differentiation
occurs and recurs; at the narrowest level, it commits to a specific
lattice structure with twenty-two quantitative retrodictions. Between
these poles lie two further levels --- observer admission and
universality classes --- that articulate intermediate structural
content.

\textbf{Level A: the observation axioms.} The framework's foundational
commitment, developed in Chapter 1, is that observation occurs: an
observer records distinguishable outcomes of interactions with a system
not wholly under the observer's control. Its indubitable core --- that
some differentiated content is registered --- is the Cartesian
\emph{cogito}, made mathematically precise and without its thinking
subject. This is the first axiom. The second axiom posits that
differentiation recurs. The structure Level A adds to that core is that
of the Chapter 1 definition, and it is physical, not mental. Level A
commits to three things: that there is something to observe (a substrate
of reality structured to support distinguishable states); that some part
of reality is structured to record outcomes (observers are embedded in
reality, not external to it); and that observation has structural
consequences (the recording itself is a physical event, not a passive
registration).

Level A is shared with the broader observer-essentiality program in
contemporary foundations of physics. The work of Chandrasekaran, Longo,
Penington, and Witten on observer-incorporated entropy in de Sitter
space (2022), Maldacena's analysis of observer's-clock dependence in
cosmological partition functions (2024), and Harlow, Usatyuk, and Zhao
on observer-dependent Hilbert spaces in closed universes (2025) all
start from analogous commitments. The two axioms give the starting point
for the constructions. A dynamics relates successive configurations at a
persisting locus. The bijective representative and the structural
hypotheses of the local reconstruction enter at the later levels.

\textbf{Level B: the memory-bearing observer class.} Chapter 1 uses C1
for hidden influence at an eligible step, C2 for persistence of a record
to readback, C3 for the quantitative capacity bound and C4 for the
history-dependence witness. Calling a substratum observer-admitting at
this level means it has a proper partition supporting that specified
memory-bearing regime. The finite-law representation also covers
memoryless records.

A finite cellular automaton can support a Level B observer if the chosen
partition, preparation and dynamics meet the stated memory-bearing
conditions. The coarse-channel mixing condition depends on the channel.
Even an exact short orbit can give a gapped compressed channel ({[}Main
§4.6{]}).

Level B commits to a structural-anthropic reading that sharpens the
conventional anthropic principle. Standard anthropic reasoning treats
fundamental parameters as contingent and explained by selection: we
observe a universe with parameters compatible with us because we could
not observe a universe without them. The Level B reading is sharper.
Observer-lacking substrata are not candidates for ``our universe'' at
all --- they are mathematical objects of a different kind, lacking the
observer-extraction structure that would make the question ``what would
observers in this universe see?'' coherent. Within the
observer-admitting subset, anthropic reasoning operates as usual; across
the observer-admitting / observer-lacking boundary, the question of why
we observe a universe with our particular features becomes the question
of why a universe must be observer-admitting at all. The framework's
answer is partly tautological --- we are observers, so the universe we
observe must admit observers --- but the tautology is informative: it
identifies which structural features of a candidate universe are forced
by the existence of observers, and which are contingent.

Level B describes a stipulated memory-bearing regime across candidate
models. A claim about a particular physical partition requires its
preparation and the stated influence, persistence, capacity and readback
conditions.

\textbf{Level C: universality classes.} Within the observer-admitting
subset, equivalence classes arise from the partial-trace observational
features that any embedded observer produces. Two
substratum-with-observer systems are \emph{observationally equivalent}
if their algebra-channel pairs --- the algebra of visible-sector
observables together with the quantum channel induced by the partial
trace over the hidden sector --- are isomorphic in a precise sense that
preserves both the algebraic structure and the channel's dynamical
content. A \emph{universality class} is an equivalence class under this
observational equivalence.

The universality-class structure is broader than the substratum gauge
group of Chapter 2. The substratum gauge group
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) relates some observationally equivalent
substrata \emph{within OI's specific structural class} --- substrata
satisfying A1--A6 of the reconstruction theorem; whether the stated
generators exhaust the relevant equivalences is open. The
universality-class equivalence operates more broadly: substrata in
different structural classes can be observationally equivalent if they
produce the same algebra-channel pair through structurally different
machinery. Two substrata that are universality-class equivalent need not
be related by any \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) transformation; the
broader equivalence allows for structural-class transitions that the
substratum gauge group does not.

Universality classes have internal sub-structure at three levels of
refinement. The most universal level is the \emph{partial-trace features
sub-class}, characterized by the exact fixed-basis representation of
supplied finite records. Conditional memory requires a readback witness,
and finite recurrence with a non-permutation rooted map gives
P-indivisibility over the cycle. The reduced-channel approximation and
the symmetry restrictions use the separate hypotheses in their
derivations. Below this is the \emph{gauge-group sub-class},
characterized by which specific emergent gauge group the marginalization
produces. Standard-Model-reproducing classes share
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\); other
classes produce different gauge groups. Below this is the
\emph{algebra-channel sub-class}, characterized by the specific algebra
of observables and specific channel dynamics --- the level at which two
specific substratum-with-observer systems become indistinguishable in
every observable.

Level C commits to a structural realism at the class level: the
universality class is what is real, with specific substratum
representatives playing the role of gauge expressions. Different members
of the same universality class are observationally indistinguishable by
definition, so the question ``which specific substratum is real?'' has
no empirical content at the universality-class level. The realism is
precisely about what survives the universality-class quotient.

\textbf{Level D: OI's specific local structural residue.} The
framework's narrowest reconstructed commitment is the three-dimensional
cubic local lattice/gauge sector with \(K=6\), the wave-equation
dynamics and the listed Standard-Model representation data, with the
qualifications developed in the technical chapters. The reconstruction
theorem establishes that the stated observed and structural inputs fix
this \textbf{local residue} under Theorem 23's conditions. It does not
uniquely determine a Bell-inclusive full representative. With one-step
own-wing setting interventions on finite regions, readouts in finite
regions outside the other wing's graph cone and a \(\pm1\) outcome in
every run, the reference cubic graph is Bell-local under measurement
independence; the adopted branch proposes preparation-indexed
state-dependent adjacency under the open hypothesis H-Bell (operational
no-signaling and the metric/Ollivier--Ricci continuum limit), with its
uniqueness left open.

Level D is where the framework's twenty-two classified quantitative
predictions live (two parameter-free structural and five conditional
structural among them): the Cabibbo angle \(1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\), the Koide
angle \(2/9\), the gauge-coupling-running calculation giving the three
SM coupling constants at the \(Z\) pole, the six-mass chain with one
empirical mass scale and the stated phenomenological and modeled inputs,
the Higgs quartic coupling from cubic-group representation theory, and
the JUNO neutrino-mixing prediction; outside that count sit the
Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) factor as a consistency relation and the MOND
acceleration scale \(cH/6\). The empirical content that distinguishes OI
from other observer-admitting frameworks is concentrated at Level D,
because Level D is where the structural commitments become specific
enough to produce specific numerical predictions.

The relationship between Levels D and C deserves a separate remark. The
structural conditions A1--A6 that define Level D are not the same as the
observer-admission conditions C1--C4 that define Level B. C1--C4 concern
the specified memory-bearing and physical persistence regime; A1--A6 are
conditions for membership in OI's \emph{specific} universality class
within the observer-admitting subset. Some A's relate to but are
distinct from C's: A1 posits finiteness of the total configuration space
and remains open as a physical premise. C3 bounds the hidden-sector
capacity needed for a given law. A2 (determinism via bijection) selects
deterministic-substratum members of a universality class, but observers
can in principle exist on stochastic dynamics that satisfy the
partial-trace observational features differently. A3--A6 (bounded
coupling, center independence, linearity, background independence) are
pure class-specific conditions, required for OI's specific
gauge-structure derivation but not necessary for observer admission. The
Level D commitment selects a specific universality class within the
observer-admitting subset, with both the empirical inputs of physics and
the framework's choice of structural assumptions playing a role in the
selection.

\textbf{The hierarchy nests.} Each deeper level is a more specific
commitment, with Level A \(\supset\) Level B \(\supset\) Level C
\(\supset\) Level D. Level A posits that observation occurs and recurs;
Level B adds that the substratum's bijection structure must support
observers; Level C adds the observational-equivalence structure that
groups observer-admitting substrata into universality classes; Level D
adds the framework's specific structural assumptions and selects the
cubic-lattice substratum. The framework commits to all four levels
simultaneously, with content at each level being more universal (broader
levels) or more class-specific (deeper levels).

\hypertarget{the-observer-admission-distinction-in-more-detail}{%
\subsection{3.3 The observer-admission distinction in more
detail}\label{the-observer-admission-distinction-in-more-detail}}

The observer-admission distinction at Level B deserves more sustained
development than the previous section allowed. It is the framework's
structural-anthropic move, and it has consequences that distinguish the
framework from both standard anthropic reasoning and the broader
observer-dependence program in contemporary foundations of physics.

Standard anthropic reasoning operates on fundamental parameters. The
cosmological constant, the masses of the fermions, the strengths of the
four forces --- these are observed to lie in narrow ranges compatible
with the existence of observers, and the anthropic principle explains
this by selection: a universe with different parameters would not
contain observers to make the observation. The reasoning is conditional.
It takes the existence of observers as given and explains the observed
parameter values by the conditioning on observer existence.

The observer-admission reading at Level B sharpens this in two ways.
First, it identifies which features the Level B models require for the
stipulated memory-bearing regime, prior to questions about specific
parameter values. The C1--C4 conditions depend on the exposed partition,
the prepared law and the dynamics. A substratum either admits observers
or it does not; the question is binary at the structural level, before
any parameter values are specified. Second, the observer-admission
reading provides a more concrete account of what ``selection'' means.
The standard anthropic principle is sometimes criticized as tautological
--- observers observe universes with observers in them --- but this
criticism misses the structural content. Observer-lacking substrata are
not failed candidates that happened not to produce observers; they lack
the stipulated features of the Level B memory-bearing regime.

A fast-mixing equilibrium and a model with protected slow modes
illustrate different retention regimes. With effective mixing and
\(\tau_{\rm mix}\ll\tau_S\), the iterated coarse channel of the first
model excludes C2-slow. A protected mode can retain a record in the
second case. Whether it supports C4 depends on the prepared law and on
whether the visible interaction reads the record.

The conditional Boltzmann-brain exclusion concerns bounded-diameter
partitions in a finite bijective model with effective mixing and
\(\tau_{\rm mix}\ll\tau_S\). These partitions fail C2-slow in the
description generated by iterating the one-step coarse channel. Uniform
erosion suppresses the readback gap there ({[}Main §§2.3, 4.6{]}). The
exclusion is time-symmetric. On an expanding homogeneous background
satisfying the null energy condition, the apparent-horizon area provides
a non-decreasing parameter, with the alignment of other arrows left
open.

The string-theory landscape problem looks different under the Level B
reading as well. The conventional landscape picture posits roughly
\(10^{500}\) metastable vacua, each a different low-energy effective
theory, with the vacuum-selection problem being to explain why our
universe is in this particular vacuum. The Level B reading reframes
this: most compactifications likely produce observer-lacking substrata
at the relevant scales, because the slow-bath, sufficient-capacity,
non-trivial-coupling conditions are non-generic. The SM-reproducing
subset of the landscape is structurally smaller than the total
landscape, because it is restricted to the observer-admitting subset.
Whether this reframing fully resolves the landscape problem is an open
technical question --- it depends on whether observer-lacking
compactifications can be characterized in string-theoretic terms, which
requires substantive work in string-theoretic landscape physics --- but
the reframing is non-trivial.

The framework's commitment at Level B is therefore structurally
substantive, not merely a definitional convention. It identifies the
observer-admission boundary as a real feature of the space of candidate
substrata, with consequences for anthropic reasoning, Boltzmann brains,
the arrow of time, and the landscape problem. The realism at Level B is
realism about the boundary itself: which substrata admit observers,
which do not, and why. The empirical content at Level B is sparse ---
most of the framework's predictions live at deeper levels --- but the
structural content is rich.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-gauge-axis}{%
\subsection{3.4 The gauge axis}\label{the-gauge-axis}}

The framework's gauge structure runs along an axis orthogonal to the
observation axis. Where the observation axis is about scope --- which
substrata fall within the framework's domain --- the gauge axis is about
transformations: which substratum-level operations leave all observables
unchanged. Like the observation axis, the gauge axis has four levels,
each with its own equivalence notion.

\textbf{Level G1: D-gauge on the emergent Hamiltonian.} The first level
of gauge freedom is the diagonal-unitary equivalence on the emergent
Hamiltonian: \(H \to D H D^\dagger\) with \(D\) a diagonal unitary in
the measurement-outcome basis. This freedom preserves transition
probabilities exactly. Energy shifts and the antiunitary reflection also
preserve them; completeness of these alternatives under the stated gap
and overlap hypotheses is conditional on the sign-aware integer
classification H-BG ({[}GR §3.3{]}; Appendix B.7). Two Hamiltonians
\(H\) and \(D H D^\dagger\) produce identical Born-rule probabilities
\(T_{ij}(t) = |\langle j | e^{-iHt/\hbar} | i \rangle|^2\) in the
measurement basis, so they are operationally indistinguishable. The
transformation rephases the measurement basis, changing off-diagonal
phases of \(H\) while leaving its diagonal entries and every transition
probability unchanged.

Level G1 operates within a single Hamiltonian realization in a single
emergent quantum mechanics --- within Level D × Level G1 in the joint
hierarchy, the framework's most specific intersection. Its content is
the bookkeeping freedom in choosing phase conventions for the emergent
basis states, with no implications beyond that.

\textbf{Level G2: the Standard Model gauge group.} The next level of
gauge freedom is the Standard Model gauge group
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\) acting on
the emergent quantum fields. Chapter 2 §2.4 developed this as the
unitary group of the bicommutant of the cubic-group action (the strict
pointwise commutant is \(\mathrm{U}(1)^3\) by Schur's lemma) on the six
internal components of OI's substratum: the cubic-group decomposition
gives multiplicities \((3, 2, 1)\), and the unitary group of the block
algebra generated by the cubic-group representation on this
decomposition is precisely
\(\mathrm{U}(3) \times \mathrm{U}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\), reducing to
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\) with a
specified charged matter action (Chapter 5 §5.6); amplitude-scale gauge
removes only the common phase. Background independence promotes this
global commutant symmetry to local gauge invariance, giving the full SM
gauge structure of standard quantum field theory.

An inclusion of Level G1 in Level G2 is not established. G2 includes the
off-diagonal gauge transformations that mix different internal
components, which G1 does not access.

Level G2 concerns the local physical gauge sector. In OI's
reconstruction the geometric six-link decomposition supplies the block
sizes. The single-copy H-link carrier and distinct-block condensate
under H-cust give the corresponding unitary stabilizer, and the
specified charged action supplies the physical gauge algebra. The local
sector of another construction can agree on the algebra while requiring
separate global data.

\textbf{Level G3: substratum observational equivalences.} Theorem 24 of
{[}Substratum{]} exhibits exact invariances for specified visible
interfaces. A single hidden permutation used identically in every
visible fibre preserves the coherent channel family with the uniform
hidden prior; an independently prepared, normalized, exactly decoupled
finite ancillary factor leaves that family unchanged. Fibre-dependent
hidden permutations preserve the rooted population transition
probabilities, but need not preserve coherences. Alphabet change
preserves observables only under the alphabet-size hypothesis; {[}SM
§2.7{]} separates results proved for every \(q\ge2\) from those that
carry \(q\). These constructions do not classify all substrata or all
observer partitions; completeness remains open.

Inclusions of G1 and G2 in G3, and a map from
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) onto the Standard Model gauge group, are
not established. The local gauge-algebra result uses the distinct-block
condensate stabilizer and the specified charged action on the
single-copy H-link carrier (Stage 2).

Level G3 differs from G1 and G2 in an important structural respect: it
is an \emph{equivalence-class symmetry}, not a Lagrangian symmetry.
There is no Lagrangian at the substratum level; the substratum is a set
(finite under A1) with a bijection on it, governed by a discrete update
rule rather than a continuous action principle. The gauge group acts on
the equivalence class of substrata defined by the observability
condition. It plays the same structural role at the substratum level
that Lagrangian gauge symmetries play at the field-theory level ---
identifying observationally indistinguishable configurations --- but
through a different mathematical mechanism.

\textbf{Level G4: universality-class equivalence.} The broadest gauge
freedom in the hierarchy operates at the universality-class level. Two
substratum-with-observer systems are universality-class equivalent if
their algebra-channel pairs are isomorphic in the precise sense
identified at Level C --- preserving both the algebraic structure of
visible observables and the channel's dynamical content. Level G4
captures equivalences that may not be expressible as transformations
within any single structural class.

Level G4 is broader than generators (i) and (iii) of
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\). Substrata related by them are
universality-class equivalent (since they produce the same
algebra-channel pair), but substrata not related by any
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) transformation may still be
universality-class equivalent if they produce the same algebra-channel
pair through structurally different machinery. The classic candidate is
the relationship between OI's cubic-lattice substratum and
string-theoretic compactifications that reproduce the Standard Model.
The two are not related by any \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) generator
--- OI's bounded-coupling, finite-deterministic structure is not
preserved by string-theoretic compactifications, which violate A2
(determinism) and A5 (linearity) at the matrix-model bridge --- but they
may produce equivalent algebra-channel pairs, making them
universality-class equivalent at Level G4 even though they are not
gauge-equivalent at Level G3.

Level G4 compares systems at a specified interface by their visible
algebra and channel. The comparison can include memoryless visible laws.
Level B refers to the designated memory-bearing regime.

\textbf{The levels of the gauge hierarchy.} The levels carry distinct
equivalence notions; inclusions among G1, G2 and G3 and a map from
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) onto the Standard Model gauge group are not
established. The framework commits to all four levels of gauge
simultaneously, with different levels of gauge being relevant to
different questions about the substratum and its emergent physics.

\hypertarget{orthogonality-multi-level-realism-and-stratified-predictions}{%
\subsection{3.5 Orthogonality, multi-level realism, and stratified
predictions}\label{orthogonality-multi-level-realism-and-stratified-predictions}}

The two hierarchies --- observation axis and gauge axis --- are
orthogonal. The observation axis is about scope: which substrata fall
within the framework's domain at each level of specificity. The gauge
axis is about transformations: which operations leave observables
unchanged at each level of breadth. A specific empirical claim or
theoretical commitment lives at a specific \emph{intersection} of the
two axes, with the intersection determining both what the claim's
content is and how it can be falsified.

The orthogonality has substantive content. Levels G1, G2, and G3 sit
within Level D --- they are gauge structures of OI's specific
universality class with its specific gauge derivation. Level G4 operates
at Level C --- it characterizes universality-class equivalence, which is
broader than OI's structural class. The two-axis structure means the
framework's strongest realism claim --- the Chapter 2 commitment to
\([(S, \varphi)] / \mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) --- operates at the Level
D × Level G3 intersection. Weaker realism claims operate at broader
intersections, with corresponding shifts in empirical content.

\textbf{What is real at each intersection.} The framework commits to
realism at four distinct levels of the two-axis hierarchy, with the
realism content differing at each level.

At Level G4 × Level C, the comparison is between algebra-channel
structures of specified observation interfaces. Every supplied law on a
finite alphabet and horizon admits a fixed-basis unitary/Born
representation. Accessible conditional memory has a C4 witness, and the
recurrence result further requires a finite representative and a
non-permutation rooted map. A near-unitary reduced channel or a
particular invariant algebra uses additional model hypotheses.

At Level G3 × Level D --- the framework's distinctive intersection ---
what is real is the \textbf{reconstructed local lattice/gauge residue
modulo} \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\). Chapter 2 shows that the
invariants of this local residue are uniquely fixed under Theorem 23's
stated conditions. Bell-inclusive completion data are not included in
that uniqueness claim: H-Bell conditions their compatibility/existence
and no result selects a unique preparation-indexed Bell rule. The
realism is therefore strongest for the reconstructed local structural
residue, not for one uniquely specified Bell-complete representative.

At Level G2 × Level D --- a narrower intersection in the gauge axis but
the same observation level --- what is real is the emergent quantum
field theory structure: the Standard Model gauge group, the matter
content of three generations (physical reading conditional on H-spin',
SM §4.7; chirality on H-χ', SM §4.8) plus one Higgs doublet, the
anomaly-free hypercharge assignment on the nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch. The
local gauge algebra in this sector uses single-copy H-link, H-cust and
the specified charged action. The spin and chirality readings retain
their named conditions, and global gauge data have separate inputs
(Chapter 5 §§5.4--5.6). The realism is about the emergent quantum field
theory rather than about any specific substratum.

At Level G1 × Level D --- the narrowest intersection --- what is real is
