its trace-out supply the same substratum and observable objects for
these questions. They do not discharge the no-go hypotheses by
themselves. Bell's ceiling still applies to a measurement-independent
deterministic completion with local responses; the adopted branch
therefore requires ontic parameter dependence and a realization meeting
H-Bell. The other cases retain their separate operational-algebra,
preparation-independence and observer-consistency assumptions. Each
conclusion follows only when its own argument and hypotheses hold.

This per-theorem verification is a genuine discipline, not a rhetorical
disadvantage. In particular, determinism by itself does not settle
Bell's measurement-independence premise. The framework \textbf{adopts}
the measurement-independent branch rather than using setting dependence
as its explanation; measurement independence is retained as a posit
about the initial condition, not derived. The required Bell violation is
instead carried by ontic parameter dependence, with operational
no-signaling checked separately. The same discipline applies to the
coherent-instrument assumptions in the other no-go theorems.

\textbf{Methodological benefit.} The benefit of the architecture-level
engagement is that the framework's structural reading of each no-go
theorem is \emph{informative}. Identifying how each assumption meets the
two-level structure explains \emph{why} quantum mechanics has the
features the no-go theorems identify, not just that it does. Bell's
theorem forces the framework to locate nonlocality precisely: in the
adopted branch it is ontic parameter dependence, not mere stochastic
outcome dependence or indivisibility. Kochen-Specker's contextuality is
informative about the partition-dependence of the trace-out. PBR
identifies a preparation-independence question for separated subsystems
that may share boundary data; the trace-out alone does not determine
whether a proposed completion satisfies that premise.
Frauchiger-Renner's inconsistency-paradox is informative about the
levels of the framework's hierarchy.

The no-go theorems become, in this reading, structural diagnostic tools
rather than obstacles. Each one identifies a specific structural feature
that any hidden-variable theory matching quantum mechanics must have.
The framework's identification of the relevant features through
hierarchy levels makes the structural content of the theorems available
for use in further work --- in particular, in identifying which features
any successful unification framework must satisfy.

\textbf{Application to new no-go theorems.} The procedure is open-ended.
Any future no-go theorem in the foundations literature can be subjected
to the same four-step analysis. The framework's commitment is to apply
the procedure honestly to each new result rather than to claim general
immunity. If a no-go theorem turns out to identify a structural property
that the framework cannot satisfy at any level --- or to require
simultaneous satisfaction of properties the framework can satisfy only
at different levels --- the framework would face genuine difficulty.

An additional no-go theorem requires an analysis of its actual
hypotheses on the proposed completion. The shared substratum and
observable descriptions identify the objects to examine, but do not
guarantee that a required premise fails or that the completion avoids
the theorem's conclusion.

The common architecture organizes the questions, while each no-go
theorem retains its own substantive test. Bell still imposes the
local-response ceiling under measurement independence, H-Bell remains an
obligation of the proposed physical realization, and the other cases
retain their separate operational, preparation and observer-consistency
assumptions.

\hypertarget{pre-registered-falsification-conditions}{%
\subsection{4.5 Pre-registered falsification
conditions}\label{pre-registered-falsification-conditions}}

A framework that derives rather than posits must be willing to specify
what would invalidate the derivation. The framework's discipline is to
pre-register specific falsification conditions, stating in advance which
observational outcomes would refute the framework's structural
commitments and which would refute only narrow predictions while leaving
the broader structure intact. The pre-registration distinguishes
structural claims --- which the framework stands or falls on --- from
solution-specific properties that lie outside the framework's scope.

The conditions are organized into three classes. Class A identifies
structural theorems whose violation would falsify the framework
directly. Class B identifies parameter-free retrodictions whose
precision-upgrade violation would falsify, with sub-classes reflecting
the rigor of the retrodiction. Class C identifies broader
framework-level commitments whose contradiction would refute particular
framework claims while leaving others intact.

\textbf{Class A --- structural theorems.} The framework derives specific
structural features of physics as theorems under the observation axioms
and the relevant structural assumptions. Each derived feature is a
falsification target if violated.

\emph{The strong-CP phase, not fixed.} T-invariance of the substratum
bijection combined with detailed balance narrows the QCD angle to
\(\theta\in\{0,\pi\}\) and gives reciprocal transition counts under the
counting hidden prior of a finite model, but does not make the emergent
Hamiltonian T-invariant, so \(\bar\theta\) is not fixed by the
construction (SM §5). The framework makes no commitment on the neutron
electric dipole moment; a measured \(\bar\theta\neq0\) would constrain
mechanisms proposed for the named condition H-det, not the T-symmetry of
the substratum.

\emph{The local Standard Model gauge algebra.} The six-link
decomposition and its distinct-block condensate give the stated unitary
stabilizer under single-copy H-link and H-cust. The specified charged
action selects the local Standard Model gauge algebra, with global
identifications and bundle data specified separately (Chapter 5
§§5.4--5.6). A measured gauge sector outside the stated charged-action
branch would test that branch's physical identification.

\emph{Three fermion generations.} Conditionally on H-link single-copy,
the framework derives the generation count of three from the link count,
\(K = 2dm\) with \(m = 1\), locking \(K = 2d = 6\) internal components
and giving three spin-\(1/2\) staggered tastes. Any observation of a
stable fourth-generation fermion with Standard Model quantum numbers
falsifies the taste-reduction derivation. Non-stable exotic states
consistent with composite or resonance interpretation do not.

\emph{Majorana neutrinos with normal mass ordering.} The framework
expects this on the branch where the singlet taste hosts the Higgs and
no gauge-singlet fermion is present (SM §8.4): Majorana because no
gauge-singlet neutrino is present, normal ordering as a heuristic
consequence of the taste-breaking structure of the neutrino mass matrix
rather than a theorem. Inverted mass ordering, confirmed to high
significance, falsifies the heuristic on that branch. Confirmed Dirac
nature of the neutrino --- for example, a null result for neutrinoless
double-beta decay at the sensitivity that would require Majorana masses
well below the framework's expectation --- falsifies the branch's
expectation that no right-handed neutrino exists in the spectrum.

\emph{The Tsirelson bound.} The value \(2\sqrt{2}\) belongs to the cited
\textbf{stochastic causal-local indivisible construction} ({[}Main
§3.3{]}), not to a Bell-local deterministic completion and not to
generic P-indivisibility. The deterministic OI layer reaches quantum
Bell violation, under measurement independence, only on the ontically
parameter-dependent branch. An observed loophole-free CHSH value above
\(2\sqrt2\) would falsify standard quantum mechanics and any claim that
the relevant OI operational lift lands in the standard quantum Bell set;
it would not, by itself, falsify P-indivisibility.

\emph{Visible-sector coherence in the physical model.} The exact theorem
represents supplied records on finite alphabets and horizons. The
near-unitary channel estimate of Chapter 1 §1.6 takes a specified
interpolation, preparation and weak coupling. The deterministic model
under these hypotheses has no intrinsic collapse. A laboratory collapse
or decoherence signal tests a specified physical model and its predicted
rates. Matter-wave interference at macroscopicity \(\mu = 15.5\)
(Pedalino et al.~2026) is a coherence test in its own regime.

\emph{Leading Lorentz-invariance-violation coefficient.} The framework
derives a specific subluminal dispersion relation with the leading
correction at order \((E/M_{\text{Pl}})^2\), with a physical,
direction-dependent anisotropy whose orientation-averaged coefficient is
\(2/15\) at one nat of entropy per boundary mode (\(2\sigma/15\) for an
entropy \(\sigma\) per mode; \(\langle\delta\rangle = 1/90\); the body
diagonals are exactly luminal). The structural content is the lattice
coefficient \(1/45\) of \(k^2\) times the squared lattice spacing and
the anisotropy pattern; the amplitude \(2\sigma/15\) carries the
undetermined entropy per mode, so it is not a parameter-free number, and
a measurement of it would constrain \(\sigma\) rather than independently
falsify the coefficient. The anisotropy's absolute orientation in space
is gauge, but its \(\ell=4\) cubic-harmonic pattern and the
direction-differences are physical --- the cubic structure is an
empirically-selected input, not a gauge choice (see the Standard Model
and Substratum papers). Two structural features of this prediction
matter for falsification. First, the dispersion has no
linear-in-\(E/M_{\text{Pl}}\) term --- any demonstration of linear
Lorentz-invariance violation at any scale falsifies the framework's
substrate-level commitment to the cubic-lattice wave equation. Second,
the dispersion is subluminal everywhere on the momentum sphere;
superluminal LIV anywhere falsifies. Current quadratic-LIV bounds from
gamma-ray-burst time-of-flight measurements reach roughly thirteen
orders of magnitude below the Planck scale, so the \(2\sigma/15\)
coefficient is not near-term testable at the magnitude level; linear-LIV
tests, by contrast, are already at sensitivities where any positive
detection would falsify. These statements describe the dispersion at
tree level; whether the absence of a relevant (low-dimension)
Lorentz-violating operator survives radiative corrections in the
interacting theory is a separate, open question --- the Lorentz
fine-tuning problem common to discrete-substrate approaches ---
discussed in the Standard Model paper. The tree-level prediction and its
falsifiers stand regardless; what is open is the loop-level protection
--- and for the rotational sector it turns on whether the emergent
theory preserves the octahedral symmetry exactly at loop level, with an
aligned condensate (Chapter 19 §19.3.7): octahedral-invariant dynamics
cannot generate the leading rotational anisotropy at any order, and the
power-divergent operator mixing that cubic symmetry permits is mixing
among angular-momentum-covariant operators rather than the generation of
a lower-dimension rotational-violating operator (see the Standard Model
paper). The protection mechanism available here (the framework not being
supersymmetric) is renormalization-group emergence --- Lorentz-violating
couplings flowing to an infrared-attractive Lorentz-invariant fixed
point (Chadha--Nielsen; Bednik--Pujolàs--Sibiryakov), natural because
the trace-out is a coarse-graining --- with the documented caveat that
the inter-species velocity flow is slow. The causal-set discreteness
results (Bombelli--Henson--Sorkin) independently confirm that a
finite-valency, locally-coupled discrete structure cannot be
microscopically Lorentz-invariant, so the invariance here is necessarily
emergent rather than fundamental.

\textbf{Class B --- parameter-free retrodictions.} The framework
produces twenty-two classified quantitative retrodictions that follow
from the structural content with no adjustable parameters beyond a small
acknowledged empirical input set and three matched coupling parameters.
These are stratified into five sub-classes reflecting their structural
status.

\emph{Class B-S (structural).} These are layer-0 or layer-1
retrodictions with no open link specific to the entry; like every Class
B entry they rest on the matter-sector hypotheses H-spin' and H-χ'. The
example in this chapter's selection is the Wolfenstein parameter
\(A = \sqrt{2/3}\) from the off-democratic projection of the cubic
generation axes. Any such entry moving outside \(3\sigma\) on precision
upgrade falsifies the framework with no recoverable error mode beyond
computational mistakes in the specific derivation.

\emph{Class B-C (conditional structural).} These are layer-1
retrodictions with no fitted input whose derivation chain has one named
open link. The Cabibbo angle \(1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\) from a single
Brillouin-zone distance is B-C, conditional on the emergent-theory
dressing of its identification with the taste-changing transition; the
Koide angle \(\theta_0 = 2/9\) from a cubic-group quadratic Casimir
(matched to \(0.001\%\)) is B-C with the Koide amplitude, whose value
\(A^2 = C_2\) is not yet derived from the dynamics. A precision-upgrade
violation would falsify the identification or the closure on which the
entry is conditional.

\emph{Class B-L (layered conditional, pending open derivations).} These
predictions follow from the structural form combined with one Layer-2
substrate input or empirical input, with a specific active research
direction whose closure would move the prediction to B-S status. The
leading-order solar value \(\sin^2\theta_{12}=1/3-1/(4\pi^2)\) is B-L.
It uses Cond 2, the separate normalization \(b_{23}=1\) and the stated
Cabibbo and flavor inputs. The retrodictive residual is \(0.07\sigma\)
to the global fit that includes the direct data. Higher orders remain
open. The mass ratio \(m_d/m_s = 1/(2\pi^2)\) is B-L, its conversion
from the Cabibbo scale running through the empirical Gatto-Sartori-Tonin
relation, and the MOND critical acceleration \(cH/6\) is B-L, using the
de Sitter temperature and specified heat input with the numerical factor
from Verlinde's emergent-gravity analysis. Other B-L predictions exist
throughout Chapter 7's quantitative content.

\emph{Class B-M (mass-chain inheritance).} These predictions inherit
their empirical match from a single upstream empirical input. The Higgs
mass \(m_H\) via Standard Model RGE running from the boundary condition
\(\lambda(M_{\text{Pl}}) = 0\), with \(m_t\) as the empirical input, is
B-M. Class B-M predictions falsify under the same precision-upgrade
protocol as B-L, but the inheritance is from an empirical input scale
rather than from an open derivation.

\emph{Class B-R (retrodictions).} The \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) and
\(\mathrm{SU}(3)\) gauge couplings at the \(Z\) pole are explicitly
retrodictions: three fitted parameters \((\delta_0, A, B)\) against
three observed couplings produces zero residual by construction. Class
B-R predictions cannot falsify in the precision-upgrade sense; their
value lies in falsifying the framework's gauge-sector structural
commitments --- universality of \(\delta_0\), the resummation form, the
structural prediction \(1/\alpha_0 = 23.25\) from the one-loop staggered
vacuum polarization, with the \(A \cdot B\) finite-lattice calculation
providing a separate model-conditional numerical cross-check that
remains inconclusive across leading-power assumptions. Any
precision-upgrade violation of the structural commitments would falsify
the framework's gauge-sector account while leaving the broader Class A
theorems intact.

The Class B split is, in honest summary: one prediction is structural
with no open link of its own (B-S), two are conditional structural
(B-C), six are layered conditional pending open derivations (B-L), two
are mass-chain inheritances (B-M), and two are retrodictions (B-R). The
thirteen Class B entries combine numerical retrodictions, conditional
formulas and inherited mass relations. Their empirical standing is
assessed individually: the gauge couplings match by construction. The
Bekenstein-Hawking coefficient \(A/(4\ell_P^2)\), conditional on the
infrared detailed-balance condition H-slope on the horizon reservoir
({[}GR §3.2{]}), is a consistency relation with no direct test ---
GW250114 constrains the area theorem --- and is not counted among them.
The quoted precision of a measured comparison does not apply to every
entry. As experimental precision improves, the discrimination power of
the B-S set increases monotonically; closure of the open derivations
would move B-C and B-L predictions to B-S over time.

\textbf{Class C --- framework-level commitments.} Two broader
commitments are implicit in the construction; each is stated with what
would contradict it.

\emph{Finite classical realizability of quantum processes.} For a
supplied law on a finite alphabet through a finite horizon, Chapter 1
§1.8 gives an exact finite reversible realization. A law with a
history-memory witness requires the corresponding hidden influence and
capacity in every faithful realization. With its quantum conditional
probabilities supplied, each finite adaptive quantum experiment has a
finite deterministic realization. The exact continuum theory at any
fixed finite carrier is excluded by the classical-dimension obstruction
({[}Main §3.4{]}). Non-Markovian models are permitted and expected (they
are how the hidden-sector correlation persistence manifests). No
finite-accuracy experiment contradicts this commitment by itself. A
memory-witness experiment would contradict the ontology only given the
coherent-preparation and instrument bridge, an outcome-independent rule
identifying fundamental open-system processes, and a constraint derived
from the completed model on what those processes must show; the last is
not established ({[}Main §4.5{]}).

\emph{The dark sector as entropy-displacement, not as a novel particle
content.} The framework's account of dark energy as boundary-entropy
bookkeeping read in the Type II running-vacuum channel, and dark matter
as frozen boundary entropy, developed in Chapter 7, is incompatible with
the direct detection of a WIMP interpretable as a fundamental particle
with Standard-Model-like interactions and no entropy-displacement
signature. A confirmed WIMP with such properties falsifies the
framework's dark-sector account while leaving the rest of the structure
intact --- it would require abandoning the boundary-entropy derivation
and either identifying an error in it or accepting that the framework's
dark-sector story is wrong even as other derivations survive.

\textbf{The cosmological commitment.} Chapter 7 gives a smooth late-time
expansion in \(H^2-H_0^2\) and considers a Type II reading with
conserved matter and running \(G\). The emergent-QFT scale estimate
\(|\nu_{\mathrm{QFT}}|\sim(M_{\mathrm{SM}}/M_{\mathrm{Pl}})^2\sim10^{-32}\)
uses the stated sourcing prescription. A null running comparison is
compatible with the near-null model and \(\Lambda\)CDM. Detectable
running would test that source estimate. Phantom crossing would test the
particular Type II history used for the comparison, and a link to
Lorentz violation requires the additional spectral and coupling
assumptions.

\textbf{The pre-registration commitment.} The author commits to treating
the Class A conditions, the Class C commitments, and a Class B
retrodiction exceeding \(3\sigma\) on precision upgrade as
framework-falsifying rather than as an invitation to post-hoc rescue. In
the case of a Class B violation, the framework will be revisited to
determine whether the violation reflects a computational error in the
specific retrodiction, an incorrect specific-bijection input, or a
structural problem with the derivation; the first two are recoverable,
the third is fatal. The framework does not reserve the right to add
structural postulates after the fact to accommodate disconfirming
evidence. The pre-registration of this commitment is itself part of the
falsifiability content of the framework --- a framework that
pre-registers its falsification conditions and then revises them
post-hoc has compromised the discipline that pre-registration was meant
to enforce.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-does-not-falsify-and-regimes-of-deliberate-silence}{%
\subsection{4.6 What does not falsify and regimes of deliberate
silence}\label{what-does-not-falsify-and-regimes-of-deliberate-silence}}

The framework's pre-registered falsification conditions define what
would refute the framework's structural commitments. The complement of
those conditions --- what lies outside the falsification schedule ---
also deserves explicit articulation. Some observational outcomes that
might appear to bear on the framework do not bear on it, because the
framework makes no commitment on the relevant question. The discipline
of pre-registering falsification conditions requires equal honesty about
what is and is not within the framework's predictive scope.

\textbf{Solution-specific properties.} The framework derives the
structural form of physics --- the local gauge algebra, the matter
content and the generation count (with single-copy H-link, H-cust, the
specified charged action and the matter conditions H-spin' and H-χ'
where applicable, Chapter 5 §§5.4--5.6), the parameter-free
retrodictions and the horizon thermodynamic relations under the
calibration premises of Chapter 7. It does not derive every contingent
feature of the observed universe. Some features are solution-specific.
Gauge-equivalent representatives agree on the data defining their
equivalence. If an output differs among candidates, the difference
describes physically distinct models for an interface that measures it.
A less informative interface may leave the candidates equivalent.

Several quantities are explicitly solution-specific in the framework's
current content.

The absolute scale of fermion masses depends on the strange-quark mass
\(m_s\) as an acknowledged empirical input. The mass chain uses the
stated cubic-group relations, the external Gatto-Sartori-Tonin relation,
the phenomenological down-sector Koide input \(Q_{\text{down}}\) and the
modeled strange-sector cross-talk normalization \(Z_S\). For fixed
auxiliary inputs, the chain gives mass ratios normalized to \(m_s\)
(Chapter 6 §6.6).

The CP-violating phases in CKM and PMNS are solution-specific. The
construction does not fix \(\bar\theta\) (§6.3): T-invariance narrows
\(\theta\) to \(\{0,\pi\}\) and gives reciprocal transition counts under
the counting hidden prior of a finite model, which leave the Yukawa
determinant phase free. The flavor-basis CP phases --- the Jarlskog
parameter, the Wolfenstein \((\rho, \eta)\), the PMNS Dirac and Majorana
phases --- are features of the basis mismatch between up-type and
down-type Yukawa mass eigenstates, not consequences of any structural
feature of the substratum, and reciprocity does not force them to vanish
{[}SM §5.4{]}. A reported computation on the staggered reconstruction,
whose driver and output are not available for verification, found that
an octahedral-equivariant emergent operator gives a vanishing Jarlskog
invariant and that restoring the observed value requires octahedral
breaking far above the rotational bounds; if it stands, it is a tension
for the flavor sector, recorded as unverified {[}SM §5.5{]}.

The Type II implementation and source attribution are additional model
choices. The near-null QFT-scale estimate is conditional on its sourcing
prescription. The Bertini et al.~(2025) fit in its own running model is
compatible with zero. A detected larger running coefficient would
require testing that sourcing and its proposed spectral link. The DESI
\(w_0w_a\)CDM model preference is a separate comparison.

Cosmic initial conditions are solution-specific. The framework derives
the structure of the dynamics --- the wave equation, the bijection, the
partition --- from which evolution proceeds. The state at any particular
cosmic time, including the time-zero conditions, is not a framework
output. The framework is compatible with any cosmic-history that
produces a C1--C4-satisfying observer-admitting regime by the time the
cosmological horizon stabilizes. Specific cosmological initial-condition
observations bear on the framework only at the boundary where they would
or would not produce the observer-admitting regime; within that boundary
they are solution-specific.

The choice among representatives related by the stated fixed-interface
invariances is not determined by the data those invariances preserve.
Uniform hidden relabelling and an independently prepared finite
decoupled enlargement give exact examples {[}Substratum Theorem 24{]}.
The same results do not classify every physical implementation or every
observer partition. A measurement using a different interface or a
sector that later couples to the observer lies outside the
fixed-interface comparison, and requires its own analysis.

\textbf{Regimes of deliberate silence.} Beyond solution-specific
properties, three regimes lie outside the framework's predictive scope
by structural construction. These are regimes where the framework's
foundational structure does not produce predictions, not because the
framework is silent by choice but because the structural conditions for
predictions to be defined do not hold.

\emph{The pre-horizon early universe.} The horizon calculations in
Chapter 7 take a specified causal partition and its boundary data as
inputs. The cosmological application proposes a retention time
\(\tau_B\sim H^{-1}\) for that partition. Applying the calculation
before a stable partition forms would require a model of the relevant
preparation, channel and readout.

\emph{The equilibrium phase of \((S, \varphi)\).} Under effective mixing
and \(\tau_{\rm mix}\ll\tau_S\), bounded-diameter partitions fail
C2-slow in the coarse-grained description generated by iterating the
one-step channel. Under uniform erosion the same model gives exponential
suppression of the readback gap ({[}Main §§2.3, 4.6{]}). An exact finite
permutation has recurrent compressions, so the scope of the exclusion is
the iterated coarse description.

\emph{Regions beyond the observer's causal horizon.} For any observer
with a finite cosmological horizon, regions beyond that horizon are part
of the observer's hidden sector. They are addressed in the framework
only through boundary effects --- the area-law entropy at the horizon
surface, which encodes the gravitational signature of the hidden-sector
content. The framework takes no observer-independent position on the
\emph{internal content} of these regions. Whether the universe beyond an
observer's horizon contains fields configured differently, contains
different gauge structures, or contains anything at all in the
observer's conceptual vocabulary, is not a question the framework's
structure can address. The framework's account is that the trace-out
over what lies beyond the horizon produces the observer's
quantum-mechanical description; the content traced over is, by
construction, inaccessible to that observer.

These scope limits follow from the physical premises used in the
respective models. The exact representation of a supplied
finite-alphabet law through a finite horizon also covers memoryless
laws, and the history-memory theorem applies where its witness is
present.

\textbf{What this section is not.} The articulation of what does not
falsify is not a list of escape routes. The framework's structural
commitments --- the Class A theorems, the Class B retrodictions, the
Class C broader commitments --- are pre-registered as falsifiable, and
the author's commitment is to treat their violation as
framework-falsifying rather than as an opportunity for post-hoc
revision. The solution-specific properties and the regimes of deliberate
silence are not categories into which falsifying observations can be
reclassified after the fact. They are explicit acknowledgments of where
the framework's commitments end and where the framework's structure has
no predictive content. The line between them is drawn before the
relevant observations are made, with the structural derivation
determining which side of the line each putative prediction falls on.

\hypertarget{what-the-framework-derives-and-what-it-compresses}{%
\subsection{4.7 What the framework derives, and what it
compresses}\label{what-the-framework-derives-and-what-it-compresses}}

A framework that advertises ``the Standard Model, gravity, and quantum
mechanics from a single object'' invites a sharp question, and the
methodological honesty of the preceding sections requires meeting it
directly: is the derivation genuine, or is the answer quietly placed in
the construction and then recovered? The answer is neither a simple yes
nor a simple no, because the framework's results do not all stand in the
same relation to its starting point. They fall into three tiers, and
naming the tier is the honest form of every claim the book makes.

The first tier is \textbf{forced}. Once the substratum is committed to
--- a simple-cubic lattice carrying the wave equation --- a great deal
follows by pure representation theory, with no remaining freedom. The
decomposition of the six lattice link-directions under the cubic point
group fixes the multiplicity pattern
\(6 = T_1(3)\oplus E(2)\oplus A_1(1)\); with single-copy H-link, the
distinct-block condensate under H-cust and the specified charged action,
it gives the local algebra associated with
\(\mathrm{SU}(3)\times\mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{U}(1)\), and on that
branch the same structure gives three candidate fermion generations
(physical generations under H-spin'), the anomaly-free hypercharges
(unique on the nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch, up to normalization), and, under
its identification hypothesis, the Cabibbo angle to
four-significant-figure agreement. These could have come out otherwise
--- a different point group, a different count, a different angle ---
and the content of the derivation is that they do not. This tier is the
framework's genuine achievement, and it is substantial: it is not
reverse-engineering, because the predictions exceed the inputs, most
visibly where the Cabibbo angle lands at \(1/(\pi\sqrt2)\) while the
competing cubic lattices miss the measured value by tens of percent.

The second tier is \textbf{selected by the world}. Several quantities
the derivation leans on are fixed not by the substratum but by
observation. The spatial dimension is three because gravity propagates,
matter is stable, and space is observed flat --- three facts read off
the universe, not consequences of the bijection. The local
reconstruction takes the isotropy, locality and site-factorization
premises and compares the stated nearest-neighbor lattice class under
its named carrier and charged-action conditions. Its implication runs
from the inputs to the local residue.

The third tier is \textbf{stipulated}. Some load-bearing moves are
decisions about what is to count as physical structure rather than facts
the bijection compels: the site factorization and the single-copy H-link
premise, which gives the count \(K=2d\) on the stated link carrier, that
couplings are nearest-neighbor, and --- at the foundation --- that the
limitation of an embedded observer takes the specific form of a fast
sector reading and writing to a slow, capacious hidden one. These
choices are principled and motivated, but they are choices.

Seeing the three tiers at once dissolves a question the framework had
carried as open --- whether its structural residue is ``genuinely
non-tautological.'' The question has no single answer because the
residue is not one kind of thing: it is non-tautological at the first
tier, world-selected at the second, definitional at the third. And no
calculation settles it, because it was never an empirical question; the
logical status of each step is fixed by the construction as written.
What the classification yields is a precise description of what the
framework \emph{is}. It is a \textbf{maximally tight compression} of
known physics onto a small set of commitments. The first tier shows
that, once those commitments are granted, the discrete structure of the
Standard Model is largely not a list of independent facts but the
unfolding of a single representation-theoretic object --- and
\emph{that} is a genuine and unusual claim about the unity of physics,
worth the book whether or not the deeper pretension holds. The second
and third tiers show that the commitments themselves are anchored in
observation and partly stipulated, so the framework is not spinning the
world out of a parameter-free principle.

This is also the place to be exact about the foundation that names the
book. ``Observation is incomplete'' --- that what we know is reached
through a partial vantage, never the whole --- is, taken by itself, not
a falsifiable claim about physics. It is close to the definition of the
empirical stance itself: every theory in science is a description built
from inside, from limited access. A thesis that cannot be false cannot,
on its own, predict. All of the framework's predictive content therefore
lives one level down, in the \emph{specific model} of the incompleteness
--- the architecture, the lattice, the dynamics --- which is precisely
where the second and third tiers locate every input. The framework's
reach and its circularity are one structure seen from two sides. Read as
the \emph{source} of the predictions, ``observation is incomplete''
claims too much. Read as the \emph{organizing principle} under which an
unusually large body of physics compresses to one structure, it is the
defensible and still-remarkable claim, and it is the claim this book
makes. The reader should hold the framework to that standard and no
other: not as a derivation of the universe from the bare fact that there
are observers, but as a demonstration that an enormous amount of what we
observe coheres as the shadow of one finite construction --- with the
construction's own starting points held up honestly to the light.

\hypertarget{what-follows-2}{%
\subsection{4.8 What follows}\label{what-follows-2}}

The methodological discipline developed in this chapter --- the
two-axiom base with its named model premises, the claim classification
by derivational rigor, the architecture-level engagement with the no-go
results, verified theorem by theorem, the pre-registered falsification
conditions and their complement of deliberate silences --- provides the
framework with a discipline that organizes its program as a research
program rather than as a single bold conjecture. The discipline is part
of the framework's content, not separate from it: the structural
commitments developed in Chapters 1 through 3 and the empirical
predictions developed in Parts II through IV are produced under this
discipline, with the discipline determining what the predictions are,
how they are classified, and what their falsification status is.

Parts II and III apply the methodology to the framework's specific
empirical content in fundamental physics. Chapters 5 and 6 develop the
Standard Model gauge and matter sectors, with twenty-two classified
observable entries, including two structural and five conditional
structural entries, in the inventory of {[}SM §7.6{]}. The four-layer
framing locates each retrodiction in the substratum-to-emergent stack,
with Layer 0 and Layer 1 predictions (gauge group, generation count,
Cabibbo, Koide, Wolfenstein) carrying the framework's strongest
structural commitments and Layer 2 and Layer 3 predictions (mass ratios
within specific operator structures, scale-setting predictions) carrying
more solution-specific content. Chapter 7 develops the gravitational
sector: the Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) coefficient and the calibration
\(\hbar = c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\) from horizon thermodynamics are
consistency relations conditional on the named horizon, frame, state and
calibration assumptions, while the vacuum-energy level distinction is
descriptive and supplies no dark-energy dynamics. The individual
classifications and empirical limits appear in Appendix A §A.4.2.
Chapter 8 develops the JUNO neutrino prediction as an L-class prediction
matched at \(0.07\sigma\), with the closure of the lepton-sector
mixing-matrix derivation as the open direction whose completion would
move the prediction to S-class. Chapter 9 develops the
universality-class structure and the framework's relationship to
alternative unification programs, with the architecture-level no-go
engagement from §4.4 applied to the analysis of cross-framework
structural relationships.

Parts III and IV develop the framework's reach into structural cascades
and applied scientific fields, with the methodological classifications
carrying through to the more applied content. The framework's
predictions in chemistry, biology, neuroscience, and quantum engineering
are not all S-class --- many are P-class or E-class, with empirical
inputs from the relevant scientific fields entering the derivation
chain. The classification scheme developed here makes the rigor of each
prediction explicit, so that readers approaching the framework from
biology or medicine can evaluate the framework's claims against the
appropriate empirical standards in those fields.

The methodology developed in this chapter is not unique to the
framework. Tracing each derivation to its premises is a general
principle of theory construction, the claim-classification scheme is a
general standard for empirical evaluation, the architecture-level no-go
engagement is a general method for analyzing structural results, and the
pre-registered falsification discipline is a general epistemological
standard. The framework's contribution is to apply this methodology
systematically rather than selectively, with every prediction carrying
its classification and every structural commitment carrying its
falsification condition. What this discipline produces, when applied to
the framework's foundational starting point --- the two-axiom
observation base --- is the content developed in the remaining chapters
of the book.

The methodological posture sketched in this chapter is developed at
length, for a philosophy-of-physics readership, in a companion paper ---
\emph{Physics Modulo Gauge} --- which treats the two-axiom foundational
commitment, constructive structural realism, the separate premise checks
of the no-go results of quantum foundations within the common substratum
and observable descriptions, and ``physics modulo gauge'' as a general
methodology. That paper is a companion to the framework's technical
sequence rather than part of this book; readers concerned specifically
with the framework's methodology and its relation to the
foundations-of-physics literature will find it the natural next text.

\hypertarget{chapter-5}{%
\section{Chapter 5}\label{chapter-5}}

\hypertarget{the-emergence-of-gauge-structure}{%
\section{The Emergence of Gauge
Structure}\label{the-emergence-of-gauge-structure}}

\textbf{Observer geometry and physical carrier.} SM §4.1 distinguishes
two claims. First, finite equivariant projection is classical and exact:
cubic symmetry is inherited by the projected Markov part and every
memory kernel, forbidding quadratic anisotropy in the scalar symbol ---
so whatever nondegenerate quadratic structure survives is isotropic ---
while allowing cubic anisotropy at quartic order. The particular
normalized nearest-neighbor operator \(A/(2d)\) additionally requires an
\textbf{observer-level} center-free kernel; microscopic center
independence alone does not imply that after correlated hidden variables
are marginalized. Second, the six signed simple-cubic links and their
exact \(3\oplus2\oplus1\) representation are unconditional geometry, but
identifying that link space with the complete physical carrier is
\textbf{H-link}; the single-copy clause gives \(K=6\), and the custodial
condensate-stabilizer reading is \textbf{H-cust}. Accordingly, any
downstream statement here that consumes \(K=6\), \(N_f=6\), the physical
SM gauge carrier, or a fixed three-sector count inherits those named
bridge conditions unless it is explicitly referring only to the six
geometric links.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-2}{%
\subsection{5.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-2}}

Part I established that any observer embedded in a finite deterministic
universe under conditions C1--C4 must use a memory-bearing formalism ---
one admitting a fixed-basis quantum representation, as every finite
observable law does, with the compressed form for processes in the
correspondence's class under (T); that observed physics together with
structural assumptions, under the reconstruction theorem's stated
conditions and its nearest-neighbor premise, fixes the \textbf{local
propagating lattice/gauge residue} while Bell-inclusive completion
remains underdetermined; and that the framework's structural-realism
position operates on a two-dimensional hierarchy with stratified
empirical commitments. The remaining question is what specific physics
the substratum produces. This chapter and the next answer that question
for the visible sector --- the Standard Model of particle physics.

The derivation has two natural phases, and the book treats each in its
own chapter. The present chapter separates an exact geometric core from
the conditional physical-carrier reading: finite equivariant projection
gives an Euclidean quadratic observer symbol; the six signed cubic links
decompose exactly with multiplicities \((3,2,1)\); \textbf{under H-link
single-copy + H-cust}, the condensate-stabilizer/background-independence
construction supplies the proposed Standard-Model gauge carrier.
Chirality and hypercharge statements retain their additional hypotheses
where stated. The second phase, Chapter 6, establishes \emph{what
specific quantitative content} this gauge structure produces: three
chiral fermion generations, one Higgs doublet
\((\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{2}, +1/2)\) taken as input and accommodated in
the \(E\) projection of the singlet taste (SM Theorem 11), gauge
couplings, and the twenty-two classified retrodictions (two
parameter-free structural and five conditional structural) including the
Cabibbo angle, the Koide relation, fermion masses, and PMNS mixing
angles.

This chapter's content is structured. Section 5.2 establishes the
minimal mathematical object --- a finite set with a deterministic
bijection of bounded coupling degree, with the coupling graph read off
from the bijection once a product factorization of the state space is
given; the factorization itself is an input the dynamics has not been
shown to select. Section 5.3 selects \(d=3\) within A4's assumed
periodic-lattice class under the continuum conditions: propagating
gravity and stable matter give the two bounds, and boundary-entropy
concordance is a further consistency check. Section 5.4 develops the
observer-level lattice-wave branch and its staggered factorization, then
states H-link: the physical carrier is a copy of the six signed links,
possibly with multiplicity, with \(K=6\) only on the single-copy branch.
Section 5.5 derives the exact six-link \((3,2,1)\) decomposition and,
under H-link + H-cust plus the stated gauge premises, the corresponding
condensate-stabilizer/local-gauge construction. Section 5.6 develops the
spin--taste grading, the open weak-chirality hypothesis H-χ' and the
anomaly calculation for the specified family on the nonzero-\(Y_Q\)
branch. Section 5.7 closes the chapter with a forward pointer to Chapter
6.

The structural status of the chapter's results is now layered. The exact
finite-observer isotropy theorem and the six-link \((3,2,1)\)
representation are forced by their stated finite/symmetry hypotheses.
The \textbf{physical Standard-Model carrier is not yet forced}: it
additionally requires H-link single-copy and H-cust, followed by the
amplitude-scale/background-independence premises already recorded. That
realization is itself empirically anchored (the lattice is selected to
match the observed gauge group, not derived from the substratum alone
--- §4.7), so the uniqueness is conditional on it rather than derived
from a parameter-free first principle. The methodological discipline
developed in Chapter 4 will organize the predictions of Chapter 6 by
derivational rigor. The exact observer-isotropy theorem and six-link
multiplicities sit at the structural tier; the physical gauge
identification sits at a conditional bridge tier because it consumes
H-link/H-cust, with the later reduction to
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\) carrying
amplitude-scale gauge and a specified charged matter action.

The chapter takes as input the framework's prior content. The
quantum-mechanical emergence theorem of Chapter 1 is invoked where
needed but not reproved. The reconstruction theorem of Chapter 2
provides the structural assumptions A1--A6 and the stated
modeling/completeness conditions and nearest-neighbor premise under
which the \textbf{local lattice/gauge residue} is uniquely fixed. The
Bell-inclusive completion is not uniquely determined by that theorem.
The hierarchy framework of Chapter 3 locates each prediction in the
multi-level structural-realism scheme. The methodological discipline of
Chapter 4 classifies each prediction by its derivational rigor. The
chapter's content is the substantive derivational chain from the
cubic-lattice substratum to the Standard Model gauge group --- the
framework's specific structural claim about \emph{why} physics has the
gauge symmetries it has.

\hypertarget{the-minimal-substratum-and-the-wave-equation}{%
\subsection{5.2 The minimal substratum and the wave
equation}\label{the-minimal-substratum-and-the-wave-equation}}

The framework's content rests on a minimal mathematical structure: a set
\(S\) (finite under the open hypothesis A1, Chapter 2 §2.4), a
deterministic bijection \(\varphi: S \to S\), and a partition of \(S\)
into visible and hidden sectors. The lemmas of Chapter 1 extracted three
structural features from this minimal object --- visible finiteness,
causal partition, determinism --- and the conditions C1--C4 identified
when an embedded observer can exist. This section develops two further
structural features of the minimal object that the Standard Model
derivation requires.

\textbf{The factorization problem.} Let \(S\) be a finite set with
\(|S| = q^N\) for some \(q \geq 2\) and integer \(N\). There are many
ways to write \(S\) as a Cartesian product
\(S = S_1 \times S_2 \times \cdots \times S_N\) with \(|S_k| = q\) for
each \(k\). Different factorizations correspond to different choices of
which elementary degrees of freedom to identify as ``local'' ---
different bases in which to decompose the configuration space. The
factorization is not given by the set \(S\) itself; it must be
determined by some additional structure.

Given a bijection \(\varphi\) and a product factorization, define the
\emph{coupling graph} \(G_\varphi\) on vertices \(\{1, 2, \ldots, N\}\),
with vertices \(i\) and \(j\) connected by an edge if the \(i\)-th
component of \(\varphi(s)\) depends on the \(j\)-th component of \(s\)
for at least one state \(s \in S\). The coupling graph is not an
additional structure imposed on the system; once the factorization is
given, it is read off from the bijection. The factorization itself is an
input --- site factorization, in the posit ledger of {[}Main §4.5{]} ---
and the dynamics alone has not been shown to select it.

Minimizing the coupling degree --- the number of edges per vertex ---
over all product decompositions does not select it. The wave equation in
one dimension is
\[x_i(t+1) = x_{i-1}(t) + x_{i+1}(t) - x_i(t-1) \mod q,\] On a ring of
four sites over \(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}\) the ring's adjacency matrix
diagonalizes, and in its eigenbasis each normal mode evolves alone,
\(c_k(t+1) = \lambda_k c_k(t) - c_k(t-1)\): the coupling graph of the
normal-mode factorization has maximum degree 1, against 3 for the
spatial one. And composing a factorization with \(\varphi\) gives one
with the same coupling graph, which differs from it whenever some
component of \(\varphi\) depends on two components; a minimizer of that
kind is therefore not unique. Whether the observable law, the observer's
registers or the dynamics select the spatial factorization within a
stated class is open.

The earlier extension from spectral dimension to a canonical \(2d_s\)
\textbf{physical internal carrier} is not established. Quasi-isometry
and heat-kernel scaling constrain large-scale geometry but do not
manufacture signed internal link channels. H-link and the exact
\((3,2,1)\) carrier construction are simple-cubic-branch statements,
computed in the spatial site factorization with the nearest-neighbour
coupling graph.

\textbf{Space as coupling structure.} Every ``spatial'' property used in
the derivation chain is a property of the coupling graph \(G_\varphi\).
The \emph{graph boundary} \(|\partial V|\) of a region \(V \subset S\)
--- the quantity the area-law bound is stated in --- is the number of
edges crossing from \(V\) to its complement. The \emph{dimension} is
extracted from the causal partial order via the Myrheim-Meyer estimator.
The \emph{area-law bound} --- that the information shared across a
region's boundary is at most proportional to the boundary rather than
the volume --- follows from the spatial Markov property on any graph
with range-1 dynamics. The \emph{dispersion relation} describing how
perturbations propagate requires translation invariance of the
underlying dynamics. The regular cubic lattice \(\mathbb{Z}^3\) is one
graph with all these properties; it is not the only one.

The framework's account of space dissolves the container problem that
has been a recurring objection to discrete models of spacetime. The
coupling graph is not embedded in a pre-existing space. There is no
ambient manifold in which the graph ``lives.'' The vertices are labels
for degrees of freedom, the edges record which degrees of freedom are
dynamically coupled. Any spatial embedding is a representation for human
convenience, not a physical fact. The coupling graph is not made of
material --- the vertices are not atoms of space and the edges are not
physical connections. A degree of freedom is a component of the state,
an abstract mathematical entity rather than an object. Asking what a
site is ``made of'' is a category error: it is a label for a variable,
not a name for a thing.

The relationship between locality and the dynamics is the precise
inverse of the conventional picture. In the conventional picture, space
exists first as a manifold, and locality is the property that nearby
points in space have causally connected dynamics. In the framework, the
dynamics exists first as a bijection, and space emerges as the topology
that locality induces on the coupling graph. Two sites are neighbors
because the bijection couples them --- because the state at one affects
the future of the other. This is a dynamical fact, not a spatial
relationship. The topology is defined by the interactions; the apparent
spatial arrangement is the topology made visible.

\textbf{The alphabet size.} The alphabet size \(q\) is the number of
distinguishable states at each lattice site. Several results hold for
every \(q \geq 2\) and contain no \(q\): the P-indivisibility theorem,
center independence, the boundary scaling of the area law, and the
dispersion relation of the observer-level operator. The gravitational
sector depends on \(q\) only through the entropy \(\sigma\) assigned to
one boundary cell, which cancels from the Bekenstein-Hawking formula; at
\(\sigma = 1\), one nat per boundary mode, neither the gap equation
\(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2 / (4G\sigma)\) derived in Chapter 7 nor the
Bekenstein-Hawking formula contains \(q\), while \(\sigma = \ln q\)
would place \(q\) in the discreteness scale
\(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\ln q}\, l_p\). Other results carry \(q\): the
period of the wave map on a ring of \(L\) sites is \(qL\) for prime
\(q\) coprime to \(L\), the coefficient of the area law and the capacity
count of the hidden sector contain \(\log q\), and the substratum
normalisation \(\alpha = 1/d\) requires \(3 \nmid q\).

That the emergent observables do not depend on \(q\) at all --- that two
substrata \((S, \varphi)\) and \((S', \varphi')\) with the same coupling
structure and different alphabet sizes produce the same emergent
transition probabilities --- is the \emph{alphabet-size hypothesis}. It
is not proved for every observable, and because the visible transition
matrices of the two substrata act on configuration spaces of different
sizes, stating it requires a correspondence between them that is not
constructed. Under the hypothesis the mod-\(q\) state space at each
lattice site plays the role of the gauge potential \(A_\mu\) and the
coupling structure with its emergent consequences that of the field
strength \(F_{\mu\nu}\). Generator (ii) of the substratum gauge group
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) developed in Chapter 2 §2.5 is stated under
this hypothesis.

The proposed amplitude-scale gauge uses affine relabellings
\(\boldsymbol{\phi}\mapsto\lambda\boldsymbol{\phi}+\mathbf c\) of a
fixed alphabet, with \(\lambda\) a unit. The affine-rule criterion
separately assumes first differences independent of the base point (SM
§4.1). Affine relabelling covariance alone allows nonlinear rules. The
alphabet-size hypothesis compares different \(q\). On the gauge branch
the amplitude-scale premise supplies at most the common phase of the
proposed observer action (SM Proposition 14a).

\hypertarget{selection-of-d-3}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{5.3 Selection of
\(d = 3\)}{5.3 Selection of d = 3}}\label{selection-of-d-3}}

The framework's structural lemmas operate at any integer dimension
\(d\ge1\). The observer-level quadratic-isotropy argument and
dimension-dependent lattice calculations can be formulated in other
dimensions, but the six-link physical-carrier construction is not a
dimension-general theorem: H-link is presently tied to the simple-cubic
signed-link representation used at \(d=3\). The question of why our
universe has three spatial dimensions is therefore a question about
which dimension produces a self-consistent observed physics. The
framework's answer is that exactly three works.

Within A4's periodic-lattice class and the continuum conditions of SM
§3.1--§3.2, propagating gravity and stable matter select \(d=3\);
boundary-entropy concordance is an additional consistency check. This is
a conditional self-consistency selection using the stated physical
inputs.

\textbf{Filter 1: Propagating gravity requires \(d \geq 3\).} The
gravitational sector developed in Chapter 7 requires propagating
gravitational degrees of freedom --- gravitational waves, the structural
content of the LIGO observations beginning in 2015. The Weyl tensor,
which captures the propagating part of the gravitational field, vanishes
identically in \(d \leq 2\): there is no gravitational radiation in two
or fewer spatial dimensions. Jacobson's thermodynamic derivation of
Einstein's equations from local causal horizons requires propagating
gravity. The filter therefore excludes \(d \leq 2\).

\textbf{Filter 2: Stable matter requires \(d \leq 3\).} The Coulomb
potential in \(d\) spatial dimensions falls off as \(1/r^{d-2}\) for
\(d \geq 3\) and gives a logarithmic potential for \(d = 2\). In
\(d \geq 4\) the Coulomb potential gives unstable atoms --- there are no
normalizable bound states of the \(d\)-dimensional Coulomb Hamiltonian,
by Ehrenfest's argument and its quantum-mechanical refinement.
Gravitational orbits are similarly unstable for \(d \geq 4\) by
Tangherlini's analysis. Without stable matter, no embedded observers
exist to define the framework's partition. The filter therefore excludes
\(d \geq 4\).

The intersection of Filter 1 and Filter 2 is already \(d = 3\) uniquely.
A third filter provides a consistency check.

\textbf{Filter 3: Boundary-entropy concordance gives \(d = 3\) exactly.}
The cosmological observation that the universe is spatially flat near
the critical density --- \(\Omega_{\text{total}} \approx 1\) --- is, in
the framework's gravitational sector developed in Chapter 7, a
structural feature rather than an initial condition. The ratio
\(\rho_s / \rho_{\text{crit}}\) between the boundary-derived entropy
density and the critical density, computed in \(d\) spatial dimensions,
satisfies \[\frac{\rho_s}{\rho_{\text{crit}}} = \frac{2}{d - 1}.\] This
ratio equals unity exactly at \(d = 3\). At \(d = 2\) the ratio is \(2\)
(overclosure); at \(d = 4\) the ratio is \(2/3\) (deficit, requiring an
unsourced gravitational contribution). The filter selects \(d = 3\) as
the unique value at which the observed spatial flatness is structurally
explained rather than fine-tuned.

Within A4's assumed periodic-lattice class and the stated continuum
conditions, the first two bounds select \(d=3\) and boundary-entropy
concordance supplies a further consistency check. The specified
Yang--Mills coupling is dimensionless at \(3+1\) spacetime dimensions;
its renormalizability result is downstream of that selection. The
six-link octahedral carrier and H-link used here are stated for the
selected simple-cubic branch. A comparison with another dimension
requires its own carrier and matter assumptions.

\textbf{Integer dimension.} The self-consistency argument assumes that
the coupling graph has a well-defined integer dimension. A general
bounded-degree graph need not have one: besides exponential growth
(\(|B(r)| \sim k^r\) for some \(k > 1\)), fractal growth
(\(|B(r)| \sim r^\alpha\) for some non-integer \(\alpha\)) and
integer-polynomial growth (\(|B(r)| \sim r^d\) for some integer \(d\)),
there are graphs of intermediate growth (Grigorchuk) and graphs with no
single growth exponent. Under A4 (Chapter 2) the integer is an input:
the coupling graph is a finite periodic lattice, the quotient of a
rank-\(d\) lattice by a finite-index sublattice, so \(|B(r)| \sim r^d\)
below the system size and none of the other classes arises.
Independently, self-consistency excludes the first two classes.

Exponential growth fails because the wave equation on
exponentially-growing graphs does not produce Lorentz-invariant
dispersion at low energies --- the spectral gap does not close in the
correct functional form --- so Jacobson's derivation of Einstein's
equations fails. Additionally, the effective dimension
\(d_{\text{eff}} \to \infty\) is incompatible with the stable-matter
filter.

Fractal growth fails because Jacobson's argument requires the
Raychaudhuri equation, which requires geodesic congruences on a manifold
structure that fractal spaces do not support. The staggered fermion
decomposition that produces the framework's three-generation structure
requires a hypercubic Brillouin-zone structure \(\eta \in \{0, 1\}^d\),
which has no fractal-graph analog. The cubic-group decomposition of
\(2d\) link directions, which constrains the gauge structure, requires
cubic lattice symmetry --- absent in fractals.

The integer \(d\) therefore enters through A4 as the rank of the
translation lattice, not through Gromov's theorem, which concerns
finitely generated groups and their Cayley graphs; statistical isotropy
alone does not supply it. Applied to the continuum description,
conditional on the continuum step of §3.1 of the SM paper, the three
filters then select \(d = 3\).

\textbf{Corollary.} \emph{Any bijection whose coupling graph is a
\(d\)-dimensional periodic lattice with \(d \neq 3\) fails at least one
of the filters E5--E7 in its emergent description. The coupling-graph
dimension is not a free parameter or a property of a specific
\(\varphi\); it is the unique value compatible with the filters.}

The argument's structure is worth marking explicitly. The framework's
definition of observation requires an embedded observer as a
constitutive element --- the partition \(V \subset S\) is defined
relative to an observer that the substratum's structure must support.
The requirement that such an observer exist, combined with the
framework-internal concordance calculation, constrains \(d\). This is
not a standard anthropic argument selecting from a pre-existing
multiverse of dimensions. The observer is a structural prerequisite for
the framework's definition to have content, not a contingent feature of
one universe among many.

Within the assumed A4 periodic-lattice class and the selected continuum
description, the E5--E7 filters select \(d = 3\). Integer rank is
supplied by A4, while the value \(3\) is selected using the physical
filters. The continuum-curvature identification remains open, as stated
in SM §3.1. This selection concerns that branch rather than every finite
bijection or embedded-observer architecture.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-emergent-qft-factorization-and-multi-component-dynamics}{%
\subsection{5.4 The emergent QFT: factorization and multi-component
dynamics}\label{the-emergent-qft-factorization-and-multi-component-dynamics}}

The cubic branch supports an observer-level lattice-wave description
whose relation to the finite bijection is governed by the projection
bridge of SM §4.1. This section develops its staggered factorization and
then separates the exact six-link geometry from H-link, the open
identification of those links with the physical internal carrier.

\textbf{Observer-level lattice Klein--Gordon branch.} The exact
projection theorem does not require a wave equation. If the projected
scalar Markov part is additionally nearest-neighbor, constant-preserving
and center-free, cubic symmetry fixes it to \(A/(2d)\), and the
reversible second-order branch is \[
\phi(\mathbf n,t+1)=\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^{d}[\phi(\mathbf n+\hat e_j,t)+\phi(\mathbf n-\hat e_j,t)]-\phi(\mathbf n,t-1).
\] Its low-momentum symbol is
\(\omega_{\mathrm{lat}}^2=(a^2/d)|\mathbf k|^2+O(a^4k^4)\) in
dimensionless update frequency. The calibrated frequency is
\(\Omega=\sqrt d\,\omega_{\mathrm{lat}}/a\). This is an
\textbf{observer-level conditional branch}, not the fundamental finite
bijection itself. A \(\beta=1\) ``maximum-speed'' reading is
unavailable: causal support travels at most one graph edge per update
independently of the coefficient, and the unnormalised \(d=3\) real lift
is unstable at \(k=0\).

\textbf{Staggered Dirac square.} For the centered staggered differences,
the squared operator gives the associated two-step lattice operator,
\(D_{\text{st}}^2=-\tfrac14\Box_{\text{lat}}\) in the convention of SM
§4.2. Solutions of \(D_{\text{st}}\chi=0\) therefore satisfy
\(\Box_{\text{lat}}\chi=0\). Matching the blocked stencil and solution
classes to the normalized nearest-neighbor observer wave above is a
separate step.

The spin--taste algebra on the stated staggered branch is used in
Chapter 6. The physical fermion identification and the map from the
realized scalar law to the determinant-pseudofermion measure require
separate inputs (SM §§4.2, 7.5).

Center independence, beyond setting the mass to zero in the bosonic
description, has a corresponding structural meaning in the fermionic
description. For site-independent center coefficients added to
opposite-parity hopping, in a ring without additive 2-torsion, on a
lattice carrying both parity sectors, the exact chiral symmetry of the
emergent staggered fermions is equivalent to the vanishing of those
center coefficients (SM Theorem 3): any non-zero center coefficient
breaks chiral symmetry. Identifying these first-order terms with center
dependence of the second-order substratum dynamics is a separate bridge
(SM §4.3). The memory-bearing sector whose phenomenology Chapter 1
develops does not come from center independence: Main's readback lemma
supplies that memory, and, on finite reversible representatives, its
recurrence-cycle theorem the P-indivisibility, independently of center
independence (SM §4.3). The Higgs mechanism developed in Chapter 6,
which gives masses to fermions in the emergent description, operates on
the chiral fermions of the center-free branch.

\textbf{Multi-component dynamics with \(K\) internal components.} The
wave equation as written above is a single-component dynamics --- one
scalar field per lattice site. The framework's gauge-emergence chain
requires the generalization to \(K\) components per site:
\(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n}, t) \in (\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^K\) for
the finite symbolic rule with coupling \(M_{\mathrm{sym}}\)
\[\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n}, t+1) = M_{\mathrm{sym}} \sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n} + \hat{e}_j, t) + \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n} - \hat{e}_j, t)\right] - \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n}, t-1)\pmod q.\]
Spatial isotropy makes the matrix \(M_{\mathrm{sym}}\) common to the
link directions. The stipulated reversible update subtracts the previous
field, and center independence removes the present onsite term. The
conditional real observer lift of SM §4.4 instead uses the normalized
update
\[\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n}, t+1) = \frac{M}{d} \sum_{j=1}^d [\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n}+\hat e_j,t)+\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n}-\hat e_j,t)]-\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n},t-1).\]

An eigenvalue \(\mu\) of \(M\) gives
\(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{lat}}=(\mu/d)\sum_j\cos(k_j a)\). In the chosen
symmetric branch \(M=I_K\), the zero-momentum frequency vanishes and all
modes have the same massless low-momentum cone. On the physical branch
with H-link and H-cust, the unitary symmetry of the pre-condensate
kinetic term is reduced by the state to the stabilizer of the
equivariant condensate \(\Sigma\) (SM Theorem 5). For distinct block
values with dimensions \((n_1,\ldots,n_r)\), this stabilizer is
\(\prod_i U(n_i)\).

\textbf{The six-link carrier and H-link.} The simple-cubic graph has
exactly six signed nearest-neighbor link directions. Their span
\(V_{\rm link}\) is therefore an exact six-dimensional geometric
representation. Coupling-degree minimization does \textbf{not} show that
diagonalizing the isotropic internal matrix assigns one field component
to one signed link; the full neighbor sum remains in every diagonal
component. A \(\delta(2d)=1\) Step 1 is therefore unavailable.

\textbf{H-link} states that the observer/gauge carrier is
\(V_{\rm link}\otimes\mathbb C^m\). The single-copy clause \(m=1\) gives
\(K=6\), but no present theorem derives \(m=1\). The later gauge and
matter calculations that use \(K=6\) are thus conditional tests of this
branch. The exact group-theoretic statement below --- the decomposition
of the six \textbf{geometric} links --- does not depend on H-link.

\hypertarget{the-cubic-decomposition-and-the-standard-model-gauge-group}{%
\subsection{5.5 The cubic decomposition and the Standard Model gauge
group}\label{the-cubic-decomposition-and-the-standard-model-gauge-group}}

The six signed simple-cubic links, defined in the spatial site
factorization with the nearest-neighbour coupling graph ({[}Main
§4.5{]}, items (viii) and (x)), form an exact six-dimensional
representation of the cubic group. This section first computes that
representation unconditionally. Its use as the \textbf{physical}
internal/gauge carrier then assumes H-link single-copy; the custodial
condensate-stabilizer step additionally assumes H-cust.

\textbf{The cubic-group representation on the six links.} The six
nearest-neighbor link directions
\(\{\pm\hat{e}_1, \pm\hat{e}_2, \pm\hat{e}_3\}\) of the cubic lattice,
with one component per link direction. The cubic rotation group \(O\)
--- the group of orientation-preserving symmetries of the cube, with
twenty-four elements --- acts on these six link vectors by permutation:
rotations of the cube permute the six link directions among themselves,
with rotations through a face center cycling four link directions and
rotations through a vertex cycling three.

The action of \(O\) on the six-dimensional space spanned by the link
directions is a representation of \(O\) with character
\(\chi(O) = 6, 0, 2, 0, 2\) at the five conjugacy classes of \(O\)
(identity, eight three-fold rotations, three two-fold rotations through
face centers, six two-fold rotations through edge midpoints, six
four-fold rotations through face centers). Computing the inner products
of \(\chi\) with the characters of the five irreducible representations
of \(O\) --- labeled \(A_1, A_2, E, T_1, T_2\) with dimensions
\(1, 1, 2, 3, 3\) --- yields the decomposition
\[6 = T_1 \oplus E \oplus A_1\] with multiplicities \((3, 2, 1)\). The
two remaining irreducible representations \(A_2\) and \(T_2\) have
multiplicity zero in the six-dimensional link representation.

The decomposition is forced by group-theoretic content rather than
chosen. The six link directions form a specific representation of the
cubic rotation group; the decomposition of this representation into
irreducibles is computed mechanically from the character table. The
framework's commitment to the cubic lattice as substratum, combined with
the requirement of spatial isotropy, makes the \((3, 2, 1)\)
multiplicity structure inevitable.

\textbf{Conditional condensate-stabilizer reading.} The link
representation itself is \(T_1\oplus E\oplus A_1\). Under \textbf{H-link
single-copy + H-cust}, the observer-level physical carrier is this
six-dimensional space and the pre-condensate kinetic structure is
custodially scalar (at the symmetric point the kinetic clause follows
from the signed-permutation symmetry of the components under H-blind,
{[}SM §4.4{]}). An \(O\)-equivariant condensate then has block form
\[\Sigma=aP_{T_1}+bP_E+cP_{A_1},\] and for generic distinct block values
its unitary stabilizer is
\[\mathrm U(3)\times\mathrm U(2)\times\mathrm U(1).\] This stabilizer
theorem is exact at those stated premises. It does not prove H-link,
select \(m=1\), or by itself perform the later
\(\mathrm U\to\mathrm{SU}\) reduction.

\textbf{Reduction to the local Standard Model gauge algebra.} The
pointwise \(O\)-commutant on the six-link space is \(U(1)^3\). The
condensate stabilizer instead has Lie algebra
\(\mathfrak{su}(3)\oplus\mathfrak{su}(2)\oplus\mathfrak u(1)^3\). The
amplitude-scale premise accounts for at most the common phase of the
assumed observer action. A specified charged matter action and anomaly
cancellation on the chiral family select the hypercharge direction (§5.6
and SM §4.9).

The resulting local gauge algebra on the stated branch is
\[\mathfrak{su}(3)\oplus\mathfrak{su}(2)\oplus\mathfrak u(1)_Y.\] The
color and weak factors use the \(T_1\) and \(E\) blocks. For the
specified charged family and Higgs, the local action has faithful image
\((SU(3)\times SU(2)\times U(1))/\mathbb Z_6\) (SM Proposition 15a). The
choice of global bundles and line operators requires independent data.

\textbf{Nearest-neighbor Bravais comparison.} On the same generic
condensate construction, the nearest-neighbor representation of
body-centered cubic is \(A_1\oplus A_2\oplus T_1\oplus T_2\), with
stabilizer \(U(3)^2\times U(1)^2\). Face-centered cubic gives
\(A_1\oplus E\oplus T_1\oplus 2T_2\) and generic stabilizer
\(U(3)^3\times U(2)\times U(1)\) before charged-action reduction. The
other eleven Bravais lattices lack a three-dimensional point-group
irrep. The simple-cubic lattice alone gives the required \((3,2,1)\)
block pattern in this nearest-neighbor comparison (SM Theorem 7b).

This comparison selects simple cubic for the stated physical gauge
branch. Under the same BZ-distance prescription, the Cabibbo values for
BCC and FCC differ from observation by \(42\%\) and \(29\%\), while the
simple-cubic value matches to \(0.04\%\). This is a retrodictive
comparison with emergent dressing open (SM §7.1).

The formal uniqueness theorem, including the character-table
decomposition for all 32 three-dimensional crystallographic point groups
and the proof that only the five cubic-system point groups admit the
required 3D irreducible representations, is developed in Appendix B.6b.

\textbf{Local gauge covariance from background independence.} The step
from global to local is what background independence (A6) supplies: the
local transformations act covariantly once the coupling data on the
links are transformed with them.

Background independence, as the reconstruction's assumption A6 states
it, is a covariance requirement: a site-dependent internal-index
transformation is a symmetry of the dynamics provided the coupling data
on the links are transformed with it. It is not the requirement that the
coupling structure be held fixed and left invariant --- for an
invertible coupling that stronger fixed-background condition holds only
for transformations that agree across every coupled pair of sites ---
and it is not the state-dependent coupling graph \(G(x)\) on which the
Bell branch of Chapter 1 rests, under which the graph itself evolves
with the state; those are different principles that share a name. Under
H-link and H-cust (§§5.4--5.5), the cubic decomposition of the link
directions fixes the block multiplicities \((3, 2, 1)\) at each site;
spatial isotropy fixes those multiplicities, not distinct block values.
The coupling on each link, \(M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_j)\), is the data the
site-dependent transformations act on; where the equivariant condensate
takes distinct block values, its stabilizer
\(\mathrm{U}(3) \times \mathrm{U}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\) (SM Theorem
5) acts at each site, and the resulting gauge transformations are
site-dependent.

Under a site-dependent transformation \(G(\mathbf{n})\) of the form
\(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n}) \to G(\mathbf{n})\,\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{n})\)
with
\(G(\mathbf{n}) \in \mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\)
at each site, the matrix wave equation is invariant provided the
coupling matrix transforms as
\(M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_j) \to G(\mathbf{n})\,M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_j)\,G(\mathbf{n} + \hat{e}_j)^{-1}\).
The link variable \(M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_j)\) transforms as a gauge
connection, with the plaquette product
\(P(\mathbf{n}, j, k) = M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_j)\,M(\mathbf{n} + \hat{e}_j, \hat{e}_k)\,M(\mathbf{n} + \hat{e}_k, \hat{e}_j)^{-1}\,M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_k)^{-1}\)
transforming in the adjoint as
\(P \to G(\mathbf{n})\,P\,G(\mathbf{n})^{-1}\). The real part of the
trace of the plaquette is gauge-invariant --- recognizable as the Wilson
plaquette action of lattice gauge theory.

The exact covariance and plaquette invariance hold for the stated link
action. The local Standard Model algebra and its charged action use the
conditions above. Selecting a physical action for the link dynamics,
such as the Wilson action, is a separate step.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{chirality-anomaly-cancellation-and-hypercharges}{%
\subsection{5.6 Chirality, anomaly cancellation, and
hypercharges}\label{chirality-anomaly-cancellation-and-hypercharges}}

The local gauge structure in §5.5 uses a specified charged action on the
condensate branch. To reproduce observation, the weak factor must act
chirally, the color coupling must be vector-like and the family charges
must satisfy the anomaly equations. The open physical chirality
hypothesis is H-χ' (SM §4.8).

\textbf{Spin--taste grading and physical chirality.} Weak
\(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) couples only to left-handed fermions in the Standard
Model. On the stated checkerboard branch the trace-out selects one
spin--taste grade, containing both spin chiralities. A spin-chiral weak
action on that grade requires H-χ'.

The starting point is the staggered Dirac structure of the wave
equation, established in §5.4. The Susskind decomposition assigns one
Dirac spinor component to each hypercube corner of the cubic lattice,
with the parity of the corner determining the ε-grade --- the product
\(\gamma_5 \otimes \xi_5\) of spin and taste chirality --- of the
assigned component. Sites with \(|\eta|\) even span the \(+1\)
eigenspace of \(\gamma_5 \otimes \xi_5\) and sites with \(|\eta|\) odd
the \(-1\) eigenspace; each grade contains both spin chiralities in
equal dimension (certified exactly by
\texttt{chirality\_grading\_probes.py}). The sublattice parity
\(\varepsilon(\mathbf{x})=(-1)^{\sum x_\mu}\) realizes this product
grading.

The staggered Dirac operator has a structural property that the
framework's chirality derivation uses: it couples only across
sublattices. The even-even and odd-odd blocks of \(D_{\text{st}}\)
vanish identically because the staggered Dirac operator anti-commutes
with the sublattice parity, \(\{D_{\text{st}}, \varepsilon\} = 0\),
which is the lattice form of chiral symmetry established in §5.4. The
full Dirac operator has the block form
\[D_{\text{st}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & D_{eo} \\ D_{oe} & 0 \end{pmatrix},\]
with off-diagonal blocks coupling the two sublattice grades and diagonal
blocks vanishing.

The framework's checkerboard partition assigns even sites --- the \(+1\)
grade of \(\gamma_5 \otimes \xi_5\), carrying both spin chiralities ---
to the visible sector \(V\), and odd sites --- the \(-1\) grade --- to
the hidden sector \(H\). This is not an arbitrary choice; it is what the
framework's structural partition produces for a cubic lattice with
bipartite coupling. The visible sector that the embedded observer reads
out is therefore one \(\gamma_5 \otimes \xi_5\) grade --- which carries
BOTH spin chiralities, so calling it the ``left-handed sublattice''
would prejudge the taste-selectivity question; the complementary grade
is part of the hidden sector that is traced over.

The trace-out structure determines the grading content of the emergent
quantum field theory; physical chirality enters through the
taste-selectivity hypothesis H-χ' (SM §4.8). Integrating out the hidden
sector (the odd sublattice) via the Schur complement --- a standard
procedure in lattice quantum field theory --- produces an effective
action whose external legs lie in the visible half of the spin⊗taste
space, where spin- and taste-chirality coincide:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{eff}} = \bar\psi_+\,(D_{eo}\,G_{oo}\,D_{oe})\,\psi_+ + \cdots,\]
where \(G_{oo}\) is the hidden-sector propagator. The hidden-grade
components appear only as internal lines; the observable external states
carry both spin chiralities, graded so that spin chirality equals taste
chirality.

The two gauge factors couple differently to this graded effective
theory. The \(\mathrm{SU}(3)\) factor acts on internal \(T_1\)
components of the cubic decomposition --- the three-dimensional
spatial-vector representation. Both left-handed and right-handed Dirac
components carry the same color charge, since the color index is
internal to the \(T_1\) block and independent of the sublattice parity.
The trace-out preserves color coupling, and \(\mathrm{SU}(3)\) remains
vector-like, coupling identically to left-handed and right-handed
components. The \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) factor acts on internal \(E\)
components --- the two-dimensional quadrupole representation. The
internal \(E\) index commutes with the grading, so the
\(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) embedding as constructed is taste-blind; its observed
spin-chirality therefore requires taste-chirality selectivity of the
physical embedding --- the named hypothesis H-χ' (SM §4.8), which the
construction does not supply.

On the stated taste-blind color embedding, \(\mathrm{SU}(3)\) is
vector-like. The chirality of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) rests additionally on
