H-χ', which is open. The framework's account of parity violation is
correspondingly conditional: the substratum supplies the ε-grading and
the visible-sector identity (spin chirality \(=\) taste chirality on the
visible half), and the remaining step --- H-χ' --- is stated as an open
hypothesis rather than derived from which sublattice the embedded
observer occupies.

\textbf{Scope of the Nielsen--Ninomiya comparison.} The lattice-fermion
no-go theorem constrains local, Hermitian, translation-invariant fermion
operators with the stated chiral symmetry. The finite symbolic rule
supplies a different starting object.

The staggered factorization supplies an operator identity on the blocked
lattice. Its spin--taste grading leaves both spin chiralities in each
grade.

The physical chiral construction requires H-χ' and a controlled operator
and measure bridge. An argument that the resulting physical theory
evades the no-go assumptions would have to concern that construction.

The staggered tastes give candidate sectors. Their physical
interpretation as generations uses H-spin' and light-spectrum selection
(Chapter 6).

\textbf{Anomaly cancellation forcing the hypercharges.} A chiral gauge
theory is consistent only if its quantum anomalies cancel. On the
specified chiral branch under H-χ', the framework must satisfy six
anomaly-cancellation conditions: three independent chiral gauge
anomalies for the \(\mathrm{SU}(3)\), \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\), and
\(\mathrm{U}(1)_Y\) factors taken in various combinations, plus mixed
anomalies involving the gravitational sector. These conditions impose
constraints on the hypercharge assignments of the chiral fermion
content.

The family assignment tested in Chapter 6 uses three candidate sectors
on the single-copy branch, with physical generations under H-spin',
chirality under H-χ' and the light-spectrum selection assumed in
specific representations of \(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2)\): a
left-handed quark doublet \(Q_L\) in \((\mathbf{3}, \mathbf{2})\), a
right-handed up quark \(u_R\) in \((\mathbf{3}, \mathbf{1})\), a
right-handed down quark \(d_R\) in \((\mathbf{3}, \mathbf{1})\), a
left-handed lepton doublet \(L_L\) in \((\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{2})\), and
a right-handed charged lepton \(e_R\) in \((\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1})\).
The supplied \(\mathrm{SU}(3)\times\mathrm{SU}(2)\) representations fix
the family on which the anomaly equations constrain
\(Y_Q,Y_u,Y_d,Y_L,Y_e\).

The six anomaly conditions are four independent constraints on these
five hypercharge unknowns. Apart from the exceptional branch
\(Y_Q = Y_L = Y_e = 0\), \(Y_u = -Y_d\) (SM Theorem 15), the remaining
one-parameter freedom is the overall hypercharge normalization, a
convention the anomaly conditions leave free (SM Theorem 15). With the
normalization fixed, the anomaly conditions determine the hypercharges
to the observed Standard Model values, uniquely up to the interchange
\(Y_u \leftrightarrow Y_d\) --- a relabeling of which quark is called
up-type, fixed by the electric-charge identification
\(Q_{\text{em}} = T_3 + Y\):
\[Y_Q = \tfrac{1}{6}, \qquad Y_u = \tfrac{2}{3}, \qquad Y_d = -\tfrac{1}{3}, \qquad Y_L = -\tfrac{1}{2}, \qquad Y_e = -1.\]

On the three-block stabilizer branch there are three abelian phase
directions. For the specified charged family and nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch
the anomaly equations select hypercharge up to normalization and the
up/down interchange. Proposition 14a of SM treats the correlated central
quotient as a separate construction.

A corollary of the hypercharge derivation deserves explicit mention: the
equality of the magnitudes of the proton and electron charges,
\(|q_p| = |q_e|\), follows on the nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch from the
framework's structural derivation rather than being a coincidence. The
proton charge \(q_p = 2 Y_u + Y_d = 2 \cdot (2/3) + (-1/3) = 1\) and the
electron charge \(q_e = Y_e = -1\) are equal in magnitude because the
anomaly conditions force the specific ratios that produce this
cancellation. The famous one-to-one ratio between proton and electron
charge magnitudes --- observed to fantastic precision in atomic
neutrality measurements --- is, on that branch, a theorem of the
framework, not a parameter fixed by observation.

\hypertarget{what-follows-3}{%
\subsection{5.7 What follows}\label{what-follows-3}}

The chapter establishes the six-link geometry and the stated
observer-level operator identities. The single-copy H-link and H-cust
assumptions yield the generic condensate stabilizer, A6 is the local
covariance premise, and the specified charged action determines the
local gauge algebra. The checkerboard grade retains both spin
chiralities. The weak coupling is spin-chiral under H-χ', and the family
charges on the nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch follow from anomaly cancellation.

The six-link representation is exact geometry. Additional stable visible
gauge structure or different charges on the specified family would test
the proposed physical branch. Global gauge data, light-spectrum
selection and the carrier identification have the separate conditions
stated above.

Chapter 6 develops the specific quantitative content this gauge
structure produces. The matter content is set out there: three candidate
fermion sectors from the staggered tastes, with physical chirality
conditional on H-χ' and the light-spectrum selection, and one Higgs
doublet \((\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{2}, +1/2)\) taken as input and
accommodated in the \(E\) projection of the singlet staggered taste (SM
Theorem 11), with three candidate tastes on the \textbf{single-copy
H-link} branch (three physical generations only under H-spin', SM §4.7);
the framework does not presently derive the copy number \(m=1\). The
strong-CP problem is treated structurally in Section 6.3, which states
what T-invariance of the substratum bijection combined with detailed
balance fixes (\(\theta\in\{0,\pi\}\) and reciprocal transition counts
under the counting hidden prior of a finite model) and what it does not
(\(\bar\theta\), open under two named conditions). The gauge couplings
at the \(Z\) pole are reproduced by a chain with one structurally
computed input, the analytic one-loop staggered vacuum polarization
\(1/\alpha_0 = 23.25\), and three threshold parameters fitted to the
three observed couplings (SM §6.3). The twenty-two classified
quantitative retrodictions developed there (two parameter-free
structural and five conditional structural; Appendix A) include the
Cabibbo angle \(1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\) matched to \(0.04\%\), the Koide angle
\(\theta_0 = 2/9\) matched to \(0.001\%\), the six-mass chain with one
empirical mass scale, the external GST relation and the auxiliary inputs
\(Q_{\text{down}}\) and \(Z_S\) (§6.6), all three PMNS mixing angles
within \(1.1\sigma\), and the Higgs quartic boundary condition
\(\lambda(M_{\text{Pl}}) = 0\), matching the RG-extrapolated value at
\(0.6\sigma\) (the \(m_H\) band \(129\)--\(132\) GeV sits \(4\)--\(7\)
GeV above observation). The framework's quantitative empirical record
outside cosmology is concentrated in Chapter 6.

Chapter 5 gave the six-link representation and the staggered

This chapter develops the specific quantitative content that the gauge

Section 6.2 gives the three candidate staggered sectors on the

The remaining sections develop the framework's quantitative

6.8 collects the twenty-two predictions in a summary table classified by

The methodological discipline of Chapter 4 organizes the predictions.
The Cabibbo angle is Class B-C (conditional structural, Layer 1,

The Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) factor --- developed in Chapter 7 --- is

2(b) bijection-specific per Chapter 2 §2.5 (the empirical mass-hierarchy
fixing which generation is electron). The framework's empirical record
in fundamental physics outside cosmology is concentrated in these

The chapter's content sits at Levels 1 and 2 of the four-layer framing
developed in Chapter 4. Layer 1 predictions (Cabibbo, Wolfenstein,
Koide) follow from pure substratum geometry or representation theory
with no operator-relation inputs; Layer 2 predictions (mass ratios
within fixed operator structures, mixing-angle values) involve specific

--- live at Layer 1 and at the Level G3 × Level D intersection of the

\hypertarget{three-generations-and-the-composite-higgs}{%
\subsection{6.2 Three generations and the composite
Higgs}\label{three-generations-and-the-composite-higgs}}

Chapter 5 states the staggered squared-operator identity on the blocked
stencil. The spin--taste analysis here uses the stated staggered branch.
The staggered decomposition produces
\(N_{\text{taste}} = 2^{\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor}\) Dirac tastes in
\(d + 1\) spacetime dimensions, with \(N_{\text{taste}} = 4\) at
\(d = 3\). The four tastes give one singlet and three candidate sectors.
The specified gauge action, H-spin', H-χ' and light-spectrum selection
give the physical chiral assignment on this branch. The singlet taste
accommodates the supplied Higgs doublet.

\textbf{The taste decomposition under the cubic group.} The four
staggered tastes can be labeled by the corners of the Brillouin zone
they originate from: the \(2^d = 8\) Brillouin-zone corners on a
\(d = 3\) lattice pair into 4 taste pairs under the corner-conjugation
\(\boldsymbol{\eta} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{1} - \boldsymbol{\eta}\).
Two corners are O-invariant under the cubic rotation group: the
\(\Gamma\) point \((0, 0, 0)\) and the \(R\) point \((1, 1, 1)\). These
two corners pair into one taste pair that transforms as the singlet
\(A_1\) representation. The remaining six corners form three
axis-aligned pairs \((X, M)\) along the three spatial directions,
transforming as the triplet \(T_1\) representation --- carried by the
signed vector action of the spin-taste matrices \(\gamma^j\); the
unsigned pair labels alone transform only as \(A_1 \oplus E\), since
sign flips act trivially on the corner components. The decomposition is
exact: \[4 = \mathbf{1} \oplus \mathbf{3}.\] One singlet taste; three
triplet tastes related by cubic symmetry.

\textbf{Spin-statistics from the lattice.} The singlet taste produces a
spin-0 field; the triplet tastes produce spin-\(1/2\) fields --- the
algebraic labels proved and probe-certified, the physical identification
the named hypothesis H-spin' {[}SM §4.7{]}. The argument runs through
the staggered-to-Dirac reconstruction. The singlet pairs \(\Gamma\) and
\(R\) in the Brillouin zone, with corresponding Dirac matrices
\(\Gamma(\boldsymbol{0}) = I_4\) (scalar) and
\(\Gamma(\boldsymbol{1}) = \gamma^1 \gamma^2 \gamma^3\) (pseudoscalar).
Both are \(\mathrm{SO}(3)\)-invariant, giving total angular momentum
\(J = 0\). The \(j\)-th triplet pair has matrices \(\gamma^j\) (vector)
and \(-i\Sigma_j\) (spin generator), giving total angular momentum
\(J = 1/2\).

The corollary, at the level of the algebraic labels: the spin-statistics
correspondence between the singlet taste (spin-0, bosonic) and the
triplet tastes (spin-\(1/2\), fermionic) follows from the lattice
representation theory --- with the physical spin identification riding
H-spin' (SM §4.7) --- not from a separate spin-statistics postulate. The
Higgs (spin-0 boson) and the fermions (spin-\(1/2\)) emerge as distinct
sectors of the same underlying staggered decomposition, with the
cubic-group representation forcing the spin content of each sector.

\textbf{Three degenerate fermion sectors.} The three triplet staggered
tastes provide three degenerate spin-\(1/2\) sectors related by cubic
symmetry --- the structural origin of the three-generation pattern of
the Standard Model. The cubic rotation group \(O\) permutes the three
spatial axes, and the three triplet tastes transform among themselves
under this permutation. The three sectors are therefore degenerate at
the level of cubic symmetry, with their Yukawa couplings to the Higgs
producing the observed fermion mass hierarchy through
generation-dependent symmetry breaking that the specific bijection
\(\varphi\) controls.

The candidate-sector count is locked at three by the same argument that
fixed \(K = 6\) --- its reading as three physical generations rides
H-spin' (SM §4.7), whose free-kernel and 4D routes are both settled
negative in Chapter 5 --- the link count under H-link jointly with the
condensate-stabilizer accounting. The chain runs as follows: the link
count under H-link gives \(K = 2dm\) on \(d = 3\), and the single-copy
clause \(m = 1\) with the stabilizer accounting fixes \(K = 2d = 6\)
(Chapter 5 §5.4); the six internal components host the \(2^3 = 8\)
Brillouin-zone corners; the corners pair into \(N_{\text{taste}} = 4\)
Dirac tastes; the cubic-group decomposition gives
\(4 = \mathbf{1} \oplus \mathbf{3}\), with one scalar taste and three
spin-\(1/2\) tastes. The generation count is not chosen from a continuum
of possibilities; it is a forced consequence of \(K = 6\) on \(d = 3\)
--- the link count under H-link single-copy together with the
single-gauge-sector accounting.

Adding a fourth fermion generation would require either expanding the
internal-component count beyond \(K = 6\) (which departs from the
single-copy clause \(m = 1\) of H-link) or finding a fourth distinct
staggered taste (which does not exist for \(d = 3\)). The framework's
structural commitment is therefore that no stable fourth-generation
fermion with Standard Model quantum numbers can exist. This is a
pre-registered falsification condition: any observation of such a
fermion would refute the framework's taste-reduction derivation at the
Class A level identified in Chapter 4 §4.5.

The formal uniqueness theorem closing the \(T_1\) generation-assignment
--- establishing that the assignment of three fermion generations to the
\(T_1\) triplet (rather than to \(3A_1\), \(A_1 \oplus E\), \(T_2\), or
other distributions) is forced by the framework's existing commitments
--- is developed in Appendix B.6c.

\textbf{The matter content on links.} The Standard Model matter
representations --- \(Q_L\) in \((\mathbf{3}, \mathbf{2})\), \(u_R\) and
\(d_R\) in \((\mathbf{3}, \mathbf{1})\), \(L_L\) in
\((\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{2})\), \(e_R\) in \((\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1})\)
--- involve cross-charged tensor products. A left-handed quark doublet
carries both color \(\mathbf{3}\) and weak isospin \(\mathbf{2}\)
simultaneously, requiring a tensor-product representation rather than a
direct-sum decomposition. The framework's link-carrier construction
provides the natural home for these representations.

The local gauge invariance established in Chapter 5 §5.5 makes the
coupling matrix \(M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_j)\) the gauge connection on a
nearest-neighbor link, transforming under local gauge transformations as
\(M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_j) \to G(\mathbf{n})\,M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_j)\,G(\mathbf{n} + \hat{e}_j)^{-1}\).
The link variable carries one gauge index at each endpoint, living in
the tensor-product space
\(V_K^{(\mathbf{n})} \otimes V_K^{(\mathbf{n} + \hat{e}_j)*}\) rather
than in a single \(V_K\). The matter content on links inherits this
tensor-product structure: a left-handed quark doublet at a link site can
have a definite color label at one endpoint and a definite weak-isospin
label at the other, with no algebraic obstruction.

The framework's content on links is therefore that matter propagates
along links and the gauge representation of a matter field is read off
from the tensor-product structure of the link's two endpoints. The three
triplet tastes distribute identical matter content across the three
candidate sectors (generations under H-spin'); the singlet taste
accommodates the Higgs doublet, taken as input, in its \(E\) projection
(the only projection that admits a gauge-invariant Yukawa coupling to
the fermion doublets, since the \(T_1\) projection is excluded on color
grounds and the \(A_1\) projection on weak grounds; SM Theorem 11). The
specified light-spectrum selection and H-χ' are needed to identify the
available representations with the three physical chiral families.

\textbf{The Higgs as a composite scalar.} A structural feature of the
framework's Higgs sector deserves explicit treatment. The Higgs is not a
fundamental scalar field. It is a composite excitation in the singlet
staggered taste of the wave equation --- the \(E\) projection of the
\(A_1 \oplus E \oplus T_1\) decomposition under the cubic group. The
Higgs's gauge representation \((\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{2}, +1/2)\) is taken
as input; the \(E\) projection of the singlet taste is the one
projection that accommodates it with a gauge-invariant Yukawa coupling
(SM Theorem 11).

The discrete pairing of the two singlet corners motivates a proposed
composite-Higgs protection mechanism (SM §8.8). The equivariant
condensate block values determine the stabilizer on the stated branch.
Establishing protection of the Higgs mass requires a continuous broken
symmetry, the Higgs Goldstone direction and a calculation of the
explicit-breaking corrections.

The origin of \(v\ll f\) also remains open. The electroweak vev is a
Layer 3 input, and the separate quartic boundary calculation uses the
inputs stated in SM §7.4.

\hypertarget{the-strong-cp-problem-what-time-reversal-fixes}{%
\subsection{6.3 The strong-CP problem: what time reversal
fixes}\label{the-strong-cp-problem-what-time-reversal-fixes}}

The strong-CP problem is one of the Standard Model's most persistent
puzzles. Quantum chromodynamics admits a CP-violating term
\(\mathcal{L}_\theta = (\theta/32\pi^2)\,\mathrm{Tr}(F\tilde F)\) where
\(F\) is the gluon field-strength tensor. This term would produce
CP-violation in strong interactions, observable as a non-zero neutron
electric dipole moment. Experimental bounds limit \(\theta\) to less
than approximately \(10^{-10}\) --- a remarkable smallness for a
parameter the Standard Model treats as free, ranging in principle over
\([0, 2\pi]\). The conventional resolution --- the Peccei-Quinn
mechanism with an associated axion --- postulates a new global symmetry
whose spontaneous breaking dynamically drives \(\theta\) to zero. No
axion has been observed at expected scales.

The framework's contribution is structural and partial: it fixes what
time-reversal symmetry of the substratum does and does not determine
about the combination \(\bar\theta = \theta + \arg\det(Y_u Y_d)\), the
physically meaningful CP-violating parameter, invariant under field
redefinitions. The answer is that T-invariance leaves \(\bar\theta\)
open, under two named conditions stated at the end of this section.
Three structural inputs carry the analysis: T-invariance of the
substratum bijection, the spatial nature of the framework's partition,
and the reciprocity of the resulting transition counts.

\textbf{T-invariance of the wave equation.} The first input is that the
discrete wave equation is invariant under time reversal. Under the
transformation \(\phi(\mathbf{n}, t) \to \phi(\mathbf{n}, -t)\), the
wave equation
\(\phi(\mathbf{n}, t+1) = \sum_j[\phi(\mathbf{n} + \hat{e}_j, t) + \phi(\mathbf{n} - \hat{e}_j, t)] - \phi(\mathbf{n}, t-1)\)
maps to itself: the time-reversed field satisfies the same equation.
T-invariance is a structural property of the wave equation, not an
additional postulate. The substratum dynamics is symmetric under time
reversal in a precise mathematical sense.

The framework's partition --- the visible/hidden checkerboard developed
in Chapter 5 --- marginalizes over spatial sites, not over temporal
data. The partition is spatial, preserving the temporal structure of the
substratum dynamics. T-invariance of the substratum implies T-invariance
of the visible-sector marginalization: the time-reversal operation
commutes with the partition's spatial projection.

\textbf{What T-invariance fixes about \(\theta\).} The \(\theta\)-term
\(\mathcal{L}_\theta\) is T-odd. The trace \(\mathrm{Tr}(F\tilde F)\)
equals \(2\,\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}\) when expressed in terms of the
chromoelectric and chromomagnetic fields, and under time reversal
\(\mathbf{E} \to \mathbf{E}\) while \(\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}\). A
T-invariant Lagrangian therefore requires \(\theta = -\theta\) modulo
\(2\pi\) --- and that equation has two solutions, \(\theta = 0\) and
\(\theta = \pi\), both of which are time-reversal-invariant points of
Yang--Mills theory. T-invariance of the emergent Lagrangian, inherited
from the substratum because the partition is spatial, narrows \(\theta\)
to \(\{0, \pi\}\); selecting the \(\theta = 0\) branch is a separate
condition, named H-top, which the symmetry does not supply.

\textbf{Detailed balance.} The second input is reciprocity of the
visible-sector transition counts. The argument runs through a counting
lemma: for each hidden state \(h\) that carries a visible initial state
\(i\) to a visible final state \(j\) under the bijection \(\varphi\),
time reversal supplies a hidden state carrying the time-reversed \(j\)
to the time-reversed \(i\), because T-invariance gives
\(\varphi = T \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ T\) and the spatial partition
preserves the visible/hidden classification under \(T\). The
correspondence is a bijection between two finite sets of hidden states,
so the transition counts agree: \(T_{ij} = T_{\theta j, \theta i}\),
where \(\theta\) is the action of time reversal on visible states ---
plain detailed balance, \(T_{ij} = T_{ji}\), when the visible states
carry no T-odd data. Since \(\varphi^n\) is a bijection with the same
property, reciprocity holds at every time scale; numerically, the
T-violation of the visible transition counts is exactly zero for ring
sizes \(L = 4, 6\), alphabet sizes \(q = 2, 3, 5\), and all times
\(n = 1, \ldots, 12\). Detailed balance is therefore not an emergent
thermodynamic property requiring equilibration; it is a direct
consequence of the substratum's bijection structure combined with
T-invariance and spatial partitioning.

\textbf{What reciprocity does not give.} Reciprocity of transition
probabilities does not make the emergent Hamiltonian T-invariant. A
four-site ring with the same complex hopping amplitude \(z = a + ib\) on
every link in one direction has \(|U_{ij}(t)|^2 = |U_{ji}(t)|^2\)
exactly at every time --- the ring has a reflection exchanging any two
sites, and a reflection reverses the loop --- yet its loop product
\(z^4\) carries a phase that no rephasing can remove and no real
Hamiltonian can have; no time-reversal operator inherited from the
substratum commutes with it. Wigner's theorem does not close the gap: it
represents a given ray transformation and does not manufacture a
physical time reversal from the equalities \(|U_{ij}|^2 = |U_{ji}|^2\).
The bipartite structure of that example is exactly the structure of the
framework's staggered sector, where the triangle phases that would
otherwise tie reciprocity to reality do not exist. So the chain from
substratum T-invariance to a T-invariant emergent Hamiltonian, and from
there to real Yukawa matrices and \(\arg\det(Y_u Y_d) = 0\), breaks at
its second step {[}SM §5.3, Proposition 20{]}.

\textbf{The strong-CP status.} T-invariance of the substratum therefore
fixes neither \(\theta\), which may be \(0\) or \(\pi\), nor
\(\arg\det(Y_u Y_d)\), and \(\bar\theta\) is not determined by the
construction {[}SM §5.3, Theorem 21{]}. The problem is open under two
named conditions: H-top, the selection of \(\theta = 0\) over \(\pi\);
and H-det, a mechanism fixing \(\arg\det(Y_u Y_d) = 0\) at the emergent
level while leaving the rephasing-invariant flavor quartets free. The
framework makes no prediction for the neutron electric dipole moment; a
measured \(\bar\theta \neq 0\) would constrain mechanisms proposed for
H-det, not the T-symmetry of the substratum, which is compatible with
any value of \(\bar\theta\).

The narrowing of the target is partly a relief. The CKM CP violation,
encoded in the Jarlskog invariant \(J \approx 3 \times 10^{-5}\), arises
from the basis mismatch between up-type and down-type Yukawa mass
eigenstates; reciprocal transition probabilities can hide exactly such
loop phases, so detailed balance at the substratum does not kill weak CP
violation, and there is no algebraic conflict between
\(\arg\det(Y_u Y_d) = 0\) and \(J \neq 0\). Conversely, a mechanism that
fixed \(\arg\det(Y_u Y_d) = 0\) by making \(Y_u\) and \(Y_d\)
simultaneously real would force the CKM matrix to be real orthogonal and
\(J = 0\) --- it would have solved too much, and that is the
falsification control on any proposed H-det. The flavor-sector CP phases
themselves are solution-specific properties of the particular bijection
\(\varphi\), treated as inputs rather than predictions; Chapter 4 §4.6
lists them among the solution-specific properties whose measurement does
not bear on the framework's structural status.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{gauge-couplings-and-the-no-gut-prediction}{%
\subsection{6.4 Gauge couplings and the no-GUT
prediction}\label{gauge-couplings-and-the-no-gut-prediction}}

The Standard Model has three gauge couplings: \(\alpha_3\) for color,
\(\alpha_2\) for weak isospin, \(\alpha_1\) for hypercharge, measured at
the \(Z\) boson mass. The values \(\alpha_3(M_Z) \approx 0.1181\),
\(\alpha_2(M_Z) \approx 0.0339\), \(\alpha_1(M_Z) \approx 0.0169\) are
taken as independent inputs in the Standard Model. The framework's
derivation of the gauge couplings extends the chain through a structural
input --- the one-loop staggered vacuum polarization --- combined with
threshold parameters that match the three couplings simultaneously. The
result is a structural account of \emph{why} the gauge couplings have
approximately the values they have, including the framework's
distinctive structural prediction of no grand unification.

\textbf{The induced coupling from the fermion determinant.} The gauge
field in the framework is not an independent dynamical degree of
freedom. It is the state-dependent coupling matrix
\(M(\mathbf{n}, \hat{e}_j)\) that Chapter 5 §5.5 identified as the gauge
connection on a nearest-neighbor link. The matter content --- the
staggered fermion field \(\boldsymbol{\phi}\) on the lattice ---
determines the coupling matrix through the wave equation. The gauge
kinetic term is therefore \emph{induced} by the fermion determinant
rather than being a separate input.

The effective action for the gauge connection, obtained by integrating
out the fermion degrees of freedom, is
\[S_{\text{eff}}[U] = -N_f\,\mathrm{Tr}\ln(D^\dagger D[U]),\] where
\(N_f\) is the number of fermion species and \(D\) is the staggered
Dirac operator coupled to the gauge connection \(U\). Expanding
\(S_{\text{eff}}\) to second order in the gauge field gives the gauge
propagator and the induced gauge coupling, computed at one loop from the
staggered vacuum polarization \(\Pi_s(0)\) --- a lattice momentum
integral over the fermion bubble with the framework's specific vertex
structure.

The induced coupling has a universal structural value. The Dynkin index
\(T(R) = 1/2\) per Dirac fermion is the same for all three gauge factors
because every component of the coupling matrix \(M\) --- with \(K = 6\)
components distributed across the \((3, 2, 1)\) cubic decomposition ---
transforms in the fundamental representation of its respective gauge
group. Combined with \(N_f = 6\) (one fermion species per internal
component, fixed by the \(K = 2d = 6\) result of Chapter 5 §5.4), the
induced inverse coupling at the matching scale \(\mu = M_{\text{Pl}}\)
--- a matching convention, the lattice scale itself being
\(M_{\text{Pl}}/\sqrt{6\sigma}\) for an entropy \(\sigma\) per boundary
mode (Chapter 7) --- is
\[\frac{1}{\alpha_0} = 6 \times \Pi_s(0) \times 4\pi = 23.25,\] with
\(\Pi_s(0) \to 0.3084\) on a robust numerical plateau as the lattice
integral converges. This is a strictly structural prediction ---
depending only on \(N_f\) and \(T(R)\), both determined by the lattice
structure --- and is universal across the three gauge factors because
the Dynkin index equality \(T_3(R) = T_2(R) = T_1(R)\) holds at the
substratum level.

\textbf{The threshold structure.} The universal coupling \(\alpha_0\) at
the matching scale \(M_{\text{Pl}}\) does not yet match the observed
couplings at \(M_Z\). Two corrections enter at the matching between the
substratum and the emergent quantum field theory: a universal threshold
\(\delta_0\) from higher-loop corrections to the vacuum polarization,
and a group-dependent threshold from gauge self-interactions
proportional to the quadratic Casimir \(C_2\) of each gauge factor.

The expansion parameter for the group-dependent threshold is
\(C_2 \cdot g_0^2 = C_2 \times 4\pi\alpha_0\), which equals \(1.08\) for
\(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) (\(C_2 = 2\)) and \(1.62\) for \(\mathrm{SU}(3)\)
(\(C_2 = 3\)). Both are of order unity at the matching scale, so
finite-order perturbation theory converges too slowly to capture the
threshold from first principles. The framework's account is that the
threshold is given by an all-orders geometric-series resummation of the
gauge self-energy, with the form
\[\frac{1}{\alpha_i(M_Z)} = \underbrace{23.25}_{1/\alpha_0} + \underbrace{10.0}_{\delta_0} + \underbrace{A \cdot \ln(1 + B \cdot C_2 g_0^2)}_{\text{resummed gauge self-energy}} + \underbrace{\frac{b_i}{2\pi}\ln\frac{M_{\text{Pl}}}{M_Z}}_{\text{SM RG running}},\]
where \(A\) and \(B\) are the threshold parameters and \(b_i\) is the
standard Standard Model beta-function coefficient for each gauge group.

The four components have distinct derivational statuses. The structural
input \(1/\alpha_0 = 23.25\) is computed analytically from the one-loop
staggered vacuum polarization, with no fitted parameters. That input is
the ambient staggered-background coefficient: the hypercharge factor's
microscopic connection is flat, so reading the number as a native
hypercharge coupling carries two further conditions --- that the
observer's state bundle carry projective curvature in that channel, and
that it couple with the vertex the calculation assumes. The non-abelian
factors do not inherit them. The universal threshold
\(\delta_0 = 10.0\), in the \(\mu = M_{\text{Pl}}\) matching convention,
is empirically fixed by the \(\mathrm{U}(1)\) row of the matching
equations; a two-loop staggered VP rebuild indicates that strict
two-loop perturbation theory does not reproduce \(\delta_0\), so it is
honestly treated as an empirical input rather than a derived value. The
\(C_2\)-dependent threshold parameters \((A, B) = (8.3, 5.59)\) are
matched to the \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) and \(\mathrm{SU}(3)\) couplings at
\(M_Z\), with the product \(A \cdot B = 46.4\) independently computed at
\(A \cdot B \approx 48\)--\(62\) depending on the assumed leading
finite-size power --- a cross-check that agrees with the fit under the
\(1/N^2\) assumption and is inconclusive across finite-size models. The
Standard Model RG running below \(M_{\text{Pl}}\) is standard.

The classification per Chapter 4 §4.5 is therefore that the three gauge
couplings at \(M_Z\) are Class B-R retrodictions: three fitted
parameters \((\delta_0, A, B)\) against three observed couplings
produces zero residual by construction. The structural content of the
framework's gauge-sector account does not lie in matching the three
coupling values --- that is achieved by the fit. It lies in the specific
value \(1/\alpha_0 = 23.25\) from the one-loop staggered VP and the
universality of \(\delta_0\) across the three gauge groups (no
group-dependent term). The finite-lattice \(A \cdot B\) computation is a
separate numerical cross-check: its extrapolated values span
\(\approx 48\)--\(62\) across leading-power models, and agreement with
the fitted product is conditional on the \(1/N^2\) assumption.

\textbf{The structural no-GUT prediction.} The stated running and
matching model has no common meeting of all three Standard Model gauge
couplings. The single-copy gauge branch has no modeled grand-unified
stage. The prediction has three layers.

At the group-theoretic level, the six-link decomposition gives the three
condensate blocks on the single-copy H-link and H-cust branch. With the
specified charged action, it gives the local Standard Model algebra
without an intermediate \(\mathrm{SU}(5)\), \(\mathrm{SO}(10)\),
\(\mathrm E_6\) or Pati--Salam stage in this model (Chapter 5
§§5.4--5.5).

At the coupling level, the universal \(1/\alpha_0 = 23.25\) at the
matching scale is shared across the three factors before gauge
self-interactions. The \(C_2\)-dependent threshold
\(A \ln(1 + B \cdot C_2 g_0^2)\) splits the couplings at matching. The
stated one-loop Standard Model running below \(M_{\text{Pl}}\) produces
pairwise crossings but no common meeting of all three lines (SM §6.7).

At the mechanism level, the gauge couplings emerge from the fermion
determinant --- a specific mechanism that string compactifications do
not share. String-theoretic gauge couplings depend on moduli
(compactification volumes, dilaton vacuum expectation values, flux
choices) and are typically not related to one another structurally. The
framework's gauge couplings, by contrast, share an origin: they all
arise from the same one-loop staggered vacuum polarization with the same
\(N_f\) and \(T(R)\), with the differences among them attributable to
the \(C_2\)-dependent threshold structure. The three couplings are not
three independent observables but three projections of a common
substructure.

The single-copy gauge branch lacks the modeled GUT gauge channel for
proton decay. An EFT estimate of
\(\tau_p \sim M_{\text{Pl}}^4/m_p^5 \sim 10^{45}\)--\(10^{46}\) years
applies if a dimension-six baryon-violating operator with coefficient of
order \(M_{\text{Pl}}^{-2}\) dominates the decay. Other baryon-violating
channels are open. Proton-decay searches constrain the relevant
operators. The absence of the modeled intermediate gauge stages also
removes their GUT-chain magnetic monopoles and cosmic strings.

The framework-specific discriminator within the no-GUT class is the
shared origin of the three gauge couplings: the structural prediction
\(1/\alpha_0 = 23.25\) as a single value shared across
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\) before
threshold corrections. Other no-GUT frameworks would generically have
three independent gauge couplings without this shared-origin structural
relation. The matching of \(\alpha_3, \alpha_2, \alpha_1\) at \(M_Z\)
uses three fitted threshold parameters against three observed couplings,
giving zero residual by construction. It therefore supplies no
independent confirmation of the shared-origin relation; the structural
input and threshold constraints are assessed separately in Chapter 5
§5.5.

\hypertarget{the-cabibbo-angle-and-ckm-structure}{%
\subsection{6.5 The Cabibbo angle and CKM
structure}\label{the-cabibbo-angle-and-ckm-structure}}

The Cabibbo--Kobayashi--Maskawa (CKM) matrix parametrizes the
misalignment between the mass eigenstates and the weak interaction
eigenstates of the down-type quarks. Its leading parameter, the Cabibbo
angle \(\lambda \approx 0.225\), controls the strength of
generation-changing weak transitions. In the Standard Model the Cabibbo
angle is a free parameter measured to be
\(\lambda = 0.22500 \pm 0.00067\). The framework obtains \(\lambda\)
from the geometry of the cubic lattice with no fitted parameters, under
an identification hypothesis whose emergent dressing is open (Class B-C;
SM §7.1), matching the observed value to \(0.04\%\) (\(0.12\sigma\)) ---
the framework's sharpest geometric prediction in the quark sector.

\textbf{The Cabibbo angle from a Brillouin-zone distance.} The three
fermion generations of the framework occupy the three triplet (\(T_1\))
staggered tastes, located at the three pairs of axis-aligned corners of
the Brillouin zone. In a normalized convention where the Brillouin zone
has dimension \(2\pi\), the three triplet corners
\(X_j = \pi\,\hat{e}_j\) sit at positions \((\pi, 0, 0)\),
\((0, \pi, 0)\), \((0, 0, \pi)\) along the three coordinate axes. The
distance between two adjacent triplet corners is
\[|X_i - X_j| = |\pi\,\hat{e}_i - \pi\,\hat{e}_j| = \pi\sqrt{2},\] a
geometric constant of the cubic lattice.

The conditional Cabibbo value on the unit-dressing branch is the inverse
of this distance: \[\lambda = \frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{2}} = 0.22508.\]
Observed value: \(\lambda = 0.22500 \pm 0.00067\) (global fit with
unitarity imposed). The framework's prediction matches to \(0.04\%\) ---
well inside experimental uncertainty.

The proposed mixing identification uses the continuum propagator at the
inter-generation momentum:
\[|S(X_j - X_i)| = \frac{1}{|X_j - X_i|} = \frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{2}}.\] The
physical matrix element requires the interaction dressing in SM §7.1.
The massless staggered taste-changing vertex has spinor structure
\(\Gamma=\gamma_\mu\) or \(\gamma_5\gamma_\mu\). In each case
\(\Gamma P_L=P_R\Gamma\) and \(\Gamma P_R=P_L\Gamma\). Since a conjugate
spinor carries the opposite projector, the corresponding vector and
axial bilinears preserve chirality and give the stated \(1/|q|\) scaling
(SM §7.1). The down-to-strange mass comparison below separately uses the
empirical GST relation.

\textbf{Comparison with other Bravais lattices.} The Cabibbo angle on
simple cubic is \(\lambda_{\text{SC}} = 1/(\pi\sqrt{2}) = 0.2251\),
matching observation at \(0.04\%\). On body-centered cubic, the triplet
sector sits at the \(H\)-points of the BCC Brillouin zone with
separation \(\pi\sqrt{6}\), giving \(\lambda_{\text{BCC}} = 0.1299\) ---
discrepant from observation by \(42\%\). On face-centered cubic, the
triplet sector sits at the \(L\)-points with separation \(2\pi\), giving
\(\lambda_{\text{FCC}} = 0.1592\) --- discrepant by \(29\%\). Among
these three lattices, the prescribed propagator comparison gives a
retrodictive match only for simple cubic. The emergent dressing of that
identification remains open (SM §7.1).

\textbf{Isolation in integer-input space.} A complementary robustness
check examines whether nearby alternatives to the specific integer
\(N = 2\) in the form \(\lambda = 1/(\pi\sqrt{N})\) also match
observation. They do not. The table below shows predictions for
\(N \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8\}\) --- the integers that arise naturally
from inter-corner distances in various cubic-lattice geometries ---
against the observed \(\lambda = 0.22500 \pm 0.00067\):

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\(N\) & \(\lambda = 1/(\pi\sqrt{N})\) & Deviation \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
1 & 0.3183 & \(+139\sigma\) \\
\textbf{2 (framework)} & \textbf{0.2251} & \textbf{\(+0.1\sigma\)} \\
3 & 0.1838 & \(-62\sigma\) \\
4 & 0.1592 & \(-98\sigma\) \\
6 & 0.1299 & \(-142\sigma\) \\
8 & 0.1125 & \(-186\sigma\) \\
\end{longtable}

The framework's \(N = 2\) is the only integer value in the nearby
alternatives that matches observation within \(1\sigma\). The
next-closest alternative (\(N = 3\)) deviates by 62 standard deviations.
The Cabibbo prediction is \emph{isolated} in the space of nearby
alternatives --- not selected from a cluster of acceptable choices.

\textbf{The Wolfenstein parameter \(A\).} The \(A_1\) (Higgs) taste sits
along the democratic direction \(\hat{h} = (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt{3}\) in the
internal space. Each generation axis \(\hat{e}_j\) makes an angle
\(\theta\) with \(\hat{h}\) satisfying
\(\cos\theta = \hat{e}_j \cdot \hat{h} = 1/\sqrt{3}\). The CKM mixing in
the \(A\) parameter is driven by the perpendicular component of the
generation axis relative to the Higgs democratic direction:
\[A = \sin\theta = \sqrt{1 - 1/3} = \sqrt{2/3} = 0.8165.\] Observed:
\(A = 0.826 \pm 0.012\). Match: \(0.8\sigma\), agreement at \(1.2\%\).
The observed value itself is less settled than the error bar suggests:
different global fits place it between roughly \(0.79\) and \(0.83\),
and the prediction sits inside that range. The geometric value is exact,
but its two uses differ in status: in the reactor angle
\(\sin\theta_{13} = A^2\lambda\) it enters protected (the second-order
correction cancels, so that comparison tests the geometry alone), while
in \(|V_{cb}| = A\lambda^2\) it enters through a second-order
coefficient whose derivation is open, so the identification with the
measured \(A\) is leading-order; the observed \(1.2\%\) deviation is
smaller than the natural \(\lambda^2 \approx 5\%\) correction scale, a
suppression that is observed rather than derived.

The combination
\(|V_{cb}| = A\lambda^2 = \sqrt{2/3}/(2\pi^2) = 0.04136\) (observed:
\(0.0408 \pm 0.0014\), agreement at \(0.4\sigma\)) provides a
cross-check at the second-order level of the Wolfenstein expansion. The
geometric \(A\) and the conditional \(\lambda\) give this comparison at
the stated order.

\textbf{A structural identity.} A non-trivial representation-theoretic
identity underlies the Wolfenstein \(A\) parameter. The off-democratic
projection-squared \(A^2 = 1 - (\hat{e}_j \cdot \hat{h})^2 = 1 - 1/d\)
for the generation axes in a \(d\)-dimensional space, combined with the
cubic-group quadratic Casimir for the vector representation
\(C_2(T_1) = d - 1\), gives the structural identity
\[A^2 = \frac{d - 1}{d} = \frac{C_2(T_1)}{d}.\] For \(d = 3\) this gives
\(A^2 = 2/3\) directly. The same Casimir-over-dimension structure
underlies the Koide prediction in §6.6 below and the PMNS angle
\(\sin^2\theta_{13}\) in §6.7. The identity is not a numerical
coincidence; it is the structural source of multiple Layer-1 predictions
in the framework.

\textbf{The down-to-strange mass ratio.} The Cabibbo derivation extends
to mass ratios through the Gatto-Sartori-Tonin (GST) relation
\(\sin\theta_C \approx \sqrt{m_d/m_s}\), a standard relation in flavor
physics with known higher-order corrections. The framework's prediction
is structural in \(\lambda\) --- the cubic-lattice derivation above ---
while the conversion to the mass ratio inherits GST's empirical status.
To leading order:
\[\frac{m_d}{m_s} = \lambda^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi^2} = 0.05066.\] Observed
(FLAG 2024 \(N_f = 2 + 1 + 1\) lattice):
\(m_d/m_s = 0.0503 \pm 0.0007\). Match: \(0.56\sigma\), agreement at
\(0.7\%\).

\textbf{The Jarlskog invariant.} The Jarlskog invariant
\(J = \text{Im}(V_{us} V_{cb} V_{ub}^* V_{cs}^*)\) measures CP violation
in the quark sector. In the Wolfenstein parametrization,
\(J \approx A^2 \lambda^6 \eta\). Substituting
\(\lambda = 1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\) and \(A = \sqrt{2/3}\):
\[J = \frac{\eta}{12\pi^6},\] where \(\eta = 0.348\) is the
solution-specific CP-violating parameter. This gives
\(J = 3.02 \times 10^{-5}\) (observed:
\((3.08 \pm 0.13) \times 10^{-5}\), agreement at \(0.5\sigma\)). The
structural suppression factor \(12\pi^6 \approx 11{,}537\) is purely
geometric.

A consistency check using the framework's \(A^2 = 2/3\) and
\(\lambda^2 = 1/(2\pi^2)\) structural inputs runs the relation in
reverse: solving \(J = A^2 \lambda^6 \eta\) for \(\eta\) at the observed
Jarlskog value \(J_{\text{obs}} = 3.08 \times 10^{-5}\) gives
\(\eta_{\text{implied}} = 0.355\). The PDG value is
\(\eta = 0.357 \pm 0.011\). The framework's structural inputs combined
with the observed Jarlskog produce an \(\eta\) consistent with the PDG
fit at \(0.15\sigma\). This consistency check is independent of the
chapter's specific solution-specific \(\eta = 0.348\) --- it asks only
whether the framework's structural \(A^2\) and \(\lambda^2\) inputs are
compatible with the observed CP-violating phase, and the answer is yes
within \(1\sigma\).

The Wolfenstein parameters \(\rho\) and \(\eta\) themselves require
complex CKM entries, arising from the specific bijection \(\varphi\)
rather than from structural cubic-group representation theory. They are
solution-specific properties of the framework's particular substratum
representative --- Layer 3 content in the four-layer framing of Chapter
4 --- and the framework makes no commitment to their numerical values
beyond the structural constraint that the Jarlskog invariant has the
form \(\eta / (12\pi^6)\).

\hypertarget{the-koide-relation-and-the-lepton-mass-chain}{%
\subsection{6.6 The Koide relation and the lepton mass
chain}\label{the-koide-relation-and-the-lepton-mass-chain}}

The Koide relation is a numerical regularity among the three
charged-lepton masses observed in 1981:
\[Q = \frac{m_e + m_\mu + m_\tau}{(\sqrt{m_e} + \sqrt{m_\mu} + \sqrt{m_\tau})^2} = \frac{2}{3}\]
to extraordinary precision --- matching observation at \(0.001\%\) with
no fitted parameters in the conventional Standard Model. The relation
has been a persistent puzzle, with multiple proposed derivations from
grand-unified, supersymmetric, and modular-symmetry frameworks. None has
produced both the value \(2/3\) and an account of why the relation
should hold in the first place. The framework derives the Koide relation
from the cubic-group representation theory of the three generations,
with both the value and the underlying structure following from
substratum-level content.

\textbf{The Koide angle from a cubic Casimir.} The three lepton
generations occupy the three triplet (\(T_1\)) staggered tastes, related
by the cubic symmetry group \(O\). The Koide relation in its angular
form \(\theta_0 = C_2/d^2\) --- where \(C_2\) is the quadratic Casimir
of the relevant cubic-group representation and \(d\) is the spatial
dimension --- provides a specific structural prediction for the value
\(\theta_0\).

For the \(T_1\) representation of \(O\) (the three-dimensional vector
representation occupied by the three lepton generations), the quadratic
Casimir is \(C_2(T_1) = d - 1 = 2\) in \(d = 3\) spatial dimensions. The
lattice bandwidth squared is \(d^2 = 9\). The Koide angle in its natural
framework form is therefore
\[\theta_0 = \frac{C_2(T_1)}{d^2} = \frac{2}{9},\] which is the phase of
the standard \(\mathbb{Z}_3\)-symmetric parametrization of three masses,
independent of the amplitude that \(Q = 2/3\) fixes (SM §7.2). The
framework's prediction matches the observed value
\(\theta_0^{\text{obs}} = 0.222225 \pm 0.000006\) at \(0.001\%\)
(\(0.4\sigma\)).

The structural interpretation is geometric: \(C_2(T_1)/d^2\) is the
anisotropy strength of the generation representation, normalized by the
lattice bandwidth squared. The cubic-group representation theory of
\(T_1\) fixes the numerator; the dimensional structure of the lattice
fixes the denominator. The value \(2/9\) follows from these two pieces
of substratum-level structure, with no fitted parameters.

\textbf{Uniqueness among alternative ratios.} Among dimensionless ratios
involving cubic-group Casimirs and lattice-dimension quantities at
\(d = 3\) and \(T_1\), the value \(\theta_0 = C_2/d^2 = 2/9\) is the
unique match to observation. Ten alternative ratios --- including
\(C_2/d\) (which gives the Wolfenstein \(A^2\) above), \(C_2/(2d)\),
\(\sqrt{C_2}/d\), \((C_2 - 1)/d^2\), and similar combinations ---
produce values discrepant from the observed Koide angle by amounts
ranging from \(11\%\) to over \(200\%\). The match at
\(\theta_0 = C_2/d^2\) is not one of several possibilities consistent
with cubic-group structure; it is the unique value forced by the
relevant Casimir-and-bandwidth combination.

\textbf{Connection to the Cabibbo identity.} The Koide angle is related
to the Cabibbo structural identity through second-order perturbation
theory. The natural cubic-lattice perturbation amplitude on the \(T_1\)
representation is \(\sqrt{C_2}/d = \sqrt{2}/3\) --- the Casimir's square
root scaled by the bandwidth. Second-order perturbation theory on the
eigenvalues then gives
\(\theta_0 \sim (\sqrt{C_2}/d)^2 = C_2/d^2 = A^2/d\), with
\(A^2 = (d-1)/d\) the structural identity of §6.5 for vector
representations. Amplitudes scale as \(\sqrt{C_2}/d\); eigenvalue shifts
scale as the square. The Koide angle and the Wolfenstein \(A\) parameter
share a common Casimir structure, with the Koide angle obtaining at the
eigenvalue level what \(A\) obtains at the amplitude level.

The first-principles derivation of the specific \(1/d\) amplitude
scaling (rather than alternatives like \(1/(2d)\)) from the
cubic-lattice Yukawa structure is complete: the amplitude prefactor has
been computed and equals one (SM §7.2; driver
\texttt{oi\_lattice\_code/fermion/n\_ratio\_pt.py}), so
\(\mathcal{N} = 1/d^2 = 1/9\) exactly at \(m \to 0\), and the empirical
match at \(0.001\%\) confirms a derived normalization rather than
constraining a chosen one. The \(1/d\) amplitude is therefore fixed by
the framework's structural commitments rather than chosen empirically,
conditional on the substrate-eigenvalue criterion that selects a loop
without a time direction (below). The Koide prediction is Class B-C,
Layer 1, because the Koide amplitude \(A^2 = C_2\) is not yet derived
from the dynamics (SM §7.2). The choice reduces to whether the
taste-mixing loop carries a time direction (\(d=4\), giving \(1/16\)) or
not (\(d=3\), giving \(1/9\)); the \(d=3\) substrate-eigenvalue origin
of the generation masses selects \(1/9\); Schur's lemma on the \(T_1\)
generations protects this against all taste-blind emergent dressing. A
cubic-invariant dressing need not be taste-blind: it may act on
\(\mathrm{Sym}^2(T_1)\) with different scalars on \(A_1\), \(E\) and
\(T_2\), as the one-loop staggered taste kernel does
(\(\lambda_E/\lambda_{A_1} \approx 0.22\)--\(0.24\)). That class is
bounded: it leaves \(\theta_0\) invariant at the \(\sqrt{m}\) level, and
on the mass pattern the observed agreement constrains it to
\(-2.5 \times 10^{-6} \lesssim \delta m/m \lesssim 1.7 \times 10^{-6}\)
at 95\% confidence; the interval is conditional on the linear response
of \(\theta_0\) to the dressing (sensitivity coefficient
\(\kappa \approx -35\), with \(\lambda_E/\lambda_{A_1}\) in the range
above) and is not a model-independent exclusion; a lepton-Yukawa loop of
order \(10^{-6}\) is compatible with that interval for either sign, by a
factor of about two, but is not a confirmed prediction (SM §7.2). What
remains is a possible loop-level cubic-breaking contribution --- the
same residual as the emergent-Lorentz radiative-stability question (SM
§7.3).

\textbf{The charged-lepton mass chain.} Given the Koide angle
\(\theta_0 = 2/9\) and one empirical input (the tau mass
\(m_\tau = 1776.93\) MeV), the parametrization
\(\sqrt{m_k} = \mu(1 + A\cos(\theta_0 + 2\pi k/3))\) is fully
determined: \(Q = 2/3\) fixes \(A = \sqrt{2}\), \(\theta_0\) fixes the
phase, and \(m_\tau\) fixes the scale \(\mu\). The two structural inputs
are \(Q = 2/3\) and \(\theta_0 = 2/9\), and the resulting masses are
\(m_e = 0.51098\) MeV and \(m_\mu = 105.656\) MeV against \(0.51100\)
and \(105.658\) observed (\(0.003\%\) and \(0.002\%\); SM §7.2). The
ratio \(m_e/m_\tau = 2.876 \times 10^{-4}\) lies within \(0.84\%\) of
\[\frac{m_e}{m_\tau} = \frac{\lambda^4}{d^2} = \frac{1}{36\pi^4} \approx 2.852 \times 10^{-4},\]
with \(\lambda = 1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\) the Cabibbo angle from the quark
sector (§6.5) and \(d = 3\) the spatial dimensionality (Chapter 5 §5.2).
The proximity plays no role in the chain: the mass point is fixed by
\(Q\) and \(\theta_0\). The assignment of \(m_e\) specifically to the
lightest charged-lepton mass eigenvalue is Layer 2(b) bijection-specific
by the gauge-invariance constraint of Chapter 2 §2.5.

Combined with \(Q = 2/3\) and the empirical \(m_\tau\), the second
structural input \(\theta_0 = 2/9\) determines all three charged-lepton
masses:

The cross-sector pattern is significant: the lepton mass spectrum
inherits \emph{both} the Wolfenstein parameter \(A^2 = 2/3\) (via the
PMNS Condition 2 sum rule of Ch08 §8.5) \emph{and} the Cabibbo coupling
\(\lambda^2 = 1/(2\pi^2)\) (via the PMNS reactor angle
\(\sin^2\theta_{13}\)) from the quark sector. The lepton-sector
structure is not freshly postulated; it inherits from the same substrate
machinery that produces the quark-sector observables.

The classification per Chapter 4 §4.5 is that the electron and muon
masses are Class B-M (mass-chain inheritance from a single upstream
empirical input \(m_\tau\) plus structural commitment); the Koide
relation \(Q = \tfrac13 + \tfrac{A^2}{6} = 2/3\) is Class B-C Layer 1
from the cubic-group Casimir through the amplitude
\(A^2 = C_2(T_1) = 2\); the phase input
\(\theta_0 = C_2(T_1)/d^2 = 2/9\) is Class B-C Layer 1 from the same
Casimir structure, with the amplitude prefactor computed equal to one
(SM §7.2); both are conditional on the dynamical closure of the Koide
amplitude, whose value \(A^2 = C_2\) is not yet derived from the
dynamics.

The magnitude content of the lepton chain is Layer 1, conditional on the
same amplitude closure: both inputs come from the cubic Casimir, the
phase input with computed unit prefactor (SM §7.2). The analogous
coefficient of Condition 2 in Ch08 §8.5 is Layer 2(b): the second-order
substrate route is excluded (SM §7.3), the leading weighted sum is
tested subject to the open higher orders, and the \(O(\lambda^3)\)
interference route is recorded, not pursued; there the framework
provides a structural identification with cross-sector content
(quark-sector inputs determining lepton-sector outputs through
cubic-group machinery), and the percent-level empirical match is
consistent with the structural identification modulo
renormalization-group running. The directional assignment (which
specific generation is \(e\), \(\mu\), or \(\tau\), and correspondingly
which eigenvalue carries which label) remains Layer 2(b)
bijection-specific by the gauge structure of Chapter 2 §2.5 and is not
derivable from substrate alone in any framework consistent with
\(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\)-invariance.

\textbf{The full six-mass chain.} The mass chain uses the empirical
scale \(m_s\), the empirical GST relation, phenomenological
\(Q_{\text{down}}\) and measured \(Z_S\):
\[m_s \;\xrightarrow{\lambda^2}\; m_d \;\xrightarrow{\sqrt{\theta_0}}\; m_u \;\xrightarrow{Q_{\text{down}}}\; m_b \;\xrightarrow{Z_S}\; m_\tau \;\xrightarrow{\theta_0}\; m_e, m_\mu.\]

The five arrows are structural relations of three different epistemic
statuses, which the chapter distinguishes explicitly:

\emph{Cubic-group derivations (parameter-free forms):} the conditional
Cabibbo value from the inter-generation Brillouin-zone distance, used
with the external GST relation \(m_d/m_s=\lambda^2\); the
\(m_u/m_d = \sqrt{\theta_0}\) from the intra-doublet splitting at the
amplitude level (Layer 1 form with Layer 2(b) alignment, SM §7.2); the
charged-lepton Koide \(Q = \tfrac13 + \tfrac{A^2}{6} = 2/3\) through the
amplitude \(A^2 = C_2(T_1) = 2\); and the Koide phase
\(\theta_0 = 2/9 = C_2(T_1)/d^2\) with computed unit prefactor (SM
§7.2). These four relations take their forms from cubic-group
representation theory with no free parameters; their classifications are
those of the Section 6.8 table, with Koide \(Q\) and \(\theta_0\)
conditional on the dynamical closure of the Koide amplitude.

\emph{Derived running factor plus measured non-perturbative
renormalization:} the down-to-tau ratio combines two components of
different character. The factor \(4.28\) is derived: tree-level
taste-independence gives \(y_b = y_\tau\), and full Standard Model RGE
running from a common \(M_{\text{Pl}}\) boundary condition gives
\(m_b/m_\tau|_{\text{tree}} = 4.276\), with a \(\sim 1\%\) systematic
from higher-loop corrections and electroweak-threshold matching (SM
§7.5). The factor \(Z_S\) is measured: the scalar-density
renormalization
\(Z_S = \langle\bar\psi\psi\rangle_{\text{int}}/\langle\bar\psi\psi\rangle_{\text{free}}\),
computed non-perturbatively on SU(3) backgrounds at the matching scale
\(m_{\text{match}} = \lambda g_0^2\), whose dimensional form is forced
by power-counting in the taste-decomposed Coleman--Weinberg potential.
At \(L = 32\), \(Z_S(\lambda g_0^2) = 1.813 \pm 0.001\) (statistical),
with the \(L \to \infty\) extrapolation \(\approx 1.83\) and a realistic
\(1\)--\(2\%\) systematic from finite volume and the regulator choice.
The prediction \(m_b/m_\tau = 4.28/Z_S = 2.361\) matches the observed
\(2.352 \pm 0.017\) at \(0.4\%\) (\(0.5\sigma\); \(\sim 0.7\sigma\) at
\(L \to \infty\)). The open Layer-2 element is the scalar prefactor in
the matching-scale identification (the \(K\) coefficient): the Monte
Carlo consistency check gives
\(m_{\text{match}}^{\text{MC}} = 0.1234 \pm 0.0002\) against
\(\lambda g_0^2 = 0.1217\) (\(1.4\%\)), and \(K = 1\) is excluded by the
same data (SM §7.5).

\emph{Phenomenological auxiliary parameter (Class P):} the down-sector
Koide invariant \(Q_{\text{down}} \approx 0.7304\) does not match any
simple cubic-group form (the closest cubic-group ratios --- \(11/15\),
\(5/7\), \(\theta_0 \cdot (3/2) \cdot (1 + \lambda^2)\) --- all deviate
from the empirical value by more than \(1\%\)). The framework treats
\(Q_{\text{down}}\) as a phenomenological input classified as Class P
per Chapter 4 §4.5, not as a structural prediction:
\(Q_{\text{down}} \approx 0.7304\) is taken as phenomenological input in
the form \((2/3)(1 + \alpha_s/\pi)\), which reproduces the PDG
mixed-scheme value to \(0.15\%\) but has no derivation (SM §7.2);
\(m_b\) then follows at \(0.9\%\). Whether \(Q_{\text{down}}\) has a
derivable structural form different from the charged-lepton sector's
\(2/3\) --- a magnitude-level question potentially closable through
lattice perturbation theory in the emergent description --- is open. The
sector-identification content (which \(Q\) values attach to down-quarks
vs charged-leptons) is bijection-specific per Chapter 2 §2.5.

The chain produces six masses from one empirical scale (\(m_s\)) plus
two further inputs (\(Q_{\text{down}}\) as a Class P phenomenological
input, \(Z_S\) measured non-perturbatively). The \(m_d/m_s\) step also
uses the external empirical GST relation. The up-quark row uses the
chained \(m_d=4.73\) MeV. Using the measured \(m_d=4.67\) MeV separately
gives \(2.20\) MeV.

\textbf{The top quark mass.} The top quark sits separately from the
chain above because its Yukawa coupling is large. The weak-scale
relation \(m_t = v/\sqrt{2}\) with \(y_t(m_t) \approx 1\) reproduces the
observed mass:
\[m_t = \frac{v}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{246\,\text{GeV}}{\sqrt{2}} = 174.1\,\text{GeV},\]
where \(v\) is the Higgs vacuum expectation value, matching the observed
\(172.5 \pm 0.3\) GeV to \(0.9\%\).

The mechanism behind this relation is open, and the honest
classification is a retrodiction rather than a structural prediction.
The natural proposal --- a compositeness-scale normalization
\(y_t(M_{\text{Pl}}) = 1\) carried to low energy by the infrared
quasi-fixed point --- does not deliver the observed value under one-loop
Standard Model running: \(y_t(M_{\text{Pl}}) = 1\) flows to
\(y_t(m_t) \approx 1.19\), giving \(m_t \approx 207\) GeV, and the IR
quasi-fixed point itself sits at \(y_t \approx 1.25\)
(\(m_t \approx 215\)--\(220\) GeV), not at unity. The attractor basin
\(y_{\text{UV}} \in [0.5, 5]\) focuses to \(m_t \in [177, 221]\) GeV, a
\(25\%\) spread. What is empirically exact is the weak-scale statement
\(y_t(m_t) \approx 1\); the compositeness-scale normalization plus IR
attraction does not produce it, and the observed top corresponds to
\(y_t(M_{\text{Pl}}) \approx 0.4\)--\(0.5\). The relation is therefore
recorded as a retrodiction of the weak-scale \(y_t \approx 1\)
coincidence, with the structural mechanism an open task; a derivation of
\(y_t = 1\) at the electroweak matching scale, or of
\(y_t(M_{\text{Pl}}) \approx 1/2\) (which runs to \(\approx 177\) GeV),
would close it.

The relation \(m_t = v/\sqrt{2}\) matches the observation to \(0.9\%\),
but as a retrodiction of the weak-scale \(y_t \approx 1\) coincidence
rather than a parameter-free structural prediction; a derivation of
\(y_t = 1\) at the electroweak matching scale, or of
\(y_t(M_{\text{Pl}}) \approx 1/2\) (which runs to \(\approx 177\) GeV),
would close the mechanism.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{pmns-mixing-angles}{%
\subsection{6.7 PMNS mixing angles}\label{pmns-mixing-angles}}

The PMNS matrix parametrizes the mismatch between neutrino mass
eigenstates and flavor eigenstates. The leading angle comparisons below
use a cubic flavor branch and the Cabibbo scale. The solar and
atmospheric values also use Condition 2, the separate normalization
\(b_{23}=1\) and the stated mass-label assignment.

\textbf{Tribimaximal mixing as the leading structure.} The starting
point is tribimaximal (TBM) mixing, derived from the alternating
subgroup \(A_4 \subset O\) of the cubic rotation group. TBM is the
specific pattern
\[\sin^2\theta_{12} = 1/3, \qquad \sin^2\theta_{23} = 1/2, \qquad \sin^2\theta_{13} = 0,\]
historically introduced as an empirical observation about the leptonic
mixing pattern and later given group-theoretic foundations. In the
framework, TBM emerges as the zeroth-order PMNS structure from the
\(A_4\) subgroup of the cubic rotation group acting on the three lepton
generations --- the same cubic group of the geometry in Chapter 5. The
local gauge identification there uses the conditional condensate and
charged-action construction.

The TBM structure is not the final answer: the experimentally measured
\(\sin^2\theta_{13} \approx 0.022\) is non-zero, and
\(\sin^2\theta_{12}\) and \(\sin^2\theta_{23}\) deviate from their TBM
values by amounts consistent with corrections of order
\(\lambda^2 = 1/(2\pi^2) \approx 0.05\). The following charged-lepton
calculation gives the leading corrections with the stated inputs.

\textbf{Ingredients of the leading calculation.}

First, the overall correction scale is the squared Cabibbo angle
\(\lambda^2 = 1/(2\pi^2)\) from §6.5. The PMNS matrix's deviation from
TBM follows from the charged-lepton sector's perturbation away from the
basis in which TBM holds exactly; the charged-lepton perturbation has
natural amplitude \(\lambda\), with second-order effects entering at
\(\lambda^2\).

Second, the charged-lepton perturbation has a specific structure: it is
\(U\)-parity odd under \(\mu\)-\(\tau\) exchange. The leading-order
generator \(A_1\) in the perturbative expansion
\(V_\ell = \exp(\lambda A_1 + \lambda^2 A_2 + O(\lambda^3))\) satisfies
\(U A_1 U^{-1} = -A_1\) under conjugation by the \(\mu\)--\(\tau\) swap
\(U\). Its negative is a proper cube rotation with the same conjugation
action. Geometrically, \(A_1\) is a rotation around the symmetric
combination \((e_2 + e_3)/\sqrt{2}\) by angle \(A^2 = 2/3\) --- with the
Wolfenstein \(A\) of §6.5 entering directly as the rotation angle. The
structural property is that this \(A_1\) produces no \(O(\lambda)\)
corrections to the TBM angles \(\theta_{12}\) and \(\theta_{23}\) (the
corrections are pushed to \(O(\lambda^2)\)), while producing the leading
reactor angle \(\sin\theta_{13} = A^2\lambda\) at order \(\lambda\).

Third, the separate normalization \(b_{23}=1\) gives
\(\Delta_{23}=\lambda^2\) at the computed order. The reactor term is
\(A^4\lambda^2\), giving \(\Delta_{13}/\Delta_{23}=A^4=4/9\) at leading
order. The solar coefficient then uses Condition 2.

\textbf{Leading angle values.} With the stated Cabibbo dressing and
mass-label assignment, and with Condition 2 and \(b_{23}=1\) for the
solar and atmospheric angles, the leading values are
\[\sin^2\theta_{12} = \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4\pi^2} \approx 0.308003,\]
\[\sin^2\theta_{23} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2\pi^2} = 0.5507,\]
\[\sin^2\theta_{13} = \frac{4}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi^2} = \frac{4}{18\pi^2} = 0.02252.\]

These leading values can be compared with the post-JUNO global fit and
the NuFIT 6.0 fit (normal mass ordering).

The comparisons differ from the quoted fits by about \(1\sigma\) or
less. The solar estimates use overlapping data.

\textbf{The JUNO measurement.} The calculated solar value is
\(0.14\sigma\) from the direct JUNO result \(0.3092\pm0.0087\) and
\(0.07\sigma\) from the global fit \(0.3085\pm0.0073\) that incorporates
it. The comparisons are retrodictive. At an illustrative future
uncertainty of \(0.0014\), unchanged central values would be about
\(0.855\sigma\) and \(0.355\sigma\) away, respectively. These
separations apply to a model taking the leading value as complete.
Testing the flavor structure also requires the stated flavor inputs and
control of the higher-order terms (SM §7.8).

The reactor squared angle
\(\sin^2\theta_{13}=A^4\lambda^2+O(\lambda^3)\) uses only \(A_1\) at the
computed order and inherits the Cabibbo dressing. The real term
\(b_{12}-b_{13}\) may enter the unsquared amplitude at order
\(\lambda^2\). The physical complex CP phase remains open (SM §7.3).

Condition 2 fixes the ratio \(b_{23}/(b_{12}+b_{13})=4/3\) and cancels
the order-\(\lambda^2\) term of the weighted angle sum. The post-JUNO
solar fit and the NuFIT 6.0 atmospheric upper-octant fit give
\(1.178\pm0.020\) by approximate quadrature assuming zero covariance.
This is a consistency comparison at about \(0.6\sigma\) and uses the
same angle estimates. The lower-octant solution gives about \(1.07\).

The ratio \(4/3=2A^2\) has the projection interpretation in SM §7.3. The
second-order substrate calculation excludes the identified route to the
ratio, so the magnitude condition remains Layer 2(b). The mass-label
assignment is a separate input attaching the coefficients to the
physical flavors. The absolute angles also use \(b_{23}=1\). The two
angle entries are Class B-L.

\textbf{Comparison with alternative patterns.} The leading weighted sum
provides a target for comparisons with TM1 and TM2 partial-TBM patterns.
Tests of the calculated relation need the atmospheric octant and control
of the higher-order terms (Chapter 8).

The framework's lepton-sector content has more structural commitments
than the three angles. The leading-order sum tests the stated Condition
2 relation with higher orders open. The exact \(7/6\) target is the
separate phenomenological model test (SM §7.8). On the branch where the
singlet taste hosts the Higgs and no gauge-singlet fermion is present
(SM §8.4; the neutrino mass mechanism is otherwise open, SM §4.7.1), the
neutrinos are Majorana rather than Dirac, and the mass ordering is
expected to be normal rather than inverted as a heuristic consequence of
the taste-breaking structure of the neutrino mass matrix developed in
Chapter 5 §5.6, not as a theorem. Each of these is a pre-registered
falsification condition per Chapter 4 §4.5: confirmed inverted ordering
would refute the taste-breaking heuristic on that branch; a confirmed
Dirac nature would refute the branch's expectation that no right-handed
neutrino exists in the spectrum.

\textbf{The Higgs mass.} A separate structural prediction completes the
chapter's quantitative content: the Higgs quartic coupling at the
compositeness scale is exactly zero. The Higgs is the singlet (\(A_1\))
taste of the staggered decomposition --- a composite scalar in the
framework's structural account, as Chapter 5 §5.5 developed --- and its
quartic self-coupling at the Planck scale receives no tree-level
contribution. The Standard Model quartic \(\lambda\) at low energies is
generated entirely by RGE running between the compositeness scale and
the experimental scale.

The structural prediction is \(\lambda(M_{\text{Pl}}) = 0\). The
observed value from Buttazzo et al.~is
\(\lambda(M_{\text{Pl}}) = -0.013 \pm 0.020\), consistent with zero at
\(0.6\sigma\). The structural commitment is therefore consistent with
the extrapolated value at the boundary-condition level.

The corresponding prediction for the Higgs mass in GeV is derived by
combining the structural boundary condition with the measured top mass
\(m_t\) as a one-input parameter and running the three-loop SM RGE. The
result is \(m_H \approx 129\text{-}132\) GeV for
\(m_t = 172\text{-}173\) GeV, against the observed
\(m_H = 125.10 \pm 0.14\) GeV. The gap is sensitive to \(m_t\) (with
\(\partial m_H / \partial m_t \approx -1.1\) GeV/GeV), and the recent
CMS measurement \(m_t = 170.5 \pm 0.8\) GeV would bring the prediction
to about \(128 \pm 2\) GeV. The structural claim
\(\lambda(M_{\text{Pl}}) = 0\) is confirmed; the specific Higgs mass in
GeV is consistent with observation within the current \(m_t\)
uncertainty.

The framework's Higgs-sector prediction has a notable convergence with
the broader physics literature. The Multiple Point Principle developed
by Bennett, Froggatt, and Nielsen in the 1990s postulated
\(\lambda(M_{\text{Pl}}) = 0\) as a fine-tuning condition, predicting
the Higgs mass at approximately the value subsequently observed.
Wetterich's asymptotic-safety analysis showed that if the Standard Model
holds to the Planck scale with an asymptotically safe gravity
contribution, the observed Higgs mass requires \(m_t \approx 171\) GeV.
The framework's structural derivation of \(\lambda(M_{\text{Pl}}) = 0\)
thus provides a substratum-level account of what an active beyond-SM
literature has been postulating as a boundary condition.

The table has twenty-four entries: eight Category A rows, one for each
relation, six in Category B, one in Category C, two in Category D, three
in Category E, two input rows (\(1/\alpha_0\) and \(\delta_0\)), one
inconclusive numerical cross-check (\(A \cdot B\)), and one open
quantity (\(\bar\theta\)). The Cat C label means composite-redundant and
is distinct from the derivational Class C. Beyond the table, the
three-generation count (Appendix B.6c) and the absence of grand-unified
gauge structure (Appendix B.6b) are further falsifiable structural
commitments, without numerical values to compare against observation.

The framework's content is concentrated at Layer 0 and Layer 1 of the
four-layer framing --- gauge structure and pure cubic-group
representation theory --- with Layer 2 and Layer 3 content
(bijection-specific operator structures and the overall mass scale)
appearing as explicit inputs rather than fitted parameters. The
structural-vs-bijection-level distinction developed in Chapter 4 §4.5 is
what makes the empirical record evaluable: the framework predicts the
\emph{angular} and \emph{ratio} structure of fermion mass relations from
cubic-group representation theory, but the overall mass scale of each
chain is set by the specific bijection and is taken as one empirical
input.

The Category A relations span five empirical channels: CKM
phenomenology, lattice QCD, PMNS mixing, lepton-mass relations, and the
Higgs sector. The structural inputs \(A^2 = 2/3\),
\(\lambda^2 = 1/(2\pi^2)\), and \(C_2(T_1)/d^2 = 2/9\) are tested
through those channels with the derivational conditions stated in the
table. The gauge-coupling product \(A \cdot B\) remains a separate,
leading-power-conditional numerical cross-check and supplies no settled
empirical match. The exact geometric comparisons in B.6b and B.6c
underpin the separately conditioned gauge and matter branches.

\textbf{Falsification commitments revisited.} The pre-registered
falsification conditions from Chapter 4 §4.5 connect directly to the
predictions developed here. Any stable fourth-generation fermion would
refute the taste-reduction derivation that locks the generation count at
three (formal uniqueness theorem B.6c). A stable extension of the gauge
sector would test the specified physical gauge branch of the exact
nearest-neighbor comparison in B.6b. Any precision-upgrade measurement
moving the Cabibbo angle outside \(3\sigma\) of \(1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\)
would refute the framework's geometric prediction. Any precision-upgrade
measurement moving the Koide relation outside \(3\sigma\) of \(2/3\)
would refute the cubic-Casimir derivation. The Category A predictions in
independent CKM, lattice-QCD, and Higgs-sector channels ---
\(|V_{cb}|\), \(m_d/m_s\), and \(\lambda(M_{\text{Pl}})\) --- provide
further falsification handles through measurements independent of the
Cabibbo channel that constrains \(\lambda\).

The Category B comparisons are conditional. The solar and atmospheric
values use the flavor-branch inputs of §6.7. Future precision tests
these values with higher-order terms and octant uncertainty included.
The mass-chain entries and Jarlskog relation have the inputs stated in
the table.

\textbf{Cross-sector universality.} A structural feature of the
framework's prediction package deserves explicit treatment: the same
numerical structural inputs that produce quark-sector observables also
produce lepton-sector observables, with no separate fitting between
sectors.

The cubic projection \(A^2=2/3\) enters \(|V_{cb}|=A\lambda^2\) and the
leading reactor expression \(A^4\lambda^2\). The leading solar and
atmospheric values use the same Cabibbo scale with the additional
conditions of §6.7. The Koide chain has its separate inputs. The
threshold product \(A\cdot B\) is a numerical cross-check with values
\(\approx48\)--\(62\) across finite-size models against the fitted
\(46.4\). Its leading-power dependence leaves the comparison
inconclusive.

The cross-sector pattern places a substantial constraint on alternative
input choices: any alternative natural input to the framework's
machinery that fits quark-sector observation would also need to fit
lepton-sector observation. Alternative natural inputs that produce
different Cabibbo angles (e.g., BCC or FCC inter-generation distances)
all deviate from \(\lambda = 1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\) by \(>20\%\) and would
correspondingly mispredict \(m_d/m_s\) and \(\sin^2\theta_{13}\) by
similar fractions. Alternative power combinations of \(A\) and
\(\lambda\) in \(\sin^2\theta_{13}\) (\(A^2\lambda^2\) at 32\%
deviation, \(A\lambda^2\) at 50\% deviation) similarly fail the
cross-sector match. The framework's specific \(A^2 = 2/3\) and
\(\lambda^2 = 1/(2\pi^2)\) inputs are consistent with observation in
both sectors simultaneously.

\textbf{What follows.} Chapter 7 develops the gravitational sector ---
the Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) factor as the ratio matched by the
horizon calibration under the conditions of §7.3 (a consistency
relation: GW250114 confirms the classical area theorem; the coefficient
has no direct test), the calibration
\(\hbar = c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\) relating the action scale to the
discreteness scale (a self-consistency condition, §7.4), the dissolution
of the cosmological constant problem at the level of two incommensurable
descriptive levels, conditional on the covariant coupling step, and the
dark-sector phenomenology with the MOND acceleration scale
\(a_0 = cH/6\) and the entropy-displacement account of dark matter. The
empirical record there is independent of and complementary to the
Standard Model content developed here: the gravitational sector tests
the substratum's boundary thermodynamics rather than its bulk gauge
structure.

Chapter 8 develops the JUNO prediction in detail, as a focused case
study of the framework's sharpest empirically matched Layer
1-plus-Layer-2(b) value (a parameter-free retrodiction). The November
2025 measurement and its discrimination from the TM1/TM2 alternatives
are presented with the experimental context that this chapter
abbreviated. Chapter 9 develops universality classes and the framework's
relationship to alternative unification programs, with the OI-string
analysis at the matrix-model level and the framework's structural
commitment to no grand unified theory developed against the broader
landscape of unification proposals.

The framework's empirical record in fundamental physics, developed
across Chapters 5 through 9, is concentrated at the Level G3 × Level D
intersection of the hierarchical structural realism developed in Chapter
3 --- class-specific predictions of the cubic-lattice substratum
representative, with substantial empirical support and pre-registered
falsifiability. The structural and methodological commitments of Part I
are made quantitatively precise here.

\hypertarget{chapter-7}{%
\section{Chapter 7}\label{chapter-7}}

\hypertarget{the-gravitational-sector}{%
\section{The Gravitational Sector}\label{the-gravitational-sector}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-4}{%
\subsection{7.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-4}}

Chapters 5 and 6 developed the framework's content in the Standard Model
sector: the gauge group
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\) from the
cubic decomposition of the substratum, three matter generations from the
staggered taste structure, twenty-two classified SM observables (two
parameter-free structural and five conditional structural; the remainder
layered, chained or fitted), with the measured comparisons spanning
\(0.0003\%\) to \(1.2\%\) across the parameter space. The content was
developed by \emph{specifying} the substratum dynamics --- the wave
equation on a cubic lattice with the link count under H-link --- and
tracing the structural consequences. The framework's content in the
gravitational sector follows a different route.

The gravitational sector uses a cosmological event horizon as a
candidate causal partition. It separates degrees of freedom in the
observer's causal reach from those outside it. The calibrated action
scale is independent of area and surface gravity at the matched horizon
conditions and counting density. The same calibration gives the
Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) coefficient on its stated counting branch.

This chapter develops seven structural results. Section 7.2 motivates
candidate coupling C1, states the Hubble-scale mixing input for C2 and
estimates capacity for a chosen laboratory demand. History readback C4
is not presently discharged. Section 7.3 derives the emergent action
scale \(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2 / (4G\sigma)\), with \(\sigma\) the
entropy of one boundary mode, by matching energy and frequency slopes
for the same transitions on the exact de Sitter branch, conditional on
the infrared detailed-balance slope of the horizon reservoir matching
the Killing period (H-slope) together with H-count, the horizon and
frame conditions, local boost structure at the horizon and the symmetric
detailed-balance rate ratio. Section 7.4 fixes the discreteness scale
\(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\,l_p\) (\(\epsilon = 2\,l_p\) at
\(\sigma = 1\), one nat per mode) as the unique simultaneous solution of
the action-scale relation and the definition of the Planck length.
Section 7.5 recovers the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy \(S = A/(4 l_p^2)\):
with the calibration the boundary-mode count reproduces it, the \(1/4\)
coefficient being the ratio of the Euclidean KMS period to the Jacobson
prefactor that the calibration matches, under the same conditions; the
waveform-based area inference for GW250114 supports the classical area
theorem. Section 7.6 treats the black hole information paradox, which
the framework does not resolve: information is never lost from the
substratum bijection \(\varphi\), bijectivity being a premise of the
framework's models; a cycle-averaged Page curve follows under the
scrambling condition H-scramble and the decoupling condition H-decouple,
taking the energy shell of the black hole and its radiation to be their
full product space, by a mechanism substantially different from that of
the quantum-extremal-surface and entanglement-island programs, with a
Page time that, for a mass-independent emission coefficient, is a fixed
fraction of the evaporation time set by the entropy the radiation
carries per unit of horizon entropy lost ---
\(t_P \approx 0.646\, t_{\text{evap}}\) when the two are equal;
H-scramble fails for every bijection acting on an initial configuration
with the bipartition aligned to the configuration coordinates, so the
Page value requires an initial superposition over many configurations or
a non-aligned bipartition, neither of which the framework specifies.
Section 7.7 proposes a dissolution of the cosmological constant problem
by identifying the emergent quantum vacuum energy and the effective
cosmological constant as properties of logically distinct descriptions
rather than commensurable quantities whose \(10^{122}\) ratio requires
