cancellation; the descriptive distinction is established, and the
dissolution is conditional on the covariant coupling step that {[}GR
§6.2{]} leaves open. Section 7.8 presents the conditional near-null Type
II reading. Section 7.9 develops the Hubble-volume normalization and the
conditional displacement law.

The three tiers of Chapter 4 distinguish the horizon normalizations,
their cosmological application and quantities depending on the specific
dynamics. The classical temperature uses the horizon first law and
boundary count. The calibration of \(\hbar\), \(\epsilon\) and the
\(1/4\) coefficient adds H-count, H-slope on identified transitions, the
horizon and frame conditions, local boost structure, and symmetric
detailed-balance rates. Interpreting the dark-sector budget requires a
physical source and the supplied baryon fraction. The MOND scale and
crossover require the de Sitter temperature, heat input and the imported
factor from Verlinde. The interpolation profile and Hawking greybody
factors require further dynamical results.

The action-scale relation holds for any horizon construction meeting its
thermal and counting conditions. It gives
\(\epsilon=2\sqrt{\sigma}\,l_p\) through the definition of the Planck
length, with \(2l_p\) at one nat per boundary mode.

\hypertarget{the-cosmological-horizon-as-causal-partition}{%
\subsection{7.2 The cosmological horizon as causal
partition}\label{the-cosmological-horizon-as-causal-partition}}

A worldline with a cosmological event horizon supplies a candidate
visible--hidden cut. The visible region is within causal reach of the
observer. The physical memory-bearing application requires the
additional conditions below.

Observers within each other's horizons can have different causal pasts.
In the calibration the area and surface gravity cancel. Horizons
satisfying the same calibration conditions share the action scale when
\(c\), \(G\) and \(\epsilon^2/\sigma\) agree.

\textbf{C1 (coupling).} The Hamiltonian and momentum constraints
correlate interior and exterior initial data. A horizon boundary term
can depend on both sets of data, motivating a candidate coupling. C1
requires hidden-to-visible influence on an accessible conditional, which
the constraint correlations alone do not establish. {[}GR §2.2{]}

\textbf{C2 (memory persistence).} The slow-bath example assumes a hidden
mixing time \(\tau_B\sim H^{-1}\sim10^{17}\) s. A laboratory scale
\(\tau_S\sim10^{-15}\) s then gives \(\tau_S/\tau_B\sim10^{-32}\).

\textbf{C3 (sufficient capacity).} The count \(N_H=A/\epsilon^2\) gives
order \(10^{122}\) boundary modes at the one-nat calibration. The
capacity estimate compares that count with the demand of a specified
laboratory register.

\textbf{Status of C4 (history readback).} A hidden-sector record of
visible history would need to affect later visible conditionals within
the accessible window. That routing is not presently discharged at the
cosmological cut.

The calibration uses H-count, H-slope on identified transitions, the
horizon and frame conditions, local boost structure and symmetric
detailed-balance rates. Cosmological readback is a separate realization
condition. The eigenstate thermalization hypothesis motivates the mixing
assumption in the slow-bath example.

\hypertarget{the-emergent-action-scale-hbar}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{7.3 The emergent action scale
\(\hbar\)}{7.3 The emergent action scale \textbackslash hbar}}\label{the-emergent-action-scale-hbar}}

The most distinctive content of the framework's gravitational sector is
the treatment of Planck's constant \(\hbar\) as an emergent action scale
whose relation to the boundary geometry is fixed by the cosmological
horizon's thermodynamics. The standard view treats \(\hbar\) as a
fundamental constant of nature, its value
\(1.055 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s}\) measured. The framework
derives \(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2 / (4G\sigma)\) from thermal
self-consistency between classical horizon thermodynamics and the
emergent quantum field theory on the horizon --- with \(\sigma\) the
entropy of one boundary mode and \(\epsilon\) the discreteness scale of
the substratum partition, fixed by self-consistency in Section 7.4 to
\(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\, l_p\); the two relations together fix only
the ratio \(\epsilon/\sqrt{\sigma} = 2\,l_p\), a self-consistency
condition rather than an independent determination of the value of
\(\hbar\).

The derivation proceeds in four steps.

\textbf{Step 1 (classical horizon temperature).} The calibration uses
the bifurcate Killing horizon of exact de Sitter, where the event and
apparent horizons agree. With the supplied Einstein first-law relation
\(dE=(c^2\kappa/8\pi G)\,dA\) and one mode of entropy \(\sigma\) per
area \(\epsilon^2\), the classical temperature is
\[k_B T_{\text{cl}} = \frac{c^2 \epsilon^2 \kappa}{8\pi G \sigma}.\]
Under H-count the total system is finite (A1), and the energy-dependent
entropy of the conserved energy shell is the boundary count. The
counting derivative gives \(\beta_E=1/(k_BT_{\rm cl})\). The
corresponding matching in dynamical FLRW remains open. {[}GR §2.3{]}

\textbf{An independent route to Einstein's equations.} Einstein's
equations would follow for the framework's emergent matter, given the
single-cone structure qualified below, from an external theorem with an
entirely different axiom base. The gravitational closure program of
Düll, Schuller, Stritzelberger and Wolz (Phys. Rev.~D 97, 084036) shows
that for matter field equations whose causal structure is that of
standard-model fields on a single Lorentzian light cone --- the class
the framework's emergent sector occupies if its single-cone structure
holds, that structure being supported by the rotational-protection
results of the companion papers, conditional on loop-level octahedral
invariance and an aligned condensate (Chapter 19 §19.3.7), and by the
symmetric-point universality of the block cones under H-blind ({[}SM
§4.4{]}) --- the requirement that matter and geometry evolve together
consistently, independently of how spacetime is sliced, forces the
gravitational action to be Einstein--Hilbert with a cosmological
constant. No thermodynamics enters that argument at all. Where the
closure route leaves Newton's constant and the cosmological constant
undetermined, the framework's relation ℏ = c³ε²/(4Gσ) and the
dark-energy analysis of the following sections take over. The closure
theorem is, moreover, one of a family of such necessity results that the
emergent sector inherits: Lovelock's theorem, which shows that in four
dimensions the only second-order, generally covariant dynamics for a
metric alone is Einstein's with a cosmological constant, and the spin-2
results of Weinberg and Deser, which show that a massless spin-two
particle coupled to a complete matter sector is forced into universal
coupling and Einstein's theory at low energy. Each of these routes would
deliver Einstein's dynamics from hypotheses the framework has not
established --- the emergent light cone, the massless spin-two bound
state, the absence of extra light gravitational modes --- and they
answer the standard objection facing every emergent-spacetime program,
that such constructions deliver the geometry of spacetime but never
Einstein's dynamics, only once those hypotheses are established. The
thermodynamic derivation of this chapter uses Einstein's equations
through Jacobson's relation and does not derive them; the covariant
field equations remain open (Chapter 19 §19.2). The behaviour of the
framework's small lattice corrections under the closure machinery
remains an open consistency check.

\textbf{Step 2: Boundary-only dependence.} The visible transition data
from which the emergent quantum field theory on the horizon is
reconstructed depend only on the hidden degrees of freedom within the
visible sector's causal cone over the elapsed time, a layer whose depth
grows with \(t\), and not on the deep content of the hidden sector
beyond it (Appendix B.4). They depend at leading order only on the
boundary modes --- the degrees of freedom at the horizon itself ---
under a posited bound on the deep sector's influence on the boundary
layer, H-BD, with influence time \(\tau_{BD}\): the corrections are then
of order \(t/\tau_{BD}\), which is \(10^{-32}\) for laboratory processes
when \(\tau_{BD} \gtrsim 1/H\), a value that is not derived, and for the
framework's linear update the bound with an influence time longer than
two update steps holds only if the deep sector does not act on the
boundary at all ({[}GR §3.2{]}). The transition data fix the emergent
dynamics in units of inverse time but not the action scale that converts
it to energy, so this step does not bear on \(\hbar\): with Step 3 it is
a consistency check, and the calibration of Step 4 fixes \(\hbar\).

\textbf{Step 3 (dimensional analysis of \(\hbar\)).} The cancellation of
surface gravity in Step 4 leaves \(c\), \(\epsilon\) and \(G\) as
dimensional inputs. Their unique combination with units of action is
\(c^3\epsilon^2/G\). The normalization follows from the thermal
matching.

\textbf{Step 4 (thermal self-consistency).} On exact de Sitter the KMS
frequency scale is set by the Euclidean period \(\tau_K=2\pi c/\kappa\)
under the stated horizon and state conditions. The corresponding
temperature is \(k_BT_Q=\hbar/\tau_K\). The calibration itself uses the
infrared slope H-slope.

The frequency slope is matched to the classical energy slope \(\beta_E\)
for the same operational transitions under H-count. Thus
\(\beta_E\hbar=\tau_K\), or \(T_{\rm cl}=T_Q\) in temperature units:
\[\frac{c^2 \epsilon^2 \kappa}{8\pi G \sigma} = \frac{\hbar \kappa}{2\pi c}.\]
The common surface gravity \(\kappa\) cancels. Solving gives
\[\boxed{\hbar = \frac{c^3 \epsilon^2}{4G\sigma}}.\]

The derivation has the structure of a gap equation: \(\epsilon\) is the
free geometric input, \(\hbar\) is the output. H-count supplies the
classical energy slope and H-slope the frequency slope for the same
operational transitions. The \(1/4\) coefficient in Section 7.5 inherits
these conditions. One prerequisite of the KMS step is carried
explicitly: Euclidean regularity at a bifurcate Killing horizon
presupposes local boost structure in the emergent description at the
horizon, so the gap equation is partially downstream of the boost
sector's protection mechanism: the symmetric-point matching under
H-blind ({[}SM §4.4{]}) and, conditional on it, the \(M_X\)-controlled
running tracked in the Lorentz-sector accounting ({[}GR §8.5{]}). At the
normalized \(d=3\) observer level the free massless branch supplies the
common infrared cone at the symmetric matching point under H-blind
({[}SM §4.4{]}); exact all-momentum boost invariance is not claimed ---
the unit-Courant cone of the one-dimensional discrete wave equation does
not carry to the three-dimensional observer branch, and away from the
body diagonals the cone holds only in the infrared ({[}GR §8.5{]}).
Conditional on that matching, the custodial symmetry forbids a
condensate-independent sector-differential counterterm, and an
interacting cross-charged calculation, reported in the companion paper
and not independently verified, gave the running a
quadratic-with-logarithm form decoupling as \((M_X/M_{\text{Pl}})^2\),
with the non-logarithmic constant that loop's own, the substratum's
component-local nonlinearity contributing only to the universal cone.
The one item shared with the Lorentz-sector accounting is that reported
running calculation; on its reported form the cross-charged mass \(M_X\)
would sit in an illustrative window of roughly two to four decades, kept
open from below by the baryon safety of the cross-charged sector, which
is of the proton-safe leptoquark class rather than the grand-unified
kind. The gap equation gives \(\hbar\) in terms of \(\epsilon\) and
\(\sigma\) on this branch.

\textbf{One boundary mode per area \(\epsilon^2\),
\(\eta = \sigma/\epsilon^2\), fixes \(\epsilon\); the internal
components fix its relation to the lattice.} The entropy-density
argument in Step 1 used \(dS = \sigma\,dA/\epsilon^2\) --- one boundary
mode per area \(\epsilon^2\). This counting fixes \(\epsilon\), the
horizon area per boundary mode being \(\epsilon^2\), rather than adding
an ansatz about the mode density. Two potential multiplicities are
settled separately. The number of internal \emph{states} per mode (the
alphabet size \(q\)) does not change the mode count; it bounds the
entropy \(\sigma\) of a mode, \(\sigma \leq \ln q\), and the
alphabet-size hypothesis of Chapter 5 does not fix \(\sigma\); the
numerical values of this chapter rest on the assumption \(\sigma = 1\),
one nat per boundary mode, which the bound makes unavailable for a
single mode with \(q = 2\). The Bekenstein-Hawking coefficient does not
depend on \(\sigma\), which cancels from the entropy law and enters only
the relation between \(\epsilon\) and the Planck length,
\(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\,l_p\) ({[}GR §3.1, §4{]}). The number of
internal \emph{components} per site (\(K = 2d = 6\)) is physical and
enters through the link count. On the single-link reading, in which the
\(K = 2d\) components are the \(2d\) link directions, each coupling
across exactly one link (not derived from the substratum dynamics, {[}SM
§4.5{]}), a horizon patch with unit normal \(\mathbf n\) is crossed by
\(\lvert n_1\rvert+\lvert n_2\rvert+\lvert n_3\rvert\) links per square
of the lattice spacing: one for a patch orthogonal to a lattice axis,
\(\tfrac32\) on average over a sphere. On the spherical horizon,
therefore, \(\epsilon^2\) is two thirds of the squared lattice spacing,
and the lattice spacing is \(\sqrt{6\sigma}\,l_p\) ({[}GR §3.1{]}); one
mode per area \(\epsilon^2\) does not establish one nat per mode.

The counting also sits at the intersection of an independent family of
results: the Bekenstein bound and Bousso's covariant entropy bound each
cap the entropy of a region by its boundary area in Planck units ---
area-law mode counting reached from quantum field theory and from
light-sheet geometry respectively. One caution keeps the logic clean:
those bounds are formulated with \(\hbar\) already in hand, and the
framework derives \(\hbar\) downstream of this counting, so the family
can serve only as downstream convergence --- the emergent theory, once
\(\hbar = c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\) is fixed, satisfies both bounds ---
and never as motivation for the counting, which stands on the
definitional argument above alone. Citing the bounds as motivation would
re-import the circularity that the definitional argument removed.

\textbf{The consequences of the gap equation.} Given \(\epsilon\), the
gap equation fixes \(\hbar\); the specific relationship
\(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2 / (4G\sigma)\) then enters three later results.
In Section 7.5 it enters the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy
\(S = A/(4 l_p^2)\) with the factor \(1/4\). In Section 7.7 it enters
the de Sitter entropy \(S_{\text{dS}}\) as the compression ratio of the
conditional cosmological constant dissolution. In Section 7.8 it enters
the Type II running-vacuum reading of the dark energy. The three
relations share the calibration; they are consequences of it, not
independent checks of it. The situation is analogous to deriving the
Schwarzschild metric with mass \(M\) as a free parameter: the derivation
has genuine content (the functional form of the metric) even though one
input is not determined from within the derivation.

The framework's relation to Jacobson's original derivation deserves
explicit comment. Jacobson's argument {[}Phys. Rev.~Lett. 75, 1260
(1995){]} uses \(\hbar\)-containing forms throughout; the present
derivation does not --- it uses the classical identity
\(dE = (c^2 \kappa / 8\pi G)\,dA\) and the classical entropy density
\(\eta = \sigma/\epsilon^2\). The logical ordering differs from
Jacobson's: his argument derives \(G\) from \(\eta\) and \(\hbar\); the
present argument takes \(G\) as a parameter of the classical Hamiltonian
and derives \(\hbar\) from \(G\) and \(\epsilon\). The two are
consistent on the spherical horizon --- substituting
\(\eta = \sigma/\epsilon^2\) and \(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\)
into Jacobson's relation \(G_{\text{eff}} = c^3/(4\eta\hbar)\) recovers
\(G_{\text{eff}} = G\), with \(\sigma\) cancelling --- but the roles of
input and output are reversed. On a planar patch with unit normal
\(\mathbf n\) the link density of Section 7.3 gives
\(G_{\text{eff}}(\mathbf n) = 3G/\big(2(\lvert n_1\rvert+\lvert n_2\rvert+\lvert n_3\rvert)\big)\),
so the relation holds for the area-averaged density of the spherical
horizon (and on patches with
\(\lvert n_1\rvert+\lvert n_2\rvert+\lvert n_3\rvert = \tfrac32\)), not
patch by patch. The Gibbons-Hawking form
\(k_B T_{\text{GH}} = \hbar \kappa / (2\pi c)\) enters as the KMS
temperature of Step 4; the calibration relates the \(\hbar\) in it to
\(\epsilon\) and \(\sigma\) through
\(\hbar = c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\).

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{self-consistency-and-the-discreteness-scale}{%
\subsection{7.4 Self-consistency and the discreteness
scale}\label{self-consistency-and-the-discreteness-scale}}

The gap equation \(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2 / (4G\sigma)\) from Section
7.3 takes \(\epsilon\) as a free geometric parameter --- the
discreteness scale of the substratum partition --- and produces
\(\hbar\) as the output. The framework's content beyond this single
relation requires that \(\epsilon\) itself be determined. The
determination comes from self-consistency with the definition of the
Planck length.

The Planck length \(l_p = \sqrt{\hbar G / c^3}\) is defined as the
unique length scale constructed from \(\hbar\), \(G\), and \(c\).
Substituting the framework's relation
\(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2 / (4G\sigma)\) into this definition:
\[l_p^2 = \frac{\hbar G}{c^3} = \frac{c^3 \epsilon^2}{4G\sigma} \cdot \frac{G}{c^3} = \frac{\epsilon^2}{4\sigma}.\]
Rearranging gives the discreteness scale:
\[\boxed{\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\, l_p.}\]

The result is, for a given \(\sigma\), the unique value of \(\epsilon\)
consistent with the framework's gap equation and the standard definition
of the Planck length. The horizon area per boundary mode is
\(\epsilon^2 = 4\sigma\,l_p^2\), so \(\epsilon\) is \(2\,l_p\), twice
the Planck length, at \(\sigma = 1\); on the single-link reading of
Section 7.3 the lattice spacing is
\(\sqrt{3/2}\,\epsilon = \sqrt{6\sigma}\,l_p\).

Here \(\sigma\) is the entropy of one boundary mode, a dimensionless
number of nats, and the Bekenstein-Hawking coefficient of Section 7.5
does not depend on it ({[}GR §3.1, §4{]}). The alphabet-size hypothesis
of Chapter 5 does not fix \(\sigma\): a mode with \(q\) internal states
carries at most \(\ln q\), so the assumption \(\sigma = 1\), one nat per
boundary mode --- an assumption about the entropy of a mode, not a
choice of units, since entropy is already measured in nats --- is
unavailable for a single mode with \(q = 2\).

\textbf{The self-consistency is algebraically equivalent to the gap
equation.} The framework contains one free geometric parameter;
self-consistency with the Planck length definition fixes its value for a
given \(\sigma\). It adds no relation beyond the structural commitment
\(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2 / (4G\sigma)\) and the definition of \(l_p\),
and its numerical value takes the measured \(\hbar\) as input. The
result is a \emph{constraint} on \(\epsilon\), not an independent
measurement.

\textbf{The discreteness scale and \(\sigma\).} With \(\sigma\)
undetermined, self-consistency fixes only the ratio
\(\epsilon/\sqrt{\sigma} = 2\, l_p\), and a Planck-scale \(\epsilon\)
additionally requires \(\sigma\) of order one. The bound
\(\sigma \leq \ln q\) limits \(\sigma\) from above for a mode with \(q\)
states, but the count bounds it from below only by \(\sigma > 0\):
\(\sigma = 10^{-12}\) would give \(\epsilon = 2 \times 10^{-6}\, l_p\).
The gap equation does not exclude discreteness scales far from the
Planck length; whether they are excluded on independent grounds is open.

The framework's content in the discreteness scale therefore has three
structural commitments: the gap equation, the Planck-length definition,
and the self-consistency between them. The result
\(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\, l_p\) is a derived quantity for a given
\(\sigma\), not a free parameter, with \(\epsilon = 2\,l_p\) at
\(\sigma = 1\), one nat per mode --- but the derivation requires
accepting the gap equation as the substratum's structural commitment
rather than \(\hbar\) as a fundamental constant.

\hypertarget{the-bekenstein-hawking-entropy}{%
\subsection{7.5 The Bekenstein-Hawking
entropy}\label{the-bekenstein-hawking-entropy}}

The Bekenstein-Hawking entropy \(S = A / (4\, l_p^2)\) assigns each
horizon a thermodynamic entropy proportional to its area, with the
proportionality constant \(1/(4\, l_p^2)\). Bekenstein (1973) introduced
the area law with a coefficient he could estimate only heuristically;
Hawking (1975) fixed the \(1/4\) from the Hawking temperature and the
first law, and the semi-classical and stringy microstate arguments
reproduce it. The framework reproduces the same ratio from its horizon
calibration: with the discreteness scale
\(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\, l_p\) fixed in Section 7.4 under the
condition H-slope, the boundary-mode count gives the area law with the
coefficient \(1/4\).

\textbf{Direct mode counting.} With \(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\, l_p\)
from Section 7.4, the number of independent boundary modes on a horizon
of area \(A\) is
\[N_{\text{modes}} = \frac{A}{\epsilon^2} = \frac{A}{4\sigma\, l_p^2}.\]
Each area \(\epsilon^2 = 4\sigma\, l_p^2\) of the horizon carries one
boundary mode of entropy \(\sigma\), giving
\(S = \sigma N_{\text{modes}} = A / (4\, l_p^2)\). This is the
Bekenstein-Hawking entropy in its standard form, and the coefficient
does not depend on \(\sigma\); the mode count
\(N_{\text{modes}} = S/\sigma\) equals the entropy only at
\(\sigma = 1\).

The factor of \(1/4\) is therefore fixed, given
\(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\, l_p\): it is the ratio
\(\epsilon^2 / (\sigma\, l_p^2) = 4\sigma\, l_p^2 / (\sigma\, l_p^2) = 4\)
in the denominator, with the \(\epsilon^2\) factor arising from the
framework's discreteness scale, the \(\sigma\) from the entropy per
mode, and the \(l_p^2\) in the denominator arising from the Planck
length appearing in the definition of \(S_{\text{BH}}\). Equivalently,
the \(1/4\) is the ratio \(2\pi / 8\pi\) between two physical
quantities: the numerator \(2\pi\) is the period of the Euclidean KMS
regularity at the horizon (thermal periodicity of QFT on a Killing
horizon), and the denominator \(8\pi\) is the Jacobson coefficient in
the Einstein-equation prefactor \(dE = (c^2 \kappa / 8\pi G)\, dA\)
(gravity's coupling). The Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) is therefore not an
arbitrary proportionality constant but the consistency condition between
gravitational thermodynamics and quantum thermal physics --- the ratio
that makes the framework's gap equation in Section 7.3 close on itself.

\textbf{Extension to black-hole horizons.} On the single-link lattice
branch, the mode count uses horizons that are spherical in the lattice
frame or have the same area-averaged link density. Applying the \(1/4\)
calibration to a black-hole horizon also requires the corresponding
stationary, state and frame conditions of Sections 7.3--7.4.

\textbf{Classical area test.} Under the classical area theorem's
hypotheses, the remnant horizon area is bounded below by the sum of the
progenitor areas. The waveform can be used to compare those areas.
GW150914 supplied an earlier pre- and post-merger test.
\href{https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.127.011103}{Isi et al.}

The LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA collaborations observed GW250114 on January
14, 2025 and reported the analysis in September. The fiducial comparison
of the inferred Kerr areas supports area increase at \(4.4\sigma\). The
significance depends on the analysis cut and modes used.
\href{https://dcc.ligo.org/public/0201/P2500421/010/GW250114.pdf}{LVK,
Fig. 5}

The gravitational-wave comparison addresses the classical areas. The
entropy coefficient has a separate thermal test. The coefficient, fixed
by the calibration of Section 7.4 as the ratio \(2\pi/8\pi\) between
Euclidean KMS periodicity and the Jacobson Einstein-equation prefactor,
is the ratio of the two normalizations that the calibration matches,
conditional on H-slope, H-count, the horizon and frame conditions, local
boost structure at the horizon and the symmetric detailed-balance rate
ratio ({[}GR §8.5{]}), with no direct empirical test at present. The
coefficient follows from the Hawking-temperature normalization, so a
measured horizon radiation spectrum would fix it. The one contingent
channel is the final evaporation burst of a primordial black hole ---
active all-sky burst searches (Fermi-LAT 2018; HAWC 2020; LHAASO 2025,
PRL 135 181005) have so far set rate-density limits only, with
next-generation sensitivity projected for CTAO; a detected burst light
curve would measure \(T(M)\) and hence the coefficient directly.
Analogue-gravity experiments probe the kinematic side of the
\(2\pi/8\pi\) ratio, not the gravitational side. The ongoing LIGO
observing runs will accumulate additional events testing the area
theorem across a range of progenitor masses and spins.

\textbf{Falsification status.} The Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) is a
consistency relation of the horizon calibration, not a counted Class B
prediction (Chapter 4 §4.5) --- conditional at the universality-class
level, holding under H-slope together with H-count, the horizon and
frame conditions, local boost structure at the horizon and the symmetric
detailed-balance rate ratio on the gap-equation chain (Section 7.1).
Falsification of the coefficient at sufficient confidence to exclude
experimental systematics would refute that chain (the connection between
the classical horizon temperature in Section 7.3 Step 1 and the
Euclidean KMS temperature in Step 4) under those conditions, and with it
the framework's structural commitment to thermal self-consistency at the
partition boundary. The coefficient currently has no direct empirical
test --- GW250114 constrains the classical area theorem, not the entropy
normalization --- the \(a_0 = cH/6\) rotation-curve family (Section 7.9)
is a conditional measured comparison, with agreement within the quoted
systematic uncertainty and the factor \(1/6\) imported.

\hypertarget{the-page-curve-and-the-information-paradox}{%
\subsection{7.6 The Page curve and the information
paradox}\label{the-page-curve-and-the-information-paradox}}

The framework's content in the Bekenstein-Hawking sector extends beyond
the area-law coefficient to the \emph{dynamics} of black hole
evaporation. The black hole information paradox --- Hawking's 1975
observation that semiclassical black hole evaporation appears to destroy
information, in tension with quantum mechanics' commitment to unitarity
--- is one of the canonical hard problems of theoretical physics. The
framework does not resolve the paradox. Information is never lost from
the substratum bijection \(\varphi\) because \(\varphi\) is bijective,
and bijectivity is a premise of the framework's models (Chapter 1), not
a result; how much of that information an observer can recover from the
radiation is a separate question, which bijectivity alone does not
settle. The Page-curve derivation below bears on it under two
conditions, H-scramble and H-decouple, neither of which is established,
and H-scramble fails for every bijection acting on an initial
configuration with the bipartition aligned to the configuration
coordinates. The conditional entropy calculation has its own dynamical
assumptions.

\textbf{The paradox in its conventional form.} Hawking's calculation of
the spectrum of radiation emitted by an evaporating black hole produced
a thermal distribution with a temperature
\(T_H = \hbar \kappa / (2\pi c k_B)\), dependent only on the black
hole's mass and angular momentum. The thermal spectrum carries no
information beyond the macroscopic horizon parameters. If the radiation
is exactly thermal --- as Hawking's semiclassical derivation suggests
--- then the radiation carries no information about the matter that
formed the black hole, and the information appears to be lost when the
black hole completes its evaporation. This is in tension with the
unitarity of quantum mechanics, which requires that any time evolution
preserve information.

The Page curve is the unitarity prediction. Don Page argued in 1993 that
if black hole evaporation is unitary, the entanglement entropy of the
radiation must follow a specific trajectory: rising as radiation
accumulates in the early phase, then turning over and decreasing at the
\emph{Page time} \(t_P\) --- defined as the moment when the radiation's
entanglement entropy equals the remaining black hole's entropy. If the
radiation's entropy equals the horizon entropy it carries off, the Page
time comes when half the black hole's initial entropy has been radiated,
and earlier if the radiation carries more; the curve's turnover is the
empirical signature of unitarity.

The dispute between Hawking's calculation (thermal radiation,
information lost) and Page's prediction (Page curve, information
preserved) was unresolved for decades. The recent
quantum-extremal-surface and entanglement-island programs of Penington,
Almheiri-Engelhardt-Marolf-Maxfield, and others have reproduced the Page
curve through replica wormhole computations in the gravitational path
integral, providing a derivation of the Page curve from semiclassical
gravity. The framework offers a conditional alternative through a
substantially different mechanism: a derivation from the scrambling
condition H-scramble and the decoupling condition H-decouple of {[}GR
Appendix A{]}. Under those conditions, and taking the energy shell of
the black hole and its radiation to be their full product space, the two
derivations give a Page curve of the same form, the framework's as an
average over the cycles of the dynamics; whether they agree on the Page
time depends on the entropy each assigns to the radiation, as set out
below.

\textbf{The observer's description: nested trace-out.} The framework's
substratum is a deterministic bijection \(\varphi\) acting on a
configuration space \(S\), finite under A1. Information is never lost
from \(\varphi\) in the framework's bijective models --- bijectivity is
the framework's structural commitment to unitarity in those models.
Bijectivity of the whole dynamics leaves the radiation's reduced law
open.

The nested calculation considers a cosmological horizon and a black-hole
horizon inside it. The configuration space decomposes as
\[S = \mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_B \times \mathcal{C}_D,\] where
\(V\) is the region between the black hole horizon and the cosmological
horizon (the external observer's visible sector), \(B\) is the black
hole interior (the secondary hidden sector), and \(D\) is the
trans-cosmological region (the primary hidden sector).

On \(V\), both a direct trace over \(B,D\) and a successive trace give
the same channel for one supplied unitary dilation and a shared product
input on \(V,B,D\) ({[}GR Appendix A.2--A.3{]}). Inferring Hamiltonians
from transition data uses the reconstruction hypotheses of {[}GR
§3.3{]}, with the diagonal-unitary, energy-origin and possible
antiunitary freedoms. If the common channel family is exactly unitary,
the generators differ only by a scalar shift. Agreement of \(\hbar\)
also requires each horizon to meet the calibration conditions with
matched \(\epsilon\) and \(\sigma\) ({[}GR Appendix A.4{]}).

\textbf{The Page curve from cycle typicality.} The framework's
derivation of the Page curve does not use the gravitational path
integral: the cycle structure of the bijection \(\varphi\) supplies
exact time averages, and the Page value enters through a typicality
condition on the substratum orbit. The relevant results are Page's mean
entropy (Page 1993) and measure concentration (Popescu, Short \& Winter
2006): for a bipartite quantum system in a Haar-random pure state, with
subsystem dimensions \(d_{\min} \leq d_{\max}\), the entanglement
entropy of the smaller subsystem lies close to Page's mean, about
\(\ln d_{\min} - d_{\min}/(2d_{\max})\) --- within half a nat of the
maximum \(\ln d_{\min}\) when the two dimensions are equal, and closer
as the larger one grows --- with deviations from that mean exponentially
unlikely in the dimension of the smaller subsystem. These results
concern Haar-random states of the full product space; on a proper energy
shell, a subspace fixed by energy conservation, the mean entropy depends
on the shell and in general differs from Page's value, so the derivation
below takes the shell to be the full product space of the black hole and
its radiation, which places no energy constraint on them; an evaporating
black hole whose radiation carries away its energy is the energy-shell
case, and that version is open ({[}GR Appendix A{]}). Applying them to
the substratum requires H-scramble: uniformity over classical
microstates is not uniformity over quantum pure states, and every finite
bijection acting on a definite configuration, with the bipartition
aligned to the configuration coordinates, visits only product states,
however uniformly it counts its energy-shell cycles ({[}GR Appendix
A{]}). H-scramble therefore fails in that setting, which is the one the
derivation counts: its initial conditions are configurations, so there
the derivation has no instance. At a bipartition aligned with the
configuration coordinates, the entanglement entropy a bijection produces
never exceeds, at any step, the entropy of the initial state's
distribution over configurations ({[}GR Appendix A{]}); a Page value
therefore requires an initial superposition over at least about
\(e^{S_{\text{Page}}}\) configurations, with \(S_{\text{Page}}\) Page's
mean entropy, or a bipartition not aligned with them. Which of these, if
either, the substratum supplies is open, and the condition is not
established.

Applied to the evaporating black hole, the relevant bipartite structure
is the radiation field outside the black hole versus the boundary modes
remaining at the shrinking horizon. Let \(n_B(t)\) denote the number of
boundary modes remaining at the horizon at time \(t\), and
\(n_R(t) = n_B(0) - n_B(t)\) the number of modes radiated. Conservation
gives \(n_B(t) + n_R(t) = n_B(0)\) --- the total number of modes is
fixed by the initial black hole entropy,
\(n_B(0) = S_{\text{BH}}(0)/\sigma\).

Under H-scramble, which carries Popescu-Short-Winter measure
concentration from the Haar ensemble to the orbit of the bijection on
the full product space of the black hole and its radiation, and under
the decoupling condition H-decouple of {[}GR Appendix A{]}, which treats
the black hole and its radiation as a closed system in a pure joint
state, the radiation's entanglement entropy, averaged over full cycles
of the dynamics at the bipartition of time \(t\), is approximately
\[\overline{S}_{\text{rad}}(t) = \min(n_R(t), n_B(t)) \cdot \ln q,\]
where \(q\) is the substratum's alphabet size, so that the state space
of one mode has dimension \(q\), with a correction of at most about half
a nat, reached at the turnover and exponentially small in
\(|n_R(t) - n_B(t)|\) away from it. Whether the entropy along a single
trajectory, whose bipartition moves with \(t\), follows the same curve
is open. The structure has two regimes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Early phase} (\(n_R(t) < n_B(t)\)): radiation has fewer modes
  than the remaining black hole; entropy rises as \(n_R(t) \ln q\).
\item
  \emph{Late phase} (\(n_R(t) > n_B(t)\)): radiation has more modes than
  the remaining black hole; entropy falls as \(n_B(t) \ln q\).
\end{itemize}

The turnover --- the Page time \(t_P\) --- occurs at
\(n_R(t_P) = n_B(t_P) = n_B(0)/2\), when half the initial boundary modes
have been radiated. Under the evaporation law \(dM/dt = -\alpha/M^2\),
with a mass-independent coefficient \(\alpha\) into which the species
content and the greybody factors enter ({[}GR Appendix A{]}), the mode
count falls as \(n_B(t) = n_B(0)\,(1 - t/t_{\text{evap}})^{2/3}\), and
the Page time is
\[t_P = (1 - 2^{-3/2})\, t_{\text{evap}} \approx 0.646\, t_{\text{evap}},\]
independent of the black hole's mass and of \(\alpha\).

The greybody factors enter a second time, through the entropy the
radiation carries. The conservation law \(n_B(t) + n_R(t) = n_B(0)\)
gives the radiation one mode of dimension \(q\) for each boundary mode
the horizon loses, so the radiation's state-space entropy grows by
exactly the amount the horizon's falls. More generally, write \(\beta\)
for the ratio of the radiation's gain in state-space entropy to the
horizon's loss, taken constant along the evaporation; when each mode
carries \(\sigma = \ln q\), \(\beta\) is the radiation's coarse-grained
entropy per unit of Bekenstein-Hawking entropy lost. The turnover falls
where
\(\beta\,[S_{\text{BH}}(0) - S_{\text{BH}}(t_P)] = S_{\text{BH}}(t_P)\),
and the same evaporation law gives (Page 2013, Eq. (8))
\[\frac{t_P}{t_{\text{evap}}} = 1 - \left(\frac{\beta}{1+\beta}\right)^{3/2},\]
which is \(0.646\) at \(\beta = 1\) and falls as \(\beta\) grows:
\(0.568\) at \(\beta = 4/3\), the value for unfiltered blackbody
emission of massless quanta. In the quasi-stationary semiclassical
regime --- a non-rotating, uncharged black hole emitting free fields
into empty space (incoming vacuum), outgoing modes in independent
thermal-form states with mean occupation
\(N = \Gamma\, n_{\text{th}}(\omega/T_H)\) for greybody factors
\(0 < \Gamma \leq 1\), and \(dS_{\text{BH}} = dE/T_H\) --- every emitted
mode carries more entropy than its energy divided by the Hawking
temperature, so \(\beta > 1\) in that regime (Page 2005, Eqs. (5)--(10);
{[}GR Appendix A{]}); its value depends on the species content and on
how the greybody factors vary with frequency --- solution-specific
content, Tier 3 in the sense of Section 7.1. For a large Schwarzschild
black hole emitting only photons and gravitons, at constant \(\alpha\),
Page's emission rates give \(\beta \approx 1.485\) and
\(t_P \approx 0.538\, t_{\text{evap}}\) (Page 2013, Eqs. (2), (8)). The
Page time \(0.646\, t_{\text{evap}}\) is therefore conditional on
\(\beta = 1\) as well as on H-scramble and H-decouple: the mode-for-mode
conservation law sets \(\beta = 1\), the semiclassical regime just
defined has \(\beta > 1\), and how much state-space entropy the
radiation acquires per boundary mode lost is open.

\textbf{Comparison with quantum extremal surfaces and islands.} The
quantum extremal surface formula and the entanglement-island
construction developed by Penington, Almheiri-Engelhardt, and others
obtain the Page curve by a different route. In the QES approach, the
Page curve emerges through an extremization principle that selects the
dominant saddle in a replica-trick computation of the radiation's
entanglement entropy. The post-Page-time saddle includes an
\emph{island} --- a region of bulk spacetime that contributes to the
radiation's entanglement entropy despite being topologically
disconnected from the radiation region. The replica wormhole geometries
connecting the replicas in the gravitational path integral are essential
to obtaining the saturating Page curve at late times.

The framework arrives at a cycle-averaged Page curve of the same form
--- rise, turnover, fall --- through a substantially different
mechanism. The cycle-typicality argument applies Popescu-Short-Winter
measure concentration to the deterministic substratum dynamics on the
full product space of the black hole and its radiation, under the
scrambling condition H-scramble and the decoupling condition H-decouple
of {[}GR Appendix A{]} --- uniformity over classical microstates is not
uniformity over quantum pure states, and neither condition is
established --- with no replica trick and no gravitational path
integral. In the QES computation the turnover comes where the island
saddle's generalized entropy, at leading order the black hole's
remaining Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, falls below the semiclassical
entropy of the radiation. The two Page times coincide when that
semiclassical entropy grows one-for-one with the horizon entropy lost,
the \(\beta = 1\) of the mode counting; in the semiclassical regime
defined above \(\beta > 1\) holds (Page 2005; for the QES setting,
Penington 2019, §2), so agreement between the two derivations on the
Page time and the Page entropy is not established. A correspondence
between the two constructions is conjectured: the \emph{island} in the
QES formulation would correspond to the post-Page-time regime in which
the black hole's boundary modes form the smaller subsystem, and the
\emph{replica wormhole} geometries to the substratum's cycle structure
on the energy shell.

This conjectured correspondence --- replica wormholes
\(\leftrightarrow\) substratum cycles --- is suggestive but not yet
rigorous. Making it precise would require constructing the gravitational
path integral as an effective description of the substratum dynamics in
the appropriate limit, a task that has not been completed. What the
framework's derivation establishes is conditional: under H-scramble and
H-decouple and with the full product space as the energy shell, a
cycle-averaged Page curve with its turnover where the radiation's state
space overtakes the black hole's follows without the replica machinery.
The Page value enters through H-scramble, not through the finite
deterministic dynamics, which from an initial configuration produces no
entanglement across an aligned bipartition and, across such a
bipartition, from any initial state at most the entropy of its
distribution over configurations. The open steps include the scrambling
condition, the decoupling condition, the value on a proper energy shell,
whether the entropy along a single trajectory follows the cycle-averaged
curve, and the radiation's entropy per boundary mode lost.

Both approaches require \emph{something} to play the role of typicality
--- Popescu-Short-Winter measure concentration in the framework's
derivation, replica saddles in QES + islands --- and both place the
turnover where the radiation's entropy reaches the black hole's
remaining entropy. If the conjectured correspondence holds, the
typicality-providing ingredient need not be gravitational at all, and
the cycle-typicality derivation would be a microscopic realization of
the entanglement-island construction; on the substratum side the
bijection alone does not supply that ingredient, since the entanglement
it can produce across an aligned bipartition is bounded by the entropy
of the initial distribution over configurations.

\textbf{The generalized second law.} A separate but related statement is
the generalized second law: the sum
\(S_{\text{matter}} + S_{\text{BH}} + S_{\text{dS}}\) is non-decreasing
in time. The matter entropy \(S_{\text{matter}}\) captures the
visible-sector matter's information content; the black hole entropy
\(S_{\text{BH}}\) is the horizon area divided by \(4\, l_p^2\); the de
Sitter entropy \(S_{\text{dS}}\) is the cosmological horizon's
contribution.

The nested dynamics gives a bound relative to a product state.
Bijectivity makes the evolution of the whole configuration space
unitary, so the joint von Neumann entropy of the visible sector \(V\),
the black hole interior \(B\) and the trans-cosmological region \(D\) is
constant. If the state at \(t = 0\) is a product over the three sectors,
subadditivity then gives
\[S(\rho_V(t)) + S(\rho_B(t)) + S(\rho_D(t)) \geq S(\rho_V(0)) + S(\rho_B(0)) + S(\rho_D(0))\]
at each time, including when the degrees of freedom are regrouped into
three sectors as the horizon moves. The inequality concerns the sectors'
von Neumann entropies. A generalized second law requires both an
identification of horizon and sector entropies and monotonicity between
times. This inequality bounds the sum relative to one product state in
both time directions. It allows the sum to rise and then fall. The
boundary-mode count does not supply the entropy identification:
\(S_{\text{BH}} = n_B\,\sigma\) counts the horizon's modes, while in the
Page-curve derivation above, where the black hole and its radiation
share a pure state, the black hole's reduced entropy equals the
radiation's and is at most \(n_R \ln q\) --- near zero early in the
evaporation, when \(S_{\text{BH}}\) is largest. Relative entropy is
contractive under a CPTP map. Separately, the von Neumann entropy of the
output is at least that of the input for every input only when the
channel is unital, and then it constrains \(S_{\text{matter}}\) alone,
not the horizon terms. A derivation of the generalized second law from
the substratum requires the area--entropy relation and monotonicity of
the combined sum. Conservation of information at the substratum level
rests, in the framework's models, on bijectivity alone and does not wait
on the generalized second law; how much of that information the observer
can recover from the radiation is the separate question the Page-curve
derivation addresses, under its own conditions.

\textbf{Empirical status and falsification.} The framework's account of
the information paradox has no direct empirical signature accessible at
current experimental precision --- black hole evaporation timescales for
astrophysical black holes vastly exceed the age of the universe, and the
Page time for a stellar-mass black hole would not occur within any
conceivable observational program. The bijective models preserve
information in the whole system. The Page-time formula concerns the
conditional radiation calculation.

Bijective dynamics is compatible with radiation that carries less
information than the matter that formed it, the remainder being held in
sectors the observer does not read, and the nested trace-out identity
holds with the common dilation and state above; a measurement of the
radiation alone therefore does not test the conservation claim, which
rests on bijectivity as a premise of the framework's models (Chapter 1).
The QES + islands computations, which obtain a unitary Page curve from
semiclassical gravity by an independent route, support unitary
evaporation without depending on the framework. The framework's content
is therefore consistent with the current theoretical and (limited)
empirical picture. Its quantitative target is the Page-time relation
\(t_P/t_{\text{evap}} = 1 - [\beta/(1+\beta)]^{3/2}\), which becomes a
sharp prediction once the radiation's entropy per boundary mode lost is
derived; at the mode-counting value \(\beta = 1\) it gives \(0.646\).

\hypertarget{dissolution-of-the-cosmological-constant-problem}{%
\subsection{7.7 Dissolution of the cosmological constant
problem}\label{dissolution-of-the-cosmological-constant-problem}}

The cosmological constant problem is conventionally described as the
worst quantitative discrepancy in physics. Quantum field theory predicts
that the vacuum energy density of the universe should be of order
\(\rho_{\text{QFT}} \sim M_{\text{Pl}}^4 \sim 10^{113}\,\text{J/m}^3\),
obtained by summing zero-point energies \(\frac{1}{2}\hbar\omega\) over
all field modes up to the Planck cutoff. The observed vacuum energy
density is \(\rho_{\text{obs}} \sim H^2/G \sim 10^{-9}\,\text{J/m}^3\),
with the ratio \(\rho_{\text{QFT}} / \rho_{\text{obs}} \sim 10^{122}\).
Standard accounts treat this as a fine-tuning problem requiring an
unknown cancellation mechanism to suppress the bare vacuum energy by 122
decimal places, re-imposed at each order of perturbation theory.

The zero-point sum and the supplied cosmological density enter different
descriptions. A dissolution of the gravitational discrepancy requires a
covariant coupling that decouples a common zero-point offset. That step
belongs to G3. {[}GR §6.2{]}

\textbf{The two levels of description.} The framework's structural
commitments produce two distinct descriptions of the universe's energy
content, operating at logically different levels.

\emph{The supplied classical background} has critical density
\(\rho_{\rm crit}=3H^2c^2/(8\pi G)\) in the flat Friedmann model. The
observed vacuum density is the supplied fraction
\(\Omega_\Lambda\rho_{\rm crit}\). Its native source remains open.

\emph{The emergent quantum field theory} assigns zero-point energy to
its modes. On the stated lattice branch the cutoff
\(M_{\rm Pl}/\sqrt{6\sigma}\) gives the order of magnitude
\(\rho_{\rm QFT}\sim M_{\rm Pl}^4\) when \(\sigma\) is of order one. A
uniform shift in the emergent generator leaves the ordinary transition
probabilities invariant. Relative differences, such as those measured in
Casimir forces, compare physical configurations. The gravitational
response requires the source map that relates the complete preparations
to stress or flux.

Which differences in the emergent energies source curvature depends on
the physical coupling.

\textbf{The proposed gravitational coupling.} The designated trace-out
takes a classical metric to define its causal partition. The proposed
Einstein dynamics would couple to the stress of the complete
pre-trace-out configurations. The native local stress or flux map
remains open.

The following conditions concern this particular trace-out and
calibration.

\emph{Definiteness.} The marginalization uses a specified partition
\(\Gamma=\Gamma_V\times\Gamma_H\) (Chapter 1). The horizon application
uses the cut supplied by the classical metric.

\emph{Non-circularity.} The causal cut uses the metric's null geodesics.
Deriving that metric solely from the output of the same trace-out would
leave its own input unspecified. An independently grounded metric can
supply the cut.

\emph{Action-scale calibration.} The matched thermal slopes in §7.3
refer to the same transitions. The calibrated action scale is shared by
horizons that match the counting and other calibration conditions.

On a common metric with a fixed physical reference, a common vacuum
offset cancels in the difference of complete conserved stress tensors.
The weak-field response retains the total energy difference, including
contributions from supports and reservoirs. The physical reference,
native stress or flux map, and response to physical vacuum changes
remain open. {[}GR §6.2{]}

\textbf{What the ordering does not yet fix.} The supplied metric at the
partition boundary leaves open the gravitational field of a laboratory
mass that the observer's description places in a spatial superposition.
Three completions are consistent with them. In the first, the field
follows the substratum configuration of the mass. In the second, the
field follows an average over the hidden sector, which is semiclassical
gravity at laboratory scales. In the third, the laboratory near field
belongs to the emergent quantum description and the classical metric of
the ordering is the metric at the partition boundary only; two masses
can then become entangled through gravity. What each completion implies
for the coherence of the superposition is not derived. Two outcomes must
be kept apart: environmental decoherence, in which which-path records
pass to unobserved degrees of freedom such as emitted radiation while
the total evolution stays unitary, which any of the completions may
produce; and an additional nonunitary effect, of the kind Chapter 4 §4.5
lists among the framework's falsifiers. The framework has not determined
which completion holds, or whether any produces the second outcome.
Fixing the completion and deriving its consequences for interferometric
tests of gravitationally mediated entanglement and for searches for
gravitational decoherence ({[}GR §6.2{]}) is what turns the
geometry-first ordering into a laboratory prediction.

\textbf{The structural origin of the \(10^{122}\) discrepancy.} The
ratio
\(\rho_{\text{QFT}} / \rho_{\text{classical}} \sim M_{\text{Pl}}^4 / (H^2 / G) \sim S_{\text{dS}} = A / (4\, l_p^2)\)
is a dimensional identity for any theory with a Planck cutoff and a
Hubble-scale density, holding up to a convention-dependent factor. The
framework reads it as the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of the cosmological
horizon in its role, identified by Section 7.5, as the
information-compression ratio of the trace-out from substratum to
emergent description; on that reading, and conditional on the coupling
step, the ``worst prediction in physics'' is the entropy of the
observer's blind spot.

The identification holds up to a convention-dependent numerical factor:
the numerator depends on where the emergent sum is cut off, at the
lattice scale \(M_{\text{Pl}}/\sqrt{6\sigma}\) in natural units or at
another Planck-scale cutoff, and on how the zero-point integral is
normalized, and the denominator on which classical density is compared.
\(M_{\text{Pl}}^4\) against \(H^2/G\) gives \(S_{\text{dS}}/\pi\); the
mode sum \(k^4/(16\pi^2)\) cut off at the lattice scale against the
critical density \(\rho_{\text{crit}}\) gives
\(S_{\text{dS}}/(216\pi^2\sigma^2)\); the conventional estimate, a mode
sum \(k^4/(16\pi^2)\) cut off at the reduced Planck mass
\((8\pi G)^{-1/2}\), against the observed dark-energy density
\(\Omega_\Lambda\rho_{\text{crit}}\) gives
\(S_{\text{dS}}/(384\pi^4\Omega_\Lambda) \approx 3.9\times10^{-5}\,S_{\text{dS}}\).
The \(10^{122}\) factor itself is the de Sitter entropy
\(S_{\text{dS}} = A_{\text{horizon}} / (4\, l_p^2)\) at the present
cosmological horizon, computed from the observed horizon area combined
with the framework's entropy formula. The factor that the conventional
QFT view treats as a discrepancy requiring cancellation is, on the
framework's reading, the information-compression ratio of the trace-out
from substratum to emergent description.

No embedded observer can determine from within whether the geometric or
the quantum description is more fundamental, and not merely as a matter
of present ignorance. Any adjudication procedure available to an
embedded observer is a function of the observer's accessible data, and
both descriptions are constructed from the same accessible data --- so
no criterion grounded in the accessible observations themselves can
separate them. (Rankings by theoretical virtue --- simplicity,
unification --- are not blocked by this factoring; but they order
presentations of the same observational content rather than track
fundamentality, and the framework's answer to the fundamentality
question is supplied at the substratum level rather than adjudicated
from within either description.) The non-adjudicability follows from the
equivalence itself, not from limited resources: a future observation
could break the equivalence, but that would be falsification of the
equivalence, not adjudication between the descriptions. Nor is this
factoring limitation an artifact of the framework's particular observer
architecture. Wolpert's limits of inference and T. Breuer's
self-measurement theorem establish barriers of the same type for any
embedded inference device under far weaker assumptions, corroborating
that the limitation is device-general rather than model-specific ---
with the scope note that those results, unlike the factoring argument,
assume free availability of the device's setups. The framework's content
here is not to identify the geometric description as ``more real'' but
to read the \(10^{122}\) factor as the compression ratio between the two
descriptions; the observed density itself is of the Friedmann scale
\(H^2/G\), as any \(O(1)\) component of a flat universe is, and its
value is an input.

\textbf{Convergence with the de Sitter observer literature.} The
framework's geometry-first dissolution converges with recent
developments in the de Sitter observer literature, in which an
unphysical phase of the de Sitter sphere partition function --- long
understood to obstruct a clean dS thermodynamic interpretation ---
cancels exactly when the formalism incorporates an observer with a
clock. Maldacena established the cancellation in 2024; Chandrasekaran,
Longo, Penington, and Witten (CLPW) showed that the von Neumann algebra
of QFT observables in a gravitational subregion promotes from type III
to type II once an observer is included, with the resulting entropy
pinned to the observer's reference data. Harlow, Usatyuk, and Zhao
established that the closed-universe Hilbert-space dimension is
determined by the observer's degrees of freedom.

The framework shares the starting point of these results: the partition
trace-out is the \emph{defining} operation rather than an added
ingredient, so the observer is present from the outset. It does not
reproduce the results themselves. It computes neither the phase of the
sphere partition function nor a type II algebra. Its observable algebra
on each finite region is a full matrix algebra, and its infinite-region
completion is a quasilocal \(C^{*}\)-algebra with no state or
representation selected ({[}GR §3.3{]}); no von Neumann closure of it,
no relation to CLPW's observer-dressed algebra and no identification of
CLPW's entropy with a substratum quantity is derived. Whether the
construction reproduces CLPW's algebra and its entropy, and whether its
trace-out yields Maldacena's cancellation, are open research questions.
The observer-essentiality literature converges with the framework on
that starting point while differing in mechanism. Chapter 9 develops the
framework's relationship to this literature in detail.

\textbf{The classical vacuum energy scale.} The reference cosmology
supplies \(\Omega_\Lambda\) and the Friedmann scale, giving the observed
vacuum contribution \(\Omega_\Lambda\rho_{\rm crit}\). Under the
proposed coupling, subtracting a common reference offset would remove
the corresponding vacuum cancellation. The physical value of the
reference source and its dynamics remain open.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{dark-energy-in-running-vacuum-form}{%
\subsection{7.8 Dark energy in running-vacuum
form}\label{dark-energy-in-running-vacuum-form}}

The proposed dark-energy account reads the boundary bookkeeping in a
Type II running-vacuum model. The considered implementation conserves
matter and uses running \(G\). Its physical source and attribution
remain open. {[}GR §7.1{]}

The field-theory curvature response could contribute to the source or
enter only the effective description. The conditional near-null estimate
uses the source split and spectral assumptions of {[}GR §7.1{]}.

\textbf{Local expansion.} With \(c=1\) and \(H_0>0\), the smooth vacuum
density can be expanded in \(H^2\) about its present value:
\[\rho_\Lambda(H)=\rho_\Lambda(H_0)+\frac{3\nu}{8\pi G}(H^2-H_0^2)+\mathcal{O}\bigl((H^2-H_0^2)^2\bigr).\]
The linear term occurs in any smooth density near \(H_0\). A quadratic
term in \(H^2-H_0^2\) can coexist with the same Type II bookkeeping. A
specific law at other epochs requires additional dynamics.

\emph{Boundary-entropy dependence.} The horizon area varies with \(H\).
How this variation enters the vacuum-like part of the budget requires
the physical source and the split from the matter-like part.

\emph{Matter conservation.} The specified Type II implementation assumes
local matter conservation. A Type I implementation specifies a
vacuum--matter exchange.

\emph{Bianchi consistency.} For the Type II implementation, conservation
with varying \(\rho_\Lambda(H)\) is maintained by running \(G(H)\).

The boundary normalization leaves the exchange condition and the native
coupling open.

\textbf{Field-theory scale estimate.} If the curvature response
contributes to the source, the estimate uses the Shapiro--Solà one-loop
expression on the supplied semiclassical background. {[}GR §7.1{]}

The Shapiro-Solà \(\beta\)-function for the vacuum-energy running
coefficient is
\[\nu = \frac{1}{48\pi^2} \sum_i a_i \frac{M_i^2}{M_{\text{Pl}}^2},\]
where the fields have masses \(M_i\) and species-dependent coefficients
\(a_i\). For Standard Model content with \(m_t\approx173\) GeV at the
upper end, the estimate is
\[|\nu_{\rm QFT}|\sim(M_{\rm SM}/M_{\rm Pl})^2\sim10^{-32}.\] This
contribution would be below the precision of the comparisons here. The
total also depends on the physical attribution and the boundary spectral
weight.

\textbf{Boundary modes.} A local two-dimensional dispersion gives
\(dN/d\omega\propto\omega\) and a small weight near the horizon
frequency. The reported free linear half-space result gives a
boundary-projected \(\omega^4\) measure. The interacting spectral
measure and its role in the source remain open. {[}GR §7.4{]}

\textbf{Observational status.} The DESI DR2 \(2.8\)--\(4.2\sigma\)
preference compares \(w_0w_a\)CDM with \(\Lambda\)CDM and depends on the
dataset combination. The inferred crossing concerns that fit.
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14738}{DESI DR2}

Bertini, Novaes, von Marttens and Shapiro fit a separate
renormalization-group-corrected \(\Lambda\)CDM model with the Type II
running structure at leading order. Using Planck 2018, DESI DR2 and
DES-Y5, they obtain
\[\nu^{\text{Bertini}} = -(2.5 \pm 1.3) \times 10^{-4},\] which is
compatible with zero at about two standard deviations. The earlier
Gómez-Valent and Solà fit used different data and a different
specification. {[}GR §7.1{]}

\textbf{Tests of the near-null reading.} A null running is compatible
with both the near-null Type II model and \(\Lambda\)CDM. Detectable
running or a confirmed crossing beyond the variation admitted by the
stated model would challenge that model. A particular attribution to the
spectral measure or to Lorentz violation would require additional
evidence.

The DESI Year 5 comparison needs a fit of a specified late-time model.

\textbf{Neutrino mass bound.} In baseline \(\Lambda\)CDM with degenerate
neutrino masses, DESI DR2 BAO plus CMB gives \(\Sigma m_\nu<0.0642\) eV
at \(95\%\) confidence. Adding oscillation information gives a
preference for normal ordering and \(m_l<0.023\) eV. The approximate
normal-ordering minimum of \(0.059\) eV uses the measured splittings and
a negligible lightest mass. The baseline upper limit is compatible with
that minimum, while the fit's tension with the oscillation lower limit
ranges from \(2.7\) to \(4.0\sigma\) depending on the statistic. The
\(w_0w_a\)CDM analysis gives a weaker bound of \(0.163\) eV. An OI Type
II joint neutrino-mass fit remains open (Chapter 8 §8.9).
\href{https://doi.org/10.1103/w9pk-xsk7}{Elbers et al.}

\hypertarget{the-dark-sector-and-the-mond-acceleration-scale}{%
\subsection{7.9 The dark sector and the MOND acceleration
scale}\label{the-dark-sector-and-the-mond-acceleration-scale}}

The proposed dark-matter account uses entropy displacement at the
cosmological boundary. Direct searches constrain the masses and
interactions they test. Detection of a particle species accounting for
the structured dark sector would contradict a boundary-only source.
{[}GR §7.2{]}

\textbf{Boundary energy and its Hubble-volume mean.} The boundary count
and classical temperature give a normalization. The interpretation as a
gravitating source requires the native coupling.

The horizon carries \(A_{\text{horizon}} / \epsilon^2\) modes and the
entropy \(S_{\text{dS}} = \sigma A_{\text{horizon}} / \epsilon^2\) by
the boundary-mode counting of Section 7.5. The classical temperature is
\(T_{\text{cl}} = c^3 \epsilon^2 H / (8\pi G k_B \sigma)\) from Section
7.3 --- computed entirely within the classical substratum with no
reference to the emergent quantum description. The total thermal energy
carried by the boundary modes is
\(E_s = S_{\text{dS}} \cdot k_B T_{\text{cl}}\). Its mean over the
Hubble volume \(V_H=4\pi c^3/(3H^3)\) is
\[\rho_s = \frac{E_s}{V_H} = \frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon^2} \cdot \frac{c^3 \epsilon^2 H}{8\pi G \sigma} \cdot \frac{3 H^3}{4\pi c^3} = \frac{3 c^2 H^2}{8\pi G} = \rho_{\text{crit}}.\]

The factors of \(\epsilon^2\) and \(\sigma\) cancel between
\(S_{\text{dS}} \propto \sigma/\epsilon^2\) and
\(T_{\text{cl}} \propto \epsilon^2/\sigma\), so the result is
independent of the specific values of \(\epsilon\) and \(\sigma\) ---
only Jacobson's \(dE = (c^2 \kappa / 8\pi G)\,dA\), an area-law entropy,
and the Friedmann volume enter the calculation. The mean equals the
supplied flat Friedmann density under those inputs.

The boundary variables are traced out in the reduced description. To
associate them with the gravitational budget requires the proposed
source identification. With that identification and the supplied baryon
fraction, the nonbaryonic contribution is \(1-\Omega_B\approx0.95\). Its
matter-like and vacuum-like split remains open.

The counted modes are on the boundary. In Newtonian gravity, a spherical
shell has zero interior force and a uniform bulk density has a field
proportional to radius inside. The equality of mean densities supplies a
normalization. A relation between the boundary deformations and the bulk
gravitational field requires the source map of §7.7.

\textbf{The MOND acceleration scale.} The framework's account of
dark-matter phenomenology --- flat rotation curves, the baryonic
Tully-Fisher relation, the radial acceleration relation --- is modeled
by entropy displacement at the cosmological boundary. The argument has
four steps, all of which inherit the conditions on the de Sitter
temperature (H-count, H-slope, H-frame, H-Hawking, local boost structure
at the horizon and the symmetric detailed-balance rate ratio; see {[}GR
§7.3{]}) and the assumption that a static configuration delivers its
full rest energy \(Q=M_Bc^2\) as heat to the boundary --- a coupling
statement belonging to the open G3 map rather than a consequence of C1.

\emph{Step 1: Entropy displacement by baryonic matter (conditional).}
The chain rests on the de Sitter temperature \(T_{\text{dS}}\), which
inherits the conditions on the gap equation (H-slope with H-count, the
horizon and frame conditions, local boost structure at the horizon and
the symmetric detailed-balance rate ratio, Section 7.3), and on the
assumption that the entire rest energy \(Q = M_B c^2\) of a static
configuration is delivered as heat to the boundary --- a statement about
how the emergent sector couples to the boundary, which the open
covariant coupling theorem ({[}GR §6.2{]}) would have to supply. With
these, the Bekenstein bound applied to a baryonic mass \(M_B\) in a de
Sitter background gives the entropy displaced from the cosmological
boundary:
\[\Delta S = \frac{M_B c^2}{k_B T_{\text{dS}}} = \frac{2 \pi M_B c^2}{\hbar H}.\]
This is the Clausius relation applied to the boundary reservoir: the
boundary's entropy reduction is \(Q/T\) for a reversible process, where
\(Q = M_B c^2\) and \(T = T_{\text{dS}}\).

\emph{Step 2: The critical acceleration \(a_0 = cH/6\) (conditional;
dimensional factor imported).} The displaced entropy redistributes over
the volume between the matter and the horizon. The proposed radial
coupling uses the acceleration conversion in Verlinde's branch. The
conversion is dimensional, and the factor is Verlinde's: in \(d\)
spacetime dimensions, the factor relating the natural Hubble
acceleration scale \(cH\) to the empirical MOND acceleration is
\((d-3) / [(d-2)(d-1)]\), which follows in his emergent-gravity analysis
from the interplay between volume-law entropy distributed over \((d-1)\)
spatial dimensions and area-law entropy scaling with \((d-2)\) surface
dimensions, together with the standard surface-density-to-acceleration
relation via Gauss's law. In our universe with \(d = 4\):
\[a_0 = \frac{d - 3}{(d-2)(d-1)} \cdot cH = \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3} \cdot cH = \frac{cH}{6} = 1.09 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m/s}^2 \quad (H_0 = 67.4\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}).\]
Under the stated coupling and horizon conditions, the imported
dimensional formula gives the factor \(1/6\) at \(d = 4\); with that
formula, the acceleration scale uses \(H\) without an additional fitted
parameter. The empirical value from the radial-acceleration-relation fit
is \((1.20 \pm 0.02 \pm 0.24) \times 10^{-10}\) m/s², so the prediction
sits at \(0.91\) of it for the Planck \(H_0\) and \(0.98\) for
\(H_0 = 73\) km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹ --- inside the fit's stellar mass-to-light
systematic, a consistency at the ten-percent level rather than an exact
match.

\emph{Step 3: The deep-MOND regime and baryonic Tully-Fisher.} For
baryonic acceleration much smaller than \(a_0\), the displaced entropy
dominates the dynamics. The proposed displacement law supplies a radial
field, giving \(g_{\text{total}} = \sqrt{g_B \cdot a_0}\) where
\(g_B = G M_B / r^2\) is the baryonic Newtonian acceleration. The
rotation velocity at radius \(r\) then satisfies
\(v^2 = r \cdot g_{\text{total}} = \sqrt{G M_B \cdot c H / 6} = \text{constant}\),
so: \[v^4 = G M_B \cdot \frac{cH}{6}.\] This is the deep-MOND baryonic
Tully-Fisher relation on the stated branch. Testing its normalization
uses measured flat rotation velocities and baryonic masses. The radial
acceleration comparison uses different observables.

\emph{Step 4: Redshift evolution.} The MOND scale depends on the Hubble
parameter, so \(a_0(z) = c H(z) / 6\) increases with redshift. The MOND
crossover radius \(r_M = \sqrt{6 G M_B / (cH)}\) correspondingly shrinks
at high redshift: for a Milky-Way-like baryon budget
(\(M_B \approx 6 \times 10^{10}\, M_\odot\) for stellar plus cold gas),
\(r_M = 8.8\) kpc at \(z = 0\) but \(5.0\) kpc at \(z = 2\) and \(3.0\)
kpc at \(z = 5\). Galaxies with effective radii comparable to or
exceeding \(r_M\) show flat rotation curves; galaxies with
\(r_{\text{eff}} < r_M\) decline, Keplerian-like, inside \(r_M\) and
approach flat beyond it. At fixed radius the baryonic share of the
acceleration, \(1/\nu(g_B/a_0)\), falls as \(a_0\) rises, so
high-redshift galaxies are less baryon-dominated than local spirals with
the same baryon distribution, and their rotation curves reach the flat
deep-MOND form at smaller radii.

\textbf{Observational comparisons.} Two observations can be compared
with the conditional dark-sector account, and both are in tension with
it.

Jiao et al.~(2023) detected a Keplerian decline in the Milky Way's
rotation curve from approximately 19 to 26.5 kpc using Gaia DR3
kinematics, with the flat rotation curve hypothesis rejected at
\(3\sigma\) significance. The conditional formula gives
\(r_M \approx 16\) kpc using a baryon budget that includes the hot
circumgalactic gas halo (\(M_B \sim 2 \times 10^{11}\, M_\odot\)), and
\(r_M \approx 9\) kpc using stellar plus cold gas
(\(M_B \sim 6 \times 10^{10}\, M_\odot\)). The observed decline lies
beyond either crossover, where the law gives a nearly flat curve:
\(v(26.5\,\text{kpc})/v(19.5\,\text{kpc}) = 0.97\) or \(0.95\) for the
two budgets treated as point masses, against \(0.86\) for a Keplerian
decline, and at least \(0.95\) in the spherical approximation for any
baryon distribution up to \(2 \times 10^{11}\,M_\odot\). A quantitative
comparison needs the Milky Way baryon model and the circular velocities
of Jiao et al.'s Jeans analysis.

The high-redshift test is Genzel et al., who report stacked rotation
curves for massive star-forming galaxies at \(z = 0.9\)--\(2.4\) showing
declining outer velocities at greater than \(3\sigma\) significance
relative to local spirals. At a fixed baryonic mass profile the
framework's law predicts the opposite trend: as the crossover radius
\(r_M\) shrinks, a galaxy becomes less baryon-dominated and its outer
curve flatter. Real high-redshift galaxies also differ from local ones
in mass distribution and pressure support, so the observed declines are
an apparent tension with the law, which a comparison modelling the
galaxies' own baryon profiles and the pressure support that Genzel et
al.~invoke alongside baryon dominance has to settle; that comparison is
not yet available. Comparison with a particle-halo model requires a
specified galaxy and halo evolution.

\textbf{Radial interpolation.} The end limits are
\(g_D\sim\sqrt{g_Ba_0}\) at small \(g_B\) and \(g_D/g_B\to0\) at large
\(g_B\). The endpoints and monotonicity admit a range of interpolation
functions. The simple MOND form \(\nu(y)=(1+\sqrt{1+4/y})/2\) is one
radial example. Its absolute correction tends to \(a_0\) at large
\(g_B\), with the fractional correction tending to zero. {[}GR §7.3{]}

The acceleration scale, crossover and deep-MOND relation require the de
Sitter temperature, the open heat input and the imported Verlinde
factor. The full interpolation and the matter-to-boundary coupling
remain open.

The calibration fixes \(\epsilon/\sqrt{\sigma}=2l_p\) under the
counting, horizon, rate and slope conditions in §§7.3--7.4. The \(1/4\)
entropy coefficient is their normalization ratio \(2\pi/8\pi\). GW250114
supplies a separate area comparison. The vacuum-energy normalization
uses the supplied Friedmann scale, with the gravitational response to an
offset open.

The horizon normalizations carry the conditions of §7.3. The Type II
reading and the MOND scale add the source and heat assumptions of
§§7.8--7.9. The interpolation profile and Hawking greybody factors
depend on further dynamics.

\textbf{Physical comparisons.} An entropy coefficient measurement would
test the calibration under its stated conditions. A crossing or running
beyond the specified near-null model would challenge that model. The
rotation-curve law is tested with measured baryonic profiles and with
pressure-support corrections where needed. The Tully-Fisher
normalization uses measured flat velocities and baryonic masses. Finding
a particle species that accounts for the structured dark sector would
contradict a boundary-only source.

The Milky Way decline compares with the conditional,
baryon-budget-dependent crossover. The Kerr areas inferred from GW250114
address the classical area theorem. The calibration coefficient needs
its own entropy or temperature measurement.

\textbf{The geometry-first account.} The classical and emergent
descriptions distinguish vacuum-energy bookkeeping without deriving its
dynamical gravitational decoupling, which remains a coupling obligation.
The \(\hbar\), \(\epsilon\) and \(1/4\) relations follow under H-count
and the named horizon conditions. The physical dark-sector
interpretation inherits those conditions and the open heat-transfer map;
its total fraction is partly the input-dependent quantity
\(1-\Omega_B\). The MOND formula uses an imported dimensional factor and
agrees within the quoted systematics. Its Tully-Fisher and crossover
consequences remain conditional. These results have distinct source
obligations and empirical standing.

The comparison between descriptions concerns their explanatory chains
and physical assumptions. A descriptive distinction between vacuum
energies does not settle their dynamical coupling, and an unobserved
entropy coefficient is not an empirical confirmation. Forward tests must
identify the conditions being tested and the measurements that
distinguish the proposed physical interpretation.

\textbf{Forward pointers.} Chapter 8 develops the JUNO comparison of the
leading solar value \(\sin^2\theta_{12}=1/3-1/(4\pi^2)\approx0.308003\).
The retrodictive residuals are \(0.14\sigma\) to direct JUNO and
\(0.07\sigma\) to the global fit that includes JUNO. The chapter
describes the experiment and the assumptions behind the leading value.

Chapter 9 develops the framework's relationship to other unification
programs --- the OI-string relationship at the matrix-model level, the
no-GUT structural commitment against the broader landscape of grand
unified theories, the universality-class character of the framework's
Tier 1 results, and the de Sitter observer literature's convergence with
the framework's geometry-first dissolution. The empirical record of
Chapters 5-8 is concentrated at the Level G3 × Level D intersection of
Chapter 3's hierarchical structural realism; Chapter 9 locates the
framework within the broader space of substratum-level theories and
articulates the universality classes that the framework's structural
commitments belong to.

The fundamental-physics inventory includes twenty-two classified
Standard Model observables, the ten entries in this chapter's table, and
seven neutrino-sector entries. It combines conditional formulas,
numerical retrodictions, observational bounds and targets awaiting data.
Part III turns to the emergence cascade through chemistry, life and
evolution; Part IV develops applications and further testable claims.
