\hypertarget{chapter-8}{%
\section{Chapter 8}\label{chapter-8}}

\hypertarget{juno-and-the-neutrino-sector}{%
\section{JUNO and the Neutrino
Sector}\label{juno-and-the-neutrino-sector}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-5}{%
\subsection{8.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-5}}

Chapter 6 §6.7 gave the leading solar mixing value
\(\sin^2\theta_{12} = 1/3 - 1/(4\pi^2) \approx 0.308003\). It is
\(0.14\sigma\) from direct JUNO and \(0.07\sigma\) from the global fit
that includes JUNO. This chapter develops the flavor calculation, its
assumptions, and the experiment's comparison with it and with other
tribimaximal mixing patterns.

The chapter opens with the experiment. Section 8.2 develops the JUNO
detector design and the reactor antineutrino source: the 20-kiloton
liquid scintillator detector 53 km from two nuclear power complexes in
southern China, the energy resolution and reactor flux that combine to
produce the world's most precise measurement of \(\sin^2\theta_{12}\) on
a much shorter timescale than was thought possible. Section 8.3 develops
the cubic-group flavor structure that produces the framework's
prediction: the three lepton generations occupying the \(T_1\) corners
of the cubic Brillouin zone, the Cabibbo angle
\(\lambda = 1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\) from a single Brillouin-zone distance, the
tribimaximal mixing pattern from the \(A_4 \subset O\) subgroup at
zeroth order.

Sections 8.4 and 8.5 develop the \(\mu\)-\(\tau\) exchange grading and
the Wilson-coefficient relation \(b_{23} = (4/3)(b_{12}+b_{13})\). That
relation preserves the tribimaximal sum
\(2\sin^2\theta_{12} + \sin^2\theta_{23} = 7/6\) through order
\(\lambda^2\).

Section 8.6 compares the leading values of the three squared mixing
angles with JUNO, the post-JUNO global fit, and the cited NuFIT 6.0
fits. Section 8.7 compares the flavor calculation with the TM1 and TM2
patterns. Section 8.8 describes what future precision can test when
higher orders are open. Section 8.9 places the separate DESI DR2
neutrino mass bounds in their cosmological models.

\hypertarget{the-juno-experiment}{%
\subsection{8.2 The JUNO experiment}\label{the-juno-experiment}}

The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) is a multipurpose
neutrino experiment located 700 meters underground in Jiangmen, southern
China. The detector consists of a 20-kiloton liquid scintillator sphere,
approximately 35 meters in diameter, instrumented with 17,612
large-aperture photomultiplier tubes and 25,600 smaller photomultiplier
tubes. The detector is designed to measure reactor antineutrinos from
the Yangjiang and Taishan nuclear power complexes, located 53 km from
the experimental site --- a baseline chosen to maximize sensitivity to
the solar mixing angle \(\theta_{12}\) at the oscillation maximum for
reactor antineutrino energies.

The detector's energy resolution is the principal experimental
innovation. JUNO achieves approximately \(3\%\) at 1 MeV, a factor of
three to five improvement over previous reactor neutrino experiments.
The improvement comes from three sources: the high photocathode coverage
(over \(75\%\) of the detector surface), the high light yield of the
scintillator, and the careful calibration program that has been ongoing
throughout the detector commissioning. The combination of high
statistics (approximately 60 events per day from the two reactor
complexes) and high energy resolution allows JUNO to resolve the fine
structure of the reactor antineutrino oscillation spectrum at
unprecedented precision.

\textbf{The first JUNO measurement.} The collaboration reported its
first measurement of reactor neutrino oscillations in November 2025. The
headline result from 59.1 days of physics data was
\[\sin^2\theta_{12} = 0.3092 \pm 0.0087,\] which is the most precise
single-experiment determination of the solar mixing angle to date --- a
factor of 1.6 improvement over all previous measurements combined. The
same dataset also produces a high-precision measurement of the
mass-squared splitting:
\[\Delta m_{21}^2 = (7.50 \pm 0.12) \times 10^{-5}\,\text{eV}^2\] for
normal ordering. \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14593}{JUNO
Collaboration}

\textbf{The post-JUNO global fit.} Capozzi \emph{et al.} include these
JUNO measurements and updated SNO+ data. Their global fit gives
\[\sin^2\theta_{12} = 0.3085 \pm 0.0073,\qquad \Delta m_{21}^2 = (7.48 \pm 0.10) \times 10^{-5}\,\text{eV}^2.\]
The direct and global solar residuals in §8.6 use overlapping data.
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21650}{Capozzi et al.}

\hypertarget{the-cubic-group-flavor-structure}{%
\subsection{8.3 The cubic-group flavor
structure}\label{the-cubic-group-flavor-structure}}

The flavor calculation uses the rotation group \(O\) of the simple cubic
lattice. Its six nearest-neighbor signed link directions decompose into
blocks of dimensions \((3,2,1)\). Chapter 5 relates this decomposition
to the gauge group through the stabilizer of a generic equivariant
condensate on the single-copy H-link and H-cust branch, with the
specified charged action. Within that nearest-neighbor comparison,
simple cubic alone supplies the required block pattern. The flavor
construction uses \(T_1\) for the lepton generations under the carrier
and spin conditions of SM §4.7.

\textbf{The cubic group \(O\) and its \(A_4\) subgroup.} The cubic point
group \(O\) is the rotation symmetry group of three-dimensional space,
with \(24\) elements isomorphic to the symmetric group \(S_4\). Its
irreducible representations decompose as
\[\mathrm{irreps}(O) = A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus E \oplus T_1 \oplus T_2,\]
of dimensions \(1, 1, 2, 3, 3\). The subgroup \(A_4 \subset O\) keeps
\(\{A_1, A_2, E, T_1\}\) but identifies \(A_2\) with \(A_1\), giving the
standard \(A_4\) content \(A \oplus A' \oplus A'' \oplus T\) of
dimensions \(1, 1, 1, 3\). The framework's structural derivation in
Chapter 5 placed the three lepton generations on the \(T_1\)
representation as one of the irreducible components of the cubic
decomposition \(6 = T_1 \oplus E \oplus A_1\) of the six
nearest-neighbor link directions.

The realization of \(T_1\) in the framework is concrete. The three
Cartesian unit vectors \(\{e_1, e_2, e_3\}\) --- corresponding to the
three spatial axes of the cubic lattice --- are acted on by the \(24\)
rotations of \(O\). The three candidate sectors --- the generations,
under H-spin' --- occupy these three Cartesian directions. The cubic
decomposition has a single democratic direction
\[\hat{h} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(e_1 + e_2 + e_3),\] which is the only
direction fixed by the \(\mathbb{Z}_3\) cyclic subgroup of \(O\). Its
perpendicular plane is the real two-dimensional complement for that
cyclic subgroup inside \(T_1\). The second column of the tribimaximal
mixing matrix is \(\hat{h}\). The first and third columns lie in the
perpendicular plane, oriented by \(\mu\)-\(\tau\) exchange.

\textbf{The Cabibbo scale from cubic Brillouin geometry.} The
perturbation parameter \(\lambda\) controlling the deviations from
tribimaximal mixing in the framework is identified with the Cabibbo
angle, fixed independently by the cubic Brillouin-zone geometry as
developed in Chapter 6 §6.5. The three generations occupy the three
\(T_1\) corners of the cubic Brillouin zone at momenta
\(X_j = \pi \cdot e_j\) for \(j = 1, 2, 3\). The inter-generation
distance in momentum space is
\[|X_i - X_j| = \pi\sqrt{2} \quad (i \neq j),\] a geometric constant of
the cubic lattice. The Cabibbo angle is the inverse of this distance:
\[\lambda = \frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{2}} = 0.22508.\]

The measured Cabibbo value is \(\lambda = 0.22500 \pm 0.00067\), a
\(0.04\%\) difference. The Brillouin-zone geometry fixes the distance
and the chirality argument gives the inverse-momentum power. The
algebraic unity of the physically projected taste-changing matrix
element and the open emergent dressing of its identification with the
Cabibbo angle have the scope of SM §7.1. The lepton calculation uses the
same \(\lambda\) for the deviations from tribimaximal mixing.

\textbf{The PMNS matrix at zeroth order.} The framework's PMNS structure
at zeroth order is the tribimaximal mixing matrix, obtained from the
\(A_4 \subset O\) representation theory. The tribimaximal matrix is
\[U_{\text{TBM}} = \begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt{2/3} & \sqrt{1/3} & 0 \\
-\sqrt{1/6} & \sqrt{1/3} & \sqrt{1/2} \\
-\sqrt{1/6} & \sqrt{1/3} & -\sqrt{1/2}
\end{pmatrix},\] with the columns corresponding to mass eigenstates
\(\nu_1, \nu_2, \nu_3\) and the rows to flavor eigenstates
\(\nu_e, \nu_\mu, \nu_\tau\). The corresponding zeroth-order mixing
angles are
\[\sin^2\theta_{12}^{\text{TBM}} = \frac{1}{3}, \quad \sin^2\theta_{23}^{\text{TBM}} = \frac{1}{2}, \quad \sin^2\theta_{13}^{\text{TBM}} = 0.\]

The observed squared angles differ from the tribimaximal values by
amounts of order \(\lambda^2 \approx 0.05\), including a nonzero
\(\sin^2\theta_{13} \approx 0.022\). The next sections calculate the
leading shifts from the \(\mu\)-\(\tau\) exchange grading, a projection
input, and two Wilson-coefficient inputs.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-u-parity-grading}{%
\subsection{8.4 The U-parity grading}\label{the-u-parity-grading}}

The \(\mu\)-\(\tau\) exchange gives a \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) grading of the
charged-lepton perturbations into \(U\)-even and \(U\)-odd components.

\textbf{The \(U\)-parity generator.} In the Altarelli-Feruglio basis
(charged-lepton mass matrix diagonal at zeroth order), the
\(\mu\)-\(\tau\) exchange operator \(U\) is the permutation that
exchanges the second and third generations:
\[U = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\]
The displayed swap has determinant \(-1\). Its negative \(-U\) is a
proper cube rotation with the same conjugation action. This action gives
a \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) grading on antisymmetric matrices: \(A\) is
\(U\)-even when \(UAU^{-1}=+A\) and \(U\)-odd when \(UAU^{-1}=-A\).

With the basis matrices
\((E_{ij})_{kl} = \delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} - \delta_{il}\delta_{jk}\) ---
the elementary antisymmetric matrices spanning the space of
\(3 \times 3\) antisymmetric matrices --- the decomposition is: -
\(U\)-even combinations: \(E_{12} + E_{13}\) - \(U\)-odd combinations:
\(E_{12} - E_{13}\) and \(E_{23}\)

The unique \(U\)-odd combination antisymmetric in \((\mu, \tau)\) is
\(E_{23}\); the unique \(U\)-odd combination relating the first
generation to the second and third is \(E_{12} - E_{13}\). The
\(U\)-even combination \(E_{12} + E_{13}\) relates the first generation
symmetrically to the other two.

\textbf{The charged-lepton perturbation expansion.} The charged-lepton
rotation matrix \(V_\ell\) in the Altarelli-Feruglio basis admits a
perturbative expansion in the Cabibbo scale \(\lambda\):
\[V_\ell = \exp\bigl(\lambda A_1 + \lambda^2 A_2 + O(\lambda^3)\bigr),\]
with \(A_1\) and \(A_2\) real antisymmetric \(3 \times 3\) matrices to
be determined from structural inputs. The expansion is the framework's
parametrization of the charged-lepton rotation: \(A_1\) controls the
leading deviations from the tribimaximal pattern at order \(\lambda\),
\(A_2\) controls the next-to-leading deviations at order \(\lambda^2\).

\textbf{Determination of \(A_1\).} The leading-order generator \(A_1\)
is fixed by three structural conditions plus the cubic geometric input.
First, the observed value \(\theta_{13} \neq 0\) requires
\(\sin\theta_{13} = O(\lambda)\), forcing \(A_1\) to contribute to the
\((1,3)\) element of \(V_\ell^\dagger U_{\text{TBM}}\). Second, the
empirical observations that both
\(\Delta_{12} \equiv \sin^2\theta_{12} - 1/3\) and
\(\Delta_{23} \equiv \sin^2\theta_{23} - 1/2\) are of order
\(\lambda^2\) --- neither shows a leading \(\lambda\) contribution ---
further constrains \(A_1\)'s structure. Third, the geometric input from
Section 8.3: each end of an inter-generation mixing vertex projects onto
the plane perpendicular to the democratic direction \(\hat{h}\),
contributing a factor \(\sin(\angle(\hat{e}_i, \hat{h})) = A\) from the
off-democratic projection of any generation axis. For a single-vertex
inter-generation transition, the total projection factor is \(A^2\) ---
one factor per vertex end.

Identifying this projection geometry with the leading \(O(\lambda)\)
contribution to \(U_{e3}\) gives the structural identity
\[\sin\theta_{13} = A^2 \lambda,\] at leading order in \(\lambda\). This
input fixes \(A_1\)'s magnitude, while the orders of \(\Delta_{12}\) and
\(\Delta_{23}\) fix its \(U\)-odd form.

The result is uniquely determined:
\[A_1 = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}(E_{12} - E_{13}).\] The generator \(A_1\) is
purely \(U\)-odd: \(U A_1 U^{-1} = -A_1\). Geometrically, \(A_1\)
represents a rotation by angle \(A^2 = 2/3\) around the axis
\((\hat{e}_2 + \hat{e}_3)/\sqrt{2}\), which reproduces
\(\sin\theta_{13} = A^2 \lambda\) as required. The structural property
is that \(A_1\) is \(U\)-odd; the magnitude \(\sqrt{2}/3\) is fixed by
the projection identity \(\sin\theta_{13} = A^2\lambda\) with
\(A^2 = 2/3\).

\textbf{Deviations from TBM at order \(\lambda^2\).} Expanding
\(V_\ell\) to second order:
\[V_\ell = I + \lambda A_1 + \lambda^2\bigl(A_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}A_1^2\bigr) + O(\lambda^3),\]
and writing the most general antisymmetric \(A_2\) as
\[A_2 = b_{12} E_{12} + b_{13} E_{13} + b_{23} E_{23},\] direct
computation of \(|U_{\text{PMNS},ij}|^2\) to order \(\lambda^2\) gives
the deviations from tribimaximal mixing:
\[\Delta_{13} = \tfrac{4}{9}\lambda^2 = A^4 \lambda^2,\]
\[\Delta_{12} = -\tfrac{2}{3}(b_{12} + b_{13})\lambda^2,\]
\[\Delta_{23} = b_{23}\lambda^2.\]

The leading squared reactor angle depends only on \(A_1\). The real
combination \(b_{12}-b_{13}\) can contribute to the unsquared reactor
amplitude \(U_{e3}\) at order \(\lambda^2\). Its interference with the
leading amplitude can enter \(|U_{e3}|^2\) at order \(\lambda^3\). The
combination drops out of all three squared angles through order
\(\lambda^2\). At this order the mixing matrix is real and the Dirac
Jarlskog invariant vanishes. A physical complex CP phase remains
unsourced. The atmospheric shift \(\Delta_{23}\) depends on \(b_{23}\)
alone at this order.

\hypertarget{the-sum-rule-and-structural-relation}{%
\subsection{8.5 The sum rule and structural
relation}\label{the-sum-rule-and-structural-relation}}

The second-order shifts involve two independent combinations of the
\(A_2\) coefficients. The \(U\)-even combination \(b_{12}+b_{13}\)
controls \(\Delta_{12}\), and the \(U\)-odd coefficient \(b_{23}\)
controls \(\Delta_{23}\).

\textbf{Condition 1 (normalization input).} Setting \(b_{23}=1\) fixes
the absolute second-order atmospheric shift with \(\lambda\) fixed
independently.

\textbf{Condition 2 (coefficient relation).} The proposed relation is
\[b_{23} = \tfrac{4}{3}(b_{12} + b_{13}).\] With Condition 1 it gives
\(b_{12}+b_{13}=3/4\) and fixes the solar shift as well. Deriving the
relation from the underlying dynamics remains open.

\textbf{The leading-order sum rule.} Adding the two shifts gives
\[2\Delta_{12} + \Delta_{23} = \bigl(b_{23} - \tfrac{4}{3}(b_{12}+b_{13})\bigr)\lambda^2 + O(\lambda^3).\]
The second-order term vanishes precisely when Condition 2 holds. Thus
the sum keeps its tribimaximal value \(7/6=2/3+1/2\) through order
\(\lambda^2\). The expansion allows higher-order terms.

The sum rule itself has a clean cubic-geometric reading:
\(7/6 = 2/d + 1/(d-1)\) for \(d = 3\) generations, with \(2/d\) being
twice the inverse generation count (the value
\(\sin^2\theta_{12}^{\text{TBM}} = 1/3\) doubled) and \(1/(d-1)\) being
the inverse partner count (the value
\(\sin^2\theta_{23}^{\text{TBM}} = 1/2\) in the doublet sector). For
three generations, \(2/3 + 1/2 = 7/6\) is forced by the representation
theory; the framework's content is that this sum rule is
\emph{preserved} at order \(\lambda^2\) by the second-order
Wilson-coefficient relation.

\textbf{The factor \(4/3\) as cubic-group identity.} Condition 2's
specific numerical coefficient is a genuine cubic-group identity:
\[\frac{4}{3} = 2A^2 = 2 \cdot \frac{C_2(T_1)}{d} = \frac{C_2(T_1)^2}{d},\]
where \(A = \sqrt{2/3}\) is the off-democratic projection of any
generation axis and \(C_2(T_1) = d - 1 = 2\) is the quadratic Casimir of
the \(T_1\) representation. The identity \(A^2 = (d-1)/d = C_2(T_1)/d\)
for \(d = 3\) is the same representation-theoretic identity from Section
6.5 that produced the Wolfenstein \(A\) parameter. The factor \(4/3\)
thus has an interpretive reading as partner-count × per-partner
projection: the \(U\)-even combination \(E_{12} + E_{13}\) couples the
first generation to its two partners \(\{\hat{e}_2, \hat{e}_3\}\), with
the per-partner projection nominally \(A^2\). The interpretation is
internally consistent but non-directional --- the same arithmetic
produces the inverse ratio \(3/4\) under alternative partner-count
assignments. The directional assertion that the \(U\)-odd coefficient
\(b_{23}\) is \emph{larger} than the \(U\)-even coefficient
\(b_{12}+b_{13}\) by this specific factor is what carries the
framework's substantive content beyond the cubic-group identity itself.

\textbf{Structural protection of the sum rule by \(A_1\) alone.} For
\(V_\ell=\exp(\lambda A_1)\), direct computation gives
\(2|U_{e2}|^2+|U_{\mu3}|^2=7/6-(14/27)\lambda^2+O(\lambda^4)\). Dividing
by \(\cos^2\theta_{13}=1-(4/9)\lambda^2+O(\lambda^4)\) cancels the
second-order offset:
\[(2\sin^2\theta_{12}+\sin^2\theta_{23})\bigm|_{A_1\text{ only}}=7/6+O(\lambda^4).\]

Condition 2 makes the sum survive the addition of \(A_2\) at order
\(\lambda^2\).

\textbf{Layer status.} The leading reactor angle depends on \(A_1\) and
inherits the open emergent dressing of the Cabibbo identification. The
leading solar and atmospheric values additionally use the normalization
\(b_{23}=1\) and the Layer 2(b) relation of Condition 2.

\textbf{Condition 2 as a Layer 2(b) bijection-specific commitment.} The
framework's \(b_{23} = (4/3)(b_{12} + b_{13})\) relation has a
multi-layer structural status that the four-layer framing of Chapter 4
§4.5 distinguishes precisely:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  Under the U-parity grading developed in §8.4, the antisymmetric tensor
  product \(T_1 \wedge T_1\) decomposes into a U-even subspace (spanned
  by \(E_{12} + E_{13}\)) and a U-odd subspace (spanned by
  \(E_{12} - E_{13}\) and \(E_{23}\)). The subspace decomposition is
  forced by group theory --- this is Layer 1 structural.
\item
  The cubic-geometric off-democratic projection \(A^2 = 1 - 1/d = 2/3\)
  for \(d = 3\) is forced by inner-product structure on \(T_1\) with
  \(\hat{h} = (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt{3}\) as the democratic axis. This is the
  same \(A^2\) that produces the Wolfenstein parameter
  \(A = \sqrt{2/3}\) in the quark sector (Chapter 6 §6.5) --- Layer 1
  structural.
\item
  The number \(4/3=2A^2\) admits a geometric reading. Identifying it
  with the coefficient ratio requires an underlying amplitude
  calculation. The specified second-order lattice route is excluded (SM
  §7.3). The recorded \(O(\lambda^3)\) interference route remains open.
\item
  The directional assertion that the \(U\)-odd amplitude exceeds the
  \(U\)-even amplitude by the specific factor of \(4/3\), with the
  labeling fixed by the observed mass hierarchy
  (\(m_e \ll m_\mu \ll m_\tau\) pinning generation 1 = electron), is
  \emph{Layer 2(b) bijection-specific} content. It depends on the
  specific bijection \(\varphi\) within the equivalence class --- the
  same kind of content as the fermion mass hierarchy itself (Chapter 19
  §19.3.1) and CKM/PMNS CP phases.
\end{enumerate}

The solar residual constrains the leading pattern under the stated
inputs. The open task is to obtain the required second-order alignment
for a candidate bijection. The proposed staggered-Yukawa calculation
concerns emergent post-trace-out operators. The specified two-hop route
to the alignment is excluded (SM §7.3).

\hypertarget{the-three-numerical-predictions}{%
\subsection{8.6 The three numerical
predictions}\label{the-three-numerical-predictions}}

Substituting \(\lambda^2=1/(2\pi^2)\) and the coefficient inputs of §8.5
gives the leading values through order \(\lambda^2\):
\[\sin^2\theta_{12} = \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4\pi^2} \approx 0.308003,\]
\[\sin^2\theta_{13} = \frac{4}{18\pi^2} \approx 0.02252,\]
\[\sin^2\theta_{23} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2\pi^2} \approx 0.5507.\]

The reactor angle uses the \(A_1\) projection input and the Cabibbo
scale. The solar and atmospheric values additionally use Conditions 1
and 2. The complex CP phase remains open (§8.4).

\hypertarget{comparison-with-tm1tm2-column-preservation-patterns}{%
\subsection{8.7 Comparison with TM1/TM2 column-preservation
patterns}\label{comparison-with-tm1tm2-column-preservation-patterns}}

Tribimaximal mixing was the leading phenomenological description of
neutrino oscillation data until Daya Bay measured a non-zero
\(\theta_{13}\) in 2012. Since then, modified tribimaximal patterns have
been the subject of a substantial literature, with the two best-known
modifications preserving one column of the original tribimaximal matrix
exactly: TM1 (first column preserved) and TM2 (second column preserved).
Each gives a one-parameter family that accommodates the observed
\(\theta_{13}\) but predicts different values for the other two angles.

\textbf{TM1 and TM2 in the post-JUNO landscape.} Post-JUNO analyses by
He and by Zhang find that TM2 is excluded at greater than \(3.5\sigma\)
while TM1 remains marginally viable. The framework's prediction sits
well below both alternatives in tension with the post-JUNO global fit:

\textbf{Three structural differences distinguish the framework from
TM\(_n\).}

\emph{Symmetry origin.} The cubic-group calculation uses
\(A_4\subset O\) on the \(T_1\) generation triplet. The simple-cubic
link and gauge interpretation carry the conditions of §8.3.

\emph{Mixing angles.} TM1 fixes \(\theta_{12}\) given \(\theta_{13}\).
The cubic-group calculation gives three leading values with the inputs
of §8.6. The comparison of precise measurements with those values
depends on the higher-order terms.

\emph{CP violation.} The surviving pattern in He's analysis predicts
\(\sin\delta_{\text{CP}}=\pm0.998\). The cubic-group mixing matrix is
real through order \(\lambda^2\). A mechanism for a physical complex
phase remains open (§8.4).

\textbf{The sum-rule comparison.} Condition 2 gives
\(2\sin^2\theta_{12}+\sin^2\theta_{23}=7/6+O(\lambda^3)\). The
approximate \(0.6\sigma\) comparison in §8.6 uses the upper-octant fit.
The lower-octant central value \(\sin^2\theta_{23}\approx0.455\) gives a
sum of about \(1.072\). TM1 and TM2 give different mixing correlations.
A precise comparison depends on the atmospheric octant and the theory
remainder.

\hypertarget{juno-sensitivity-and-tests-of-the-flavor-pattern}{%
\subsection{8.8 JUNO sensitivity and tests of the flavor
pattern}\label{juno-sensitivity-and-tests-of-the-flavor-pattern}}

The JUNO sensitivity study projects uncertainties on
\(\sin^2\theta_{12}\) of about \(0.0016\) after six years and \(0.0010\)
after twenty years under its forecast inputs. The comparisons below use
an illustrative uncertainty of \(0.0014\).
\href{https://juser.fz-juelich.de/record/911312/files/Abusleme_2022_Chinese_Phys._C_46_123001.pdf}{JUNO
sensitivity study, Table 6}

\textbf{The leading solar value and the minimal truncation.} If a model
takes \(0.308003\) as its complete solar prediction, unchanged direct
and global central values would differ from it by about \(0.855\sigma\)
and \(0.355\sigma\), respectively, at the illustrative precision. Higher
orders matter to a test of the proposed structure. In the minimal
truncation \(V_\ell=\exp(\lambda A_1+\lambda^2 A_2)\) with
\(-0.5\le b_{12}-b_{13}\le1\), the higher orders of that exponential
shift \(\sin^2\theta_{12}\) by \(+0.0032\) to \(+0.0044\). Independent
terms in the full expansion are open.

\textbf{Comparison with TM1 and TM2.} The solar values \(0.3184\) and
\(0.3408\) for TM1 and TM2 are separated from the leading value by about
\(7.4\) and \(23\) times the illustrative uncertainty, respectively.
Within the specified minimal truncation the corresponding separations
are about \(4.3\)--\(5.1\) and \(20\)--\(21\) times that uncertainty.
These are separations between model values on the chosen experimental
scale.

\textbf{Sensitivity to Condition 2.} At fixed \(b_{23}\) and \(\lambda\)
and ignoring higher orders, a fractional shift \(\epsilon\) in \(4/3\)
changes \(\sin^2\theta_{12}\) by \(\epsilon\Delta_{23}/2\) to first
order, with \(\Delta_{23}=1/(2\pi^2)\). A \(10\%\) shift gives about
\(0.0025\), about \(29\%\) of the direct first-result uncertainty. The
direct, global, and illustrative future solar uncertainties translate to
about \(34\%\), \(29\%\), and \(5.5\%\) on the coefficient under these
conditions.

\textbf{What the measurements test.} Solar data compare directly with a
model taking the leading solar value as complete. A test of the proposed
cubic-group flavor structure uses the TBM and Cabibbo inputs, the
separate normalization and Condition 2, and a controlled higher-order
remainder. More precise solar and atmospheric data can test the exact
\(7/6\) sum as an additional phenomenological commitment. Testing the
perturbative Condition 2 uses that correlation through order
\(\lambda^2\), with the atmospheric octant, covariance as applicable,
and theory remainder included. Reactor data test the stated \(A_1\) and
Cabibbo inputs through the leading squared reactor angle, also subject
to higher orders.

\hypertarget{desi-dr2-and-the-neutrino-mass-bound}{%
\subsection{8.9 DESI DR2 and the neutrino mass
bound}\label{desi-dr2-and-the-neutrino-mass-bound}}

The flavor calculation and the cosmological mass bound compare different
quantities. The framework heuristically favors a hierarchical normally
ordered spectrum on the branch described in SM §8.4.

\textbf{The DESI DR2 + CMB bound.} The baseline \(\Lambda\)CDM fit with
degenerate neutrino masses gives
\[\Sigma m_\nu < 0.0642\,\text{eV} \qquad (95\%\,\text{CL}).\] In the
analysis with additional oscillation information, the lightest mass is
bounded by \(m_l<0.023\) eV and normal ordering is preferred. The
approximate normal-ordering minimum, \(0.059\) eV, uses measured
splittings and a negligible lightest mass,
\(\Sigma m_\nu^{\min}\simeq\sqrt{\Delta m_{21}^2}+\sqrt{\Delta m_{31}^2}\).
The baseline upper limit is compatible with this value.
\href{https://doi.org/10.1103/w9pk-xsk7}{Elbers et al.}

\textbf{Dependence on the dark-energy model.} The reported tension
between the baseline cosmological fit and the oscillation lower limit
ranges from \(2.7\) to \(4.0\sigma\) depending on the statistic. The
same study obtains a weaker upper limit, \(0.163\) eV, in \(w_0w_a\)CDM.
Bertini \emph{et al.} separately constrain the running-vacuum parameter
\(\nu\). A joint neutrino-mass fit in the OI Type II model remains open.
\href{https://doi.org/10.1103/w9pk-xsk7}{Elbers et al.} ·
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24026}{Bertini et al.}

neutrino
sector}\label{chapter-close-the-frameworks-empirical-record-in-the-neutrino-sector}}

The leading solar value \(0.308003\) lies \(0.14\sigma\) from direct
JUNO and \(0.07\sigma\) from the overlapping global fit. The cited
reactor and atmospheric comparisons give about \(1.01\sigma\) and
\(0.7\sigma\). The approximate \(0.6\sigma\) comparison with the leading
sum uses those solar and atmospheric estimates on the upper-octant
branch.

The flavor calculation shares the Cabibbo scale and the off-democratic
projection with the quark-sector calculations. The solar and atmospheric
shifts also require the independent normalization and Condition 2. The
observed values constrain the proposed leading flavor pattern, with no
parameter fitted to the solar measurements. New precision can test
specified flavor models once their higher-order terms are controlled.

The separate cosmological comparison is with an upper bound on the mass
sum. The normal-ordering near-minimum value uses measured splittings and
the negligible-lightest-mass assumption.

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-6}{%
\subsection{9.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-6}}

Chapters 5 through 8 developed twenty-two classified Standard Model
observable entries (two parameter-free structural and five conditional
structural), seven gravitational-sector entries and seven
neutrino-sector entries. The numerical comparisons have different
evidential roles: selected flavor retrodictions have percent or
sub-percent agreement, fitted gauge couplings match by construction, and
the neutrino mass sum is constrained by upper bounds. The gravitational
formulas carry the conditions of Chapter 7; the MOND acceleration agrees
within quoted systematics, and the Bekenstein-Hawking coefficient is a
consistency relation, conditional and without a direct test. GW250114
tests the classical area theorem. Appendix A records each entry's
classification and empirical standing.

This chapter is different. The framework's content is \emph{not} a
competitor to other unification programs that operate at the same level
--- it is a structural framework at a different level than string
theory, loop quantum gravity, or grand unified theories. Locating the
framework within the broader theoretical landscape, articulating what
classes of results the framework establishes at the universality-class
level rather than at the specific-bijection level, and identifying
convergences and divergences with mainstream physics literature ---
these are the chapter's content.

Seven pieces occupy the chapter.

Section 9.2 develops the framework's hierarchical structural realism:
the framework operates at multiple levels of abstraction simultaneously,
with different chapter contents living at different levels. Some results
are \emph{universality-class} results (the classical horizon temperature
of the boundary count and the finite counting of boundary modes
unconditionally; the Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) coefficient and the
action-scale relation \(\hbar = c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\) from
partition geometry, consistency relations conditional on H-count and the
horizon conditions named in Chapter 7; the descriptive distinction
behind the cosmological constant dissolution) --- they hold for any
finite deterministic substratum satisfying the framework's structural
conditions at its cosmological horizon, regardless of the specific
bijection. Other predictions are \emph{substratum-specific} (the
conditional Cabibbo angle and the solar angle on the flavor branch of
Chapter 8) --- they require the specific cubic-lattice realization
developed in Chapters 5-6.

Section 9.3 develops the Tier 1 results, and the conditional results
built on them, as universality-class content. The framework's
gravitational-sector content (Chapter 7) and the memory-bearing quantum
phenomenology with its universal representation (Chapter 1) are largely
universality-class --- the accessible memory statement uses C1/C3/C4 and
an accessible history witness, with C2 treated separately. The
representation is exact for a supplied finite-alphabet law at a finite
horizon. The gravitational calibrations use H-count and the named
horizon conditions. The empirical record at Tier 1 tests the framework's
commitments at the level of \emph{structural classes of substrates},
with the cubic-lattice realization being one example within the class.
Section 9.4 develops the corresponding Tier 2 and Tier 3 content and
clarifies which empirical predictions test which level.

Section 9.5 develops the framework's relationship to string theory at
the substratum level. The two programs operate at different levels and
answer different questions. The framework's specific commitments to a
deterministic bijection (finite under A1) are not equivalent to string
theory's commitments to a continuum quantum gravity with extra
dimensions; the apparent overlap in their predictions reflects shared
universality-class content rather than substratum-level equivalence.
Section 9.6 develops the string-landscape multiplicity problem: the
framework's gauge-group derivation does not dissolve the landscape
problem because the framework operates at a structurally different level
than string compactification.

Section 9.7 compares the Danielson--Satishchandran--Wald horizon
decoherence calculation in curved-spacetime QFT with the framework's
causal partition. The BEC proposal of Chapter 15 tests a separate
finite-capacity model.

Section 9.8 develops adjacent observer-emergent literature: the
Chandrasekaran-Longo-Penington-Witten (CLPW) construction of observer
algebras in de Sitter space, the Maldacena and Harlow-Usatyuk-Zhao work
on observer-essentiality in quantum gravity, the Slagle-Preskill
experimental program for entanglement structure in gravitational
systems. These are \emph{adjacent convergences} with the framework's
substratum-emergent operator distinction, each addressing a related
question from a different theoretical starting point.

Section 9.9 closes the chapter by locating the framework's content
within the broader theoretical landscape: the framework's epistemic
position relative to other unification programs, the empirical record
concentrated at the Tier 1/Tier 2 boundary, and the framework's openness
to embedding string-theoretic or loop-quantum-gravity content as
universality-class members rather than as competing claims.

The chapter is a \emph{positioning} chapter rather than a
\emph{content-development} chapter. The framework's empirical content
has been developed in Chapters 5 through 8; here it is located within
the space of substratum-level theories and articulated relative to
alternative programs. The pedagogical value is to clarify what the
framework claims at which level, with the universality-class character
of the strongest empirical predictions being one of the framework's
distinctive features.

\hypertarget{the-frameworks-hierarchical-structural-realism}{%
\subsection{9.2 The framework's hierarchical structural
realism}\label{the-frameworks-hierarchical-structural-realism}}

The framework operates simultaneously at multiple levels of abstraction.
Chapter 3 §3.4 introduced the hierarchical structural realism that
organizes the framework's content; this section develops it concretely
against the empirical content of Chapters 5 through 8 and identifies
where each chapter's results live in the hierarchy.

\textbf{The hierarchy.} The framework distinguishes four levels of
structural commitment, organized along two orthogonal axes.

The first axis is \emph{observation level}. Level O1 is the emergent
quantum field theory accessible to embedded observers --- the level
where the Standard Model, GR, and standard quantum mechanics operate.
Level O2 is the substratum, where the framework's bijection \(\varphi\)
and partition structure are defined. The framework's content cuts across
both levels: O1 is where predictions are tested, O2 is where the
structural commitments live.

The second axis is \emph{gauge level}. Level G1 is the framework's
general structural axioms (deterministic bijection, classical
probability, causal partition) with the open hypothesis A1 (finite
substratum). Level G2 is the structural properties of the substratum
(the six properties developed in Chapter 5: isotropy, sublattice
structure, link content, anomaly cancellation, taste content, generation
count). Level G3 is the specific bijection within the equivalence class
\([(S, \varphi)] / \mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\). Level G4 is the
universality class to which any specific bijection belongs --- multiple
bijections within \(\mathcal{G}_{\text{sub}}\) produce identical
observables.

The framework's predictions stratify across these levels. Different
chapters live at different (O × G) intersections.

\textbf{Where each chapter's content lives.}

\emph{Chapter 1 (Quantum Mechanics from Embedded Observation).} The
exact theorem represents a supplied law on a finite alphabet at a finite
horizon by a reversible finite realization and its fixed-basis quantum
form (\(S\iff D\iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\)). C1/C3/C4 characterize the
accessible history-memory sector. C2 is record persistence, with a
mixing hypothesis for its slow-bath implication. Phase locking uses its
own hypotheses. The five completion conditions characterize the coherent
instrument algebra on a finite carrier within complex matrix kinematics
taken as given. Native physical sourcing remains open ({[}Main §3.4{]},
{[}GR §3.3{]}).

\emph{Chapter 5 (Gauge Structure).} The exact Level O2 × Level G2
content is the observer-isotropy theorem together with the six-link
cubic representation; the latter decomposes as \((3,2,1)\). Identifying
that representation with one physical Standard-Model carrier is H-link
single-copy, with H-cust and the later matter hypotheses entering
downstream. The geometric decomposition is therefore structural; the
physical gauge-group reading is a conditional bridge construction rather
than a consequence of a \(K=2d\) minimization theorem.

\emph{Chapter 6 (Matter Content).} The quantitative predictions of
Standard Model parameters live at Level O1 × Level G3 --- the specific
cubic-lattice bijection produces specific values for the Cabibbo angle,
Koide relation, gauge couplings, and other observables. The Cabibbo
angle prediction \(\lambda = 1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\) tests the framework's
commitment to the cubic Brillouin geometry at Level G3.

\emph{Chapter 7 (Gravitational Sector).} Predictions stratify across
multiple levels. The classical horizon temperature of the boundary
count, the finite boundary-mode count and the two-level distinction
behind the cosmological constant dissolution are Tier 1 results at Level
O2 × Level G4; the Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\) coefficient and the
action-scale relation \(\hbar = c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\), consistency
relations, sit at the same level conditional on H-count and the horizon
conditions of Chapter 7 §7.3, the dynamical form of the dissolution is
conditional on the coupling theorem of {[}GR §6.2{]}, and the Type II
running-vacuum form is not derived (Chapter 7 §7.8). The MOND
acceleration scale \(a_0 = cH/6\) and the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation
are Tier 2 results at Level G2, inheriting the conditions on the de
Sitter temperature with the dimensional factor imported from Verlinde.
The MOND interpolation steepness is Tier 3 at Level G3.

\emph{Chapter 8 (JUNO and Neutrino Sector).} The leading solar and
atmospheric angles use Condition 2, the separate normalization
\(b_{23}=1\), the mass-label assignment and the Cabibbo dressing.
Condition 2 cancels the \(O(\lambda^2)\) term in the weighted sum. The
exact \(7/6\) target is the stated phenomenological model commitment (SM
§7.8). The neutrino-mass comparison uses measured splittings and upper
bounds. An OI Type II joint fit remains open.

\textbf{Multi-level structural realism.} A single empirical prediction
can carry content at multiple levels simultaneously. The GW250114
area-theorem result illustrates the level structure (noting that it
tests classical horizon dynamics, not the \(1/4\) coefficient, which has
no direct empirical test): - Level G4: the universality-class commitment
to thermal self-consistency at the partition boundary. - Level G2: the
framework's specific implementation of the thermal self-consistency
through the gap equation chain. - Level G3: the cubic-lattice
realization being one example within the universality class.

The same observation provides evidence at multiple levels. The empirical
record is therefore not just a record of ``does the framework's specific
cubic-lattice bijection match observation?'' but ``does the framework's
structural commitment at each level match observation?'' The cumulative
case across the framework's empirical chapters is strongest at Level G2
and G4 --- the framework's structural commitments at the
substratum-properties level and the universality-class level are
extensively tested, with the cubic-lattice realization at Level G3
providing one specific way the structural commitments are met.

\textbf{Why the hierarchy matters.} The hierarchical structure clarifies
what the framework's empirical case actually tests. Critics sometimes
claim that frameworks like this one are too flexible --- that any
empirical result could be accommodated by adjusting the specific
substratum bijection. The hierarchical structure shows this concern
misplaced: most of the framework's strongest empirical predictions test
Level G4 (universality-class) and Level G2 (structural-properties)
content, which is \emph{not} adjustable by varying the bijection.

The Bekenstein--Hawking \(1/4\) follows for the stated horizon
calibration with H-count, H-slope and the horizon conditions of Chapter
7 §7.3 and {[}GR §8.5(b){]}. Thermal matching identifies the energy and
frequency slopes of the same operational transitions. The GW250114
inferred-area comparison tests classical area increase.

Similarly, the MOND acceleration scale \(a_0 = cH/6\) is determined at
the structural-properties level: the dimensional factor \(1/6\) arises
from the cubic-lattice geometry combined with the \(d = 4\) spacetime
structure, common to any substratum with these properties. The
descriptive distinction behind the proposed cosmological constant
dissolution is determined at the structural-properties level, regardless
of the specific bijection; the dissolution itself is conditional on the
coupling step that {[}GR §6.2{]} leaves open.

The framework's empirical case is therefore largely a case at the
\emph{structural} levels --- universality-class and
substratum-properties --- with the substratum-specific (Level G3)
content concentrated in the flavor sector and the dark-sector
interpolation function. This is what distinguishes the framework from
frameworks operating at a single specific level: the framework's
predictions are stratified, with most of the empirical exposure at
structural levels where the predictions are robust to
substratum-specific choices.

\hypertarget{tier-1-results-as-universality-class-content}{%
\subsection{9.3 Tier 1 results as universality-class
content}\label{tier-1-results-as-universality-class-content}}

The framework's strongest structural results are concentrated at the
universality-class level (Level G4 in §9.2's hierarchy, Tier 1 in
Chapter 7's tier classification, together with the conditional results
built on it). This section develops what universality-class content
means structurally and traces the universality-class status of those
results, including the named conditions the calibrations inherit.

\textbf{What universality-class content means.} A universality-class
result is a structural commitment that follows from a small set of
structural conditions and holds across multiple substratum realizations.
The classic example in condensed matter is the renormalization-group
universality of critical phenomena: different microscopic Hamiltonians
(Ising model, \(\phi^4\) field theory, certain lattice gauge theories)
produce identical critical exponents at their phase transitions because
they belong to the same universality class.

C1--C4 specify the admission criterion for an observer in the stated
memory-bearing sector. Class membership additionally requires
equivalence of the chosen observable algebra and its dynamics
{[}Structure §9.1{]}. Partial trace on a finite deterministic
realization can also give a Markov law.

The framework's Tier 1 results, and the conditional results built on
them, are properties of the universality class as a whole, not of the
specific cubic-lattice realization; the conditions they carry are
statements about the horizon, the hidden sector's density of states and
the emergent dynamics rather than about the specific realization, so
they do not reintroduce bijection-specific content. Three examples
illustrate.

\emph{The Bekenstein-Hawking entropy.} \(S = A/(4 l_p^2)\) is recovered
in Chapter 7 §7.5 from boundary-mode counting combined with thermal
self-consistency at the cosmological horizon, conditional on H-slope and
the further conditions of {[}GR §8.5(b){]}. On the stated finite shell
with one mode per cell of area \(\epsilon^2\), the counting gives
\(S = \sigma A/\epsilon^2\) for entropy \(\sigma\) per mode; the
coefficient enters through \(\epsilon^2 = 4\sigma\,l_p^2\), from which
\(\sigma\) cancels, which the gap equation chain --- classical horizon
temperature equals emergent KMS temperature --- fixes under those
conditions, and the chain is a property of any substratum with the
framework's structural conditions at its horizon. The specific
cubic-lattice substratum is \emph{one way} C1--C4 are satisfied at the
horizon, but alternative substrata satisfying C1--C4 differently would
give the same \(1/4\) coefficient under the same conditions. A direct
test of the coefficient would probe the universality-class commitment,
not the cubic-lattice specifics; GW250114, which compares areas and does
not measure entropy, does not provide one.

\emph{The cosmological constant dissolution.} The descriptive
distinction behind the proposed dissolution in Chapter 7 §7.7 follows
from the two-level description: the classical substratum carries the
vacuum energy \(\rho_{\text{crit}} \sim H^2/G\), while the emergent QFT
has vacuum energy \(\rho_{\text{QFT}} \sim M_{\text{Pl}}^4\). The
two-level description is a property of any substratum with the
framework's structural conditions; the specific substratum dynamics do
not enter. The distinction holds for any member of the framework's
universality class. That gravity couples to the classical substratum and
that the emergent zero-point energy does not gravitate --- the dynamical
form of the dissolution, in which the effective cosmological constant
tracks \(H^2/G\) --- is conditional on the covariant coupling theorem
that {[}GR §6.2{]} leaves open.

\emph{The action-scale relation from partition geometry.}
\(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\) follows in Chapter 7 §7.3 from
thermal self-consistency at the cosmological horizon, conditional on
H-slope and the further conditions of {[}GR §8.5(b){]}, with the
discreteness scale \(\epsilon\) and the entropy \(\sigma\) per boundary
mode the only substratum-specific inputs. The functional form is
universal across the framework's universality class; the specific value
of \(\epsilon\) would vary across alternative substrata, with
self-consistency requiring \(\epsilon = 2\sqrt{\sigma}\,l_p\) for any
member of the class.

\textbf{The universality-class character of Tier 1 results.} The
framework's Tier 1 results are therefore \emph{not} claims about the
specific cubic-lattice substratum but claims about the broader
universality class of substrata satisfying the framework's structural
conditions. This has three consequences.

First, the empirical confirmations at Tier 1 are evidence for the
framework's universality-class commitments, not for the specific
cubic-lattice realization. A competing substratum theory giving the same
Tier 1 comparisons would agree on those tests. Equivalence of the chosen
observable algebra and dynamics is a separate requirement. The
framework's distinctive empirical exposure is at Tier 2 and Tier 3,
where substratum-specific content can in principle differ across
alternative realizations.

Second, a revision of the cubic-lattice realization can retain each Tier
1 result by preserving its hypotheses, including the respective thermal
and boundary conditions where used. The framework's commitment to
specific cubic-lattice content is therefore \emph{less load-bearing}
than its commitment to the universality-class structural conditions.

Third, the framework's content is \emph{embeddable} within other
frameworks at higher levels of abstraction. A meta-framework that
produced multiple universality-class members --- perhaps string theory's
landscape of compactifications, or a more general
bijection-on-finite-set construction --- would have the framework as one
structural commitment among many. The framework's epistemic stance is
therefore not ``this is the unique theory of fundamental physics'' but
``this is one structural framework that meets a set of
universality-class commitments, with specific bijection content tested
empirically.''

\textbf{The framework's universality-class commitments.}

The framework's universality-class commitments --- the conditions that
define membership in the framework's universality class --- are six
structural properties of the substratum, organized as follows.

\emph{Finiteness.} The substratum \(S\) has finite cardinality --- as a
claim about nature, the open hypothesis A1, not adopted. This is
load-bearing for the recurrence route specifically: the recurrence
theorem (Chapter 18 §18.7) requires finiteness for the exact recurrence
of a finite bijection, which supplies recurrence-scale P-indivisibility.
It is not required for accessible non-Markovianity, which has its own
finite-horizon route through readback, nor for the imported
representation, which is gated by (T).

\emph{Deterministic bijection.} The substratum dynamics
\(\varphi: S \to S\) is a bijection. Bijectivity is load-bearing because
it preserves information at the substratum level (the premise of
information conservation in Chapter 7 §7.6) and produces the recurrence
structure (Chapter 18 §18.7).

\emph{Causal partition.} The specified factorization
\(S=\mathcal C_V\times\mathcal C_H\) and preparation determine the
visible law. The supplied finite law admits the fixed-basis
representation. History readback, when witnessed, marks the sector with
accessible memory.

\emph{C1 (coupling).} The visible and hidden sectors are non-trivially
coupled. This is necessary for non-Markovian dynamics; failing C1
produces memoryless (Markovian) dynamics rather than the memory-bearing
sector --- fixed-basis quantum representability itself is universal,
memoryless laws included ({[}Main §3.4{]}).

\emph{C2 (memory persistence).} The record survives to its readback. A
slow bath with \(\tau_B\gg\tau_S\) is one mechanism under the stated
mixing conditions. Dynamics that conserves and routes the record can
also realize persistence ({[}Main §1.3{]}).

\emph{C3 (sufficient capacity).} The hidden sector must carry
information capacity at least the history's demand,
\(\log_2|\mathcal{C}_H| \geq I^*\) for the specified realization. This
capacity is necessary for the hidden sector to have room to store the
correlations the read-write cycle generates.

These conditions specify the observer-admission criterion on the stated
finite representative. Membership in a universality class also compares
its observable algebra and channel. The classical horizon and
Bekenstein--Hawking comparisons have the separate horizon count and
thermal conditions of Chapter 7. The MOND acceleration comparison is
Tier 2 (§7.9).

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{tier-2-and-tier-3-stratification}{%
\subsection{9.4 Tier 2 and Tier 3
stratification}\label{tier-2-and-tier-3-stratification}}

The framework's empirical content beyond Tier 1 stratifies into two
further tiers, with the empirical exposure shifting from
universality-class commitments to substratum-properties content (Tier 2)
and to specific-bijection content (Tier 3). The chapter's hierarchical
structural realism makes the stratification explicit; this section
traces the framework's empirical record at the corresponding levels.

\textbf{Tier 2: substratum-properties content.} Tier 2 results follow
from the framework's structural commitments to the substratum's
properties --- the six structural properties developed in Chapter 5
(isotropy, sublattice structure, link content, anomaly cancellation,
taste content, generation count) --- combined with the
universality-class conditions C1--C4. Tier 2 results are \emph{not}
universal across all members of the framework's universality class; they
require the substratum to have the specific properties Chapter 5
develops, but they do \emph{not} require the specific bijection.

The Tier 2 gauge branch has the local Standard Model algebra and no
modeled GUT gauge stage under single-copy H-link, H-cust and the
specified charged action (Chapters 5--6). H-spin', H-χ' and
light-spectrum selection enter the physical reading of the three taste
sectors. The MOND scale, baryonic Tully--Fisher relation and redshift
evolution of the crossover radius have their own conditions (Chapter 7
§7.9).
