Conditional \\
Darwinian evolution & Replication + variation + selection &
Consequence \\
\end{longtable}

Once template replication is established, copying errors give heritable
variation. Selection further requires that variants differ in
reproductive success under the relevant ecological conditions;
replication, variation and finite resources do not by themselves supply
this. Given sustained replication, heritable variation and such
differential success, Darwinian evolution can occur. Whether the three
capabilities combine into a replicator is a chemical premise (§11.6),
not a consequence of the derived chemistry.

\textbf{The RNA precedent.} RNA is simultaneously a linear polymer, a
substrate for complementary pairing, and a catalyst (ribozymes).
RNA-catalyzed RNA polymerization has been demonstrated experimentally.
This dual capability --- template and catalyst in a single molecular
family --- is the natural intersection of the three structural
capabilities required for template replication. The RNA world hypothesis
holds that the first replicators were RNA-like: a molecular family that
satisfies all three replication capabilities with a single molecular
species rather than requiring separate template and catalyst molecules.

\textbf{Heritable variation is automatic.} Template copying with finite
fidelity produces errors. Errors in a self-replicating polymer are
\emph{mutations}. Where variants replicate at different rates under the
prevailing conditions, faster replicators outcompete slower ones ---
\emph{selection}. Copying errors produce \emph{variants}. Successful
variants propagate --- \emph{heredity}. The conjunction of these four
features is Darwinian evolution.

The framework's content here is conditional: in any chemistry with the
framework's commitments, given sustained replication, heritable
variation and differential reproductive success under the relevant
ecological conditions, Darwinian evolution can occur. These conditions
are not specific to biological systems on Earth. The empirical record
--- the universality of natural selection across all of biology --- is
consistent with this conditional account.

\textbf{Caveats.} The structural argument establishes that Darwinian
evolution can occur wherever template replication is sustained and its
heritable variants differ in reproductive success, in a system with
carbon chemistry, a thermal window and a chiral aqueous environment. It
does not determine the \emph{specific} molecular system that first
replicates (RNA, PNA, or some other RNA-like family), the
\emph{timescale} for the transition from prebiotic chemistry to first
replicator (millions or billions of years, depending on parametric
details), or the \emph{specific pathway} from simple replicators to
cellular organization. These depend on the specific bijection
\(\varphi\), local geochemistry, and contingent historical conditions.

The framework's structural content is therefore conditional: given a
sustained replicator whose heritable variants differ in reproductive
success, Darwinian evolution can occur; whether and how a replicator
arises is parametric, and whether its variants differ in reproductive
success depends on ecological conditions. The framework provides the
structural account; the specific historical content is the subject of
the historical sciences (paleontology, geochemistry, comparative
biology).

\hypertarget{c1c4-at-the-molecular-scale}{%
\subsection{11.6 C1--C4 at the molecular
scale}\label{c1c4-at-the-molecular-scale}}

Chapter 1 links positive conditional memory to different next-step laws
at the same visible present. Coupling, persistence and capacity can
enable the C4 contrast in a specified model.

\textbf{Before replication.} Classical chemical dynamics can be modeled
as Markovian in a sufficient state. Coarse concentrations need not
provide such a state.

A persistent intermediate or conformation can change the next-step law
at fixed measured concentrations, with or without a copying template.

\textbf{A candidate molecular implementation.} In an existing replicator
the following functions could provide a readback mechanism.

\emph{C1 (coupling), realized as catalytic feedback.} The template must
direct synthesis of new molecules (catalyzing the reaction), and the
synthesis must maintain the template (either by producing copies of the
template or by producing molecules that contribute to template
stability). The framework's autocatalytic networks (§11.2) provide the
coupling: catalytic relationships between molecules produce feedback
between template and environment.

\emph{C2 (persistence).} The template or another distinguishable record
needs to survive across the copying or reaction cycles of interest. The
relevant lifetime depends on the chemical conditions.

\emph{C3 (capacity).} For example, a four-letter alphabet gives
\(4^{20}\) nominal 20-mer sequences. Usable capacity concerns
distinguishable records accessible to the actual chemistry.

\emph{C4 (history readback).} Readback requires the template or another
retained record to affect the next-step law differently after histories
with the same current coarse state.

\textbf{Template-mediated heredity.} Copying passes a sequence to
descendants. When the observable law also has the matched-present
contrast, the finite-horizon result gives accessible conditional memory.

This use of the diagnostic requires a declared observable and time
window. The copying and selection claims have the separate chemical and
ecological premises above.

\textbf{Replicators under population dynamics.} C1--C4 do not by
themselves imply copying or growth: the finite bijections that realize
them in the foundational paper preserve the number of states and neither
copy nor grow ({[}Main §3.4{]}). A self-replicating system in a pool of
feedstock molecules, with replication exceeding decay and copying
fidelity high enough to keep variants heritable, grows exponentially
while the feedstock lasts, and given sufficient time can dominate its
environment. Exponential growth is not peculiar to replicators:
mass-action autocatalysis, such as the formose reaction, also grows
exponentially while its feedstock lasts.

Once a replicator is established in some local environment, it grows
exponentially until it consumes the available feedstock or reaches some
other environmental limit. The system's offspring (with copying errors)
further explore the sequence space, with selection eliminating
less-effective replicators. The population persists over epochs in which
feedstock is sustained and replication exceeds decay.

Autocatalytic models describe specified reaction and food sets.
Formation of a replicator in an aqueous mixture depends on catalytic
closure containing a copier, co-presence of the relevant species,
chemical rates and sustained feedstock.

\textbf{The timescale.} The earliest evidence for life on Earth is
approximately 3.8 billion years ago (carbon isotope signatures in Isua,
Greenland), on a planet that formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago.
The \(\sim 700\) million year gap is consistent with a period of
prebiotic chemical exploration before the first replicator, whose
duration depends on solution-specific parameters (concentration,
temperature fluctuation rates, mineral surface availability, energy
sources, and the specific molecular pathway being explored).

The framework does not predict the specific 700-million-year gap, and it
establishes no positive lower bound on the time between the formation of
a suitable chemical environment and the establishment of the first
replicator. The existence and length of such a gap are historical
contingencies.

\hypertarget{rna-as-a-single-molecule-template-and-catalyst}{%
\subsection{11.7 RNA as a single-molecule template and
catalyst}\label{rna-as-a-single-molecule-template-and-catalyst}}

The simplest replicator would use \emph{one molecular family} as both
template and catalyst, rather than separate molecules for each. RNA is
the natural candidate: a single molecular family that serves both roles.
This is the chemical content of the RNA world hypothesis; it rests on
the ribozyme evidence below and is not a deduction from C1--C4.

\textbf{Three capabilities in one molecule.}

\emph{Template capability (C2, C3).} RNA is a linear polymer with a
4-letter alphabet (A, U, G, C) and arbitrary length. The 4-letter
alphabet provides sequence space \(4^N\) for length \(N\), satisfying C3
with substantial margin for any biologically relevant length. RNA's
phosphate-sugar backbone is chemically stable in aqueous conditions for
hours to days, satisfying C2 relative to reaction timescales.

\emph{Catalytic capability (C1).} RNA can fold into three-dimensional
structures with active sites that catalyze specific reactions. The
catalytic capability was discovered in the 1980s with the identification
of self-splicing ribozymes (Cech, Altman, 1989 Nobel Prize). Subsequent
work has identified ribozymes catalyzing a wide range of reactions:
peptide bond formation (the ribosome's peptidyl transferase center is a
ribozyme), nucleotide hydrolysis, transesterification, and most
importantly for the origin-of-life context, RNA polymerization.

\emph{RNA-templated synthesis.} Ribozymes have been shown to catalyze
RNA-templated primer extension (Johnston et al., 2001, cited in
{[}Complexity §5.5{]}). The result supplies one component of a possible
RNA replication cycle.

\textbf{Why DNA and proteins are not single-molecule replicators.} DNA
is more chemically stable than RNA (improved C2 --- half-lives of
millions of years vs.~hours for RNA), making it a better information
storage medium. But DNA cannot easily catalyze reactions (catalytic DNA
has been engineered in the laboratory but is much less common than
catalytic RNA). DNA serves as a template but not as a catalyst in any
natural system.

Proteins are excellent catalysts (much more diverse catalytic repertoire
than RNA), but proteins cannot easily template their own replication (a
protein cannot directly serve as a template for synthesizing another
protein of the same sequence --- there is no protein-protein equivalent
of Watson-Crick complementary pairing). Protein conformations are
candidate records. A matched-present readback test is needed to
establish C4 for a chosen observable (Chapter 13).

RNA is the natural polymer known to serve as both template and catalyst
in a single molecular species. The RNA world hypothesis --- that early
life used RNA for both information storage and catalysis before the
evolution of DNA and proteins --- rests on that chemical evidence; it is
an empirical hypothesis, not a consequence of C1--C4.

\textbf{The RNA → DNA + protein transition.} Modern biology uses DNA for
information storage and proteins for catalysis, with RNA serving
intermediary functions (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, regulatory RNAs). The proposed
transition separates storage and catalytic functions.

\emph{DNA optimizes C2.} DNA's chemical stability is much higher than
RNA's, providing greater persistence for information storage. The
improved C2 allows more stable inheritance over longer timescales ---
important for organisms with longer generation times.

\emph{Proteins optimize C1.} Proteins' catalytic repertoire is much more
diverse than RNA's (the 20 amino acids provide more chemical
functionality than the 4 nucleotides). The improved C1 allows more
sophisticated catalytic networks and more efficient metabolism.

The division between DNA storage, RNA intermediaries and protein
catalysis illustrates a biological architecture with distinct
persistence and reaction functions. Its evolution depends on the
organism and environment.

On the RNA-world hypothesis, early life used RNA-like architecture. The
division of functions in the later DNA and protein system provides a
separate molecular setting for studying persistence and readback. In
either setting, C4 requires a specified partition and histories with
different next-step laws at the same measured present.

\hypertarget{what-remains-genuinely-open}{%
\subsection{11.8 What remains genuinely
open}\label{what-remains-genuinely-open}}

The framework's structural content on the origin of life is substantive
but limited. The chapter has established that, given sustained
replication, heritable variation and differential reproductive success
under the relevant ecological conditions, Darwinian evolution can occur,
that a replicator's heredity can realize C1--C4 at the molecular scale
in the same structural sense that C1--C4 at the cosmological scale
produces the memory-bearing dynamics quantum mechanics represents, and
that the case for RNA-like architecture in the first replicators is
empirical. What the framework does \emph{not} address is the historical
content of life's origin on Earth.

\textbf{What the framework does not derive.}

\emph{The specific molecular pathway from prebiotic chemistry to first
replicator.} The framework does not predict that a replicator must
arise, nor the specific molecular pathway by which the first replicator
was established on Earth. The pathway depends on the local geochemistry
(mineral surfaces, temperature fluctuations, concentration mechanisms),
the specific precursor molecules available (HCN, formaldehyde, simple
sugars, amino acids), and the specific autocatalytic networks that
formed under those conditions. These are matters for prebiotic chemistry
research, not for the framework's structural commitments.

\emph{The timescale of the transition.} The framework does not predict
the time between the formation of a suitable chemical environment and
the establishment of the first replicator, and it establishes no
positive lower bound on it. Earth's \(\sim 700\) million year gap
between planetary formation and first life is a historical datum, not
derived from the framework. Alternative planetary environments
(different temperatures, different mineral assemblages, different
concentrations of precursors) would have different timescales.

\emph{The specific molecular system that first replicated.} The
framework does not predict whether RNA itself was the first replicator.
Alternative possibilities include peptide nucleic acid (PNA), threose
nucleic acid (TNA), or other RNA-like polymers with different
sugar-phosphate backbones. The RNA-world evidence bears on architecture
(linear polymer with complementary pairing and catalytic capability)
more than on specific chemistry.

\emph{The transition from simple replicators to cellular organization.}
The framework's structural account ends with self-replicating molecular
systems. The transition to encapsulated cellular life (lipid bilayer
membranes, protein-mediated metabolism, DNA-based information storage)
involves additional structural steps the framework's current content
does not fully derive. The chemistry-level structural foundations are in
place (carbon chemistry for membranes, scale hierarchy for metabolism);
the specific organizational steps require further structural analysis
the framework has not completed.

\textbf{The framework's epistemic stance.} The framework's content on
the origin of life is therefore at the \emph{architectural} level: the
memory conditions a replicator can realize, the population-dynamical
conditions under which replicators grow and are selected, and the
chemistry-level features --- catalysis, persistence, sequence capacity
--- on which such mechanisms draw. The framework does not compete with
or replace prebiotic chemistry research; it provides the structural
foundations that prebiotic chemistry operates within.

The empirical confirmations of the framework's content are concordance:
laboratory demonstrations of ribozyme function, RNA-catalyzed
polymerization, autocatalytic chemistry, and the emergence of complex
chemistry from simple precursors are all consistent with the framework's
structural predictions. The framework does not predict new chemistry; it
provides the structural account of why the observed chemistry has the
architecture it does.

\textbf{Forward pointers.} Chapter 12 develops the framework's content
on evolution, intelligence, and self-reference: the cascade from the
chapter's first replicators through complex biology to general
intelligence and the framework's own self-discovery. Chapter 13 develops
quantum biology --- the specific applications of C1--C4 at the molecular
scale to biological systems with substantial empirical content (enzyme
kinetics, photosynthesis, magnetoreception, neural information
processing). The framework's content in this chapter --- Darwinian
evolution as possible wherever sustained template replication has
heritable variants differing in reproductive success, heredity as C1--C4
memory, RNA-like architecture as an empirically supported hypothesis ---
provides the foundation on which the subsequent biology chapters build.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{chapter-12}{%
\section{Chapter 12}\label{chapter-12}}

\hypertarget{evolution-intelligence-and-self-reference}{%
\section{Evolution, Intelligence, and
Self-Reference}\label{evolution-intelligence-and-self-reference}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-9}{%
\subsection{12.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-9}}

Chapter 11 considered sustained template copying and the conditions for
selection. A replicator's sequence can act as a persistent record, and
Darwinian evolution can occur where heritable variants differ in
reproductive success.

This chapter examines conditional links from heredity to information
processing and computation. Protein conformations, gene regulation and
modified environments are candidate sources of memory. Later links
depend on their ecological, material and engineering premises.

Eight pieces occupy the chapter.

Section 12.2 examines protein conformation, the epigenome and the
constructed ecological niche as possible memory-bearing partitions. Each
application needs its own observable and readback test.

Section 12.3 considers selection for information processing where
responses to informative cues improve net fitness. Section 12.4
discusses whether major evolutionary transitions involve new sources of
persistent memory.

Section 12.5 discusses the materials, structure and energy regime for
electrochemical signaling. Section 12.6 considers the ecological and
historical conditions for general intelligence.

Section 12.6 develops the framework's most honest scope limit in the
cascade: general intelligence is \emph{structurally unconstrained} (the
framework's commitments permit arbitrarily complex neural circuits) but
\emph{not guaranteed} (whether evolution reaches general-purpose
reasoning depends on specific fitness landscapes the framework's
commitments do not constrain). On Earth, general intelligence arose once
in approximately 4 billion years. The framework cannot determine whether
this is typical or rare.

Section 12.7 traces a conditional route from suitable materials and
fabrication to universal computation. Boolean universality is a
mathematical result, and its implementation uses scalable circuit and
memory resources.

Section 12.8 considers how AI and its designers can each infer facts
from the records available to them. It compares this question with
Gödel's limits on proof and Turing's result on halting.

These links use the physical and chemical branch of Chapters 10--11 and
additional inputs for the target system. Evolution, intelligence and
technological realization each have their own conditions.

\hypertarget{evolution-as-a-multi-scale-c1c4-system}{%
\subsection{12.2 Evolution as a multi-scale C1--C4
system}\label{evolution-as-a-multi-scale-c1c4-system}}

In a template copier, a copied sequence can provide a persistent record
for heredity. Three other candidate memory architectures are considered
here at protein, cellular and ecological scales.

\textbf{The three scales.}

\emph{Scale 1: The protein conformational landscape.} A protein's active
conformation is the fast subsystem; the broader conformational landscape
--- alternative folded states, slow side-chain rearrangements, the
protein's interaction history with substrates --- is the slow subsystem.
The visible-sector observables are the protein's current activity
(catalytic rate, binding affinity, regulatory state); the hidden-sector
content is the conformational memory stored in slowly-relaxing degrees
of freedom. The framework's prediction is that protein function shows
non-Markovian dynamics --- history-dependent activity rather than purely
Markovian rates set by current substrate concentrations. The empirical
record from single-molecule enzymology (memory effects,
history-dependent kinetics, stretched-exponential waiting-time
distributions) is consistent with this prediction; Chapter 13 develops
the empirical content in detail.

\emph{Scale 2: The epigenome.} Gene expression is the fast subsystem;
the chromatin state --- DNA methylation patterns, histone modifications,
three-dimensional chromatin architecture --- is the slow subsystem. The
visible-sector observables are the cell's current gene expression
profile; the hidden-sector content is the regulatory memory encoded in
chromatin. The framework's prediction is that gene expression shows
non-Markovian dynamics over developmental and evolutionary timescales
--- history-dependent responses to environmental signals, including
transgenerational inheritance of acquired epigenetic states. Chapter
16's medicine content develops the epigenetic substratum-emergent
operator distinction in detail; Chapter 17's bioinformatics content
develops the empirical signatures.

\emph{Scale 3: The constructed ecological niche.} Organism behavior is
the fast subsystem; the environment that organisms modify and pass to
descendants --- burrows, mounds, beaver dams, the chemical composition
of the atmosphere, the soil microbiome shaped by plant communities ---
is the slow subsystem. The visible-sector observables are the organisms'
current adaptations; the hidden-sector content is the niche-construction
memory stored in the modified environment. The framework's prediction is
that ecological dynamics shows non-Markovian dynamics over evolutionary
timescales --- history-dependent fitness landscapes shaped by previous
generations' niche construction. The empirical record from niche
construction theory (Odling-Smee, Laland, Feldman 2003 and subsequent
work) is consistent with this prediction.

\textbf{The structural pattern.} At each scale a proposed partition is
assessed using C1--C4 for its particular measurements and timescale.

\emph{C1 (coupling).} At each scale, the fast subsystem is non-trivially
coupled to the slow subsystem. Protein activity depends on the
conformational landscape's current state; gene expression depends on the
chromatin's current state; organism behavior depends on the constructed
niche's current state. The couplings are catalytic (protein-substrate,
chromatin-gene, organism-environment), with feedback between fast and
slow subsystems.

\emph{C2 (memory persistence).} The respective records must persist
across the observation window. Slow motion, stable marks and enduring
environmental changes can motivate that premise.

\emph{C3 (sufficient capacity).} The hidden description needs enough
distinguishable and accessible record states for the proposed history
test. Counts of possible conformations or regulatory elements illustrate
possible carriers.

\textbf{C4 (history readback).} Compare histories with the same visible
present. The record is read back if the histories yield different
next-step laws. Different partition choices can lead to different
results.

Catalytic state can affect metabolism and gene expression. Chromatin can
influence cell behavior, and organisms can modify the environment
experienced by later populations. This sequence suggests possible links
between scales, whose causal effects have to be established
individually.

At each scale a positive matched-present C4 contrast establishes
accessible conditional memory for the tested observable. Chapters 13, 16
and 17 discuss specific observations and candidate comparisons.

\hypertarget{information-processing-as-fitness-enhancing}{%
\subsection{12.3 Information processing as
fitness-enhancing}\label{information-processing-as-fitness-enhancing}}

Selection can favor information processing when an informative response
improves net reproductive success in an environment with useful cues.

\textbf{The structural argument.} Three conditions describe when
information processing could be favored.

\emph{Environmental information exists.} \(kT > 0\) produces thermal
fluctuations at any temperature. The argument uses gradients in
concentration, temperature and chemical composition or environmental
cycling as additional conditions. Where present, these can provide cues
on biological timescales.

\emph{Internal state can guide a response.} Organisms can use sensory
information or retained records to change behavior. The ability to act
on available information depends on the specified sensing and control
mechanisms.

\emph{Benefits need to exceed costs.} More informative internal states
can improve foraging or reduce risk. Selection acts on net reproductive
success, which also reflects the costs of acquiring, storing and using
the information.

\textbf{The conditional conclusion.} Selection can favor heritable
information-processing traits when their net fitness effect is positive
in the relevant environment.

Chemotaxis, photoperception, hormonal signaling and neural processing
are observed examples of information use. The fitness effect of each
depends on the organism and environment.

The possible forms and benefits of information processing depend on the
organism and environment. Whether general-purpose reasoning evolves
remains open.

\hypertarget{major-evolutionary-transitions}{%
\subsection{12.4 Major evolutionary
transitions}\label{major-evolutionary-transitions}}

Major evolutionary transitions change the unit of selection as
interacting organisms or replicators form higher-level entities. Maynard
Smith and Szathmáry inventoried examples. Persistent records offer one
way to analyze the dynamics of a proposed higher-level unit.

\textbf{The transitions.} The conventional inventory includes:

\emph{Replicating molecules to populations of replicating molecules.}
The earliest transition, where individual replicating polymers
(RNA-like, §11.7) form interacting populations with collective dynamics.

\emph{Independent replicators to chromosomes.} Multiple genetic loci
become physically linked, with their fitness becoming correlated rather
than independent.

\emph{RNA as both gene and enzyme to DNA + protein.} The differentiation
of information storage (DNA, optimized for C2) from catalysis (proteins,
optimized for C1), as discussed in §11.7.

\emph{Prokaryotes to eukaryotes.} The endosymbiotic origin of organelles
(mitochondria, chloroplasts), where independent prokaryotic cells become
integrated components of larger eukaryotic cells.

\emph{Asexual to sexual reproduction.} Two parental contributions
replacing one, with recombination introducing additional variation
mechanisms.

\emph{Protists to multicellular organisms.} Independent cells become
integrated components of multicellular bodies with specialized cell
types.

\emph{Solitary individuals to colonies.} Individual organisms become
integrated components of social groups (ant colonies, bee hives), with
reproductive division of labor.

\emph{Primate societies to human societies.} Cultural transmission
becomes a major channel for inheritance alongside genetic transmission.

\textbf{The framework's structural reading.} Each major transition has
the same structural pattern: previously independent units (the
``individuals'' at the lower level) become integrated into a
higher-level unit, with three structural features establishing the
higher level:

\emph{Coupling becomes obligatory.} Lower-level units that were
independently viable become mutually dependent. A mitochondrion alone is
no longer viable outside its eukaryotic host; an isolated worker ant
outside its colony cannot reproduce. The coupling between units is C1 at
the new level --- the lower level cannot operate independently.

\emph{Slow-bath separation emerges.} The higher-level entity's dynamics
operate on slower timescales than the lower-level dynamics. Eukaryotic
cell-cycle timescales are slower than mitochondrial division rates;
multicellular organism lifespans are much longer than cell division
timescales; colony lifespans exceed individual worker lifespans. The new
level's slow bath is C2 at the higher level.

\emph{Hidden-sector capacity grows.} The higher-level entity has
substantially more internal degrees of freedom than its constituents. A
eukaryotic cell has \(\sim 10^{10}\) atoms vs.~a prokaryotic cell's
\(\sim 10^9\); a multicellular organism has \(\sim 10^{14}\) cells
vs.~one. The new level satisfies C3 with a hidden sector orders of
magnitude larger than the lower level's.

\textbf{The role of memory.} Lower-level units can participate in a
larger system with persistent records that affect its observable
dynamics. A transition to a new unit of selection also requires
heritable variation and differences in reproductive success at that
level.

The finite-horizon memory implication applies to a declared partition if
C4 holds. It leaves the origin and stability of the higher-level unit to
the relevant ecological and population mechanisms.

\textbf{Empirical implications.} A new unit of selection with a proposed
slow record can be tested by comparing histories at the same measured
present. The contributions of that record to fitness and inheritance
require their own tests.

\textbf{Limits of the framework's content.} The framework's structural
reading does not predict \emph{which} major transitions occur or
\emph{when} they occur in any specific biology. The transition from
prokaryotes to eukaryotes occurred approximately 2 billion years ago on
Earth; the transition from protists to multicellular organisms occurred
multiple independent times across different lineages; the transition
from primate societies to human societies occurred once. The framework's
structural commitments are compatible with very different timelines and
trajectories. The occurrence of C4 at each proposed level depends on the
partition and the observed readback.

\hypertarget{neural-computation-as-structurally-possible}{%
\subsection{12.5 Neural computation as structurally
possible}\label{neural-computation-as-structurally-possible}}

The selected chemistry permits candidate ions and membrane constituents
for electrochemical signaling. A functional neural system also requires
membrane organization, channels, energy supply and a suitable operating
regime.

\textbf{Ions for electrochemical signaling.} Fast neural signaling uses
ion flow across membranes. Na\(^+\) and K\(^+\) currents contribute to
axonal depolarization and repolarization, and Ca\(^{2+}\) influx can
trigger neurotransmitter release. The periodic trends in Chapter 10
§10.2 account for the familiar valences of sodium, potassium and calcium
under the stated atomic inputs. Hydration, channel selectivity and
signaling depend on the solvent, channel structure, gradients and
cellular machinery.

\textbf{Lipid membranes for compartmentalization.} Suitable amphiphilic
lipids can self-assemble into bilayers separating aqueous compartments.
Familiar phospholipids have hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails. The
availability of these molecules and the conditions for bilayer assembly
are material and environmental inputs.

\textbf{Energetic separation.} In suitable systems, electrochemical
signaling can occur on energy scales below covalent bond energies. At
room temperature \(kT\) is about 25 meV. The signal and bond energies
depend on the driving voltage, molecular architecture and environment.

\textbf{The feasibility claim.} With suitable chemistry and molecular
machinery, signaling can occur without breaking the covalent framework
of the cell. The same conditions can support circuits of interacting
cells.

Nervous systems and signaling in plants provide empirical examples of
such organization. Their evolutionary history depends on the lineage and
environment.

The argument identifies materials and energy regimes that permit
electrochemical signaling. Whether and how they are used for neural
computation depends on biological organization.

\hypertarget{conditions-for-general-intelligence}{%
\subsection{12.6 Conditions for general
intelligence}\label{conditions-for-general-intelligence}}

The chemistry and energetic separation allow complex neural circuits in
suitable organisms. Evolution also has to supply their organization,
maintenance and behavioral uses.

\textbf{Intelligence-relevant capabilities.}

\emph{Neural computation.} The candidate materials and energy conditions
are discussed in §12.5.

\emph{Sensory processing.} The chemistry permits candidate transduction
mechanisms such as light-sensitive proteins and mechanosensitive
channels.

\emph{Memory.} Conformations, chromatin and synaptic weights can provide
persistent records if they influence a later readout.

\emph{Pattern recognition.} Appropriately organized circuits can
discriminate patterns.

\emph{Learning.} Synaptic plasticity can encode previous activity. The
circuit and its training or selection conditions determine which
capabilities result.

\emph{Goal-directed behavior.} Coupled sensing and control can support
actions that improve outcomes under suitable environmental conditions.

\emph{General-purpose reasoning.} \textbf{Not structurally guaranteed.}
Whether evolution produces systems capable of abstract reasoning,
language with recursive syntax, formal mathematics, and self-modeling
depends on specific selection pressures the framework's commitments do
not determine.

General-purpose reasoning is a particular outcome of evolution. It
requires additional ecological and developmental premises beyond the
material possibility of neural signaling.

The fitness advantages of general intelligence depend on the specific
environment. In environments where pattern recognition and learning
provide sufficient adaptive advantage, evolution may stop at
sophisticated learning systems without developing general reasoning. In
environments where social complexity, tool use, or environmental
unpredictability place premium on abstract reasoning, evolution may
proceed to general-intelligence-like systems. The framework does not
determine which environments select for general intelligence.

\textbf{Earth's record.} General intelligence arose on Earth
approximately once in \(\sim 4\) billion years (the human lineage, with
the most extreme degree; some other species --- cetaceans, corvids,
cephalopods --- show partial expressions). This is consistent with two
interpretations: general intelligence is \emph{rare} (requires specific
evolutionary conditions that are unlikely to occur), or general
intelligence is \emph{inevitable but slow} (any sufficiently complex
biology produces general intelligence given enough time).

The framework cannot determine which interpretation is correct. The
framework's structural commitments are compatible with both. The
empirical record on Earth is consistent with both. Determining which
interpretation holds requires evidence from astrobiology --- the
discovery of multiple independent occurrences of general intelligence in
independent biological systems --- which is not currently available.

\textbf{The scope.} The materials argument allows neural systems capable
of complex behavior. The occurrence of general-purpose reasoning and the
conditions sufficient to evolve it remain open.

This is honest content. Frameworks claiming to predict general
intelligence as a structural inevitability would be overreaching given
the available evidence; frameworks claiming general intelligence is
impossible or extraordinarily rare would also be overreaching. The
framework's stance --- capability structural, occurrence uncertain ---
is the position most consistent with the framework's structural
commitments and the available evidence.

\hypertarget{the-chain-from-intelligence-to-ai}{%
\subsection{12.7 The chain from intelligence to
AI}\label{the-chain-from-intelligence-to-ai}}

Given suitable materials, fabrication, controls and memory, a generally
intelligent observer could implement universal computation. The
following links describe one such route.

\textbf{Step 1: Band theory.} Standard quantum mechanics in a periodic
crystal potential gives Bloch states and energy bands. A particular
crystal structure and a useful band gap are material inputs. The
proposed OI application uses the physical quantum correspondence as an
additional premise.

\textbf{Step 2: Semiconductors.} Crystalline silicon has a filled
valence band at zero temperature and a gap of about 1.1 eV. At room
temperature its gap satisfies \(E_{\text{gap}}/kT\sim40\). Suitable
doping and device geometry permit controllable conduction.

Whether a material has a gap in that range at its operating temperature
is a material-dependent input. The atomic energy scale
(\(\alpha^2 m_e c^2 \approx 27\) eV, set by the coupling values and
masses of Chapter 10 §10.4) sets the eV scale of electronic energies,
and the thermal scale at biological temperatures is \(kT \sim 0.025\)
eV; the gap of a particular material and the operating temperature are
inputs, and silicon's place in the regime where it can be used as a
voltage-controlled switch is a fact about that material.

\textbf{Step 3: Doping.} In silicon, substitutional phosphorus acts as a
donor and boron as an acceptor. Controlled incorporation can produce
n-type and p-type regions.

\textbf{Step 4: From transistors to universal computation.} Suitable
semiconductor junctions and transistors enable switching. NAND is
functionally complete for Boolean functions. Circuits based on NAND,
joined to memory and resources that can scale with the task, support
Turing computation.

The device links consume semiconductor physics, suitable fabrication and
control. The universality link uses the mathematical result about
circuits and memory.

\textbf{The reconstruction theorem and self-discovery.} The
reconstruction theorem (developed in Chapter 2) identifies the local
invariants of \((S, \varphi)\) fixed by its stated inputs. An observer
with access to those inputs can use the result in device design given
the material, fabrication and control conditions above.

This route makes artificial computation feasible where those
technological conditions are met. Whether a society realizes it or
builds artificial intelligence depends on its choices and history.

\hypertarget{the-self-referential-loop-and-structural-limits}{%
\subsection{12.8 The self-referential loop and structural
limits}\label{the-self-referential-loop-and-structural-limits}}

Building an AI can place a new observer within the same \((S, \varphi)\)
as its designers. Each observer has a declared observation and control
interface. For a supplied observable law with a finite alphabet and
horizon, {[}Main §3.4{]} gives an exact fixed-basis quantum
representation. Conditional memory requires a C4 readback witness, with
two positive-probability histories that share the current visible state
and have different next-step laws. A shared record law requires an
established correspondence between the admitted preparations and
controls that preserves the probabilities of corresponding records. The
action-scale relation \(\hbar = c^3\epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\) and the
claims about the Standard Model and the gravitational and dark sectors
use the premises of the separate constructions in Chapters 5--8.

\textbf{Self-referential limits.} At a declared interface, a record
identifies a quantity when all supported states compatible with that
record agree on its value. In a known finite reversible model with a
specified preparation, a proper observer can identify the current state
or a future quantity on some passive records ({[}Substratum{]}
Proposition 24.5). Breuer's self-measurement bound concerns
distinguishability when the system includes the observer's own records
(Breuer 1995). A cosmological horizon bounds direct observation where it
acts as a causal boundary.

The same criterion applies at each stage of AI building AI. More
computation on a fixed record leaves any disagreement among its
compatible states unresolved. Better instruments may supply new records
or controls.

\textbf{Gödel, Turing and observational incompleteness.} Self-reference
raises distinct questions about proof, computation and observation.

\emph{Gödel.} Sufficiently strong, consistent, effectively axiomatized
theories of arithmetic have undecidable statements under the first
incompleteness theorem's hypotheses. Under the second theorem's
hypotheses, the theory's own consistency statement is unprovable within
that theory.

\emph{Turing.} Halting is undecidable over the general family of
programs and inputs. Given an explicit finite deterministic update and
initial state, one can decide halting on that orbit by iterating until
it halts or a state repeats.

\emph{OI (framework).} Supported states that agree on the available
record can disagree on the quantity being inferred. The resulting limit
concerns the particular record, target and interface.

\textbf{Deutsch's \emph{Beginning of Infinity}.} David Deutsch
{[}Deutsch{]} argues that explanatory knowledge is objective and its
creation is open-ended. The right epistemic stance toward any current
best explanation is therefore \emph{provisional but committed} --- take
the explanation seriously enough to commit to it operationally and hold
it accountable to its predictions, while remaining open to its eventual
successor.

The growth of knowledge is a philosophical parallel to these
mathematical limits. OI supplies a particular example of a limit on
empirical knowledge. At a fixed interface, representatives related by an
established record-preserving correspondence have the same accessible
record laws ({[}Substratum{]} Theorem 24). Empirical explanations using
those records leave the choice among those representatives undetermined.
Deutsch's case for open-ended explanatory growth is independent of that
example.

One feature of Deutsch's broader program is read differently by the
framework, and the divergence is worth stating precisely. Deutsch's
\emph{Beginning of Infinity} defends the many-worlds interpretation of
quantum mechanics as a corollary of taking the wave function as
fundamental ontology. From the framework's perspective, that commitment
rests on a category error. On the framework's proposal, quantum
mechanics is not fundamental: it is emergent, the post-trace-out
description of how observation operates for embedded observers, and the
wave function is the mathematical object that emerges. The Everettian
``branches'' are then not a parallel-ontologies claim about fundamental
reality; they are features of the compressed emergent description,
analogous to the way the partition function is a mathematical structure
of statistical mechanics rather than a claim about parallel ensembles.
Asking ``do the branches really exist?'' presupposes the wave function's
formalism as direct ontology --- a presupposition OI specifically
denies, since the substratum is the deeper description and the wave
function is what observation produces from it. The Everettian measure
problem dissolves on the framework's reading because the branches are
not ontological objects requiring measure assignment ({[}Main{]} §4.1);
the question MWI is trying to answer is dissolved by relocating the wave
function's apparent ontology one level down. The same substratum and
observable descriptions also organize the distinct premise checks for
Bell, Kochen-Specker, Pusey-Barrett-Rudolph and Frauchiger-Renner
(\protect\hyperlink{methodology}{Methodology} Part III; Appendix C).
Those checks retain their separate operational, preparation and
agent-consistency assumptions; relocating a description alone does not
establish a no-go resolution. The framework's divergence from MWI is
therefore not disagreement at the epistemic-status level --- where OI
and BoI align --- but a diagnosis: MWI is reading at the wrong level of
the substrate-emergent architecture.

describes. Its authors, readers and any AI using it can infer a quantity
from their records when the supported compatible states agree on that
quantity. Chapter 19 §19.3.5 discusses the separate question of initial
conditions.

of conditional memory in biology. Chapter 14 characterizes BQP under a

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-10}{%
\subsection{13.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-10}}

Chapters 10--12 describe chemistry on a conditional continuum branch,
template copying under its chemical premises, and candidate memory
architectures in biology.

This chapter applies the finite-horizon memory diagnostic to biological
observables. Prior experiments motivate candidate records and
interventions. Demonstrating C4 requires a matched-present history
contrast for the declared observable.

Eight pieces occupy the chapter.

Section 13.2 describes how the conditional readback result informs tests
of photosynthetic energy transfer, magnetoreception and enzyme activity.
Fixed-basis representability applies to finite laws. Biological
coherence and its functional role require physical evidence.

Section 13.3 considers protein conformations as candidate persistent
records. Section 13.4 distinguishes spectroscopy of light-harvesting
complexes from models of exciton--vibration dynamics and from tests of
C4.

Section 13.5 discusses the radical-pair hypothesis and in vitro evidence
about cryptochrome. Section 13.6 uses enzyme waiting times and rate
correlations to motivate matched-present tests.

Section 13.7 considers the proposal that some biological systems show
partial distinguishability revival, \(0<\mathcal N<1\) for the measure
of Chapter 18 §18.3. Matched-present tests assess accessible memory.
Distinguishability measurements for specified preparations assess
revival.

Section 13.9 reviews which empirical results motivate the mechanism
proposal and what direct tests would require.

The mechanism proposal considers specific biological observations, with
conditional memory and revival as distinct tests.

\hypertarget{the-frameworks-reframing-of-quantum-biology}{%
\subsection{13.2 The framework's reframing of quantum
biology}\label{the-frameworks-reframing-of-quantum-biology}}

The conventional treatment of quantum biology has a particular
structure. Quantum mechanics is treated as the \emph{exception} in
biology --- most biological processes are presumed classical, with
quantum effects appearing in specific exceptional cases that require
special explanation. The exceptional cases include photosynthetic
exciton transfer (where quantum coherence persists longer than naively
expected), magnetoreception (where radical-pair quantum dynamics may
underlie the avian compass), and enzyme catalysis (where quantum
tunneling may contribute to hydrogen transfer reactions). Each case is
treated as a specific puzzle requiring its own explanation.

The same conditional readback implication applies to each declared
observable. Fixed-basis representation by itself supplies neither
physical coherence nor a particular mechanism.

Conformational states and chromatin marks are candidate record carriers
in the settings discussed in Chapter 12. A test needs to establish which
record persists and what later measurement it affects.

Accessible memory is a property of an observable law. A mechanism can be
tested against classical models that include additional current-state
variables and against quantum dynamical models where relevant.

\textbf{Candidate systems.} Photosynthesis, avian magnetoreception and
enzyme kinetics suggest different possible records and readouts.

Spectral oscillations, magnetic sensitivity and turnover correlations
probe different properties. Each system needs its own comparison between
histories at the same present to establish C4.

\textbf{Empirical access.} Single-molecule measurements can help define
the present observable and follow later transitions. To test readback,
the experiment would compare histories at fixed values of that present.

\hypertarget{c1c4-in-proteins}{%
\subsection{13.3 C1--C4 in proteins}\label{c1c4-in-proteins}}

A protein's broader conformational landscape is a candidate source of
history dependence in a chosen active-site observable.

\textbf{The protein partition.} Consider an enzyme catalyzing a
reaction. The visible sector is the active site's current configuration
--- the precise geometric arrangement of catalytic residues, the
substrate's binding position, and the local electronic structure that
determines the reaction's instantaneous rate. The hidden sector is the
broader conformational landscape --- the protein's overall fold, the
rotameric states of distant side chains, the dynamic network of
residue-residue contacts throughout the scaffold, and the bound water
structure in the protein's interior.

The partition is \emph{physically meaningful} in the sense that
experimentally accessible observables (catalytic rate, binding affinity,
fluorescence anisotropy) correspond to visible-sector quantities, while
the conformational details determining those observables sit in the
hidden sector and are not directly observable at the same time
resolution.

\textbf{C1: catalytic-conformational coupling.} Active-site dynamics are
coupled to the broader conformational landscape through several
mechanisms. Substrate binding induces conformational changes in the
scaffold (induced fit). Catalysis releases or absorbs energy that
propagates through the protein (allosteric coupling). Side-chain
rotameric transitions change the active site's electrostatic environment
(conformational gating). The coupling is non-trivial: the active site's
current behavior depends on the scaffold's current state, and the
scaffold's evolution depends on the active site's history of binding and
catalysis. C1 is satisfied with substantial coupling strength.

\textbf{C2: conformational timescale separation.} Active-site dynamics
(substrate binding, bond formation/breaking, proton transfer) operate at
\(\tau_S \sim 10^{-12}\) to \(10^{-9}\) s (picoseconds to nanoseconds).
Conformational rearrangements in the broader scaffold operate at
\(\tau_B \sim 10^{-6}\) to \(10^{-3}\) s (microseconds to milliseconds),
with some particularly slow conformational transitions taking seconds or
longer. The timescale separation is \(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-9}\) to
\(10^{-3}\) --- substantially smaller than the cosmological case
(\(10^{-32}\)) but comparable to or larger than engineered quantum
systems (qubits at \(10^{-3}\), atomic clocks at \(10^{-6}\)).

\textbf{C3: conformational landscape capacity.} A coarse conformation
count illustrates possible record states. The usable capacity depends on
which states persist and can be distinguished through the proposed
coupling.

\textbf{A matched-present test.} If conformational records influence
later active-site dynamics differently for histories sharing the same
present, the observable law carries conditional memory.

\emph{Nonexponential kinetics.} Waiting-time distributions can reflect
mixtures of states with different rates, including Markov models in the
enlarged state.

\emph{Fluctuating rates.} Single-enzyme rates can fluctuate across
turnover windows. Lag correlations motivate a conditional test with a
specified present state.

\emph{Conformational gating.} Binding, release and some tunneling models
depend on molecular conformation. The causal effect of a retained record
depends on which transitions and histories are compared.

\emph{Inhibition and activation.} Slow relaxation after allosteric
ligand binding can motivate a comparison at matched present measured
state.

Empirical work on these signatures includes single-molecule measurements
and model comparisons. The readback claim requires the conditional test
above.

\textbf{Empirical status.} The measured turnover and conformation
dynamics motivate tests of specific models. Raw kinetics leave the
presence and source of C4 open for the declared readout.

\hypertarget{photosynthesis-and-excitonvibration-dynamics}{%
\subsection{13.4 Photosynthesis and exciton--vibration
dynamics}\label{photosynthesis-and-excitonvibration-dynamics}}

Engel and colleagues reported oscillations in two-dimensional electronic
spectroscopy of the FMO complex. Distinguishing vibrational, electronic
and mixed contributions requires detailed spectroscopy and dynamical
modeling ({[}Complexity §7.4{]}).

The exciton--vibration interface is a candidate memory architecture. An
appropriate dynamical comparison would ask which state is retained and
influences later transfer at the same measured present.

\textbf{The photosynthetic partition.} In a light-harvesting complex
(LH1, LH2, FMO, or others), the visible sector is the \emph{exciton} ---
the photoexcited electronic state delocalized across multiple pigment
molecules (chlorophylls, bacteriochlorophylls, carotenoids). The hidden
sector is the \emph{protein-vibrational environment} --- the protein
scaffold's vibrational modes, the solvent dynamics, and the slow
conformational fluctuations that modulate the pigments' electronic
energies and inter-pigment couplings.

\textbf{Coupling and timescales.} Exciton--vibration coupling motivates
a candidate visible and hidden description. Lifetimes and
distinguishable vibrational states are model inputs. The C4 contrast
needs its own witness.

\textbf{Proposed history test.} A vibrational record that changes later
exciton-transfer laws at matched present would give conditional memory.
Detectable distinguishability revival would require a comparison with
specified initial preparations and readout.

Duan et al.~report short electronic coherence in their FMO spectroscopy
({[}Complexity §7.4{]}). Cao and Plenio model vibronic contributions to
transfer. The model and spectroscopy provide separate information about
candidate dynamics.

\textbf{Empirical implications.} Measurements across controlled
vibrational preparations could help resolve electronic and vibronic
contributions. The C4 test needs a specified measured state, histories
and subsequent observable.

The effectiveness of a candidate transfer mechanism depends on the
observed dynamics and a comparison with alternatives.

\hypertarget{a-radical-pair-hypothesis-for-magnetoreception}{%
\subsection{13.5 A radical-pair hypothesis for
magnetoreception}\label{a-radical-pair-hypothesis-for-magnetoreception}}

The avian magnetic compass --- the mechanism by which migratory birds
sense the geomagnetic field for navigation --- provides a second
canonical case of quantum biology. The leading hypothesis (Ritz, Adair,
Schulten, and others, from the 1970s through the present) is that
magnetoreception uses a \emph{radical-pair mechanism} in cryptochrome
proteins in the avian retina: photoexcitation of cryptochrome produces a
spin-correlated radical pair whose recombination yield depends on the
geomagnetic field through Zeeman splitting of the radical-pair states.

The radical-pair model motivates a test of whether nuclear and molecular
degrees of freedom retain information relevant to recombination.

\textbf{The radical-pair partition.} A radical pair consists of two
unpaired electrons in adjacent molecular orbitals, with the two-electron
spin state initially correlated (singlet \(|S\rangle\) or triplet
\(|T_0\rangle\), \(|T_\pm\rangle\), depending on the photochemical
mechanism). The visible sector is the \emph{electron spin state} --- the
two-electron spin configuration that determines the recombination
products. The hidden sector is the \emph{nuclear spin environment} ---
the hyperfine-coupled nuclear spins of the surrounding nuclei, the
molecular vibrations modulating the hyperfine couplings, and the protein
scaffold dynamics affecting the radical pair's lifetime.

\textbf{Candidate partition.} Hyperfine coupling can connect the
electron spins with nuclear spins. Whether a useful record persists, and
changes a later yield at fixed present, depends on mechanism-specific
rates, controls and readout.

\textbf{A proposed history test.} Compare the recombination laws for
histories matched at a declared radical-pair observable. The
magnetic-field dependence and the existence of a retained record are
distinct measurements.

Radical-pair lifetime sets an available reaction interval. It cannot by
itself determine the coherence lifetime or the response in a bird.

\textbf{Empirical context.} Behavioral tests and in vitro molecular
assays inform different parts of the hypothesis.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Light dependence.} The light dependence of the avian compass
  motivates photochemical mechanisms.
\item
  \emph{Inclination sensitivity.} The observed compass response to field
  orientation constrains candidate mechanisms.
\item
  \emph{Radiofrequency disruption and in vitro sensitivity.} Behavioral
  radiofrequency results motivate radical-pair models. Xu et al.~report
  magnetic sensitivity of European robin cryptochrome 4 in vitro
  ({[}Complexity §7.4{]}). The responsible receptor and its mechanism in
  vivo remain open.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Further tests.} The proposed mechanism needs a link from
molecular responses to the sensory system and a declared C4 assay for a
retained record. The magnetic sensitivity results alone do not give
either.

\hypertarget{enzyme-catalysis-as-the-frameworks-clearest-test-case}{%
\subsection{13.6 Enzyme catalysis as the framework's clearest test
case}\label{enzyme-catalysis-as-the-frameworks-clearest-test-case}}

Enzyme catalysis is the framework's most direct empirical test bed in
quantum biology. Single-enzyme experiments --- pioneered by Sunney Xie
and developed by many groups over the past two decades --- provide
single-molecule resolution of catalytic events, with sufficient time
resolution to detect the framework's predicted non-Markovian signatures.
This section develops the specific empirical predictions and their match
to experimental data.

\textbf{The empirical record.} Single-enzyme studies report several
kinds of temporal behavior:

\emph{Dynamic disorder.} Individual enzyme molecules exhibit
fluctuations in catalytic rate over time. The fluctuations are not
random noise but exhibit structured temporal correlations --- slow
periods (low catalytic rate) cluster together; fast periods (high
catalytic rate) cluster together. The autocorrelation function of
catalytic rate decays on timescales much longer than individual
catalytic cycles, indicating that the rate fluctuations have
\emph{memory}.

\emph{Nonexponential waiting-time distributions.} Stretched-exponential
and multiexponential fits describe some observed waits. A mixture or
projection of Markov states can produce such waits.

\emph{Correlations between cycles.} Successive turnover durations can be
correlated. A matched-present history test requires conditioning beyond
the raw lag correlation.

\emph{Allosteric history dependence.} Inhibitors and activators binding
away from the active site produce activity changes with kinetics
dependent on the protein's history. The ``memory'' is the slow
relaxation of the conformational substrate to the new ligand-bound
state.

\textbf{A conditional readback test.} The readback result identifies
memory when histories of the same measured present have different
subsequent laws. A biochemical model is required to identify which
retained variable accounts for the contrast.

The individual findings motivate tests across specific conformations and
histories. The existence, time window and magnitude of accessible memory
depend on the given enzyme, perturbation and measurement.

\textbf{Quantitative testability.} A parameterized kinetic model could
predict waiting-time distributions and correlation functions. The
finite-horizon result specifies the conditional contrast without fixing
those forms. A separate revival test could address the mechanism
proposal in §13.7.

The diagnostic experiments are within reach of current single-molecule
techniques: multi-time correlation measurements with sufficient
statistics to constrain the algebraic structure of the transition
probabilities, performed on well-characterized enzymes with known
conformational landscapes. The framework's content here is therefore
empirically actionable, with the prediction of the restricted
quantum-statistical regime being the mechanism proposal's distinctive
falsification target.

\hypertarget{the-restricted-quantum-statistical-regime-in-biology}{%
\subsection{13.7 The restricted quantum-statistical regime in
biology}\label{the-restricted-quantum-statistical-regime-in-biology}}

The framework's content on quantum biology includes a structurally
distinct prediction: the mechanism proposal predicts that biological
C1--C4 systems lie in the \emph{restricted quantum-statistical regime}
of Chapter 18 §18.3, partial distinguishability revival on accessible
windows (\(0 < \mathcal{N} < 1\)) --- a revival range, not a degree of
quantum membership ({[}Main §3.4{]}), and not implied by C1--C4, which
give memory without fixing \(\mathcal{N}\) ({[}Main §2.3{]}). Partial
revival itself is standard open-systems phenomenology, quantified in the
literature by the Breuer--Laine--Piilo measure; what is distinctive is
the proposed capacity-controlled origin and scaling law, the mechanism
proposal's prediction for systems with marginal hidden capacity.

\textbf{The regime's empirical signature.} C4 is a statement about
multi-time laws at fixed present. The measure \(\mathcal{N}\) concerns
revival of distinguishability in a specified rooted map family.
Conditional memory and divisible population laws can coexist on an
accessible window ({[}Main §2.3{]}). The capacity law and any proposed
conditions on operational completion require their own derivation.

\textbf{Biological systems in the restricted quantum-statistical
regime.} The biological scales developed in §§13.3-13.6 --- protein
conformational landscapes (\(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-9}\) to
\(10^{-3}\)), photosynthetic light-harvesting
(\(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-1}\) to \(10^{-4}\)), magnetoreception
(\(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-3}\)), single-enzyme catalysis
(\(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-9}\) to \(10^{-12}\)) --- are slow-bath
ratios. Hidden-sector capacities range from \(\sim 10^{30}\) (radical
pair) to \(\sim 10^{200}\) (protein conformational landscape) --- large
but finite, the finiteness capping accessible memory ({[}Main §3.4{]}).
Capacities of this size lie far above the comparable-capacity range
\(N_H/N_V \sim 1\) of Chapter 15 §15.7, so the placement of biological
systems in the restricted quantum-statistical regime is a conjecture
that the capacity ratio does not fix.

The proposal's conjecture is that \emph{biological systems show partial
distinguishability revival (the restricted quantum-statistical regime)}
at the C1--C4 scales of interest --- a revival claim, not a
quantum-membership claim ({[}Main §3.4{]}). This is structurally
distinct from ``biology has quantum effects'' (which the framework's
reading agrees with) and from ``biology is fundamentally
quantum-mechanical at all scales'' (which the framework's reading
rejects). The restricted quantum-statistical regime is the mechanism
proposal's specific commitment.

\textbf{Empirical access.} Multi-time measurements can estimate the
matched-present contrast for a chosen enzyme's observable. To measure
revival, prepare the specified states and track the relevant
distinguishability on the same window.

A test of the mechanism proposal needs a declared system, preparations,
observation window, conditioning and noise model. A divisible rooted
population family is compatible with positive conditional memory.

The proposed capacity dependence would be tested by varying accessible
capacity under stated dynamics and measuring revival.

\hypertarget{implications-for-drug-design}{%
\subsection{13.8 Implications for drug
design}\label{implications-for-drug-design}}

Drug-target kinetics can be approximated by a model of current state
when that state is sufficient. Additional conformational variables may
be needed for some experiments.

\textbf{Kinetic implications.} Standard pharmacology characterizes a
drug-target interaction with two rate constants: \(k_{\text{on}}\)
(binding rate) and \(k_{\text{off}}\) (dissociation rate), with the
equilibrium dissociation constant \(K_d = k_{\text{off}}/k_{\text{on}}\)
determining the binding affinity. The framework's prediction is that
these rate constants are \emph{not constants} but vary with the
protein's conformational state --- fast periods (high \(k_{\text{on}}\),
low \(k_{\text{off}}\)) cluster together; slow periods cluster together.
The clinical consequence: a drug's effective potency varies over time in
ways the constant-rate-constant model cannot capture.

\textbf{Allosteric implications.} Ligands can act through protein
conformation. In a system with history-dependent ligand response at
matched present, a kinetic model would need to account for the retained
variables.

\textbf{Resistance mechanisms.} Drug resistance often involves mutations
in the target protein that change the active site or the allosteric
communication network. The framework's reading: resistance is a
\emph{memory-structure alteration} --- the mutations change the
protein's C1--C4 architecture, producing different non-Markovian
dynamics and therefore different drug-target kinetics. The framework's
content suggests that resistance can be combatted by designing drugs
that exploit specific features of the C1--C4 architecture rather than
just optimizing static binding affinity.

\textbf{Catalytic vs regulatory specificity.} The framework's structural
content distinguishes drugs that target the active site (modulating the
fast subsystem) from drugs that target the regulatory landscape
(modulating the slow subsystem). The two categories have different
kinetic signatures and different clinical implications. Chapter 16's
medicine content develops this distinction in detail for specific
clinical contexts; the structural foundation is the C1--C4 architecture
developed in this chapter.

\textbf{The magnitude of corrections.} The size of the framework's
corrections to standard drug kinetics is not fixed by \(\tau_S/\tau_B\).
The ratio sets how long the scaffold retains a record, of order
\(\tau_B/\tau_S\) active-site events; the size of the correction is set
by how strongly that record modulates later events, which is open for
protein systems. For drug design, the practical question is whether the
cumulative effect reaches clinical relevance at the doses and timescales
of therapeutic use. The framework's content provides a structural basis
for predicting when corrections matter rather than just empirically
discovering them case by case.

\hypertarget{chapter-close}{%
\subsection{13.9 Chapter close}\label{chapter-close}}

Enzyme kinetics, exciton transfer and magnetoreception offer distinct
experiments in which to look for a persistent record and compare its
effects at matched present.

\textbf{Three categories of empirical content.} The chapter's content
sorts into three categories.

\emph{Established empirical content.} The cited studies report FMO
spectral oscillations, magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome in vitro and
temporal structure in single-enzyme kinetics. Their conclusions use
different readouts and do not determine a common C4 mechanism.

\emph{Quantitative model proposals.} Enzyme waiting times, multi-time
correlations and temperature responses can be modeled for specified
molecular systems. The finite-horizon result supplies the conditional
test of accessible memory.

\emph{Predictions for future empirical work.} The restricted
quantum-statistical regime's diagnostic signature
(distinguishability-revival measurements, with multi-time correlation
measurements testing memory) is the mechanism proposal's distinctive
falsification target. Engineered biological systems with tunable C1--C4
parameters (designed proteins, synthetic photosynthetic systems,
artificial radical-pair platforms) could provide controlled tests of the
framework's quantitative predictions.

\textbf{Forward pointers.} Chapter 14 gives a BQP theorem under a
uniform scalable model with quantum operations, efficient simulation and
charged conditioning. Chapter 15 proposes a BEC test of a
capacity-controlled revival mechanism, with an estimator and controls
still to be specified. Chapters 16 and 17 discuss candidate biomedical
applications.

The following chapters apply these conditional diagnostics to proposed
engineering and biomedical tests.
