A long retention window motivates a search for a matched-present history
effect. A divisibility test and a measurement of any logical or sensing
benefit are separate comparisons.

The remaining sections develop the framework's specific engineering
content at each of these scales, with testable predictions for current
and near-future quantum hardware platforms.

\hypertarget{superconducting-qubits-and-tls-noise}{%
\subsection{15.3 Superconducting qubits and TLS
noise}\label{superconducting-qubits-and-tls-noise}}

Superconducting qubits --- transmons, fluxonium, and similar
architectures --- are the leading commercial platform for quantum
computing. Companies including IBM, Google, Rigetti, and IQM have
demonstrated processors with hundreds to thousands of physical qubits,
with active programs targeting fault-tolerant quantum computing at
scale. The framework's content provides specific predictions for the
noise structure that limits current performance and the design
principles that could improve it.

\textbf{The TLS bath.} Superconducting qubits are fabricated as
thin-film Josephson junctions on amorphous oxide substrates. The
amorphous oxide contains \emph{two-level systems} (TLS) --- structural
defects that flip between two configurations at characteristic rates
determined by the local atomic environment. The TLS distribution is
broad, with rates ranging from microseconds to seconds, and the TLS
density is approximately \(10^4\)-\(10^6\) per cubic micrometer for
typical aluminum-oxide barriers. A transmon qubit typically couples to
several hundred to several thousand TLS through its electromagnetic
field.

\textbf{The framework's C1--C4 conditions for the transmon-TLS system.}

\emph{C1 (coupling).} The TLS couple to the transmon through their
electric dipoles, with coupling strengths varying from kHz to MHz
depending on the TLS proximity to the qubit's electric field maxima. The
coupling is continuous and bidirectional --- qubit excitations can
transfer to TLS and vice versa.

\emph{C2 (memory persistence).} Transmon gate operations occur on
\(\tau_S \sim 10\)-100 ns timescales. The TLS bath has correlation times
\(\tau_B \sim 1\)-100 \(\mu\)s. The ratio:
\(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-3}\) for typical operating conditions. This is
twenty-nine orders of magnitude larger than the cosmological case,
placing transmon-TLS dynamics squarely in the framework's slow-bath
regime, with a retention window of \(\sim 10^3\) gates.

\emph{C3 (capacity).} A TLS bath has candidate record states. Its usable
capacity depends on which states can retain distinguishable histories
and influence the measured qubit.

\emph{C4 (history readback).} A TLS record would satisfy C4 if histories
with the same measured present gave different next-step laws through
that record. The contrast and its attribution require measurements.

\textbf{A test of memory-bearing noise.} Compare the next error law
after different histories matched at the present. A characteristic ratio
\(\tau_B/\tau_S\sim10^3\) gates motivates a choice of windows in the
illustrative bath. It does not determine the size or even the existence
of a readback effect.

Independent errors are a standard comparison. A Markov model with
leakage, drift or a latent state can also produce correlated error
records.

\textbf{Candidate empirical tests.}

\emph{Lagged correlations.} Error correlations across gate separations
can guide choice of timescales for the matched-present test.
Correlations can persist in a Markov model with additional state
variables.

\emph{Higher-order statistics.} Conditional multi-time comparisons can
test a declared history effect. P-indivisibility requires a separate
witness for a specified map family.

\emph{Surface-code logical errors.} A model of physical noise and a
specified decoder can be used to predict and compare logical errors.

Correlated errors have been reported for several carriers, including
cosmic-ray events and quasiparticles. The Willow comparison reported in
{[}Complexity §8.2{]} finds an aggregate trend with depth relative to
its detector-error model. The stricter analysis yields no defensible
individual detections, and the backflow proxy is null in those streams.
Carrier attribution and a measured decoder gain remain open.

\hypertarget{correlation-aware-error-correction}{%
\subsection{15.4 Correlation-aware error
correction}\label{correlation-aware-error-correction}}

A history-aware decoder can use diagnostic past observations in addition
to the current syndrome. Its performance depends on the code, noise,
decoder comparison and implementation costs.

\textbf{A proposed decoder comparison.} Test a correlation-aware decoder
against a specified baseline at matched physical operating conditions.
The illustrative \(\tau_B/\tau_S\) gives one candidate range of lags.
The test needs to estimate which past observations add predictive
information and how that information affects logical error.

The size of the reduction is not derived: converting the correlation
length into an overhead requires a code, decoder and noise spectrum
(§15.9).

Compare noise models and decoders on the same device regime at matched
code distance, physical error rate and readout. The comparison should
account for training, decoding latency and the resources needed at the
target logical error rate.

Any overhead reduction would depend on those measured system and decoder
properties.

\textbf{Falsification conditions.} A matched comparison can reject a
predicted gain for the specified noise model, decoder and device regime.
A separate test of C4 can reject a proposed history effect on the chosen
window.

The aggregate syndrome observations motivate these comparisons. They
leave the performance and mechanism tests open.

\hypertarget{coherence-extension-through-engineered-baths}{%
\subsection{15.5 Coherence extension through engineered
baths}\label{coherence-extension-through-engineered-baths}}

An engineered bath could extend usable coherence if its dynamics
restores the phase-sensitive signal needed by the device. This requires
a comparison with matched controls.

\textbf{A candidate mechanism.} In a model with coherent coupling to a
slow bath, some quantum information can transfer to and return from the
bath. Which part returns to the logical or readout degrees of freedom
depends on the model.

An exponential \(e^{-t/T_2}\) is a common coherence benchmark. A rooted
population revival certifies a divisibility failure for that map family.
To claim coherent recovery, measure phase-sensitive revival for the
relevant state preparations and controls.

How long the recovered signal persists depends on amplitude, coupling
and other decoherence channels. The timing ratio alone leaves the
achievable coherence extension open.

\textbf{Concrete platform: qubit coupled to a spin chain.} A specific
platform implementing the framework's prediction is a qubit coupled to a
linear chain of \(L\) ancillary spins. The chain serves as the
engineered hidden sector. Its correlation timescale scales as
\(\tau_B \sim L^z\) (where \(z\) is the dynamical exponent --- for a
Heisenberg chain, \(z = 1\)). Its capacity scales exponentially as
approximately \(2^L\) states.

By tuning the chain length \(L\) --- the lengths below are illustrative
estimates from \(\tau_B \sim L^z\), not derived critical lengths --- the
framework's prediction is:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Short chain (\(L \lesssim 5\), \(\tau_B \sim \tau_S\)): how far the
  dynamics departs from the Markov benchmark, and whether any record
  survives to readback, depends on the coupling, the chain's conditional
  mixing and its readback; the ratio \(\tau_B/\tau_S\) alone establishes
  neither memorylessness nor record survival.
\item
  Long chain (\(L\gtrsim20\), \(\tau_B\gg\tau_S\)): a longer retention
  window in the illustrative model can allow readback if the retained
  state affects later visible laws at fixed present. Coherent recovery
  and population indivisibility require their respective measurements.
  Whether a record survives to readback depends on the chain's
  conditional mixing, not on a threshold in \(\tau_B/\tau_S\); where a
  record survives and the chain reads it back (C4), the visible law
  carries accessible finite-horizon memory. On a fixed finite reversible
  representative, where recurrence returns the visible map to the
  identity and a readback gap forces a non-permutation rooted map, that
  memory also shows up as stochastic indivisibility of the visible
  population law across the recurrence cycle. Neither statement is a
  claim about generic open-system non-Markovianity of a quantum channel,
  which is a different notion and does not follow from either.
\end{itemize}

Spin chains, controllable nuclear spin baths and phonon modes offer
candidate platforms. A platform test must verify that the returned
record affects the chosen coherent signal and compare it with the
appropriate control.

\textbf{Implications for hardware development.} The bath-as-resource
philosophy has implications for hardware-development priorities. Current
investment is concentrated on isolation and noise reduction. The
framework's prediction is that complementary investment in
engineered-bath architectures could produce comparable or larger gains
at lower hardware cost. Whether this prediction generates commercial
uptake depends on whether early demonstrations of the framework's
predicted coherence extension are achieved at sufficient scale to be
competitive with continued isolation improvements.

\hypertarget{quantum-sensing-with-nv-centers}{%
\subsection{15.6 Quantum sensing with NV
centers}\label{quantum-sensing-with-nv-centers}}

Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are the leading platform for
room-temperature quantum sensing --- magnetic field measurement,
temperature sensing, biological imaging, and related applications.
Current NV sensitivity is limited by the spin coherence time \(T_2\) of
the NV electron spin, with standard Markovian models predicting that
improvements in sensitivity require improvements in \(T_2\). The
framework proposes that sensitivity can be improved beyond the Markovian
\(T_2\) limit through exploitation of information backflow from the
diamond lattice's slow phonon and nuclear-spin baths, where those baths'
return revives distinguishability.

\textbf{The C1--C4 architecture of NV centers.} The NV center's electron
spin couples to multiple baths in the diamond lattice: phonons (acoustic
vibrations of the diamond crystal), nuclear spins (\(^{13}\)C nuclei in
natural-isotope diamond, P nuclei in synthetic diamond), and
paramagnetic impurities (other defect centers). Each bath contributes to
decoherence at characteristic timescales.

The relevant timescale separations are: NV electron-spin dynamics at
\(\tau_S \sim 10\)-100 ns; phonon-bath correlation times
\(\tau_B \sim 1\)-10 ms; nuclear-spin bath correlation times
\(\tau_B \sim 1\)-100 ms. The ratio: \(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-5}\) to
\(10^{-6}\) --- within the framework's slow-bath regime where memory
effects become predictable.

\textbf{The proposed sensing mechanism.} An NV-center bath can affect
the time dependence of the measured signal. A population revival or a
slow bath mode leaves open whether the phase-sensitive signal used by
the protocol recovers.

The sensing proposal is to look for recovered phase sensitivity and
choose a readout time on the basis of that signal. Performance depends
on the reference protocol and available resources.

\textbf{Sensitivity.} In a simplified fixed-visibility benchmark,
\(\delta B\sim 1/(\gamma\sqrt{T_2T_{\text{meas}}})\), where \(\gamma\)
is the gyromagnetic ratio and \(T_{\text{meas}}\) is total measurement
time. Using a different interrogation time requires measuring visibility
and noise under the actual readout.

Sensitivity depends on interrogation time, visibility, noise and readout
under the same resource budget. A measured revival is relevant if it
improves the signal-to-noise comparison with a specified reference
protocol.

\textbf{Empirical test.} Characterize the bath and measure the
phase-sensitive signal across candidate interrogation times. Compare the
resulting sensitivity at matched total resources with the reference
protocol. A gain then has the scope of that device and protocol.

The comparison would estimate any change in integrated sensitivity for
the tested device and protocol. A null result would constrain the
proposed sensing benefit in that regime.

\hypertarget{the-restricted-quantum-statistical-regime-in-engineered-systems}{%
\subsection{15.7 The restricted quantum-statistical regime in engineered
systems}\label{the-restricted-quantum-statistical-regime-in-engineered-systems}}

Beyond the revival effects developed in §§15.3-15.6 where a slow bath's
return revives distinguishability, the mechanism proposal predicts a
\emph{restricted quantum-statistical regime} at marginal hidden
capacity: partial distinguishability revival, \(0 < \mathcal{N} < 1\)
(Chapter 18 §18.3). In this regime --- on the mechanism proposal's
hypothesis --- engineered systems exhibit dynamics whose memoryless
operational modeling --- divisible-channel accounts of preparation and
intervention --- gives out, while the quantum representation at the
transition-statistics layer is retained ({[}Main §3.4{]}); any stronger
operational-failure reading is a mechanism-proposal claim, stated as
such, and the regime is distinguished from complete revival and from no
revival by distinguishability-revival measurements, not by the memory
test alone.

\textbf{The structural condition.} C3 is sufficient memory capacity ---
\(N_H \gg N_V\) is the comfortable physical regime, not the condition
itself ({[}Main §3.4{]}) --- and is required for the memory-bearing
sector at full strength. Capacity bounds memory without fixing revival.
The capacity floor caps \(M_t\) at \(\log_2|\mathcal{C}_H|\), so a
one-state hidden sector forces \(M_t = 0\) ({[}Main §3.4{]}). A capacity
margin does not by itself produce revival: adjoining an idle hidden
register to the XOR control of {[}Main §2.3{]} enlarges its hidden
capacity without changing its visible law, which carries memory with
\(\mathcal{N} = 0\) on a window containing that memory. The mechanism
proposal hypothesizes that comparable capacities, \(N_H/N_V \sim 1\),
produce partial revival --- the restricted quantum-statistical regime,
explicitly not a quantum-membership scale, since every finite law at
every \(\mathcal{N}\) admits both the quantum representation and a
deterministic hidden realization (\(S \iff D\), {[}Main §3.4{]}).

In engineered systems, the hidden capacity is \emph{controllable}. By
designing the hidden-sector capacity (the number of TLS in a
superconducting qubit's substrate, the number of nuclear spins in an NV
center's bath, the length of an engineered spin chain), the engineer
sets the capacity ceiling on accessible memory --- the theorem-level
content; the mechanism proposal hypothesizes that this choice positions
the system on the revival scale \(\mathcal{N}\). This is a new design
degree of freedom whose predicted empirical consequences, on that
proposal, are distinct from continuous-decoherence accounts of the
quantum-classical boundary.

\textbf{The framework's prediction.} In the restricted
quantum-statistical regime, the mechanism proposal predicts that
multi-time correlation functions show structural signatures distinct
from both memoryless quantum modeling and memoryless classical
probability --- proposal-level claims about the accessible dynamics, not
about representability ({[}Main §3.4{]}). Specifically:

\emph{Multi-time joint distributions.} C4 excludes a memoryless Markov
description of the declared visible statistics. A rooted map family can
still be P-divisible on that window. Revivals require a separate
distinguishability comparison. The fixed-basis representation applies to
the finite law in both cases ({[}Main §3.4{]}).

\emph{Memory saturation.} Accessible memory is capped by hidden
capacity, \(M_t \le \log_2|\mathcal{C}_H|\) ({[}Main §3.4{]}). The
mechanism proposal predicts that distinguishability revival falls below
its saturated value at marginal capacity, \(r = N_H/N_V < 1\), with the
form \(\mathcal{F}(r)\) below; no further saturation pattern is
specified.

\emph{Capacity dependence.} The mechanism proposal's model gives the
normalized revival measure as \(\mathcal{F}(r)\), with
\(\mathcal{F} \to 1\) for \(r \gg 1\) (saturated revival,
\(\mathcal{N} = \mathcal{N}_{\max}\) at small \(\tau_S/\tau_B\), §15.8),
\(\mathcal{F} \to 0\) for \(r \ll 1\) (no revival), and
\(\mathcal{F}(r) = 2r - r^2\) for \(r < 1\), increasing on that range.
This functional form is distinctive and falsifiable: it is the
framework's PROPOSED model prediction --- proposed, not theorem-derived
(see below) --- for how revival falls from saturated to none as capacity
is reduced.

\textbf{The functional form \(\mathcal{F}(r) = 2r - r^2\).} The
quadratic dependence is MOTIVATED by the \(1/\omega\) Planckian spectral
falloff combined with the framework's structural conditions in the
marginal-capacity regime. A detailed derivation is not packaged in this
release, and the functional form is accordingly a proposed model
prediction rather than a theorem-derived one (prediction-status
appendix); the structural heuristic is that the lowest-frequency modes
(which carry the most entanglement) are removed first as capacity is
reduced, with the quadratic form being the integrated effect of this
preferential removal.

The functional form distinguishes the proposal's prediction from the
alternative accounts considered. The particular alternative models
analyzed in §15.8's control set produce either continuous exponential
decay of the revival measure (with no structural transition) or
first-order linear behavior \(\mathcal{F}(r) = r\) at marginal capacity
--- a claim about that comparison class, not about open-system models
generically. The quadratic \(2r - r^2\) form is distinctive of the
proposed mechanism among the alternatives considered, and is empirically
diagnostic of it.

\textbf{Candidate test platforms.} The model associates marginal revival
with comparable \emph{accessible} capacities, \(N_H/N_V\sim1\).
Realizing that regime requires a measurement model and independent
calibration.

\emph{BEC analogue-gravity systems.} Varying \(L_{\text{super}}\)
changes the modeled modes in §15.8. Their effective capacity also
depends on the measured flow and condensate parameters.

\emph{Engineered spin chains.} Varying chain length changes the nominal
dimension. Which chain states are accessible depends on coupling,
preparation and readout.

\emph{Designed photonic systems.} Controllable defect modes could
provide a way to vary capacity. The experiment would need to determine
the modes used by the measured dynamics.

\textbf{Diagnostic measurements.} The mechanism proposal's prediction of
the restricted quantum-statistical regime is diagnosable through
distinguishability-revival measurements. The key observable is the
revival measure \(\mathcal{N}\) of Chapter 18 §18.3: the largest
increase, over the accessible window, of the total-variation distance
between the visible population laws of two initially distinguishable
preparations evolved through the system (the trace distance of their
diagonal states). Its dependence on \(r\) --- on the proposal, the
\(2r - r^2\) form --- is the proposed empirical signature.

The next section considers a BEC experiment for the proposed capacity
law.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{the-bec-analogue-gravity-experiment}{%
\subsection{15.8 The BEC analogue-gravity
experiment}\label{the-bec-analogue-gravity-experiment}}

A flowing BEC with sonic horizons offers a candidate test of the
proposed capacity-dependent revival form \(\mathcal F(r)=2r-r^2\). The
experiment needs a calibrated map from the apparatus to the model and a
measured revival for two preparations.

\textbf{The analogue-gravity setup.} A flowing BEC produces a sonic
horizon where the flow velocity equals the speed of sound. Phonons
emitted in the supersonic region cannot propagate against the flow back
into the subsonic region --- exactly analogous to how photons inside a
black hole event horizon cannot escape to infinity. The Hawking-Unruh
effect predicts that the sonic horizon should emit thermal phonons at a
temperature determined by the flow's velocity gradient --- analogue
Hawking radiation.

The Steinhauer group at the Technion has demonstrated this
experimentally over the past decade. Their setup uses a Rb-87 BEC in an
elongated trap, with a step in the trap potential producing a region of
supersonic flow that acts as the analogue horizon. The experimental
observation of analogue Hawking radiation and the measurement of its
thermal spectrum has been progressively refined; their 2016 paper
provided the first observation, with subsequent work refining the
measurement.

\textbf{The framework's modification.} The framework's content goes
beyond reproducing analogue Hawking radiation. The mechanism proposal
predicts that the distinguishability revival \(\mathcal{N}\) of the
subsonic-region phonon dynamics depends on the \emph{capacity} of the
supersonic-region (hidden-sector) phonon modes, with the dependence
following the proposed model form \(\mathcal{F}(r) = 2r - r^2\) for
\(r = N_H^{\text{eff}}/N_V < 1\).

The model varies capacity with \(L_{\text{super}}\) through the
calibrated inputs of the formula below. For \(r\geq1\) the capacity
factor saturates. For \(0<r<1\) it is reduced according to the proposed
quadratic form. The observable amplitude also includes the timing factor
and the scale \(\mathcal N_{\max}\).

\textbf{The framework's full prediction.} Including both the capacity
(C3) and the memory-timescale (C2) factors, the framework's prediction
is
\[\frac{\mathcal{N}(L_{\text{super}})}{\mathcal{N}_{\max}} = \mathcal{F}\!\left(\frac{N_H^{\text{eff}}(L_{\text{super}})}{N_V}\right) \cdot \left(1 - \frac{\tau_S}{\tau_B(L_{\text{super}})}\right),\]
with
\(N_H^{\text{eff}} = \min(L_{\text{super}}/\pi\xi,\; \kappa_s L_{\text{super}}/\pi c_s)\)
(where \(\xi\) is the healing length, \(\kappa_s\) is the surface
gravity, \(c_s\) is the speed of sound),
\(N_V = \kappa_s L_{\text{sub}}/\pi c_s\) (where \(L_{\text{sub}}\) is
the subsonic region length), and
\(\tau_B = L_{\text{super}}/|v - c_s|\).

The test needs an independent calibration of the parameters in
\(r=N_H^{\text{eff}}/N_V\), the timing factor and the amplitude scale
\(\mathcal{N}_{\max}\). A large-\(r\) configuration with small
\(\tau_S/\tau_B\) is a candidate reference for the scale.

\textbf{The experimental protocol.} The proposal uses a
black-hole--white-hole pair in a flowing BEC. The proposed scan in
\(L_{\text{super}}\) illustrates the range over which one would
calibrate the modes and estimate revival.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Prepare the BEC and allow Hawking radiation to reach stationarity
  (approximately 10 ms).
\item
  Measure the density profile at a sequence of times separated by
  approximately 0.1 to 1 ms.
\item
  Repeat approximately \(10^3\) times per \(L_{\text{super}}\) value.
\item
  Compute \(G_{\text{sub}}^{(2)}(\Delta t)\) as an auxiliary measure of
  temporal density correlations. Its oscillations or nonmonotonicity
  cannot estimate the revival of distance between two preparations.
\item
  Prepare two specified initial perturbations and estimate their visible
  population distributions at matched times and controls. Use the
  total-variation distance \(D(t)\) and test for an increase across the
  declared window to estimate \(\mathcal N\) for those preparations.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Controls.} A comparison must measure or hold fixed the capacity
and timing factors that the model does not intend to vary.

\emph{Reference without the supersonic region.} Estimate the same
two-preparation quantity in a matched reference as a baseline for
intrinsic dynamics and readout artifacts.

\emph{C2 test.} When changing flow at fixed \(L_{\text{super}}\),
measure \(\kappa_s\), \(c_s\) and \(\xi\) and verify or model any change
in \(r\). The timing factor can be tested separately if the capacity
ratio and other relevant conditions are controlled.

\emph{Thermal test.} Temperature changes can affect the sound speed,
healing length, surface gravity and relaxation. Measure or match the
capacity ratio and timing factor across thermal controls before
attributing a residual change.

\textbf{Size of the modeled effect.} For calibrated \(r=0.5\) and
\(r=0.25\), the capacity factor alone is 0.75 and 0.4375 respectively.
Actual normalized revival multiplies these values by the timing factor.
The lengths that yield the quoted ratios depend on the measured BEC
parameters.

The noise of density autocorrelation measurements constrains that
auxiliary observable. Uncertainty in the revival statistic depends on
estimation of two distributions, preparation and measurement errors, and
temporal sampling.

Estimate uncertainty for the chosen two-preparation statistic, including
time correlations, finite-sample bias from estimating distances and
maxima, and uncertainty in the calibration of \(r\) and
\(\mathcal N_{\max}\). The achievable precision remains to be
established for that protocol.

\textbf{Comparison with backgrounds.} The proposed \(2r-r^2\) dependence
can be compared with alternatives at matched timing and readout. An
experiment needs models of the same revival observable for the relevant
backgrounds.

\emph{Bogoliubov--de Gennes dynamics.} Standard BdG calculations
describe mode mixing and occupation in the given flow. A quantitative
comparison requires computing the two-preparation statistic under the
same conditions.

\emph{Other backgrounds.} Interaction-driven dynamics, losses and trap
noise can affect the measured signal. Their effects need independent
controls and an uncertainty estimate on the actual statistic.

\textbf{Relation to DSW horizon decoherence.} The BEC analogue-gravity
test is structurally related to the Danielson-Satishchandran-Wald (DSW)
horizon decoherence program developed in Chapter 9 §9.7. DSW prove
within standard QFT in curved spacetime that Killing horizons impart
fundamental decoherence on nearby quantum superpositions, with rate
determined by horizon geometry. The framework's BEC analogue-gravity
test extends DSW's analysis to the \emph{capacity-controlled regime}
(marginal hidden capacity) that DSW does not address.

The convergence is theoretical. DSW derive within standard physics a
feature the framework's universality-class commitments share ---
horizons impose decoherence, with geometry setting the relevant
parameters --- and add no empirical evidence for the framework. The BEC
analogue-gravity test provides empirical access to the framework's
distinctive content (capacity-controlled revival in the restricted
quantum-statistical regime) in a laboratory apparatus. The two are
complementary: DSW for theoretical convergence at the universality-class
level, BEC for an empirical test of the distinctive content of the
restricted quantum-statistical regime.

\textbf{Implications.}

Agreement with \(\mathcal F(r)=2r-r^2\) after the calibration and
background comparisons would support the proposed capacity-dependent
mechanism in the tested system.

A calibrated null result could constrain the mechanism in the tested
range if the experiment has adequate power for the predicted amplitude.

A reliably different dependence on capacity under matched conditions
would reject the proposed curve for that setup.

The BEC scenario defines a possible mechanism test. Feasibility depends
on implementing the paired-preparation readout, calibrating the model
inputs and estimating the uncertainty.

\hypertarget{chapter-close-2}{%
\subsection{15.9 Chapter close}\label{chapter-close-2}}

This chapter proposes engineering comparisons for accessible memory,
revival and device performance.

\textbf{Engineering tests.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \emph{Correlation-aware error correction.} Compare specified decoders
  at matched code and noise conditions (§15.4). The size of any gain
  remains open.
\item
  \emph{Coherence extension through engineered baths.} Test
  phase-sensitive recovery and its duration under specified bath and
  control dynamics (§15.5).
\item
  \emph{Backflow-aware NV sensing.} Compare measured sensitivity with a
  matched reference. The result depends on coherent signal recovery,
  readout and resource accounting (§15.6).
\item
  \emph{Restricted quantum-statistical regime.} Engineered systems at
  marginal hidden capacity (\(N_H/N_V \sim 1\)) are predicted, on the
  mechanism proposal, to show the proposed \(\mathcal{F}(r) = 2r - r^2\)
  form (§15.7). Diagnosable through distinguishability-revival
  measurements.
\item
  \emph{BEC analogue-gravity test.} Calibrate capacity and timing, and
  estimate revival from two preparations with suitable controls (§15.8).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Three categories of empirical exposure.}

The chapter's content sorts into three empirical categories.

\emph{Decoder benchmark.} Reported aggregate syndrome trends motivate a
matched comparison of logical error and resource costs.

\emph{Signal tests.} The engineered-bath and NV proposals need readout
for the relevant coherent signal and matched reference protocols.

\emph{Capacity test.} The BEC and other candidate platforms need
calibration of the parameters and a revival estimator.

The effect on logical error, coherence or sensitivity is a separate
outcome in each specified device test.

These comparisons apply the finite-horizon memory and divisibility
diagnostics to proposed hardware mechanisms.

\textbf{Forward pointers.} Chapters 16 and 17 develop candidate clinical
and bioinformatics applications with their own empirical and modeling
premises.

The framework's empirical reach across Chapters 13-17 is concentrated at
the application level --- specific predictions for biology, computing,
engineering, medicine, and bioinformatics. The framework's content here
in quantum engineering is the bridge between the foundational chapters
(1-9) and the applied chapters (13-17), demonstrating that the
framework's structural commitments at the substratum level produce
specific quantitative predictions across multiple engineering domains.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{chapter-16}{%
\section{Chapter 16}\label{chapter-16}}

\hypertarget{medicine}{%
\section{Medicine}\label{medicine}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Status --- conjectural extension.} The cited observations
include reversal after Mecp2 reactivation in a mouse model of Rett
syndrome. They motivate tests of the proposed mechanisms. Comparative
therapeutic windows and clinical benefits remain open.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-13}{%
\subsection{16.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-13}}

Chapter 13 develops tests of conditional memory. Chapter 14 uses a
scalable model with quantum control, efficient simulation and charged
conditioning for its BQP result. Chapter 15 proposes controlled
engineering tests. This chapter considers medical applications with
their own experimental premises.

This chapter discusses proposed memory mechanisms and tests in
pharmacology, neurodegeneration, immune signaling and epigenetics. It
draws on prior experimental and clinical observations with the endpoints
reported in those studies.

The chapter has explicit two-half structure.

The \emph{first half} (§§16.2--16.8) discusses candidate records in
checkpoint kinase regulation, CaMKII dynamics and reconsolidation,
bacterial persistence, T-cell exhaustion, use-dependent cardiac channel
block and JAK signaling. The proposed mechanisms depend on what persists
and whether it affects later outcomes at the same measured present.

Sections 16.9--16.12 compare measurable chromatin features with
expression and function. The operator distinction of Chapter 6 motivates
an analogy. The evidence concerns particular molecular observations and
clinical endpoints.

Section 16.13 closes the chapter with a unifying therapeutic principle:
\emph{memory asymmetry}. When a disease process depends on non-Markovian
signaling dynamics that the corresponding normal tissue does not,
therapies can target the \emph{memory structure} rather than the
\emph{catalytic function} --- predicting wider therapeutic windows
because memory dependence is more disease-specific than catalytic
activity.

Guy et al.~(2007) observed neurological reversal after reactivating
Mecp2 in symptomatic adult mice. This provides a prior comparison for
the proposed role of reader restoration. A wider therapeutic window
across disorders is a separate prediction.

\hypertarget{the-enzyme-as-a-read-write-system}{%
\subsection{16.2 The enzyme as a read-write
system}\label{the-enzyme-as-a-read-write-system}}

Enzyme regulation supplies candidate mechanisms for writing, retaining
and reading molecular records. The proposed role of a record in disease
depends on the particular system and what its later activity reveals.

\textbf{Molecular memory mechanisms.} The following mechanisms can
create states that persist across catalytic cycles.

\emph{Multisite post-translational modification.} PTMs ---
phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, methylation --- covalently
alter specific residues, changing the protein's conformational landscape
and activity. For \(N\) sites with \(k\) possible states each, \(k^N\)
is the count of possible patterns if every combination is available.
Treating approximately ten Chk1 regulatory phosphorylation sites as
binary gives about \(2^{10} \approx 1{,}000\) nominal patterns.
Gunawardena (2012) describes how the same cellular condition can produce
different modification patterns depending on prior history.

\emph{Sequential phosphorylation.} Wilsker et al.~(2008) found
S317-dependent S345 phosphorylation in the DNA-damage response. They
distinguished a mitotic mode of S345 phosphorylation independent of
S317. The sequence is a biochemical result. A C4 test requires comparing
histories at the same declared visible state.

\emph{Conformational hysteresis.} Proteins can occupy conformations with
different lifetimes. The binding and release of the endogenous Chk1
repressor Chk1-S is a candidate slow process.

\emph{Persistent chromatin marks.} DNA damage induces histone
modifications (\(\gamma\)H2AX, H4K20me) that can persist for hours to
days.

\textbf{The memory hierarchy.} These examples span different timescales
and illustrate possible persistence and storage. C4 requires different
next-step laws for histories that end at the same measured present.
