Additional candidate records in nervous tissue include synaptic LTP/LTD
changes (hours to days), circuit engram-cell ensembles (days to months),
hippocampal-cortical interactions (months to years) and distributed
cortical representations (years to decades). A readback claim at any
layer uses a specified partition and comparison.

A perturbation at one layer could affect a longer-lived state in
another. Linking a clinical time course or treatment response to such a
state requires evidence for the proposed links between layers.

\textbf{The core therapeutic principle.} \emph{Memory asymmetry} is the
proposal that an intervention can exploit differences in how diseased
and normal tissue depend on a retained signaling state. A wider
therapeutic window requires a selective effect on that state and a
direct comparison with the relevant treatment baseline.

\hypertarget{cancer-pharmacology}{%
\subsection{16.3 Cancer pharmacology}\label{cancer-pharmacology}}

Checkpoint kinases and their regulatory regions give candidate fast and
slow variables in the DNA-damage response. Testing their contribution to
cancer pharmacology requires a specified model and readout.

\textbf{Checkpoint kinase inhibitors and sensitization.} Parsels et
al.~report preclinical gemcitabine sensitization by Chk1 inhibition in
pancreatic cancer cells. The catalytic and regulatory domains motivate a
proposed partition. Coupling and retained post-translational states need
their own matched-present readback test ({[}Medicine §3.1{]}).

The proposed Chk1 mechanism is that prior activation changes the next
response through a retained modification or conformation. Testing it
requires a history comparison at the same declared present state.

\emph{A selectivity hypothesis.} Tumor and normal cells can depend
differently on checkpoint pathways. The specific role of a persistent
Chk1 state in selectivity is open.

\emph{Why schedule matters.} Preclinical schedule effects motivate a
readback hypothesis. A Markov model including present damage and
cell-cycle state can also yield order effects. A matched-present
comparison would test whether additional history affects sensitization.

\textbf{Radiation adaptive response.} Priming responses in particular
experimental systems motivate a hypothesis involving retained chromatin
changes. A history contrast with controlled current state and measure of
the candidate record is required to assess that mechanism.

\textbf{Distinguishing predictions for cancer pharmacology.}

\emph{Memory-selective scheduling.} Measure candidate checkpoint
relaxation and compare schedules at matched present and exposure in a
controlled model. Whether the timing predicts sensitization is open.

\emph{Low-dose memory priming.} A controlled preclinical comparison
could measure history effects at matched exposure and the same recorded
present state. Exposure and toxicity require a specified comparator and
direct measurements.

\emph{Memory-targeted drugs.} Drugs that specifically disrupt the
\emph{memory structure} without blocking catalysis: accelerating the
regulatory domain's slowest conformational mode (decreasing \(\tau_B\))
to erase checkpoint memory without blocking checkpoint activation. Such
a drug would be invisible to standard kinase inhibitor screens, which
measure catalytic inhibition.

These cancer applications propose measurements of checkpoint readback
and treatment response. A therapeutic index benefit would need its own
evidence.

\hypertarget{neurodegeneration}{%
\subsection{16.4 Neurodegeneration}\label{neurodegeneration}}

Lecanemab and donanemab trials reported slower decline in early
Alzheimer's disease without restoration of cognition ({[}Medicine
§4.1{]}). Those endpoints do not establish the proposed kinase mechanism
below.

\textbf{CaMKII as a candidate memory system.} CaMKII participates in
synaptic plasticity. The following features motivate a test of
accessible readback:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{C1.} The kinase domain is coupled to the regulatory/association
  domain through the autoinhibitory segment.
\item
  \emph{C2.} Autophosphorylation at T286 creates a bistable switch with
  persistence time of minutes to hours --- much longer than individual
  calcium transients (\textasciitilde ms).
  \(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-5}\).
\item
  \emph{C3.} CaMKII forms dodecameric holoenzymes with 12 subunits, each
  independently phosphorylatable --- \(2^{12} = 4{,}096\) distinct
  modification states.
\item
  \emph{C4.} Test whether a measured synaptic response differs between
  histories of the same measured present through a retained state.
  CaMKII is implicated in synaptic plasticity. Its contribution to an
  accessible C4 contrast and to a disease mechanism requires direct
  evidence.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Kinase dynamics as a disease hypothesis.} The proposal is that
changes in the relaxation time \(\tau_B\) of a regulatory mode
contribute to some neurodegenerative outcomes.

\emph{Normal aging.} One hypothesis is that oxidative damage changes
conformational relaxation and thereby affects plasticity.

\emph{Alzheimer's disease.} Test whether A\(\beta\) oligomers change
CaMKII regulatory kinetics and whether those changes affect plasticity
or tau phosphorylation.

\emph{Parkinson's disease.} Test whether aggregate-associated changes in
regulatory kinase kinetics contribute to neuronal dysfunction.

\textbf{Candidate \(\tau_B\)-normalizing interventions.} Test whether
restoring a measured regulatory relaxation time improves a specified
synaptic endpoint independently of changes in aggregate burden.

\emph{Testable prediction.} Measure CaMKII conformational dynamics (by
FRET or HDX-MS) in neurons exposed to A\(\beta\) oligomers versus
controls. The framework predicts that A\(\beta\) shifts \(\tau_B\) of
CaMKII's regulatory domain. A compound that reverses this \(\tau_B\)
shift should rescue synaptic plasticity (measurable by long-term
potentiation induction) independently of A\(\beta\) clearance.

\textbf{PTSD and reconsolidation.} Intrusive memories motivate a
candidate persistence model. A clinical treatment effect and the
responsible memory mechanism require separate evidence.

Brunet et al.~reported a benefit with propranolol and trauma
reactivation. Roullet et al.~found no overall PTSD symptom advantage
over reactivation with placebo ({[}Medicine §4.5{]}). A proposed effect
on noradrenergic re-encoding remains a mechanistic hypothesis.

Generalizing a reconsolidation intervention requires identifying the
relevant memory component, checking its sensitivity to the timing of
treatment and measuring the outcome.

\textbf{Focused ultrasound as a candidate perturbation.} Focused
ultrasound can open the blood--brain barrier in controlled protocols.
Whether it changes the relaxation time of a particular kinase requires a
molecular measurement.

The proposed comparison measures the candidate \(\tau_B\) and asks
whether it mediates an independently measured response.

Ye et al.~(2025) reported an exploratory open-label blood--brain barrier
opening study in six people with Alzheimer's disease. The study did not
measure CaMKII conformational dynamics or molecular timescale
normalization ({[}Medicine §4.6{]}). A controlled comparison is needed
to estimate efficacy.

\textbf{Proposed tests.} Compare variation in pulse timing against a
measured relaxation time, with matched conditions and controls for
nonspecific effects. Measure the molecular and clinical endpoints
separately.

A test must distinguish the proposed kinase mechanism from other effects
of the intervention.

\hypertarget{antibiotic-resistance}{%
\subsection{16.5 Antibiotic resistance}\label{antibiotic-resistance}}

Phenotypic tolerance and genetic resistance are distinct. A persistent
cellular state is a candidate contributor to tolerance, and the proposed
mechanism needs a specified readout and matched-present comparison.

\textbf{Persister cells and candidate records.} The hypothesis is that
part of the stress response persists across observations and affects a
later response. A model with explicit current-state variables provides a
comparison.

A history contrast would ask whether different prior exposures affect
the next measured response at fixed present. That result would constrain
the observation law. Assigning the effect to a particular mechanism
would require additional evidence.

\textbf{Memory-optimized antibiotic scheduling.} The framework's reading
implies that \emph{scheduling} of antibiotic doses matters in ways
standard pharmacokinetics does not capture. Specifically:

\emph{Continuous exposure.} The conventional ``keep antibiotic above MIC
for as long as possible'' strategy maximizes SOS memory accumulation and
therefore persister formation. This is the worst possible scheduling
from the framework's perspective.

\emph{Pulsed exposure with \(\tau_B\)-matched intervals.} Antibiotic
pulses separated by intervals matching the SOS memory's \(\tau_B\) allow
the memory to relax between pulses, preventing the cumulative
accumulation that produces persisters. The framework predicts this
pulsed scheduling produces fewer persisters than continuous exposure at
equivalent total drug exposure.

\emph{Combination scheduling.} Combinations of antibiotics targeting
different memory architectures (different bacterial signaling pathways
with different \(\tau_B\)) can interfere with each other's memory
dynamics, producing effects beyond simple additive killing. The
framework predicts specific combinations and timings that exploit memory
interference.

\textbf{Distinguishing predictions.}

\emph{\(\tau_B\)-matched pulsed dosing.} The framework predicts that
pulsed dosing with \(\tau_B\)-matched intervals produces fewer persister
cells than continuous dosing at equivalent total drug exposure. The
prediction is testable in animal models of chronic bacterial infection
with measured RecA filament dynamics. Standard pharmacokinetic models
predict no benefit to pulsed dosing if total exposure is matched; the
framework predicts a specific benefit from \(\tau_B\) matching.

\emph{Anti-persister drugs.} Drugs that specifically accelerate RecA
filament dissociation (decreasing \(\tau_B\) of the SOS memory) should
eliminate persisters without killing growing bacteria. This is a new
drug class that the framework predicts is pharmacologically distinct
from standard antibiotics; such drugs would be invisible to
growth-inhibition screens.

\emph{Memory-erasing combinations.} Combinations of \(\beta\)-lactams
(acting on rapidly-growing bacteria) with memory-erasing agents
(preventing persister formation) should produce dramatically improved
outcomes in chronic infections. The framework predicts specific drug
combinations from the memory architecture of bacterial signaling
networks.

\hypertarget{immunotherapy-and-t-cell-exhaustion}{%
\subsection{16.6 Immunotherapy and T-cell
exhaustion}\label{immunotherapy-and-t-cell-exhaustion}}

T-cell exhaustion is a loss of T-cell effector function during chronic
antigen exposure. Checkpoint inhibition can partly restore function.
Regulatory states in T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling are candidate
records for studying how prior stimulation contributes to exhaustion.

\textbf{Candidate records in TCR signaling.} The cascade involves
components including Lck, ZAP-70 and LAT, with regulatory
phosphorylation and links to downstream transcription factors. Slow
changes in regulator levels and modification patterns provide possible
persistence and storage.

The proposed mechanism links retained PTM patterns to upregulated
inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIM-3, LAG-3) and reduced effector function.
C4 requires differences in a subsequent signaling response after
distinct stimulation histories at the same defined present. Attributing
such a difference to the PTM patterns requires evidence for that
mediator.

\textbf{Therapeutic implication.} Under the proposed mechanism,
targeting kinases or phosphatases that control the relevant PTM pattern
could complement PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibition. Synergy requires a
comparison with the component interventions.

\emph{Specifically:} The serine/threonine kinases responsible for the
exhaustion-specific phosphorylation patterns (likely candidates: PKC,
MAPK, and downstream effectors) are framework-predicted to be the
\emph{upstream writers} of the exhaustion state. Inhibiting these
writers should prevent exhaustion development; activating the
corresponding erasers should reverse established exhaustion. This is a
new therapeutic axis distinct from standard checkpoint blockade.

\textbf{Distinguishing prediction: kinase regulatory-domain
accelerators.} Drugs that accelerate the regulatory-domain dynamics of
TCR-pathway kinases (decreasing \(\tau_B\) without blocking catalytic
activity) should reverse exhaustion. These drugs would be invisible to
standard kinase inhibitor screens, which measure catalytic inhibition.
The framework predicts that screening compound libraries against
measured regulatory-domain dynamics (rather than catalytic inhibition)
would identify a new class of immuno-oncology agents.

\hypertarget{cardiac-pharmacology}{%
\subsection{16.7 Cardiac pharmacology}\label{cardiac-pharmacology}}

Some cardiac antiarrhythmics (including lidocaine, propafenone and
flecainide) exhibit \emph{use-dependent block}. Channel block can change
across repeated activations. The observed dependence motivates testing
whether slow channel conformations mediate a history effect beyond the
declared present measurements.

\textbf{Candidate history readback in use-dependent block.}
Voltage-gated ion channels have closed, open and inactivated
conformations with different transition times. Opening and closing on
microsecond timescales and inactivation on longer timescales in some
channels motivate a candidate partition. C4 requires that two activation
histories giving the same recorded present lead to different next-step
laws for the specified readout.

In a candidate mechanism, rapidly cycling channels accumulate occupancy
of an inactivated state and bind a drug that favors that state more
avidly. Testing that mechanism requires measuring the relevant
conformations and drug response.

\textbf{Therapeutic implication.} Use-dependent block can favor action
in rapidly firing tissue. A therapeutic-window benefit from the proposed
inactivated state depends on its contribution to both efficacy and
toxicity in the tissues being compared.

\textbf{Distinguishing predictions.}

\emph{Optimal dosing intervals.} The framework predicts that the optimal
interval between antiarrhythmic doses depends on the channel's
\(\tau_B\) at the inactivated state. Dose intervals matching \(\tau_B\)
maximize the memory-write while minimizing baseline blockade; intervals
much shorter or longer reduce therapeutic index. Current dosing is
empirically optimized; the framework predicts calculable optima from
channel kinetics.

\emph{Memory-targeted antiarrhythmics.} Drugs that accelerate channel
recovery from inactivation (decreasing \(\tau_B\) of the inactivated
state) should eliminate arrhythmias by erasing the memory-accumulation
that produces them. This is a new therapeutic axis distinct from
standard channel-blocking antiarrhythmics; such drugs would not show
standard channel-blocking pharmacology and would be invisible to
standard antiarrhythmic screens.

\emph{Frequency-selective combinations.} Combinations of drugs with
different channel memory profiles (different \(\tau_B\) values) can
produce frequency-selective effects beyond simple additivity. The
framework predicts specific combinations and dosing for arrhythmias at
different cycle lengths.

\hypertarget{autoimmune-disease}{%
\subsection{16.8 Autoimmune disease}\label{autoimmune-disease}}

Cytokine signaling involving Janus kinases (JAKs) is involved in several
autoimmune diseases. JAK inhibitors include tofacitinib, baricitinib and
upadacitinib. Persistent JAK--STAT regulation is a candidate mechanism
for effects of prior cytokine exposure on later responses.

\textbf{Response to partial JAK inhibition.} Clinical responses can
occur under partial inhibition. A nonlinear dose response can arise in
models of the current state. Testing C4 requires a history contrast at
the same measured present.

The proposed mechanism is that accumulated phosphorylation mediates a
history effect and that partial inhibition can alter that state.
Explaining a clinical response with this mechanism requires evidence for
the history effect and its mediation.

\textbf{Therapeutic implication.} The framework predicts that JAK
inhibitor dose-response curves should show \emph{threshold behavior} ---
clinical efficacy emerges above a specific dose threshold corresponding
to disruption of memory accumulation, rather than linear with kinase
inhibition. Below threshold: minimal efficacy regardless of partial
inhibition. Above threshold: substantial efficacy from memory
disruption. This pattern matches the clinical observation of ``minimum
effective dose'' thresholds with rapid efficacy gains above threshold.

\textbf{Distinguishing prediction: optimal scheduling.} The framework
predicts that \emph{intermittent} JAK inhibitor dosing (with intervals
matching the cytokine memory's \(\tau_B\), typically hours to days)
should produce equivalent or superior efficacy to continuous dosing at
lower cumulative drug exposure. Standard pharmacokinetic models predict
continuous dosing is optimal; the framework predicts intermittent dosing
exploiting memory dynamics could improve therapeutic index.

A second distinguishing prediction: combinations of JAK inhibitors with
phosphatase activators (drugs that accelerate the memory erasure of the
JAK-STAT pathway) should be synergistic, producing equivalent clinical
effect at lower JAK inhibitor doses. This combination would be invisible
to standard pharmacology screens that focus on catalytic inhibition.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{epigenetics-as-biological-hidden-sector}{%
\subsection{16.9 Epigenetics as biological hidden
sector}\label{epigenetics-as-biological-hidden-sector}}

The second half examines chromatin features as candidate records and
gene expression and phenotype as possible readouts. The relation
motivates an analogy to the operator distinction from Chapter 6 §6.3.

\textbf{A candidate chromatin partition.} Observations of
transcriptional machinery define a possible visible sector. DNA
methylation, histone modifications, chromatin compaction and
three-dimensional architecture provide candidate hidden variables. C4
needs a matched-present history contrast in transcription or another
declared readout.

\emph{C1 (coupling).} The transcriptional machinery and chromatin state
are coupled through multiple mechanisms: direct physical coupling
(nucleosome positioning controls promoter access, DNA methylation
modulates transcription factor binding, histone tail modifications
recruit reader proteins), writer-reader feedback (transcription recruits
chromatin-modifying enzymes that alter the chromatin state, which
modulates future transcription), and structural coupling (chromatin
looping by CTCF and cohesin brings distal regulatory elements into
proximity with promoters).

\emph{C2 (memory persistence).} The chromatin state changes on
timescales far slower than individual transcription events. The
hierarchy is multi-scale:

\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mechanism
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\(\tau_B\)
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
\(\tau_S/\tau_B\)
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
DNA methylation (CpG) & Cell generations & \(\sim 10^{-6}\) \\
Histone methylation & Hours to days & \(\sim 10^{-3}\) to \(10^{-2}\) \\
Histone acetylation & Minutes to hours & \(\sim 10^{-1}\) to \(1\) \\
Chromatin compaction & Cell generations & \(\sim 10^{-6}\) \\
CTCF/cohesin loops & Hours to cell generations & \(\sim 10^{-3}\) to
\(10^{-6}\) \\
\end{longtable}

These timescales give candidate retention windows. If persistence
controls the available record, methylation can motivate tests at longer
lags than acetylation. A history effect at a given lag also depends on
how the record is read back.

\emph{C3 (capacity).} Treating about \(28 \times 10^6\) human CpG sites
as independent binary sites gives \(2^{28 \times 10^6}\) nominal
patterns. The distinguishable patterns available to the proposed
mechanism determine its storage capacity.

\textbf{Cancer as pathological epigenetic memory.} Cancer is, in the
framework's language, a disease of the epigenetic hidden sector. The
malignant transcriptional program is maintained not only by genetic
mutations but by an aberrant epigenetic memory state --- stable patterns
of DNA methylation and histone modifications that lock the cell into a
proliferative program. This memory is self-reinforcing: the malignant
transcription writes further aberrant marks through recruited chromatin
modifiers, which stabilize the malignant transcription.

The framework predicts that disrupting the memory \emph{structure} (the
stability and capacity of the epigenetic hidden sector) is a more
selective anti-cancer strategy than disrupting the memory \emph{content}
(reactivating specific silenced genes). A memory-structure drug would
reduce \(\tau_B\) of the aberrant methylation and histone marks (making
them less stable), not affect \(\tau_B\) of constitutive marks
(housekeeping genes, developmental identity), and selectively
destabilize the tumor's pathological memory without affecting normal
cellular memory.

\textbf{Aging as memory accumulation.} Aging involves progressive
accumulation of epigenetic marks --- the ``epigenetic clock'' of Horvath
2013 --- that alter gene expression in ways associated with declining
function. In the framework's language, aging is the accumulation of
memory in the slowest epigenetic layers (DNA methylation, chromatin
compaction) beyond the cell's ability to maintain functional
homeostasis.

Long autocorrelation times in aging-associated gene expression would
suggest lags for a readback test. C4 requires different next-step laws
for histories ending at the same measured present. Partial reprogramming
through transient Yamanaka factor expression erases recent epigenetic
memory while preserving deeper developmental identity. Conditional on
the marks eroding on their retention times, the framework predicts that
pulses long enough to erase recent marks but short compared with the
\(\tau_B\) of developmental memory preserve identity; how identity
changes for longer pulses, gradually or sharply, depends on the identity
network's mixing, coupling and readback, and is model-dependent unless a
specific mechanism establishes it.

\hypertarget{the-substratum-emergent-operator-distinction-at-chromatin}{%
\subsection{16.10 The substratum-emergent operator distinction at
chromatin}\label{the-substratum-emergent-operator-distinction-at-chromatin}}

The proposal distinguishes measurable chromatin states from measured
downstream expression and function. The relationship depends on the
particular molecular system.

\textbf{Chromatin state and downstream readout.}

\emph{Molecular state.} Bisulfite sequencing, ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq
address different features of DNA methylation, histone modifications and
chromatin accessibility.

\emph{Downstream response.} RNA-seq and functional assays measure gene
expression or cellular phenotype.

Transcriptional machinery and other regulatory mechanisms relate these
layers. Their molecular observables can have different dynamics.

\textbf{Empirical comparisons at chromatin.}

\emph{iPSC reprogramming residuals.} Lin et al.~(2024) describe residual
source-cell epigenetic features in studied systems after a change in
cell identity. Buckberry et al.~(2023) show that resetting depends on
the reprogramming protocol ({[}Medicine §9.4{]}).

These comparisons illustrate that epigenetic marks and phenotype can
change differently. The residual marks and their magnitude depend on the
protocol.

\emph{Bivalent chromatin states.} Bernstein et al.~(2006) reported
coexisting H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 at lineage-control loci with low or
poised expression. The observation concerns the marks and expression,
without a conservation or exact-cancellation result.

\emph{Multi-timescale chromatin dynamics.} Single-molecule and
single-cell measurements directly observe distinct dynamics on subsecond
and minutes timescales for the same histone modifications on the same
nucleosomes (Stasevich et al.~2014; Saxton et al.~2023). Histone
acetylation modulates transcriptional burst frequency rather than burst
size (Nicolas-Phillips et al.~2018), a stochastic-emergent-output
pattern consistent with the framework's prediction that emergent
operators have specific functional relationships to substratum operators
rather than being identical to them.

These results motivate studying chromatin marks and measured output
separately.

Applying the formal physical operator distinction would require a
specified molecular model and correspondence.

The observed chromatin and expression comparisons supply inputs to that
proposal.

\hypertarget{reader-writer-and-eraser-pharmacology}{%
\subsection{16.11 Reader, writer, and eraser
pharmacology}\label{reader-writer-and-eraser-pharmacology}}

Current epigenetic therapeutics are organized along three axes that
correspond directly to the framework's substratum-emergent operator
distinction at the operational drug-development level. The three-axis
pharmacology --- \emph{readers}, \emph{writers}, \emph{erasers} --- is
the structural pattern of any therapeutic approach to a
substratum-emergent operator pair: target the substratum maintenance
machinery (writers and erasers, which establish and remove substrate
marks) or the substratum-to-emergent translation machinery (readers,
which couple substrate state to downstream function).

\textbf{The three axes.}

\emph{Writers.} DNA methyltransferase inhibitors (DNMT inhibitors):
5-azacytidine, decitabine. Histone methyltransferase inhibitors (HMT
inhibitors): EZH2 inhibitors (tazemetostat for follicular lymphoma),
DOT1L inhibitors (under investigation). Writers act on the
substratum-maintenance machinery --- they prevent or accelerate the
writing of substrate-level marks.

\emph{Erasers.} Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDAC inhibitors):
vorinostat, romidepsin (approved for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma),
panobinostat. Histone demethylase inhibitors (LSD1, KDM5 family
inhibitors under investigation). Erasers act on the substratum-erasing
machinery --- they prevent or accelerate the removal of substrate-level
marks.

\emph{Readers.} BET bromodomain inhibitors: JQ1 (preclinical), ZEN-3694,
BI 894999 (clinical investigation). Methyl-lysine reader inhibitors
(under investigation). Readers act on the substratum-to-emergent
translation machinery --- they prevent the substrate-level marks from
being read as downstream functional output.

\textbf{The framework's structural reading.} The three-axis organization
follows structurally from the operator distinction. Any therapeutic
approach to a substratum-emergent operator pair must target one of three
functional roles: substratum maintenance (writers), substratum erasure
(erasers), or substratum-to-emergent translation (readers). The
empirical organization of epigenetic drugs into exactly these three
classes is the framework's substratum-emergent operator distinction made
operational.

\textbf{Combination and scheduling hypothesis.} The proposed link
between measured relaxation times and combination scheduling can be
tested for particular targets and regimens.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Writer + reader.} The cited p300/CBP and BET work reports
  preclinical combination results in NUT carcinoma.
\item
  \emph{Eraser + reader.} HDAC inhibitor + BET inhibitor combinations
  are under clinical investigation in NUT carcinoma and other contexts.
\item
  \emph{Writer + eraser.} DNMT and HDAC inhibitor combinations have
  preclinical evidence. Trial E1905 compared azacitidine with and
  without entinostat in MDS/AML ({[}Medicine §9.5{]}). It did not
  measure a relaxation-time-matched optimum.
\end{itemize}

Clinical activity and preclinical synergy are distinct outcomes.
Schedule comparisons need specified doses, timing, and endpoints.

The proposed test asks whether a measured \(\tau_B\) predicts
combination response at a specified interval.

\hypertarget{a-therapeutic-window-hypothesis-for-reader-writer-disorders}{%
\subsection{16.12 A therapeutic-window hypothesis for reader-writer
disorders}\label{a-therapeutic-window-hypothesis-for-reader-writer-disorders}}

Rett mouse rescue provides prior evidence of reversibility after
restoring Mecp2. A wider therapeutic-window pattern across disorders and
mechanisms is a separate comparative hypothesis.

\textbf{The reader-writer disorder class.} Several genetic disorders are
caused by mutations affecting epigenetic reader or writer proteins:

\emph{Rett syndrome.} MECP2 (methyl-CpG binding protein 2) --- a reader
of DNA methylation. Loss-of-function mutations produce severe
neurodevelopmental disability primarily in females.

\emph{Fragile X syndrome.} FMR1 --- controls RNA binding and
translation. Loss-of-function produces intellectual disability. Strictly
an RNA-binding protein rather than a chromatin reader, but with
structural similarities to chromatin readers in its functional role.

\emph{Angelman syndrome.} UBE3A --- ubiquitin ligase. Loss-of-function
on the maternal allele produces severe developmental disability. Related
to chromatin biology through ubiquitin-mediated histone modification.

\emph{Kabuki syndrome.} KMT2D is an H3K4 methyltransferase, and KDM6A
removes H3K27 methylation. Pathogenic variants in either gene can cause
Kabuki syndrome ({[}Medicine §10.7{]}).

\emph{ATR-X syndrome.} ATRX --- chromatin remodeler involved in
heterochromatin maintenance. Loss-of-function produces
\(\alpha\)-thalassemia with X-linked intellectual disability.

\textbf{The framework's hypothesis.} Compare the age or time after onset
at which targeted restoration still improves a specified endpoint with
that for a defined alternative. The usable window depends on the
disorder, intervention, restored activity and outcome.

Guy et al.~(2007) observed neurological rescue including in symptomatic
adult mice after reactivating endogenous Mecp2, and recovery of
hippocampal long-term potentiation. The study establishes reversibility
under that intervention in the mouse model.

The comparison motivating a wider window for some reader-writer
disorders would require matched treatment ages or stages, restored
activity and endpoints. Methylation preservation and its relevance to
rescue need separate evidence.

\textbf{Proposed generalization.} Test reversibility across disorders
with appropriately matched comparisons and measured restoration of
function.

\emph{Fragile X.} A proposed test is whether restoration of FMR1
improves a specified functional endpoint after symptom onset. The
outcome and its dose dependence need to be established.

\emph{Angelman syndrome.} Topoisomerase inhibitors and antisense
oligonucleotides targeting UBE3A-ATS show preclinical efficacy with
restored UBE3A function. The framework predicts substantive phenotypic
improvement at partial restoration levels.

\emph{Kabuki syndrome and ATR-X.} Studies could test whether restoring
affected chromatin machinery improves a declared outcome at different
stages. Responsiveness across disorders remains open.

A class-wide pattern requires comparisons that distinguish timing and
extent of response from other influences on phenotype.

\textbf{The cancer methylome classifier comparison.} Capper et
al.~developed an earlier CNS tumor classifier and reported diagnostic
changes in up to 12\% of a prospective series. Sill et al.~report 95\%
subclass accuracy in nested cross-validation for Heidelberg v12.8 (see
Chapter 17 §17.7). These are results for specific classifiers and
validation designs.

The clinical classification results motivate comparing the information
in methylation with other assays on the same target and cohort. They do
not show that the methylation state remains unchanged or establish an OI
mechanism.

\hypertarget{chapter-close-memory-asymmetry-as-unifying-principle}{%
\subsection{16.13 Chapter close: memory asymmetry as unifying
principle}\label{chapter-close-memory-asymmetry-as-unifying-principle}}

The framework's content across the chapter is organized by a single
therapeutic principle: \emph{memory asymmetry}. When a disease process
depends on non-Markovian signaling dynamics that the corresponding
normal tissue does not depend on (or depends on differently), therapies
can target the memory structure rather than the catalytic function. The
framework predicts wider therapeutic windows for memory-structure
therapies because memory dependence is more disease-specific than
catalytic activity.

\textbf{The unifying principle across the chapter's content.}

\emph{Cancer.} Preclinical Chk1 sensitization and scheduling results
motivate matched-present tests of regulatory memory and an independent
therapeutic comparison.

\emph{Neurodegeneration.} Test whether kinase kinetics mediate a
synaptic response independently of amyloid clearance. Propranolol trials
in reconsolidation give mixed clinical evidence, and the exploratory
focused ultrasound study leaves the molecular mechanism untested.

\emph{Antibiotic response.} Persistent cellular states can motivate
tests of a history-dependent response. A treatment effect and mechanism
need evidence under specified conditions.

\emph{Immunotherapy.} A proposed test is whether changes to a candidate
persistent signaling state alter exhaustion-related outcomes while
preserving acute responses.

\emph{Cardiac pharmacology.} Use-dependent block can be modeled through
channel state. A conditional-memory test requires histories matched on a
declared present readout.

\emph{Autoimmune disease.} A memory-mediated account of nonlinear
responses to partial inhibition is a hypothesis to test against
alternative signaling models.

\emph{Epigenetics.} Mouse Rett rescue motivates comparative tests of
targeted functional restoration. Therapeutic windows in other disorders
are open.

\textbf{Three categories of empirical content.}

The chapter's content sorts into three empirical categories.

\emph{Prior observations.} Adult mouse rescue, specific methylation
classifier results and preclinical Chk1 scheduling effects provide
comparisons. Each supports the finding at its measured endpoint.

\emph{Proposed tests.} Controlled timing comparisons and molecular
readouts could assess the Chk1, CaMKII and focused-ultrasound
mechanisms. The reader-writer window hypothesis requires
disorder-specific comparisons.

\emph{Open clinical development.} The framework predicts new drug
classes --- memory-targeted drugs (Chk1 regulatory-domain accelerators),
\(\tau_B\)-normalizing drugs (neurodegeneration), anti-persister drugs
(antibiotic resistance), regulatory-domain accelerators (immunotherapy)
--- that are pharmacologically distinct from current standards. These
drug classes are not currently in development; they would require
dedicated screening programs measuring regulatory dynamics rather than
catalytic inhibition.

The medical proposals share a conditional readback diagnostic. Their
mechanisms and intervention effects require independent evidence.

The observed comparisons motivate further tests of the specified
mechanisms and clinical hypotheses.

\textbf{Forward pointers.} Chapter 17 discusses limits of prediction
with a declared observation set, tissue-specific benchmarks and
descriptive evolutionary trends, together with tests of candidate
mechanisms.

The applications in Chapters 13--17 range from empirical comparisons to
proposed tests. The claims depend on their stated observables,
interventions and models.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{chapter-17}{%
\section{Chapter 17}\label{chapter-17}}

\hypertarget{bioinformatics}{%
\section{Bioinformatics}\label{bioinformatics}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Status --- conditional information result and conjectural
applications.} The empirical comparisons below predate the framework. A
common mechanism and a relation between accessible capacity and Hurst
scaling are proposed tests.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-14}{%
\subsection{17.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-14}}

Chapter 16 describes prior observations including mouse Rett rescue
after Mecp2 reactivation. Its comparative therapeutic-window and
molecular-mechanism hypotheses remain open.

This chapter applies an identification limit to specified bioinformatics
tasks and discusses observational comparisons in molecular evolution.

A target that differs between hidden-sector completions sharing the law
of the available transcriptome observations is unidentified from those
data. The existence and magnitude of such a gap for a given biological
target have to be established.

The evolutionary comparisons include reported substitution-count
dispersion, phylogenetic rate autocorrelation and mean fitness trends in
the Long-Term Evolution Experiment. They describe different observables.

Eight pieces occupy the chapter.

Section 17.2 states the information bound for a specified target and
observation design. The effect of adding a molecular assay depends on
the information it carries about that target.

Sections 17.3--17.6 relate the conditional bound to particular benchmark
results. Section 17.7 discusses methylation-based tumor classification
and its validation.

Section 17.8 proposes a stratified variant-effect benchmark. Section
17.9 distinguishes descriptive evolutionary trends from tests of
conditional memory.

The conditional result identifies when a target is unresolved by
available observations. The applications ask whether specific
measurements or independently justified assumptions resolve it.

\hypertarget{the-information-theoretic-ceiling-on-transcriptome-only-methods}{%
\subsection{17.2 The information-theoretic ceiling on transcriptome-only
methods}\label{the-information-theoretic-ceiling-on-transcriptome-only-methods}}

Gene expression and chromatin assays measure different variables. To
determine what can be recovered from RNA alone requires a target and a
precise account of the available observations.

\textbf{The structural argument.} Chapter 16 §16.10 discusses the
distinction between measured molecular marks and downstream readouts. In
the finite-law result, several hidden completions can share the same
observable law.

If those completions differ in a target such as a regulatory edge, that
target cannot be uniquely recovered from their shared observation law.
Any feature common to those completions can still be identifiable.

\textbf{The information-theoretic bound.} Let \(Y\) be a discrete
target, \(T\) the observations available for prediction and \(S\)
additional molecular measurements. If a predictor uses only \(T\), data
processing gives \(I(Y;\widehat{Y})\le I(Y;T)\). Added measurements
improve optimal log-loss risk by
\(H(Y\mid T)-H(Y\mid T,S)=I(Y;S\mid T)\). A strict gap for the specified
assay requires \(I(Y;S\mid T)>0\).

With squared loss, the optimal prediction is the conditional mean from
the known inputs. The conditional law can also identify variance and
quantiles where the relevant target is observed. Comparing practical
methods requires the target, observation design and evaluation metric.

\textbf{Scaling with fixed information.} More training data can help
estimate the observable law. Where completions still share that law and
differ in the target, improving its estimate leaves that part of the
target unidentified.

The size of a possible prediction improvement depends on the added
measurements and the loss.

\textbf{Empirical motivation.} Benchmark underperformance can come from
data limitations, model fit or evaluation choices. Independent contrasts
are needed to establish the proposed identification gap.

\hypertarget{trajectory-inference-and-the-rna-velocity-paradigm}{%
\subsection{17.3 Trajectory inference and the RNA velocity
paradigm}\label{trajectory-inference-and-the-rna-velocity-paradigm}}

Trajectory inference methods attempt to reconstruct cell-state
transitions from single-cell snapshot data. RNA velocity (La Manno et
al.~2018) is the dominant paradigm: by comparing spliced and unspliced
mRNA, the method estimates the rate of change of expression for each
gene, producing a vector field that points each cell toward its
predicted future state. The method has been widely adopted in
developmental biology, cancer research, and stem cell biology.

\textbf{The framework's structural reading.} RNA velocity measures one
specific time-derivative signature in the visible-sector data
(spliced-unspliced ratio) and projects it onto a low-dimensional
cell-state manifold. The method assumes that this projection captures
the relevant dynamics. The framework's prediction: this assumption fails
when cell-state transitions depend on substratum memory not visible in
the transcriptome.

Velocity methods infer local dynamics under their kinetic assumptions.
Chromatin is one candidate variable affecting rates, while model
assumptions and sampling can also influence direction estimates.

\textbf{Documented failures.} Gorin et al.~(2022) describe failures
including trajectory reversal on particular data ({[}Bioinformatics
§2.2{]}). Which modeling or measurement assumption causes a particular
error needs a separate test.

An RNA-only method can improve where its kinetic model or estimation is
at fault. An unidentifiable direction under the entire RNA observation
law would require assumptions or observations that distinguish competing
completions.

\textbf{Multi-omic velocity.} MultiVelo (Li et al., 2022) includes
chromatin accessibility with RNA. It reports benefits on specified
datasets. Later multi-modal methods extend the available models and
comparisons ({[}Bioinformatics §2.4{]}).

A paired benchmark can test whether added data improve the target under
matched conditions.

\hypertarget{gene-regulatory-network-inference}{%
\subsection{17.4 Gene regulatory network
inference}\label{gene-regulatory-network-inference}}

Gene regulatory network (GRN) inference attempts to reconstruct the
causal regulatory architecture of cells from expression data. The
methodological problem is well-defined: given expression measurements
across many conditions or single cells, infer the regulatory
relationships (which gene regulates which) that produced the observed
patterns. Methods range from correlation-based (co-expression networks)
through linear models (LASSO, regression-based methods) to deep-learning
approaches.

\textbf{Benchmark results.} Some GRN evaluations report that causal
methods match or underperform correlation baselines under the chosen
reference networks and data design ({[}Bioinformatics §3.1{]}).

\textbf{A candidate information limit.} DNA binding, chromatin and other
unmeasured states can affect transcription. Their omission matters for
identification if different regulatory mechanisms remain compatible with
the observed data.

Where a regulatory target differs across completions sharing the RNA
law, the differing part remains unidentified. Association estimators can
recover quantities defined by the RNA law.

The conditional result leaves the performance of particular causal and
correlation estimators to benchmark tests.

\textbf{Multi-modal methods.} Additional measurements may distinguish
the target if they resolve a difference among observationally equivalent
completions.

SCENIC+ and LINGER incorporate accessibility or external priors and
report performance on specific regulatory tasks ({[}Bioinformatics
§3.3{]}). The reported comparisons depend on the data and reference
targets.

The information increment for a specified added modality depends on the
target and on what is already observed.

\hypertarget{perturbation-prediction-and-the-failure-of-scaling}{%
\subsection{17.5 Perturbation prediction and the failure of
scaling}\label{perturbation-prediction-and-the-failure-of-scaling}}

Perturbation prediction is the bioinformatics task of predicting
cellular response to genetic, chemical, or environmental perturbations
from training data on related perturbations. The task is central to drug
discovery (predicting effects of small molecules from training
compounds) and functional genomics (predicting effects of CRISPR
perturbations from training screens).

\textbf{The empirical failure of deep learning.} The bioinformatics
community has invested substantial resources in foundation models
trained on scRNA-seq data --- large-scale neural networks trained on
millions of single cells from public datasets. Models including scGPT
(Cui et al.~2023, replaced by 2024 versions), Geneformer (Theodoris et
al.~2023), and scFoundation have been positioned as the bioinformatics
analog of language model foundation models, with the promise that
scaling will produce comparable improvements.

\textbf{Perturbation benchmarks.} Ahlmann-Eltze et al.~(2025) compared
deep-learning approaches including GEARS with simple mean and linear
baselines on the reported datasets. The evaluated models did not
consistently outperform those baselines. Kedzierska et al.~(2025)
address separate zero-shot tasks ({[}Bioinformatics §4.2{]}).

Several explanations can contribute to these outcomes, including the
available information, training design, model fit and evaluation setup.

\textbf{The conditional explanation.} For an unseen perturbation,
consider whether completions agreeing on the observed inputs predict
different outcomes. In that case the difference is unresolved under
those inputs.

A competitive training-set mean baseline does not show that models have
reached the best possible risk given the observed data.

\textbf{Use of biological priors.} GEARS and related methods use
biological representations to constrain predictions. Whether those
priors improve a specific target is assessed by matched model and data
comparisons.

A useful prior can distinguish target-relevant models or improve
estimation. It can also impose assumptions that need validation.

\textbf{Compositional generalization.} Predicting unseen combinations
from single-perturbation training depends on assumptions about the joint
response.

If several joint responses fit the same single-perturbation law, treated
combinations or an independently supported response model can help
distinguish them.

The benchmark results motivate testing which perturbation tasks have
identification gaps and which benefit from different measurements or
models.

\hypertarget{multi-omics-integration-and-timescale-aware-methods}{%
\subsection{17.6 Multi-omics integration and timescale-aware
methods}\label{multi-omics-integration-and-timescale-aware-methods}}

Multi-omics integration combines transcriptome data with other molecular
measurements --- proteome, epigenome, metabolome, single-cell chromatin
accessibility --- into unified analyses. The methodological challenge is
that different omics modalities operate at different timescales:
transcript abundance changes on minutes-to-hours timescales, protein
abundance on hours-to-days, chromatin state on days-to-cell-generations,
DNA methylation on cell-generations-to-organism-lifetime.

\textbf{The timescale problem.} Measurements taken together can reflect
biological processes with different delays. Static covariance and lagged
effects address different relationships.

Histone marks, methylation, expression and chromatin organization can
change on different timescales. The timescales must be measured or
modeled for the experiment in question.

A time-indexed model can use lag structure when the sampling and target
make it identifiable. Its predictive effect requires a matched
comparison.

MultiVelo fits time-dependent chromatin and expression components.
Lineage and time-series methods use other sources of temporal
information. The studies' conclusions have their own benchmarks and
endpoints.

Testing the timing hypothesis requires comparing specified dynamic and
static models on the same data and target.

\hypertarget{cancer-methylome-classification}{%
\subsection{17.7 Cancer methylome
classification}\label{cancer-methylome-classification}}

Methylation profiles support tumor classification in specific clinical
and validation settings. The following comparisons distinguish
classifier performance from a possible molecular explanation.

\textbf{Heidelberg CNS tumor classifiers.} Capper et al.~(2018)
developed a classifier on 2,801 reference samples and reported
diagnostic changes in up to 12\% of prospective cases. Sill et
al.~report 95\% subclass accuracy in nested cross-validation for v12.8,
trained on 7,495 profiles with 184 subclasses ({[}Bioinformatics
§6.1{]}). The percentage pertains to that design.

\textbf{A proposed molecular interpretation.} Some diagnostic
methylation features could preserve information about a cell of origin.
The classification result leaves the stability of the entire methylome
open.

Comparisons with transcriptomic or histological methods require matched
clinical targets, assays and samples.

\textbf{Cross-cancer extension.} Methylation-based classifiers have been
studied in sarcomas and other cancers. Performance depends on the
reference set and validation design.

A follow-up test could ask whether alteration of a specific maintenance
process explains accuracy differences across tumors at controlled
sampling and reference coverage.

\textbf{Unclassifiable tumors.} Drexler et al.~(2024) studied v11.4
groups defined with calibrated score thresholds of 0.84 and 0.3
({[}Bioinformatics §6.4{]}). Low purity, reference coverage and clinical
sampling are among the factors that can affect confidence.

Altered methylation maintenance could contribute to low classifier
scores for some cases. Its contribution remains to be separated from
differences in sampling, purity and tumor types.

A test could compare predefined maintenance-associated features across
cases matched for tumor type, purity and relevant clinical covariates.

\hypertarget{variant-pathogenicity-for-readerwritereraser-genes}{%
\subsection{17.8 Variant pathogenicity for reader/writer/eraser
genes}\label{variant-pathogenicity-for-readerwritereraser-genes}}

Variant-effect predictors supply computational scores. Their performance
can be tested by variant and gene class against independent evidence.

\textbf{Candidate gene groups.} MECP2 is a reader, KMT2D writes H3K4
marks, KDM6A removes H3K27 methylation and ATRX remodels chromatin.
Their phenotypic effects and responses to restoration require
disorder-specific evidence.

The proposed benchmark compares score behavior and functional readouts
across prespecified groups.

\emph{Graded outcomes.} Compare residual activity and independently
measured phenotypic severity within and across specific genes.

\emph{Pathogenicity and severity.} Test whether the relationship between
a computational score and a separate severity measure differs across
groups.

\emph{Predictor performance.} Compare discrimination and any probability
calibration on the same held-out data, with appropriate controls for
gene, variant and reference-label differences.

\textbf{Proposed test.} The comparison could use published variant
scores and suitable independent reference labels.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  Prespecify the functional groups and assignment criteria, including
  readers, writers, erasers and remodelers.
\item
  Compare sensitivity and specificity at defined thresholds and use AUC
  for discrimination. To evaluate calibration, compare predicted
  probabilities with observed frequencies.
\item
  Compare associations with independently measured severity, with
  uncertainty and relevant covariates accounted for.
\end{enumerate}

These comparisons are proposed. Performance estimates will depend on the
reference labels and data split.

\textbf{Clinical interpretation.} A computational score is one possible
line of evidence. Clinical significance requires independent evidence
and variant interpretation under the applicable standards
({[}Bioinformatics §7.4{]}).

\hypertarget{evolutionary-observations-and-candidate-memory-tests}{%
\subsection{17.9 Evolutionary observations and candidate memory
tests}\label{evolutionary-observations-and-candidate-memory-tests}}

Studies of substitution rates and adaptation report statistical patterns
at different evolutionary scales. Those patterns motivate tests of
particular dynamical models.

C4 gives history dependence at a fixed recorded present. It does not
force a particular count variance, autocorrelation function or mean
fitness trend.

\textbf{Molecular clock overdispersion.} The molecular clock ---
Zuckerkandl and Pauling's proposal that protein and DNA substitutions
accumulate at approximately constant rates over time --- has been
recognized to violate strict Poisson statistics since the 1980s. The
index of dispersion \(R(t) = \text{Var}/\text{Mean}\) for substitutions
on a single lineage should equal 1 for a Poisson process; empirical
measurements consistently exceed this value.

Positive conditional memory need not imply \(R(t)>1\). For example, the
finite binary law \(B,0,1-B\) for a fair bit \(B\) has one event in
total. At the middle time the next outcome depends on the earlier bit
even though the present is fixed.

Reported dispersion indices depend on taxa, genes and method. The cited
mammalian analyses include estimates around \(R(t)\approx5\). Bedford
and Hartl and the cited Drosophila analyses report different values in
their datasets.

A gamma mixture of Poisson rates can give negative-binomial
overdispersion without establishing a matched-present history effect.
The Bedford--Hartl comparisons motivate testing models of
substitution-rate heterogeneity.

\textbf{Phylogenetic rate autocorrelation.} Correlation between inferred
rates is a statistic of the fitted evolutionary model. Relating it to C4
requires a declared present observable and a conditional contrast.

Tao et al.~(2019, \emph{Molecular Biology and Evolution}) applied
CorrTest to large phylogenies across the tree of life and found
``extensive rate autocorrelation in DNA and amino acid sequence
evolution of mammals, birds, insects, metazoans, plants, fungi,
parasitic protozoans, and prokaryotes.'' The fitted autocorrelation
parameter \(1/\nu\) ranges from 1.2 to 40 across datasets, with both
synonymous and nonsynonymous rates showing significant autocorrelation.

Differences across substitution types can inform models of rate
variation. The strength and explanation of the correlation depend on the
phylogeny and fitted model.

\textbf{LTEE mean fitness trajectories.} A mean trend is distinct from
the temporal dependence of deviations about that trend. Inferring
stochastic memory requires a process model or a separate analysis of the
residual trajectory.

Wiser, Ribeck and Lenski (2013) reported a power-law fit
\(w(t)=(1+t/\tau)^\beta\) to the measured mean fitness trend in the LTEE
and discussed a model with clonal interference and diminishing returns.

The fitness-trend exponent does not determine a stochastic Hurst
exponent. The latter requires a specified scaling law and suitable
time-series data.

The value \(0.79\pm0.03\) in {[}Complexity §8.11{]} is a retrospective
description of selected kinetic and spectral inputs under stated
conversions. It supplies no estimate for taxa. Whether memory scaling
varies with accessible capacity remains open.

\textbf{Punctuated equilibrium.} Stasis and intervals of rapid change
can motivate models with slow variables. Establishing a particular
history mechanism requires comparison with other processes that produce
the same pattern.

The fossil pattern is a comparison for candidate models, with the
aspects of the past available to the data defined by the setting.

\textbf{Evolutionary capacitance.} A buffering mechanism can retain
variation that becomes visible under a change in conditions. Its history
dependence can be tested for a declared present and perturbation.

The cited Hsp90 experiments motivate such tests in a particular
buffering system. A change after stress leaves open the kinetics of the
proposed readback.

Overdispersion, autocorrelation, mean fitness fits and buffering concern
different observables. Each motivates tests with a specified present
state and candidate record.

These are comparisons with prior observations. The proposed connection
to a common capacity-dependent model remains to be demonstrated.

\hypertarget{chapter-close-the-structural-roadmap-forward}{%
\subsection{17.10 Chapter close: the structural roadmap
forward}\label{chapter-close-the-structural-roadmap-forward}}

The identification limit applies to targets that vary across completions
of the available observation law. Existing methodological and
evolutionary comparisons suggest where to test for that gap or for a
specific history effect.

\textbf{Three components of the roadmap.}

\emph{Multi-modal data.} Test whether the added assay resolves
differences in the target left open by the existing data.

\emph{Knowledge graphs and prior structure.} Test whether a justified
prior improves prediction relative to matched estimation on the same
data.

\emph{Explicit memory state.} A parameterized dynamical model can
represent candidate slow states. Predictive benefits and identifiability
need testing on the chosen task.

\textbf{Five predictions for empirical work.}

(P1) Under observational equivalence, an unseen perturbation target that
differs among completions is unidentified from the common transcriptome
law.

(P2) Test whether additional molecular measurements improve the optimal
prediction or distinguish otherwise equivalent target models for a
specified perturbation.

(P3) Compare variant scores across declared groups with held-out
performance and appropriate calibration measures.

(P4) Test whether measured chromatin-maintenance features predict
classification outcomes after accounting for reference coverage and
sample characteristics.

(P5) Test whether independently estimated stochastic memory scaling
varies with calibrated accessible capacity in prespecified systems.

The empirical studies motivate additional experiments. Their conclusions
retain the scopes of their measurements and validation designs.

The information limit and readback criterion specify conditional tests.
The proposed biological causes require evidence independent of
compatibility with existing comparisons.

\textbf{Forward pointers.} The chapter closes the chapter sequence of
the book. Chapter 18 has already developed the framework's distinctive
forward predictions beyond standard QM and GR. Chapter 19 has developed
the systematic inventory of resolved and open problems in fundamental
physics. The remaining work consists of the back-matter appendices:
prediction status (Appendix A), mathematical derivations (Appendix B),
and the new common objections appendix (Appendix C) that systematically
addresses the most frequent challenges to the framework's content.

Chapters 13--17 connect conditional results to particular biological and
engineered systems. The applications include prior observations,
reported benchmark outcomes and proposed mechanism tests.

The evidence for each application and for the underlying physical claims
is assessed under its own premises.

\hypertarget{chapter-18}{%
\section{Chapter 18}\label{chapter-18}}

\hypertarget{beyond-quantum-mechanics-and-general-relativity}{%
\section{Beyond Quantum Mechanics and General
Relativity}\label{beyond-quantum-mechanics-and-general-relativity}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Status --- conjectural extension.} This chapter applies the core
framework to consciousness, and is offered as a \emph{conjecture}, not
an established result: no empirical test is proposed; the claim is a
structural correspondence between embedded observation --- the trace-out
of an observer's own inaccessible degrees of freedom --- and the
character of a bounded first-person perspective, offered as a
possibility the framework raises rather than a result it establishes. It
carries no evidential weight for the core framework --- which stands or
falls independently on its physics --- and should be read as a
structural possibility to be tested, not as support for the framework.
\end{quote}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-15}{%
\subsection{18.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-15}}

Chapters 5 through 16 developed the framework's content where standard
physics and the framework agree at high empirical precision. The
Standard Model gauge group, the gravitational sector, the JUNO neutrino
prediction, the dark sector phenomenology --- all are sectors where the
framework reproduces or refines standard predictions, often with sharper
structural commitments and parameter-free quantitative agreement. The
empirical case for the framework is concentrated in those chapters.

This chapter is different. The framework predicts content that
\emph{goes beyond} standard quantum mechanics and general relativity ---
phenomena that standard physics has no commitment to, structural
features that standard physics treats as postulates rather than
derivations, observable signatures distinguishing the framework's
specific commitments from the broader landscape of foundational
accounts. The empirical record on this content is incomplete because the
relevant experiments either have not yet been performed or have not yet
reached the precision required. The chapter is therefore forward-looking
rather than retrospective: what the framework predicts that current
physics does not yet test.

Ten pieces of content occupy the chapter.

Section 18.2 develops the framework's \emph{account} of the Born rule
--- the read-write-cycle equilibrium reading of the cosmological
realization, a mechanism proposal layered on the representation-level
fact that every finite-horizon law admits Born-rule fixed-basis readout
({[}Main §3.4{]}), with the common coherent operational extension
remaining open --- and the transient deviations it implies in the very
early universe if the hidden sector began away from equilibrium, a
conditional prospect for CMB tests of the primordial power spectrum and
non-Gaussianity. Section 18.3 develops the quantum-classical boundary as
a sharp C1--C4-determined threshold, together with the mechanism
proposal's restricted quantum-statistical regime --- partial
distinguishability revival, with a proposed capacity-controlled origin
and scaling law; partial revival itself is standard open-systems
phenomenology, the origin claim the proposal's own. Section 18.4
develops the epistemic character of quantum randomness --- quantum
outcomes are deterministic but inaccessible rather than fundamentally
indeterminate, with implications for what kinds of accounts of physics
are compatible with the framework.

Section 18.5 develops the framework's cumulative case on quantum
gravity: the descriptive cosmological constant account (Chapter 7 §7.7),
the black hole information account (Chapter 7 §7.6), and the proposed
lattice cutoff are framework-level interpretations and conditional
results, with covariant unification open (G3). Section 18.6 takes up
gravitational wave echoes: {[}GR §8.4{]} gives no echo mechanism from
the external observer's horizon partition. Standard ringdown is
inherited conditional on recovering GR dynamics.

The middle of the chapter takes up the framework's foundational
commitments and their consequences. Section 18.7 develops, under A1, the
finite-information character of the substratum and its consequence of
exact recurrence, at a period no larger than the largest order of a
permutation of \(S\) (Landau's function \(g(|S|)\)), which the framework
does not compute since \(|S|\) is not fixed by visible data. Section
18.8 develops the arrow of time as emergent from the partition's initial
conditions rather than from a fundamental temporal asymmetry --- the
substratum is T-symmetric, and the thermodynamic and cosmological arrows
trace to the partition's low-entropy initial state.

The latter sections engage two structural questions the framework has
been silent on in earlier chapters. Section 18.9 develops the
framework's position on cosmic spatial topology: the substratum is
locally a cubic lattice of spacing \(\sqrt{6\sigma}\,l_p\), with
\(\sigma\) the entropy of one boundary mode, but the global
identification structure (whether the universe is topologically trivial
\(\mathbb{R}^3\), a 3-torus, a Klein-bottle quotient, or some other
compact identification) is not determined by the framework's structural
commitments. Janna Levin's compact-universe proposal is engaged as one
specific instantiation of finite cosmic extent compatible with the
framework but not predicted by it.

Section 18.10 develops the framework's position on consciousness. The
position is asymmetric: the framework's mathematical operation of
observation (partition-and-trace-out with C1--C4 structure) is a
necessary but not sufficient condition for consciousness. The framework
imposes structural constraints on physics-based consciousness theories
--- deterministic substratum rules out fundamental-indeterminism
accounts; the C1--C4 architecture provides necessary structural
conditions for the non-Markovian information processing conscious
systems must exhibit; the framework's content is compatible with
integrated information theory and several other accounts that supply
additional sufficient conditions. The hard problem of consciousness
proper --- the explanatory gap between structural and phenomenal facts
--- is not addressed; the framework has no bridge from one to the other
and is honest about that limitation.

Section 18.11 closes the chapter by identifying which of the framework's
forward predictions are most accessible to near-term experimental
engagement, which require new instrumentation, which proposed mechanisms
remain conditional prospects without a specified observable response,
and which lie outside foreseeable empirical reach. The chapter is the
book's forward-looking content: the framework's substantive commitments
beyond current physics, with the empirical record yet to be developed.

The framework's content in this chapter has a particular epistemic
structure. Predictions like the restricted quantum-statistical regime in
biological systems and the BQP computational ceiling (developed in
Chapter 14) are \emph{testable}. The Born rule's dynamical equilibrium
is a \emph{conditional prospect}: a proposed mechanism that would bear
on the CMB's primordial statistics, without yet a specified observable
response (§18.2). Predictions like the asymmetric position on
consciousness are \emph{structural commitments with limited empirical
access}. The chapter is honest about which is which. The framework's
value here is not the empirical record (which is what Chapters 5-17
developed) but the structural commitments --- what the framework says
about the world beyond what current physics tests.

\hypertarget{the-born-rule-as-dynamical-equilibrium}{%
\subsection{18.2 The Born rule as dynamical
equilibrium}\label{the-born-rule-as-dynamical-equilibrium}}

The Born rule --- that the probability of measuring a quantum system in
state \(|x\rangle\) given wave function \(|\psi\rangle\) is
\(P(x) = |\langle x | \psi \rangle|^2\) --- is one of the most
empirically successful predictions in physics. It is also one of the
most foundationally puzzling. In standard quantum mechanics, the Born
rule is an \emph{independent postulate}: it holds always, for all
systems, at all times, with no underlying mechanism producing it. The
various interpretive programs (many-worlds, QBism, Bohmian mechanics,
dynamical collapse) take different positions on what the Born rule
means, but they share the structural feature of treating it as
fundamental rather than derived.

The framework's account is layered. At the representation level the Born
rule is part of the exact equivalent description: every finite-horizon
law has a unitary representation with Born-rule fixed-basis readout
(\(S \iff D \iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\), {[}Main §3.4{]}). This
representation exhibits the Born form without selecting its quadratic
exponent; the physical origin of the quadratic probability rule remains
open ({[}Main §3.1{]}), as does the common coherent operational
extension to arbitrary noncommuting instruments and composites. On top
of that sits the cosmological-realization \emph{mechanism proposal}: the
equilibrium reading of the read-write cycle between the visible and
hidden sectors --- the observer reads the visible sector through
measurement, writes correlations into the hidden sector through the
coupling \(H_{VB}\), and reads back those correlations on subsequent
measurements --- with Born-rule probabilities as the stationary
statistics of the cycle for the equilibrated hidden prior. That
stationary-distribution reading is the account's load-bearing step, and
it is a structural commitment of the realization, not a proved theorem
of the foundational paper.

On this mechanism proposal, the Born rule would be a \emph{dynamical}
equilibrium rather than a fundamental postulate. The system would
approach Born-rule statistics on a characteristic timescale set by the
hidden sector's equilibration time \(\tau_{\text{eq}} \sim \tau_B\),
where \(\tau_B\) is the hidden sector's correlation time from condition
C2. For the cosmological partition \(\tau_B\) is the horizon time,
\(\tau_B(t) \sim H(t)^{-1}\): about \(10^{17}\) seconds today and far
shorter in the early universe. Two quantities must be kept apart. The
ratio \(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-32}\) is the per-step loss of a stored
record under C2; it sets how long a stored record survives, not the size
of memory effects or the distance from equilibrium. The quantity that
tracks the approach to equilibrium is instead the accumulated number of
relaxation times,
\(\int dt/\tau_{\text{eq}} \sim \int H\,dt = \ln(a/a_i)\), but that
count does not by itself fix how a deviation decays. If the observed
deviation \(\delta\) obeys a closed relaxation law
\(\dot\delta = -\lambda H\delta\), a deviation present when relaxation
began at scale factor \(a_i\) decays as \((a_i/a)^{\lambda}\); the
identification \(\tau_{\text{eq}} \sim H^{-1}\) fixes neither that
closed law nor the coefficient \(\lambda\), which it constrains only to
be of order one. Under such a law the epoch-local reading is required:
with \(\tau_{\text{eq}}\) fixed at today's value, of order \(H_0^{-1}\),
the age of the universe would amount to about one relaxation time and
would leave a fraction of order \(e^{-\lambda}\) of any initial
deviation in place today, a departure that laboratory tests of the Born
rule exclude unless the initial deviation was itself negligible. On the
epoch-local reading the same law suppresses the residual in any current
or foreseeable laboratory experiment by the factor
\((a_i/a_0)^{\lambda}\), and the Born rule is exact for all practical
purposes. If the hidden sector began at equilibrium there is no
transient to relax, and the account reduces to the maximal-entropy
measure posited in {[}Main §4.5{]}. (Status of this estimate: the
identification \(\tau_{\text{eq}} \sim \tau_B\) and its epoch-local
reading are heuristic content of the mechanism proposal, and the closed
relaxation law and its coefficient \(\lambda\) are further assumptions
the proposal does not derive; none of these is a theorem of the
foundational paper.)

\textbf{Transient violations in the very early universe.} If the hidden
sector began away from its stationary distribution, the Born rule was
\emph{not} exact in the very early universe: until the hidden sector
equilibrated, measurement statistics deviated from
\(|\langle x | \psi \rangle|^2\). Whether it began away from equilibrium
is a question about the cosmological initial conditions that the account
does not settle; if it began at equilibrium, there were no such
violations. Any deviations are parametrized by
\[P(x, t) = |\langle x | \psi(t) \rangle|^2 + \sum_k c_k(t) \langle x | \hat{O}_k | \psi(t) \rangle,\]
where the operators \(\hat{O}_k\) encode the measurement history and the
coefficients \(c_k(t)\) parameterize possible history-dependent
departures. Their decay would require an additional effective relaxation
law, such as the closed law considered above, applicable over a
specified finite epoch. Neither asymptotic convergence to zero nor a
universal decay rate follows from the finite reversible substratum
dynamics, which is recurrent under A1 (§18.7); microscopic recurrence
and a possible effective relaxation over a finite epoch are distinct.
(Status: the expansion is the proposal's \emph{parametrization} of the
deviation --- the form an eventual derivation would have to fill in ---
not a derived spectral decomposition.)

The structural source of any transient violations is the hidden sector's
initial state. In the framework's substratum dynamics, the hidden sector
begins in a specific initial configuration set by the cosmological
initial conditions. If that initial state is away from the stationary
distribution, then before the visible-hidden coupling has driven the
hidden sector there, the read-write cycle's input statistics differ from
the Born rule, and the observer reads visible-sector outcomes with
probabilities that deviate from \(|\langle x | \psi \rangle|^2\) in ways
that depend on the specific initial state.

This connects to Valentini's \emph{quantum relaxation} hypothesis in de
Broglie-Bohm theory, where Valentini proposed that Born-rule violations
in the early universe would leave observable imprints. The mechanism
proposal offers a structural mechanism for what Valentini's program
postulates: hidden-sector equilibration would drive relaxation toward
the Born rule on the heuristic timescale
\(\tau_{\text{eq}} \sim \tau_B\). Valentini's program postulated the
relaxation; the account locates a candidate mechanism for it in the
partition's read-write architecture. Both take the initial departure
from equilibrium as an assumption about the cosmological initial
conditions.

\textbf{Observational signatures in the CMB.} If primordial Born-rule
violations were present during inflation, their empirical signature
would be modified statistics of the primordial fluctuations. A change in
the variance alone alters the primordial power spectrum without
entailing any non-Gaussianity --- a Gaussian distribution with a changed
variance has no connected moments beyond the second --- so a
non-Gaussian signature arises only if the departure also carries higher
connected moments. Standard inflationary models predict approximately
Gaussian primordial perturbations, and the Planck 2018 analysis detects
no primordial non-Gaussianity: for the local shape,
\(f_{\text{NL}} = -0.9 \pm 5.1\) (68\% CL). The framework does not yet
supply an amplitude to compare with this bound or with the measured
power spectrum.

Standard local, equilateral, and folded non-Gaussianity shapes arise
from specific inflationary mechanisms (multi-field inflation,
non-canonical kinetic terms, modified initial vacuum states). Which
moments a Born-rule departure would modify, and with what scale
dependence or bispectrum shape, depends on the source dynamics of the
relaxation, the family of initial deviations and the map from the
hidden-sector deviation to the observed fluctuations, none of which the
proposal specifies; whether such a departure produces any
non-Gaussianity, and whether its shape would differ from the standard
ones, is open.

The empirical accessibility of the proposal depends on inputs it does
not yet fix: the source dynamics of the relaxation through inflation,
the family of initial deviations, the rule for a mode's evolution after
horizon exit, and the map from a residual deviation to the measured
power spectrum or non-Gaussianity. The residual on a given scale is set
by the initial deviation and by the relaxation accumulated between the
onset of relaxation and the imprinting of that scale, not by the
relaxation timescale alone: even rapid relaxation leaves almost the
entire deviation on a scale imprinted shortly after relaxation begins,
and no relaxation history leaves a residual if the initial deviation is
zero. Once the observable map is derived, the Planck measurements would
constrain the combination of initial deviation and relaxation history;
no bound on \(\tau_{\text{eq}}\) follows before then. The epoch-local
reading above places \(\tau_{\text{eq}} \sim H_{\text{inf}}^{-1}\).
Under a closed relaxation law, if a mode's relaxation stops at its
horizon exit, the residual on observable scales depends on how many
e-folds of relaxation preceded that exit and, for scale-independent
initial deviations, is largest on the largest scales; if relaxation
continues to a common later epoch, that scale dependence cancels; and
scale-dependent initial deviations can cancel or mimic either trend. The
account fixes none of these.

\textbf{Status ledger for §18.2.} Layer by layer: the
representation-level Born status is a theorem ({[}Main §3.4{]}: admitted
universally, coherent operational extension characterized by five named
conditions in {[}GR §3.3{]}); the read-write equilibrium reading is a
mechanism \emph{proposal} whose stationary-distribution step is a
structural commitment; the equilibration timescale, its epoch-local
reading and the deviation parametrization above are the proposal's
heuristic quantitative content, and the closed relaxation law and rate
coefficient on which a decay law rests are further assumptions it does
not derive; the observable form of a departure --- a power-spectrum
change, non-Gaussianity, or both --- is not derived; and the F7 entry
--- transient deviations if the hidden sector began away from
equilibrium, observed through the CMB's primordial statistics --- is a
conditional prospect: it becomes a testable prediction only once the
source dynamics, the family of initial deviations and the map to
observables are specified, and it is detectable only if a nonzero
residual survives on observable scales when they are imprinted. No entry
in this section is a theorem of the foundational paper.

CMB-S4 (the upcoming ground-based experiment) and LiteBIRD (the planned
space-based experiment) will tighten the non-Gaussianity constraints by
roughly an order of magnitude over the next decade. Whether these
experiments bear on the proposal depends on the source dynamics, the
family of initial deviations and the map to observables, none of which
the proposal yet specifies. Once they are specified, a predicted
departure above the new sensitivity would be tested by these
experiments, and a smaller one would leave the proposal unconstrained by
them.

\textbf{History-dependent corrections at late times.} Even after the
hidden sector has equilibrated, the Born rule receives history-dependent
corrections. Their size is not fixed by the timescale ratio:
