\(\tau_S / \tau_B \approx 10^{-32}\) for the cosmological partition sets
how long the hidden record survives, while the size of the correlations
is set by the coupling and the readback, which the framework does not
quantify for that partition. The bath's motion contributes an absorbable
Hermitian drift at first order in the ratio and genuine non-unitarity at
second order ({[}Main §3.2{]}). The \emph{structure} of the corrections
is predicted: successive quantum measurements are not exactly
independent samples from the Born distribution. They carry correlations
encoding the deterministic structure of the substratum bijection
\(\varphi\).

The conceptual content of the late-time correction is significant.
Standard quantum mechanics treats measurement outcomes as fundamentally
independent random samples from the Born distribution. The framework
predicts that this independence is approximate --- there exist
correlations between successive measurements, generated by the
deterministic substratum dynamics, that persist in the frozen-bath limit
\(\tau_S / \tau_B \to 0\), where the hidden record is retained longest.
The framework's substratum is deterministic; the apparent randomness of
quantum mechanics is the observer's incompleteness rather than
fundamental indeterminism. The late-time corrections are the structural
signature of this underlying determinism; their magnitude is not fixed
by the timescale ratio.

\hypertarget{the-quantum-classical-boundary-and-the-restricted-quantum-statistical-regime}{%
\subsection{18.3 The quantum-classical boundary and the restricted
quantum-statistical
regime}\label{the-quantum-classical-boundary-and-the-restricted-quantum-statistical-regime}}

The quantum-classical boundary is one of the most pragmatically
important features of physics and one of the most foundationally
ambiguous. Standard quantum mechanics applies universally in principle:
a rock, a cat, and an electron are all described by wave functions, with
the rock's wave function being too entangled with environmental degrees
of freedom to show interference effects. The pragmatic boundary between
``quantum'' and ``classical'' is set by decoherence rather than by any
structural distinction --- macroscopic objects appear classical because
they are quantum-but-decohered, not because they obey different physics.

The framework's account is structurally different. The boundary it draws
is \emph{determined by whether the framework's conditions C1, C2, C3, C4
are satisfied} --- and it is a boundary in the memory currency, not in
representability, which is universal (\(S \iff D \iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\),
{[}Main §3.4{]}). A system satisfying all four carries the
memory-bearing sector --- accessible non-Markovian statistics,
\(M_t > 0\), with unavoidable hidden predictive memory in every
completion; a system failing C1, C4 or the persistence form of C2 has
that sector empty --- not ``quantum but decohered'' but genuinely
described by memoryless classical stochastic dynamics, its quantum
representation trivial; a system failing C2 only in its timescale form
has it suppressed, not shown to be empty, and limited capacity caps it
(below). The boundary drawn by C1, C4 and the persistence form of C2 is
structural rather than approximate.

\textbf{The four conditions as criteria.} Recall from Chapter 1 the
framework's four conditions for an embedded observer's reduced
description to carry the memory-bearing sector --- the discriminating
content, the representation itself being universal ({[}Main §3.4{]}): -
C1 (coupling): the subsystem must interact non-trivially with a hidden
sector; - C2 (memory persistence): the hidden sector must retain a
record of the subsystem's past across the accessible window,
\(\tau_B \gg \tau_S\) with \(\tau_B\) the coarse-grained mixing time ---
slow hidden dynamics is one sufficient mechanism, not the condition
itself ({[}Main §1.3{]}); - C3 (capacity): the hidden sector must have
capacity sufficient for the process's conditional memory --- the
capacity floor \(\log_2 |\mathcal{C}_H| \geq I^*\) ({[}Main §3.4{]});
\(N_H \gg N_V\) is the comfortable physical regime, not the condition; -
C4 (history readback): hidden degrees of freedom must carry the visible
past into future visible conditionals --- the readback gap that makes
the stored memory accessible ({[}Main §1.3{]}).

A system implementing C1--C4 with all four conditions strongly satisfied
has a memory-bearing reduced description --- the framework's
identification applies in full at its stated layer --- the
memory-bearing description with its quantum representation, correctly
given by unitary evolution on a Hilbert space at the
transition-statistics layer, the coherent operational lift still to be
established ({[}Main §3.4{]}). A system failing C1 (no hidden-sector
coupling) has memoryless classical stochastic dynamics --- the
memory-bearing sector is empty, the quantum representation trivial. A
system failing C2 in its timescale form (a hidden sector that
equilibrates faster than the visible-sector dynamics, its records eroded
before readback) has emergent dynamics whose accessible memory effects
are suppressed. A hidden sector of limited capacity caps accessible
memory --- the capacity floor \(M_t \le \log_2|\mathcal{C}_H|\) ({[}Main
§3.4{]}); the mechanism proposal hypothesizes that marginal capacity
produces partial distinguishability revival, the restricted
quantum-statistical regime of Chapter 15 §15.7, with memoryless
operational modeling failing while the transition-statistics layer
remains representable ({[}Main §3.4{]}).

\textbf{The restricted quantum-statistical regime.} The mechanism
proposal adds a revival scale to the distinction between memoryless and
memory-bearing visible laws, and names one range of it. The scale is the
revival measure \(\mathcal{N}\). On an accessible window
\(W = \{0, \ldots, K\}\), let \(d_t\) be the distinguishability at time
\(t\) of two initial preparations under the visible dynamics --- the
total-variation distance of their visible population laws, equivalently
the trace distance of the corresponding diagonal states --- and let
\(\mathcal{N}\) be the largest increase \(d_t - d_s\) over pairs of
preparations and times \(s < t\) in \(W\), with \(\mathcal{N} = 0\) when
distinguishability never increases. \(\mathcal{N}\) is the peak revival
on the window, a single increase, so \(0 \le \mathcal{N} \le 1\). It is
not the Breuer--Laine--Piilo measure, which sums every increase over the
window. That cumulative backflow is kept separate: on a finite
reversible system the rooted laws are periodic ({[}Main §2.3{]}), so a
revival in one recurrence period recurs in every later one, and the sum
grows without bound as the window lengthens. \(\mathcal{N} > 0\) on a
window certifies P-indivisibility there, since a P-divisible family
never increases distinguishability; the converse fails ({[}Main
§2.3{]}). Memory does not fix \(\mathcal{N}\): the XOR control of
{[}Main §2.3{]} carries memory on a window on which its family is
P-divisible, so \(\mathcal{N} = 0\) there, and \(\mathcal{N}\) measures
revival, not memory. Three ranges are named on a window: no revival
(\(\mathcal{N} = 0\)), partial revival (\(0 < \mathcal{N} < 1\)) and
complete revival (\(\mathcal{N} = 1\)). The mechanism proposal calls
partial revival the \emph{restricted quantum-statistical} regime. The
name records that the quantum description supplied there is the
representation at the transition-statistics layer, with the operational
layer built on it not supplied; that restriction holds at every value of
\(\mathcal{N}\), so the regime is fixed by its revival range, and the
name marks neither a partial nor a complete quantum theory and is not a
quantum-membership scale: every finite law at every \(\mathcal{N}\)
admits the quantum representation and a deterministic hidden realization
({[}Main §3.4{]}).

By definition the regime lies strictly between no revival
(\(\mathcal{N} = 0\)) and complete revival (\(\mathcal{N} = 1\)). In
standard quantum mechanics, a decohered system is still described by a
density matrix --- it is quantum but mixed. In the framework the regime
is a statement about the DYNAMICS, not about representability: every
stochastic transition family admits the one-step ancilla dilation
({[}Main §3.1{]}), so no process lacks a Hilbert-space representation at
the transition-statistics layer. What varies across the regime is the
size of the largest distinguishability revival on the window; a positive
revival certifies indivisibility, while indivisibility without revival
is possible ({[}Main §2.3{]}). What a system in the regime may lack is
the stronger OPERATIONAL structure built on top of that representation:
coherent preparations of the represented states, the instrument algebra
governing interventions, and representation-consistency across horizons
--- each of which the framework leaves open or bounded rather than
delivered ({[}Main §3.4{]}). The quantum description is restricted in
that precise sense: the transition-statistics layer is available
throughout the regime, as at every value of \(\mathcal{N}\), while the
operational layer is available only to the extent those questions are
settled, so the representation is not a complete operational quantum
theory; and \(\mathcal{N}\) records the largest revival, not a distance
from the divisible families.

Partial distinguishability revival itself is standard open-systems
phenomenology --- the Breuer--Laine--Piilo measure quantifies
trace-distance revival, and the Rivas--Huelga--Plenio measures quantify
departures from complete-positivity divisibility, a different property;
what is distinctive here is the proposed capacity-controlled origin and
the specific scaling law. Standard accounts treat quantum and classical
as endpoints of a spectrum (with decoherence interpolating between
them), but the framework separates memoryless from memory-bearing
visible laws ({[}Main §3.4{]}), and the mechanism proposal adds a
revival scale inside the memory-bearing case --- the restricted
quantum-statistical regime for partial revival --- all of it
quantum-representable ({[}Main §3.4{]}).

\textbf{Where to look for the restricted quantum-statistical regime.}
The mechanism proposal, layered on the capacity theorem, conjectures
where partial revival occurs: in systems whose hidden sector has
capacity comparable to the visible sector's, with protein conformational
dynamics and single-enzyme kinetics as the biological candidates Chapter
13 conjectures, which the capacity ratio does not by itself place there.
The timescale ratio \(\tau_S/\tau_B\) does not by itself place a system
on the revival scale. A fast bath that erodes the stored record
uniformly suppresses the readback gap exponentially in \(\tau_S/\tau_B\)
at every order \(k \geq 2\) ({[}Main §2.3{]}); a slow bath does not by
itself give memory or revival --- a static bath whose record is never
read back carries no memory ({[}Main §2.3{]}).

The framework's content is not ``quantum effects in biology'' ---
standard quantum mechanics allows quantum effects at any scale, and the
literature documents many examples. The framework's content is the
distinction between memoryless and memory-bearing visible laws, all
quantum-representable ({[}Main §3.4{]}), together with the mechanism
proposal's conjecture that partial revival occurs at marginal hidden
capacity.

\textbf{Observational signatures.} Single-molecule enzyme experiments
already show non-Markovian kinetics --- history-dependent reaction
rates, stretched-exponential waiting-time distributions, transition
statistics that cannot be fitted with a Markovian rate equation. The
framework's prediction is that these signatures are not artifacts of
poorly-characterized rate constants but features the mechanism proposal
attributes to partial revival. Two tests are distinct. Whether the
multi-time statistics admit a memoryless (Markov) description at the
accessible horizon decides memory; whether the distinguishability of two
preparations revives on that horizon decides \(\mathcal{N} > 0\), which
certifies indivisibility. A memory-bearing system can show no revival
({[}Main §2.3{]}); the mechanism proposal predicts memory together with
partial revival --- a proposal-level claim ({[}Main §3.4{]}).

The distinction is empirically testable. A memoryless (divisible)
density-matrix description requires specific algebraic constraints on
the transition probabilities --- positivity, completeness, certain
inequality relations between multi-time correlators. The mechanism
proposal predicts that protein conformational dynamics and single-enzyme
kinetics violate at least some of these constraints. The experimental
program would require multi-time correlation measurements with
sufficient statistics to constrain the algebraic structure, which is
within reach of current single-molecule techniques.

The restricted quantum-statistical regime is the mechanism proposal's
testable conjecture, with experimental targets in the biological
sciences that the framework's quantum-biology chapter (Chapter 13)
develops in detail.

\hypertarget{the-epistemic-character-of-quantum-randomness}{%
\subsection{18.4 The epistemic character of quantum
randomness}\label{the-epistemic-character-of-quantum-randomness}}

The framework's commitment to a deterministic substratum has a striking
consequence for the foundations of quantum mechanics: quantum randomness
is \emph{epistemic} rather than ontic. The apparent indeterminism of
quantum measurement outcomes is the observer's incompleteness, not a
fundamental feature of physical reality. The substratum bijection
\(\varphi\) is deterministic; the memory-bearing description --- with
its admitted quantum representation --- emerges from the framework's
structural conditions applied to embedded observation of this
deterministic dynamics ({[}Main §3.4{]}); the randomness the observer
sees is the result of marginalizing over the hidden sector.

This is a substantive position, and it has consequences both for the
foundations of quantum mechanics and for what kinds of accounts of
physics are compatible with the framework.

\textbf{Deterministic but inaccessible.} The framework's substratum
dynamics is given by the bijection \(\varphi\) acting on the
configuration space \(S\). Each state \((x, h)\) --- visible coordinates
\(x\) paired with hidden coordinates \(h\) --- maps to a unique
successor \(\varphi(x, h) = (x', h')\). There is no randomness in the
dynamics; the substratum is strictly deterministic.

The apparent randomness arises because the observer sees only \(x\), not
\(h\). Different hidden states \(h_1, h_2, \ldots\) compatible with the
same visible state \(x\) lead to different successor visible states
\(x_1', x_2', \ldots\) under the bijection. From \(x\) alone the
observer cannot distinguish among the hidden states; they appear as a
probability distribution over the possible successors. The probabilities
are \emph{not} features of the dynamics --- the dynamics is
deterministic --- but features of the observer's reduced description of
the dynamics, given the observer's incomplete information about the
hidden-sector configuration.

This is what ``deterministic but inaccessible'' means in the framework:
the outcomes are fully determined by the substratum dynamics, but the
observer cannot in principle access the complete state that determines
them. The randomness is unavoidable for any embedded observer, but it is
not fundamental --- it is the cost of partial observation.

\textbf{Bell's theorem and the chosen nonlocality.} Bell does not rule
out determinism by itself; it rules out reproducing the observed
correlations with a response-complete deterministic completion that
records a \(\pm1\) outcome in every run and is both
measurement-independent and parameter-independent. Chapter 1 proves the
corresponding Bell ceiling: if the setting interventions, applied at one
step, each read and write only their own wing, the Bell-relevant
coupling range does not connect the wings before readout, every run
records a \(\pm1\) outcome, and one setting-independent pre-setting
ensemble is used, then \(|S_{\rm CHSH}|\le2\). The framework therefore
declines the measurement-dependent/superdeterministic horn and takes
\textbf{ontic parameter dependence}. In the specific SM/GR realization
the target mechanism is preparation-indexed adjacency in the already
state-dependent graph \(G(x)\) (or an equivalent ontically nonlocal
response), so a prepared microstate response may depend on the remote
setting while the reference vacuum/uniform graph remains geometric and
bounded-range. Whether those prepared graphs keep the operational
distribution no-signaling and preserve the continuum-curvature limit is
the open hypothesis H-Bell. The \(2\sqrt2\) theorem for the causal-local
indivisible stochastic description is a separate weaker-layer result,
not a locality theorem for the deterministic completion.

One proposed physical realization of that preparation-indexed parameter
dependence uses non-localized cosmological-boundary modes. This is a
candidate realization, not an established Bell mechanism: any such
prepared long-edge/response structure must satisfy H-Bell, i.e.~preserve
operational no-signaling and the metric/Ollivier--Ricci continuum limit
used by the gravitational reconstruction. What distinguishes it from a
superluminal signaling mechanism is operational no-signaling, not ontic
parameter independence.

\textbf{Practical consequences are absent.} The distinction between
epistemic and ontic randomness has no consequence observed at current
experimental precision --- quantum random number generators, quantum key
distribution protocols, and other applications that rely on ``true
randomness'' function identically under either interpretation. What
these applications rely on is unpredictability to the parties who can
observe or act on the source, not the ontic or epistemic status of its
randomness. Determinism does not by itself guarantee that
unpredictability: an embedded observer whose actions reach the hidden
state driving a deterministic source can, for some sources, predict its
output better than chance. Whether a source stays unpredictable to
observers of bounded memory, whether they act on it or only read it,
depends on the source, and the framework does not establish it for the
hidden sector of the physical realization.

The framework's content here is therefore conceptual rather than
empirical at near-term experimental scales. The framework's commitment
to deterministic substratum changes what physics-based accounts are
compatible with the framework --- but it does not change near-term
experimental predictions in any observable way.

\textbf{Conceptual consequences.} The deeper conceptual consequence is
significant. The universe is deterministic in the framework. Quantum
indeterminacy is the cost of partial observation, not a feature of
reality. At the fixed-basis level the measurement problem receives an
observer-relative account: no collapse, no branching and no objective
randomness in the substratum; which operational protocols the completion
settles is open (Chapter 19 §19.2.5). There is a bijection, a partition,
and an observer who cannot see the whole.

This has implications for what classes of physics-based accounts of
consciousness, the foundations of probability, the relationship between
determinism and free will, and various other foundational questions are
compatible with the framework. Accounts that require fundamental
indeterminism in physical reality --- Penrose's orchestrated objective
reduction is the most prominent example in consciousness research ---
are incompatible with the framework's deterministic substratum. Accounts
that treat quantum probabilities as derivable from incomplete
information rather than as fundamental are compatible with and supported
by the framework.

The framework does not claim to settle these foundational questions; it
makes structural commitments that constrain which accounts are
compatible. Sections 18.9 and 18.10 develop two of these constraints in
detail --- what the framework says about cosmic spatial topology and
what it says about consciousness --- but the broader pattern is that the
framework's commitment to deterministic substratum is a substantive
structural feature that constrains the foundational landscape.

The framework's quantum randomness is therefore epistemic, exact in its
predictions for any embedded observer's empirical access, and
consequential for the classes of foundational accounts compatible with
it. The empirical record is silent at the \(10^{-32}\) level; the
conceptual record is substantial.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{quantum-gravity-the-cumulative-case-at-the-framework-level}{%
\subsection{18.5 Quantum gravity: the cumulative case at the framework
level}\label{quantum-gravity-the-cumulative-case-at-the-framework-level}}

The framework gives a geometry-first reading of three quantum-gravity
problems: the cosmological constant problem, the black hole information
paradox, and the non-renormalizability of perturbative quantum gravity.
For the cosmological constant, the two levels of description can be
distinguished, and the gravitational coupling remains open. Bijectivity
preserves substratum information, and the Page curve is conditional. The
proposed lattice supplies a microscopic cutoff, with recovery of the
covariant effective theory open at G3. This section brings those
readings together.

\textbf{The conventional formulation.} Standard treatments of quantum
gravity attempt to quantize the gravitational field by analogy with the
quantization of the Standard Model forces. The metric tensor
\(g_{\mu\nu}\) is treated as a quantum field, decomposed into a
classical background plus fluctuations, and the fluctuations are
quantized through canonical or path-integral methods. Three obstacles
arise.

The cosmological constant problem: the QFT vacuum energy summed over all
field modes up to the Planck cutoff is of order
\(M_{\text{Pl}}^4 \sim 10^{113}\,\text{J/m}^3\). The observed vacuum
energy density is \(\sim 10^{-9}\,\text{J/m}^3\). The ratio \(10^{122}\)
is treated as a fine-tuning problem requiring an unknown cancellation
mechanism.

The black hole information paradox: Hawking's 1975 semiclassical
calculation produces thermal radiation that appears to carry no
information about the black hole's initial state. If the radiation is
exactly thermal, information is destroyed when the black hole completes
evaporation --- in tension with quantum mechanics' commitment to
unitarity.

Non-renormalizability: perturbative quantum gravity treated as a quantum
field theory in flat spacetime is non-renormalizable. Infinitely many
independent counterterms are required to absorb divergences at
successively higher orders, with no UV completion within the standard
quantization framework.

The framework starts with causal geometry in the classical substratum.
In the proposed description, an embedded observer traces out degrees of
freedom across a boundary defined using that geometry. This ordering is
needed for that trace-out construction.

\textbf{The first component: the cosmological constant.} Chapter 7 §7.7
distinguishes two scales. The Friedmann equation sets the
critical-density scale \(\rho_{\text{crit}} \sim c^2 H^2/G\). The
observed vacuum density is a supplied fraction of that scale. Summing
QFT zero-point energies up to a Planck cutoff gives
\(\rho_{\text{QFT}} \sim M_{\text{Pl}}^4\) in natural units. Their large
ratio is of the order of the de Sitter entropy
\(S_{\text{dS}} = A/(4 l_p^2)\) under these scale estimates. The
framework reads this comparison as an information compression ratio
between the substratum and the observer's emergent description.

The gravitational comparison requires a native coupling at G3. A common
offset cancels in a difference of complete conserved stress tensors
evaluated on the same metric with a fixed reference. The native stress
or flux map and the gravitational response to physical vacuum changes
remain open.

\textbf{The second component: the black hole information paradox.}
Chapter 7 §7.6 developed the framework's account of the information
paradox. A bijective substratum preserves information. Whether the
radiation carries it is a separate question. For a common dilation and
initial state, the nested-partition formalism gives the same reduced
channel from the direct and sequential trace-outs. The Page curve
additionally needs H-scramble and H-decouple. The paper rules out that
condition for a definite initial configuration with the bipartition
aligned to the configuration coordinates (Chapter 7 §7.6).

The derivation runs through a mechanism substantially different from the
quantum-extremal-surface and entanglement-island computations --- cycle
typicality on the configuration space rather than replica wormhole
computation in the gravitational path integral --- and the
correspondence between the two is conjectural. For a mass-independent
emission coefficient (Chapter 7 §7.6), its Page time is a fixed fraction
of the evaporation time set by the entropy the radiation carries per
unit of horizon entropy lost: \(t_P \approx 0.646\, t_{\text{evap}}\)
when the two are equal, and earlier when the radiation carries more, as
it does in the semiclassical emission regime defined in Chapter 7 §7.6.

The two-level description makes it possible for information preserved by
bijectivity to reside in sectors that the emergent description traces
out. Whether and when this information becomes accessible in the
radiation requires the separate dynamical argument.

\textbf{The third component: non-renormalizability.} In the usual
continuum effective field theory of gravity, perturbation theory about
the Einstein--Hilbert action requires new counterterms at successive
orders. The effective theory is predictive order by order at low energy.
\href{https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.50.3874}{Donoghue}

The framework proposes a physical lattice with spacing
\(\sqrt{6\sigma}\,l_p\) under the link count and horizon calibration of
Chapter 7 §§7.3--7.4. That spacing would set the microscopic cutoff. The
covariant effective description would apply at wavelengths large
compared with that spacing.

On this proposal the lattice dynamics would take over at scales
approaching \(\sqrt{6\sigma}\,l_p\). Matching those dynamics to
covariant field equations with their sources remains open at G3 ({[}GR
§8.7{]}).

\textbf{The shared structural feature.} In each case the geometry-first
proposal distinguishes the substratum from the observer's description.
For the cosmological constant it distinguishes the horizon scale from
the zero-point estimate. For the information paradox it distinguishes
preservation by bijectivity from accessibility in the radiation. For
perturbative gravity it distinguishes the proposed microscopic cutoff
from its open matching to the long-wavelength covariant theory.

These readings motivate a common substratum model \((S,\varphi)\) for
quantum records and gravity. G3 remains open (Chapter 19 §19.2.1). The
framework's treatment carries conditional and consistency relations,
including the horizon calibration with its \(1/4\) ratio, the
descriptive vacuum-energy distinction, the dark-sector reading, and the
MOND scale \(a_0 = cH/6\) conditional on the open coupling map with its
factor \(1/6\) imported. Its forward exposure is listed in Appendix A.5.

\hypertarget{gravitational-wave-echoes}{%
\subsection{18.6 Gravitational wave
echoes}\label{gravitational-wave-echoes}}

Several quantum-gravity proposals --- firewall scenarios, fuzzball
proposals, certain wormhole models --- predict that a black hole's
horizon partially reflects outgoing gravitational radiation, producing
delayed echoes after the ringdown, with amplitudes that depend on the
microstructure assumed. Echo searches in LIGO/Virgo data (Abedi, Dykaar
and Afshordi 2017; Westerweck et al.~2018; Tsang et al.~2018; and the
LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA Collaboration on the merger catalog through O3) have
found no statistically significant signal.

\textbf{The framework's statement.} {[}GR §8.4{]} uses the cosmological
horizon for the external observer's partition. In the stated
configuration the merger and the infalling matter stay inside that
observer's visible sector. The external trace-out therefore supplies no
mechanism for an echo, a comb, or a reflecting wall at the black-hole
horizon. No echo amplitude is derived. Inheriting standard ringdown
requires recovery of the relevant GR dynamics at G3.

\textbf{The conceptual content.} The more informative gravitational
comparison is the Milky Way outer rotation curve (Chapter 7 §7.9), whose
reported Keplerian decline beyond the crossover is in tension with the
dark-sector law. The GW250114 result tests the classical area theorem.
The \(1/4\) calibration retains its own conditions.

The chapter's broader content on forward predictions continues with the
framework's substratum commitments --- finite information under A1, the
arrow of time, cosmic topology, and consciousness --- that test the
framework at scales and levels distinct from the direct empirical
exposure of the gravitational and quantum sectors.

\hypertarget{finite-information-and-exact-finite-recurrence}{%
\subsection{18.7 Finite information and exact finite
recurrence}\label{finite-information-and-exact-finite-recurrence}}

The hypothesis A1 of a finite substratum has structural consequences
that extend beyond the empirical predictions of fundamental physics.
Under A1 the universe is described by a finite configuration space \(S\)
with bijection dynamics \(\varphi: S \to S\). Finiteness is not a
calculational convenience but load-bearing under A1: it guarantees exact
recurrence of the substratum dynamics --- the finite-bijection form of
recurrence, stronger than what Poincaré's theorem gives for a
finite-measure system --- which, together with a non-permutation rooted
map, produces P-indivisibility at the embedded-observer level; a
fixed-basis unitary quantum representation is internal and universal
({[}Main §3.4{]}), the compressed form supplied across the
correspondence's class under (T), with P-indivisibility fixing its
nontriviality. The recurrence route in the framework's logic chain
requires finite \(S\).

\textbf{Finite information content.} The substratum's information
content is \(\log_2 |S|\) bits --- finite for any finite \(S\). This is
distinct from the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy
\(S_{\text{BH}} = A/(4 l_p^2)\), which bounds the \emph{accessible}
information at any given partition (the capacity of the visible sector
and the boundary layer). The total information content of \(S\) is at
least that of the boundary layer at the cosmological horizon; whether it
exceeds the Bekenstein-Hawking bound is not fixed by visible data, and
under the finiteness posit A1 (Chapter 2 §2.4) it is finite.

A clarification is essential. The cardinality \(|\mathcal{C}_D|\) of the
deep hidden sector is \emph{gauge} in the framework: different values of
\(|\mathcal{C}_D|\) produce the same visible transition data exactly for
a deep sector beyond the reach of the dynamics over the times
considered, and at leading order on accessible timescales under the
posited influence bound H-BD of {[}GR §3.2{]}. The ``total information''
of the universe is therefore not fixed by those data. But the
\emph{finiteness} of \(|\mathcal{C}_D|\) --- for the recurrence route
specifically, that there exists some finite value, even if its specific
magnitude is not observable --- is load-bearing. Infinite hidden sectors
would break the recurrence argument that drives recurrence-scale
P-indivisibility; that route would close. P-indivisibility itself does
not require finite \(S\): any revival of distinguishability between the
visible laws of two roots implies it, whatever the size of the hidden
sector. For the selected linear update on the infinite lattice, with
prime \(q\), a nonzero coupling coefficient, a uniform product prior on
the hidden sites and lattice-convex visible windows, no such revival
occurs, and the process is P-divisible at every horizon. Accessible
non-Markovianity would survive through readback, and the imported
representation is gated by (T) rather than by recurrence, so an infinite
substratum removes this route rather than the framework's quantum
representation.

The hypothesis of finite information (A1) is therefore neither a
quantitative claim about the specific cardinality nor a metaphysical
preference for finitism. It is a structural requirement for one
particular route --- the recurrence-based P-indivisibility result, which
needs every root's visible law to return to certainty at a common time,
\(\Gamma_n = I\), almost surely over the hidden prior. A bijection of a
finite set supplies that return at its order
(\(\varphi^N = \mathrm{id}\) gives \(\Gamma_N = I\)); the Poincaré
recurrence theorem for a finite-measure system does not, since it
returns almost every state at its own time. The substratum's finiteness
is what makes this particular route to P-indivisibility available.

\textbf{Exact finite recurrence.} A bijection \(\varphi\) acting on a
finite set \(S\) is a permutation. Every permutation on a finite set has
finite order: there exists a smallest positive integer \(N\) such that
\(\varphi^N = \mathrm{id}\), the identity map. After \(N\) time steps,
it returns to its exact initial state. A bijection of a finite set is
therefore strictly periodic, with period \(N\) determined by the
bijection's cycle structure.

The recurrence period can be astronomically large. For an arbitrary
bijection of \(S\), two upper bounds with different growth rates bear on
it. \emph{A bound valid for every permutation:} \(N\) is the least
common multiple of the cycle lengths, each at most \(|S|\), so \(N\)
divides \(\mathrm{lcm}(1, 2, \ldots, |S|)\). Its logarithm is
Chebyshev's function, \(\ln \mathrm{lcm}(1, \ldots, n) = \psi(n)\), with
\(\psi(n) \sim n\) by the prime number theorem. \emph{The largest period
any permutation attains:} this is Landau's function \(g(n)\), the
maximum order of a permutation of \(n\) points, with
\(\ln g(n) \sim \sqrt{n \ln n}\) (Landau 1903). Since \(\sqrt{n \ln n}\)
is \(o(n)\), \(g(n)\) lies far below \(\mathrm{lcm}(1, \ldots, n)\), and
no permutation has order near \(e^{n}\). Typical-permutation order
estimates require a specified probability law for \(\varphi\), which the
framework does not adopt; Chapter 3 §3.2 holds that random permutations
of finite sets typically lack the structure C1--C4 require.

The substratum's cardinality is not fixed by visible data. {[}Substratum
§4{]} bounds only the visible-plus-boundary sector,
\(|\mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_B| \le e^{10^{122}}\) at the de
Sitter horizon; the deep sector's cardinality is gauge (above). For
illustration only, if \(|S|\) were of order \(e^{10^{122}}\), the first
bound would give
\(N \le \mathrm{lcm}(1, 2, \ldots, |S|) = e^{\psi(|S|)} \sim e^{e^{10^{122}}},\)
in the sense \(\ln N \le \psi(|S|) = (1 + o(1))\,|S|\). The second is
sharper: no bijection of that set has period above \(g(|S|)\), with
\(\ln g(|S|) \sim \sqrt{|S| \ln |S|} \sim 10^{61}\, e^{5 \times 10^{121}}\).

The exactly linear rule on a fixed coupling graph is far more
constrained than an arbitrary bijection. Under linearity (A5, Chapter 2
§2.4) the update is an invertible linear map of
\(S = (\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^D\), where \(D\) counts every stored
component, including the previous-time copy that a second-order rule
carries. Its powers \(\varphi^0, \ldots, \varphi^{N-1}\) are distinct
and nonzero, and they lie in the ring generated by \(\varphi\), which by
the Cayley--Hamilton theorem has at most \(q^D\) elements. Hence
\(N \le q^D - 1 = |S| - 1\) for every alphabet size \(q \ge 2\). For
prime \(q\) some linear maps attain \(q^D - 1\), but the wave rule falls
far short of it: on a ring of \(L\) sites, with \(q\) prime and
\(\gcd(L, q) = 1\), its period is exactly \(qL\), against
\(|S| = q^{2L}\) (Appendix B, Theorem B.3.1). The bound does not cover
the other maps the corpus uses: the state-dependent-geometry map
\(F(u, v) = (v, \mathrm{WE}_{G(v)}(v) - u)\) of {[}SM §3.1{]}, which
carries the gravitational sector, and the rounded bijection of {[}SM
§4.2{]}, whose proposed stationary law is meant to support full-shell
sampling, are bijections but not linear maps, and for them only
\(N \le g(|S|)\) and \(N \mid \mathrm{lcm}(1, \ldots, |S|)\) hold. The
period of the three-dimensional rule at cosmological size is not
computed in the corpus.

The return itself is definite: a finite model returns to its exact
initial state after \(N\) substratum time steps, where \(N\) is fixed by
the cycle structure of \(\varphi\). It is at most \(g(|S|)\) for any
bijection and below \(|S|\) for the exactly linear rule. The framework
bounds \(N\) rather than computing it, and it supplies no lower bound on
\(N\).

A finite model is periodic with period \(N\), the least common multiple
of the bijection's cycle lengths. For a rule fixing the zero
configuration on a nontrivial state space, no single cycle passes
through every configuration. The exact linear rule of {[}SM §4.2{]} has
this property and therefore at least two cycles. The cycle-ergodicity
question that {[}SM §4.2{]} treats concerns sampling within an energy
shell. Within a single cycle no state function increases throughout; a
direction of the observer's experience is fixed by boundary conditions
on a stretch of the cycle (the arrow of time discussed in the next
section), and at the substratum level the dynamics has no preferred
direction.

\textbf{Implications for the framework's logical structure.} The
recurrence theorem connects three structural features of the framework:
substratum finiteness (the hypothesis A1, \(|S| < \infty\)), bijection
dynamics (the bijectivity premise of the framework's models), and
P-indivisibility at the recurrence scale. The connection runs in three
steps. Finiteness of \(S\) guarantees exact recurrence
(\(\varphi^N = \mathrm{id}\)). Recurrence together with C1 acting at the
first step --- which makes the one-step matrix a non-permutation under
the uniform hidden prior, the cheapest non-permutation rooted map ---
gives returns of information from hidden to visible over the recurrence
timescale (P-indivisibility across the recurrence cycle, not on
accessible windows); the coupling is load-bearing rather than
decorative, since for an uncoupled partition
\(\varphi = \varphi_V \times \varphi_H\) the visible sector evolves
autonomously, its two-time family is divisible, and no
distinguishability is ever restored --- recurrence notwithstanding. With
a full-support visible prior this indivisibility is equivalent to memory
at some order below the recurrence time; the memory-bearing sector is
the one in which C4 places that memory at an accessible order, and every
finite law, memory-bearing or not, admits the quantum representation.

The hypothesis of finite information (A1) is therefore load-bearing for
the recurrence route specifically, not for representability or for
accessible non-Markovianity: readback at order \(k\) has its own
finite-horizon route, and the imported representation is gated by (T)
rather than by recurrence, so those routes do not exclude an infinite
deep hidden sector, which would need its own normalized state or measure
and well-defined dynamics ({[}Main §2.3{]}, §3.1; Chapter 2 §2.3).
Removing finiteness --- replacing \(|S| < \infty\) with \(|S| = \infty\)
--- would remove the recurrence route rather than the framework's
quantum representation.

\hypertarget{the-arrow-of-time}{%
\subsection{18.8 The arrow of time}\label{the-arrow-of-time}}

The framework's substratum dynamics is given by the bijection
\(\varphi: S \to S\). The bijection has \emph{no arrow of time}. Both
\(\varphi\) and its inverse \(\varphi^{-1}\) are equally valid maps on
the configuration space, and the substratum dynamics is unchanged under
the exchange \(\varphi \leftrightarrow \varphi^{-1}\). The framework's
commitment to T-symmetric substratum dynamics is the same commitment
that gives reciprocal transition counts under the counting hidden prior
of a finite model in Chapter 6 §6.3 (and narrows \(\theta\) to
\(\{0,\pi\}\) without fixing \(\bar\theta\)) --- T-invariance at the
substratum level is a structural feature that propagates through the
framework's emergent descriptions.

This raises an obvious question. The universe we observe has an
unambiguous arrow of time: entropy increases, biological systems age,
memories form of the past but not the future, the universe expands
rather than contracts. If the substratum dynamics is T-symmetric, where
does the observed arrow come from?

\textbf{The arrow as observer-emergent.} The framework's answer is that
the arrow of time is \emph{emergent from the observer's coarse-grained
description}, not from the substratum dynamics. The substratum dynamics
is T-symmetric; the observer's reduced description of a non-equilibrium
initial condition is not. The asymmetry enters through the trace-out of
a non-equilibrium initial condition --- the marginalization over the
hidden sector that produces the embedded observer's reduced description;
under the invariant measure the trace-out alone produces none. The arrow
of time is therefore a feature of embedded observation of such a
condition, in the same way that quantum mechanics, the dark sector, and
the Born rule are.

The mechanism is the standard Boltzmann argument applied to the
framework's partition. The visible sector starts in a particular
configuration that is, in some sense, ``low entropy'' relative to the
typical configurations accessible at later times. The hidden sector
starts in a configuration that contains all the correlations needed to
specify the visible sector's future evolution. As the dynamics evolves,
correlations flow from hidden sector to visible sector and back, with
the time-reversibility of the underlying dynamics fully preserved at the
substratum level. But the observer, who sees only the visible sector,
sees an irreversible flow: information about the past is encoded in the
visible sector's current state (entropy increasing), while information
about the future is encoded in the hidden sector (inaccessible to the
observer).

The arrow of time is therefore \emph{the observer's incompleteness}
expressed temporally. The same partition that produces quantum
randomness (by hiding the substratum information that determines
outcomes) produces the arrow of time (by hiding the substratum
information that would let the observer reverse the dynamics). Both are
aspects of the same structural feature: the observer's reduced
description is asymmetric in ways that the substratum dynamics is not.

\textbf{Detailed balance and the thermodynamic arrow.} The framework's
content on detailed balance from Chapter 6 §6.3 has a direct implication
for the arrow of time. For a time reversal that preserves the partition,
and the counting prior on hidden states, the visible transition
probabilities satisfy reciprocity, \(T_{ij} = T_{\theta j, \theta i}\)
at all timescales, with \(\theta\) the action of time reversal on
visible states; when the visible states carry no T-odd data this is
detailed balance, \(T_{ij} = T_{ji}\) --- the rate of transition from
\(i\) to \(j\) equals the rate of transition from \(j\) to \(i\). This
follows from \emph{substratum-level} T-symmetry: the dynamics has no
preferred direction.

The thermodynamic arrow of time emerges not from any asymmetry in the
transition probabilities but from the partition's \emph{initial
conditions}. The universe starts in a configuration that is far from
equilibrium relative to the substratum's full state space, with most of
the substratum's degrees of freedom on the hidden side of the partition
and the visible sector occupying a small, structured region. As the
dynamics evolves, the system moves toward equilibrium relative to the
substratum's state space --- entropy increasing in the observer's
coarse-grained description --- until the entire substratum is fully
mixed. The arrow of time runs in the direction of this equilibration.

The relation to detailed balance is that the H-theorem --- the standard
derivation of entropy increase from microscopic dynamics --- is a
theorem about the \emph{coarse-grained} description, not about the
underlying transition probabilities. The H-theorem assumes a particular
kind of initial condition (low entropy at the coarse-grained level) and
derives entropy increase from there. Detailed balance at the microscopic
level is fully consistent with the H-theorem at the coarse-grained
level, because the H-theorem is about how the observer's information
about the system evolves rather than about the system's underlying
dynamics.

\textbf{The cosmological arrow.} Whether the thermodynamic arrow and the
cosmological arrow --- the direction in which the universe expands ---
are aligned is open in the framework: it is neither established nor
refuted. The cosmological partition has a specific initial condition:
the universe begins in a low-entropy configuration with most degrees of
freedom on the hidden side of the cosmological horizon. On an expanding
FRW background satisfying the null energy condition, the
apparent-horizon area is non-decreasing. Its assigned entropy has that
interpretation under the stated calibration assumptions; whether this
behavior aligns with boundary correlations or hidden-sector disorder
remains open.

Both arrows are traced to the same initial conditions of the
cosmological partition. That is a common boundary condition, not a
derived mechanism: that the thermodynamic arrow within the visible
sector tracks the cosmological arrow is not established. The universe
started with low entropy at the cosmological level, as an initial
condition; at the cosmological boundary, coupling C1, persistence C2 and
capacity C3 are verified, while history readback C4 is a named
realization condition not presently discharged (Chapter 7 §7.2); the
cosmological boundary is the primary partition for any embedded
observer.

\textbf{Why the framework reframes rather than explains.} The
framework's content on the arrow of time is not an explanation of
\emph{why} the universe has a preferred direction; it is a
\emph{reframing} of the question. Standard accounts of the arrow of time
treat it as an asymmetry that requires explanation --- why is entropy
increasing in the direction we call ``future'' rather than the direction
we call ``past''? The framework's answer is that there is no asymmetry
in the substratum dynamics; the asymmetry is in the observer's reduced
description, which inherits the initial conditions of the partition.

The reframing places the explanatory burden on a different question.
Instead of asking ``why does the universe have a preferred direction of
time?'', the framework asks ``why does the universe start in a
low-entropy partition?'' The latter question is a question about
\emph{initial conditions} --- addressable by inflationary cosmology,
anthropic arguments, or other initial-condition mechanisms --- rather
than a question about \emph{dynamics}. This is the same kind of
reframing the framework applies to the cosmological constant problem
(Chapter 7 §7.7): the conventional formulation treats the small observed
value as a fine-tuning problem in the dynamics; the framework treats it
as a feature of the partition's structure that does not require
dynamical explanation.

The arrow of time is therefore one more case where the framework's
substratum-emergent distinction does substantive work. The substratum is
T-symmetric (the dynamics has no arrow). The emergent description is not
T-symmetric (the observer sees an arrow). The asymmetry is structural
--- inherited from the partition's initial conditions --- rather than
dynamical. The framework's content here is not to solve the
arrow-of-time problem in the conventional sense but to locate it
precisely: the arrow is at the level of partition initial conditions,
not at the level of substratum dynamics.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{cosmic-spatial-topology}{%
\subsection{18.9 Cosmic spatial
topology}\label{cosmic-spatial-topology}}

The framework's structural commitments determine the \emph{local}
structure of the substratum but are silent on its \emph{global}
structure. The substratum is a cubic lattice of spacing
\(\sqrt{6\sigma}\,l_p\) (Chapter 7 §§7.3--7.4). The local cubic
structure produces the gauge group, the matter content, and the
framework's quantitative predictions across Standard Model and
gravitational sectors. But whether the lattice extends globally as
\(\mathbb{R}^3\), identifies as a 3-torus, has a Klein-bottle quotient,
or admits some other global identification structure --- that is not
determined by the framework's structural commitments. The framework is
locally specific and globally agnostic.

The framework's local calculations use the properties of the partition
at scale \(\epsilon\). A global identification can affect what enters an
observer's causal neighborhood. The finite-window comparison below
specifies when two models give the same local records.

\textbf{Janna Levin's compact-universe proposal.} Levin developed in the
late 1990s and early 2000s the proposal that the universe could have a
non-trivial spatial topology --- specifically, that spatial sections
could be \emph{compact} (a 3-torus, a Klein-bottle quotient, or other
compact identifications) rather than infinite. The motivation was partly
cosmological (compact topology produces specific signatures in the CMB
power spectrum at the largest angular scales) and partly philosophical
(an infinite universe creates conceptual difficulties around uniqueness
and the anthropic principle, addressed at book length in Levin's
\emph{How the Universe Got Its Spots} in 2002).

The Klein-bottle specifically refers to non-orientable compact spatial
topologies in which a parity-reversing identification connects opposite
``sides'' of the universe. The proposal is one example within the
broader family of compact-universe possibilities --- others include the
3-torus (orientable, no parity reversal), the Poincaré dodecahedral
space (constant positive curvature, no parity reversal), and various
lens-space identifications. Levin's work, with collaborators Cornish,
Spergel, Starkman, Weeks, and others, developed the empirical program
for testing compact-universe proposals through their characteristic CMB
signatures.

\textbf{The empirical program: matched-circle signatures.} A topological
image of the observer can have a last-scattering sphere that intersects
ours. In that case the same region of the last-scattering surface can be
seen in two directions, producing correlated temperature patterns along
a pair of circles.

Cornish, Spergel, Starkman, and Komatsu (2004) developed a statistical
method for detecting matched circles. WMAP and Planck temperature maps
have been searched for these patterns.

Planck found no statistically significant matches in the configurations
it searched. The resulting bounds constrain suitable topological loops
through our position on scales comparable to the diameter of the
last-scattering surface. A topology can have shorter loops elsewhere and
still evade this bound.
\href{https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201525829}{Planck 2015 results
XVIII} · \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02603}{COMPACT, Part I}

\textbf{The framework's compatibility with Levin's proposal.} Levin's
compact-universe proposal is \emph{consistent with} but \emph{not
predicted by} the framework. Three structural points clarify this.

First, a compact identification can give a finite periodic lattice. With
finitely many states per site and the specified finite-carrier dynamics,
this is one way to realize A1 in a model.

Second, A1 can also hold on a finite lattice region with prescribed
boundary conditions and finitely many states per site.

Third, the local finite-window laws agree across two topology choices if
the local updates agree, the relevant dependency cones are identified,
and the joint law of their inputs agrees (GR Appendix B). This gives a
test for when a global identification can be ignored in a local
comparison.

The framework leaves global topology open. Consequences of a particular
identification depend on the model and the observer's causal
neighborhood.

\textbf{The CMB as joint testing ground.} Both Levin's matched-circle
program and the framework's Born-rule transient violations (§18.2) are
CMB-data-driven empirical programs. They are structurally distinct ---
matched-circles tests global identification, Born-rule transient
violations tests boundary thermodynamics at inflation --- but they use
overlapping observational data. Planck 2018 constrains the standard
non-Gaussianity shapes, and CMB-S4 and LiteBIRD will tighten those
constraints; whether they bear on the Born-rule proposal depends on the
quantities §18.2 does not yet fix.

The framework's CMB content does not compete with Levin's. The
matched-circle test depends on the spatial extent and structure of
topological identifications. The framework's Born-rule transient
violations, if present, depend on the temporal evolution of the
visible-hidden coupling during inflation. The two tests probe orthogonal
physical content using the same data sets --- analogous to how the JUNO
experiment probes neutrino mixing and the same reactor antineutrino flux
probes other oscillation parameters.

\textbf{Open question: non-orientability and chirality.} On Chapter 5's
H-link/H-cust branch and under the physical identification H-spin', the
staggered trace-out gives a vector-like \(\mathrm{SU}(3)\) coupling;
chiral \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) additionally requires the open
taste-selectivity hypothesis H-χ' (SM §4.8). A separate question is
whether a non-orientable global topology (Klein-bottle specifically, or
other non-orientable compact identifications) interacts non-trivially
with the framework's local-lattice chirality.

On the stated local lattice branch, the chirality scale is microscopic.
A global identification on a cosmological scale would be separated from
it by roughly 60 orders of magnitude at \(\sigma = 1\). Whether global
phase or sign factors can affect the local chirality structure remains
open.

This is an open question the framework has not addressed. Resolving it
would require a calculation: starting from a specific non-orientable
compact topology (Klein-bottle or otherwise), determining whether the
framework's local chirality derivation acquires global corrections, and
computing the observable signatures of any such corrections. The
framework does not currently have the calculation; the question is
pre-registered as an open theoretical task.

The framework leaves cosmic spatial topology open. Levin's
compact-universe proposals illustrate one way to model A1 under the
conditions above. The effect of non-orientability on the local chirality
argument requires a separate calculation.

\hypertarget{the-frameworks-position-on-consciousness}{%
\subsection{18.10 The framework's position on
consciousness}\label{the-frameworks-position-on-consciousness}}

The framework's mathematical object --- the partition with C1--C4
structure --- defines an \emph{observer} in a structural sense. The
observer is not yet a \emph{conscious entity}. Whether the structural
conditions for observation are also sufficient conditions for
consciousness is a separate question, with the framework's commitments
having implications for what answers are possible.

This section develops the framework's substantive position on
consciousness: observation is \emph{necessary but not sufficient} for
consciousness. The framework provides structural necessary conditions
for conscious systems and imposes constraints on what physics-based
consciousness theories are compatible with its commitments. The hard
problem of consciousness proper --- the explanatory gap between
physical/structural facts and phenomenal experience --- is not
addressed, and the framework is explicit about this scope limitation.

\textbf{Mathematical observer is not equivalent to conscious entity.}
The framework's observer is a partition \(V\) of the substratum's
configuration space combined with the conditions C1 (coupling to hidden
sector), C2 (record persistence --- slow-bath separation the route; a
physical-regime premise in {[}Main{]}'s typing), C3 (sufficient
hidden-sector capacity), and C4 (history readback --- the load-bearing
memory condition). The partition is a mathematical object that has
dynamical consequences (the trace-out producing the reduced law whose
representation carries the emergent QFT), thermodynamic consequences
(entropy displacement producing dark matter phenomenology), and
empirical consequences (the JUNO prediction, the BH entropy, the dark
sector).

The partition is not, by itself, a conscious entity. A thermostat
coupled to room temperature implements a partition in a degenerate sense
(the thermostat's internal state interacts with the room's thermodynamic
state). A cosmological horizon implements a partition with
\(\tau_S/\tau_B \sim 10^{-32}\). A protein interior implements a
partition. Nothing in the framework attributes phenomenal experience to
any of them. The framework's mathematical observer is therefore a
structural object, not a phenomenal one, and the framework does not
claim equivalence between mathematical observation and conscious
experience.

\textbf{The asymmetric position.} The framework's substantive content on
consciousness is the asymmetric claim: any conscious system must
implement a partition with C1--C4 structure, but not every C1--C4
partition is conscious. The framework provides structural necessary
conditions for consciousness without specifying sufficient conditions.
The two directions below differ in standing: Direction 2 follows from
the definition of observation, which detectors and horizons satisfy;
Direction 1 is a conjecture about consciousness, motivated by the role
of memory in conscious information processing, and not a theorem of the
framework. Evidence in the framework's sense is perspective-neutral ---
a record bears its evidential relations through its correlations at the
partition, whether or not a conscious system takes it up; whether
evidence as experienced requires a conscious perspective is an
epistemological question the framework does not address.

The claim has two directions worth distinguishing.

\emph{Direction 1: Consciousness requires observation.} Any conscious
system must implement a partition with substantial C1--C4 structure. A
system that fails C1 (no coupling to a hidden sector) cannot be
conscious because it has no environment to be aware of. A system that
fails C2 (hidden sector equilibrates faster than visible-sector
dynamics) cannot be conscious on the framework's account with C2 read in
its timescale form: the memory it retains, which would support
integration over time, is suppressed. A system that fails C3
(insufficient hidden-sector capacity) cannot be conscious because it
cannot store the information that conscious experience would require.
The C1--C4 architecture is necessary for the non-Markovian information
processing that conscious systems must exhibit.

\emph{Direction 2: Observation does not require consciousness.} The
cosmological horizon, proteins, and engineered C1--C4 systems implement
observation structurally, and nothing in the definition requires that
they be conscious. The framework's observation has structural
consequences (the memory-bearing quantum representation, dark sector
phenomenology) at the level of the partition's emergent dynamics, but it
does not entail phenomenal experience. Whatever distinguishes the
conscious C1--C4 systems from the non-conscious ones is some
\emph{additional feature} beyond the bare C1--C4 architecture ---
biological substrate, neural architecture, integrated information
\(\Phi\), global workspace dynamics, recurrent processing, or some
combination --- that the framework's structural commitments do not
specify.

The asymmetric position is more conservative than alternatives like
dual-aspect monism (where structural observation and phenomenal
consciousness are necessarily co-occurring) and panpsychism (where every
C1--C4 system is conscious to some degree). The framework's content
allows but does not require these stronger positions.

\textbf{Substantive constraints on consciousness theories.} The
framework's commitments constrain what physics-based theories of
consciousness are compatible with it.

\emph{Deterministic substratum rules out fundamental-indeterminism
accounts.} The framework's substratum is deterministic: the bijection
\(\varphi\) maps each state to a unique successor. Quantum randomness is
epistemic, not ontic (§18.4). Theories of consciousness that
\emph{require} fundamental indeterminism in physical reality are
incompatible with the framework. The most prominent example is Penrose's
orchestrated objective reduction (Penrose-Hameroff), which posits that
conscious experience arises through gravitationally-induced quantum
collapse in microtubules --- a specific form of fundamental
indeterminism that the framework's deterministic substratum forbids. The
framework's commitments make Penrose-Hameroff structurally incompatible.

\emph{C1--C4 architecture is necessary for non-Markovian information
processing.} Conscious systems must exhibit memory effects,
history-dependent dynamics, and readback of stored correlations between
subsystems --- the structural signatures of non-Markovian dynamics that
emerge from the framework's C1--C4 architecture. Theories of
consciousness that treat conscious systems as fundamentally Markovian
(instantaneous, memoryless processing) are incompatible with the
framework's account of how cognitively non-trivial information
processing must work. Strict feed-forward computational accounts of
consciousness face this constraint.

\emph{The substratum is finite under A1.} Under A1 the framework's
finite substratum (§18.7) would constrain theories of consciousness that
posit infinite information content for conscious experience. Theories
requiring genuinely infinite degrees of freedom (some forms of
mathematical Platonism applied to consciousness, for instance) face this
constraint.

These are real constraints rather than vacuous ones. The framework rules
out a substantial class of physics-based consciousness theories while
remaining compatible with the broader landscape of accounts that supply
additional sufficient conditions for consciousness beyond the
framework's necessary ones.

\textbf{Integrated information theory as adjacent content.} Integrated
information theory (IIT), developed primarily by Giulio Tononi, is the
most prominent physics-adjacent consciousness theory and has substantive
content overlap with the framework. IIT proposes that consciousness
corresponds to integrated information \(\Phi\), a quantitative measure
of how much a system's parts inform each other beyond what their
individual contributions predict. Systems with high \(\Phi\) are
conscious; systems with low \(\Phi\) are not.

There is a real structural relationship between the framework's C1--C4
architecture and IIT's \(\Phi\). C1 (non-trivial coupling) is necessary
for non-zero \(\Phi\) --- without inter-part coupling, integrated
information cannot be non-trivial. C2 (record persistence --- realized
here by slow-bath separation) is necessary for IIT's information
integration over time --- the framework's persistence requirement, met
via \(\tau_B \gg \tau_S\), provides the memory architecture that
integration requires. C3 (sufficient hidden-sector capacity) is
necessary for the system's state space to be large enough to support
meaningful integration. A system satisfying C1--C4 with substantial
margins (large \(\tau_B/\tau_S\), large \(N_H/N_V\)) is a system with
substantial \(\Phi\); a system satisfying C1--C4 marginally has low
\(\Phi\).

The relationship is not exact identity. C1--C4 are \emph{necessary
conditions} for non-Markovian dynamics in the framework's specific
sense, while \(\Phi\) is a \emph{quantitative information-theoretic
measure} in IIT's specific formulation. But the conditions overlap
substantially. The framework's content here is compatible with IIT as a
candidate sufficient-condition theory: the C1--C4 architecture provides
the necessary structural conditions for the framework, and IIT's
\(\Phi\) provides the additional sufficient content for consciousness
within that architecture. The framework does not endorse IIT's
identification claim (that \(\Phi\) \emph{is} consciousness), but it
provides structural foundations that IIT-like accounts can build on.

The relationship runs in both directions. The framework's structural
account of subjecthood --- what makes a system a subject of observation
in the framework's mathematical sense --- is compatible with IIT's
account of what makes a system conscious. Conversely, IIT's predictions
about which systems are conscious provide quantitative content that
complements the framework's structural necessary conditions. The two
accounts engage at different levels and are not in tension.

\textbf{The hard problem is not addressed.} The framework's content on
consciousness is necessary-condition content. The framework provides
structural conditions that conscious systems must satisfy; it provides
constraints on what theories of consciousness are compatible with the
framework's commitments; it provides empirical predictions about the
structural features conscious systems must exhibit. None of this
addresses the hard problem of consciousness proper --- the question of
\emph{why} phenomenal experience accompanies physical processes at all.

The hard problem is a question about the relationship between
structural/physical facts and phenomenal facts. The framework provides a
structural account (the partition with C1--C4 structure produces the
emergent dynamics that conscious systems must satisfy). What it does
\emph{not} do is bridge the explanatory gap from such a structural
account to phenomenal experience. The framework predicts which systems
should be conscious as a necessary-condition claim, but it does not
explain \emph{why} implementing those necessary conditions should
produce subjective experience rather than functional information
processing ``in the dark.''

This scope limitation is honest rather than evasive. No physics-based
framework currently bridges the explanatory gap; claiming that the
framework does so would be overreaching. The framework's value here is
its discipline: necessary-condition content with substantive constraints
on theories, combined with explicit acknowledgment that the hard problem
is not addressed. This is more than the strict scope often adopted in
physics frameworks (which decline to engage consciousness at all) and
less than the overclaiming sometimes seen (where physics frameworks
announce solutions to the hard problem they cannot actually deliver).

\textbf{Empirical predictions and constraints.} The framework's
necessary-condition conjecture implies structural expectations about the
features conscious systems should exhibit; they are consistency checks
on the conjecture, not evidence for the framework.

Conscious systems should exhibit non-Markovian information processing
--- memory effects, history-dependent dynamics, readback of stored
correlations between subsystems. The C1--C4 architecture is empirically
detectable in neural systems; the prediction is that systems we identify
as conscious (humans, mammals, possibly other complex biological
systems) should exhibit these signatures at their relevant timescales.
Neuroscience evidence --- synaptic plasticity, neuromodulator gradients,
glial dynamics, slow oscillations supporting cognitive integration ---
is consistent with this prediction. The framework's content is
structurally aligned with the broader neuroscience consensus on the
architecture of conscious information processing.

Conscious systems should \emph{not} be possible in architectures that
strictly fail C1--C4. The framework predicts that strictly feed-forward
neural network architectures (without recurrent connections, without
memory states, without integration over time) cannot produce
consciousness --- they fail C2 by lacking the temporal integration
architecture. This is consistent with the empirical finding that
consciousness in humans is associated with recurrent processing rather
than purely feed-forward processing. The framework's content here is a
structural constraint that aligns with empirical neuroscience.

The framework's bioinformatics content from Chapter 17 is structurally
related. The molecular clock overdispersion, rate autocorrelation across
the tree of life, and LTEE power-law fitness trajectory are all
empirical signatures of non-Markovianity in evolutionary biology
systems. The framework predicts that similar non-Markovian signatures
should be detectable in conscious systems at their relevant timescales
--- the brain's analog of the molecular clock's overdispersion would be
the variability of neural processing rates across timescales, predicted
by the framework to be non-Markovian rather than Markovian. The
empirical program connecting these structural predictions to
consciousness research is open.

The framework's content on consciousness is therefore disciplined
necessary-condition content with substantive empirical predictions, real
constraints on theory choices, and explicit honesty about the limits of
its scope. The hard problem of consciousness proper is not solved or
dissolved by the framework. The framework's value in consciousness
research is structural --- what makes a system the kind of system that
\emph{could} be conscious --- rather than phenomenal.

\hypertarget{chapter-close-3}{%
\subsection{18.11 Chapter close}\label{chapter-close-3}}

This chapter has developed the framework's distinctive forward content
beyond standard quantum mechanics and general relativity. The empirical
record of Chapters 5 through 17 establishes the framework's content
where it agrees with current physics at high precision; this chapter has
developed the framework's content where it makes predictions current
physics does not yet test.

\textbf{Four categories of forward content.} The chapter's content sorts
into four categories distinguished by their empirical accessibility.

\emph{Testable forward predictions.} The restricted quantum-statistical
regime (§18.3) is testable through distinguishability-revival
measurements in single-molecule kinetics, accessible to current
laboratory techniques. The BQP computational ceiling (Chapter 14) is
exposed to any demonstrated super-BQP computation --- which would
falsify the global-coverage premise first, the framework-plus-model
conjunction only with further argument. The framework's content in this
category is empirically engaged at near-term experimental scales.

\emph{Conditional prospects.} The Born rule's dynamical equilibrium
(§18.2) is a proposed mechanism without a specified observable response.
It would become testable through CMB measurements of the primordial
power spectrum and non-Gaussianity, such as CMB-S4 and LiteBIRD, only
once the source dynamics, the family of initial deviations and the map
to observables are specified; until then it carries no quantitative
prediction.

\emph{Structural commitments with limited empirical access.} The
epistemic character of quantum randomness (§18.4) is consequential for
foundations but has no consequence observed at current experimental
precision. The cumulative case on quantum gravity (§18.5) reframes three
problems but has no direct empirical signature beyond the predictions
already developed in the cosmological constant, BH information paradox,
and renormalization treatments. The arrow of time (§18.8) is
observationally manifest but is not directly testable as a framework
prediction because all physics-based accounts of the arrow generate the
same empirical signature. The framework's content in this category is
structurally consequential without producing additional empirical
handles beyond those already developed in Chapters 5-17.

\emph{Framework's scope limits.} Cosmic spatial topology (§18.9) remains
open. Local comparisons between models of different topology require
matching causal-window inputs. The hard problem of consciousness
(§18.10) is explicitly outside the framework's scope; the framework
provides necessary-condition content on consciousness but does not
bridge the explanatory gap from structural to phenomenal facts. The
framework's content in this category is honest acknowledgment of what
the framework does not address.

\textbf{Forward pointers.} Chapter 19 develops the framework's content
against the standard list of open problems in fundamental physics. The
chapter is a systematic inventory: ten problems the framework addresses
with a resolution, dissolution, conditional construction or partial
treatment, its table giving each one's status (quantum gravity in three
components, covariant unification open, the cosmological constant, dark
matter, dark energy, the measurement problem, BH information, hierarchy,
gauge group origin, generation puzzle, dark sector budget), two
split-status entries (the Born-rule origin --- representation level
settled, coherent operational extension characterized by five named
conditions; strong CP --- open under two named conditions) and five
scope limits where the framework does not provide a derived value (the
flavor problem with structured open task; baryogenesis, which §19.3.3
reclassifies as solution-specific --- the baryon asymmetry is downstream
of the framework's flavor-sector CP input; inflation and initial
conditions; the Hubble tension; the cosmological initial state). Each
entry cross-references where in the book the relevant content is
developed, with Chapter 19 functioning as a reference resource for
readers wanting to understand how the framework positions itself
relative to the recognized hard problems of fundamental physics.

\textbf{Cumulative case.} The framework's content across the empirical
chapters (5-17) and this forward-predictions chapter (18) forms a
cumulative case for the framework's structural commitments. Of the
twenty-two Standard Model observables, two are parameter-free structural
retrodictions and five are conditional structural ones, and the
remainder are layered, chained or fitted; the seven gravitational-sector
entries are conditional relations and estimates, two of them compared
with measured values (G6, G8) and one with upper bounds (G12); the seven
neutrino-sector entries include retrodictions and bound-only
comparisons. The framework's content in biology (Chapters 11-13 and
16-17) makes specific predictions that align with the empirical record
across non-Markovian dynamics, evolutionary signatures, and clinical
pharmacology. The forward content of this chapter extends the
framework's reach to phenomena standard physics has no specific
commitments on --- Born-rule equilibrium, the capacity-controlled origin
of partial revival, computational ceilings, and the arrow of time. The
consciousness conjecture of §18.10 is not part of this case.

The framework's evidential standard is parameter-free structural
prediction matching observation. The cumulative case across the book is
retrodictive --- exact structural values matching existing data across
physics, biology, and computation --- and the pre-registered standard
properly applies to the forward content of this chapter, which awaits
its data. The framework's physical content beyond conventional physics
is structural extension of the same framework that produced the
empirical predictions of Chapters 5-17, not speculative addition to an
empirical base.

The chapter is honest about what it does not address. The hard problem
of consciousness is not solved. The cosmological initial state is not
explained. Several other open problems remain in the framework's
residue. Chapter 19 develops these residues in detail, alongside the
resolved-problem inventory that makes the framework's cumulative
empirical reach explicit.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{chapter-19}{%
\section{Chapter 19}\label{chapter-19}}

\hypertarget{resolved-and-open-problems-in-fundamental-physics}{%
\section{Resolved and Open Problems in Fundamental
Physics}\label{resolved-and-open-problems-in-fundamental-physics}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{what-this-chapter-develops-16}{%
\subsection{19.1 What this chapter
develops}\label{what-this-chapter-develops-16}}

The framework's content across the empirical chapters (5 through 17) and
the forward-predictions chapter (18) constitutes a substantial body of
structural commitments and quantitative predictions. This chapter
inventories the framework's content against the \emph{standard list of
open problems} in fundamental physics --- the canonical questions every
framework in physics is expected to address.

The inventory has two parts. Section 19.2 develops the problems for
which the framework claims a resolution, dissolution, conditional
construction or partial treatment --- including quantum gravity, the
cosmological constant discrepancy, dark matter and dark energy, the
measurement problem, black-hole information, hierarchy, gauge structure,
generation structure, and the dark-sector budget --- together with
split-status entries: the origin of the Born rule, whose fixed-basis
representation is settled exactly while the coherent operational
extension is characterized by five named conditions (§19.2.12), and the
strong CP problem, where the construction supplies a mechanism that does
not reach the Standard Model. Each entry pairs the standard status of
the problem (how it is conventionally formulated) with the framework's
status (how the framework engages it), with a cross-reference to the
chapter and section where the relevant content is developed.

Section 19.3 develops six problems the framework does \emph{not}
resolve. The fermion mass hierarchy (flavor problem) has a defined
research program with initial computational results and three tractable
open targets, but the full quantitative content has not yet been
derived. The Hubble tension remains open. The specified near-null Type
II model has negligible running at current precision. Baryogenesis is
solution-specific: the framework provides standard leptogenesis
ingredients but the baryon asymmetry is downstream of the flavor-sector
CP phases the framework inputs rather than derives, so \(\eta_B\)
inherits that input status (§19.3.3). Inflation and initial conditions
are \emph{not addressed}: the framework reproduces the Standard Model
structure but does not address the very early universe's dynamics, with
three possibilities outlined but none developed. The initial state of
\((S, \varphi)\) is partially gauge (within the reconstruction theorem's
equivalence class) and partially the framework's irreducible mystery
(why this equivalence class rather than another). The sixth entry is the
chirality hypothesis H-χ' (§19.3.8) --- a framework-specific structural
hypothesis rather than one of the seventeen standard problems, so the
headline tally's ``five open'' counts the standard entries --- now in
sharpened form: the minimal SU(2) embedding is certified taste-blind ---
vector-like, exactly as color's is --- and the hypothesis asks whether a
non-minimal mechanism (a taste-asymmetric condensate structure) restores
