\(6 Y_Q - 3(Y_u + Y_d) + 2 Y_L - Y_e = 6 Y_Q - 6 Y_Q - 6 Y_Q - Y_e = -6 Y_Q - Y_e = 0\),
so \(Y_e = -6 Y_Q\).

From the electroweak completion of \(L\): the doublet \(L\) contains
\(\nu_L\) (electrically neutral) and \(e_L\) (charge \(-1\)). The charge
formula \(Q_{\text{em}} = T_3 + Y\) gives
\(Q_{\text{em}}(\nu_L) = +1/2 + Y_L\), requiring \(Y_L = -1/2\) for
\(\nu_L\) to be neutral. Therefore \(Y_L = -1/2\) and \(Y_Q = 1/6\).

This gives \(Y_u + Y_d = 1/3\) and \(Y_e = -1\).

To separate \(Y_u\) and \(Y_d\), the \(\mathrm{U}(1)^3\) anomaly (A5)
provides the remaining constraint. Substituting \(Y_Q = 1/6\),
\(Y_L = -1/2\), \(Y_e = -1\):
\[6 (1/6)^3 - 3 Y_u^3 - 3 Y_d^3 + 2 (-1/2)^3 - (-1)^3 = 0\]
\[6 \cdot 1/216 - 3 Y_u^3 - 3 Y_d^3 - 2/8 + 1 = 0\]
\[1/36 - 3(Y_u^3 + Y_d^3) - 1/4 + 1 = 0\]
\[3(Y_u^3 + Y_d^3) = 1/36 + 3/4 = 1/36 + 27/36 = 28/36 = 7/9\]
\[Y_u^3 + Y_d^3 = 7/27\]

Combined with \(Y_u + Y_d = 1/3\): using
\(Y_u^3 + Y_d^3 = (Y_u + Y_d)^3 - 3 Y_u Y_d (Y_u + Y_d)\), we get
\(7/27 = 1/27 - Y_u Y_d\), so \(Y_u Y_d = 1/27 - 7/27 = -6/27 = -2/9\).

The roots of \(x^2 - (1/3) x - 2/9 = 0\) are
\(x = (1/3 \pm \sqrt{1/9 + 8/9})/2 = (1/3 \pm 1)/2\). The two roots are
\(2/3\) and \(-1/3\). The anomaly conditions are symmetric under
\(Y_u \leftrightarrow Y_d\), so the system does not itself order the
pair; the assignment \(Y_u = 2/3\), \(Y_d = -1/3\) is fixed by the
electric-charge identification \(Q_{\text{em}} = T_3 + Y\) for the
up-type quark.

\textbf{Conclusion.} The complete hypercharge assignment is
\[Y_Q = 1/6, \quad Y_u = 2/3, \quad Y_d = -1/3, \quad Y_L = -1/2, \quad Y_e = -1\]
determined by the six anomaly conditions with no free parameters beyond
the overall normalization (fixed above by the neutrality of \(\nu_L\))
and the \(Y_u \leftrightarrow Y_d\) root labeling (fixed by the
electric-charge identification). \(\square\)

\textbf{Corollary.} On the nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch, \(|q_p| = |q_e|\) is
a \emph{theorem}, not a coincidence.

Proton charge: \(q_p = 2 q_u + q_d = 2(2/3) + (-1/3) = 4/3 - 1/3 = 1\).
Electron charge: \(q_e = Y_e + T_3 = -1 + 0 = -1\) (since \(e_R\) is a
singlet, \(T_3 = 0\)). So \(|q_p| = |q_e| = 1\), with the equality
forced by anomaly cancellation. This is one of the framework's
distinctive structural predictions: the proton-electron charge equality,
which is a free parameter in the Standard Model, is a theorem of the
framework on that branch.

\hypertarget{b.6-gauge-theoretic-derivations}{%
\subsection{B.6 Gauge-theoretic
derivations}\label{b.6-gauge-theoretic-derivations}}

\emph{Main-text reference: Chapter 5 §5.3-5.5.}

Two key gauge-theoretic results from Chapter 5 are presented here in
full: the conditional link-count proposition giving \(K = 2dm\) internal
components per site, and the cubic-rotation-group decomposition fixing
the block multiplicities at \((3, 2, 1)\).

\textbf{The coupling-degree minimization.} The framework's substratum is
a deterministic bijection on a \(d = 3\) spatial cubic lattice. The
site-internal structure is described by \(K\) scalar components per
site. The minimal \(K\) supporting a chiral gauge structure is the
structural question. Coupling-degree minimization does not answer it:
the argument below is stated and then shown not to close, and the
surviving content is the conditional link-count proposition together
with the exact representation theorem that follows it.

\textbf{Why coupling-degree minimization does not fix \(K\).} The
natural argument runs: the discrete Laplacian on a \(d\)-dimensional
cubic lattice couples \(2d\) nearest neighbours, so the internal space
needs one component per direction and \(K \geq 2d\). The step fails.
Diagonalizing the internal matrix decouples its eigenvectors, but it
does not assign an eigenvector to a single signed spatial neighbour: in
the displayed wave operator every internal component receives the WHOLE
neighbour sum, so nothing forces a component-per-direction
correspondence. A smaller \(K\) is not excluded by this argument, and
the \(\delta(2d)=1\) substitution that would supply the correspondence
is an operator replacement rather than a consequence of the dynamics.

\textbf{Proposition B.6.1 (\(K = 2dm\), conditional on H-link).}
\emph{Let
\(V_{\rm link}=\operatorname{span}\{e_{+1},e_{-1},\ldots,e_{+d},e_{-d}\}\)
be the space spanned by the \(2d\) signed lattice links. If the physical
internal space satisfies}
\(V_{\rm physical}\cong V_{\rm link}^{\oplus m}\) \emph{(hypothesis
H-link), then} \(K=2dm\), \emph{and the single-copy case \(m=1\) gives
\(K=2d\), hence \(K=6\) at \(d=3\).}

\emph{Proof.} Immediate from \(\dim V_{\rm link}=2d\). \(\square\)

The content of the proposition is entirely in its hypothesis. H-link
identifies the geometric link space with the physical carrier, and
\(m=1\) asserts a single copy; neither is derived here, and \(K=6\) is a
consequence of those premises rather than a prediction of the wave
operator. What is unconditional is the representation theorem that
follows, which is a statement about the six geometric links themselves
and holds whether or not they are the carrier.

\textbf{The cubic rotation group decomposition.} The proper cubic
rotation group \(O\) acts on the six signed geometric links. Its
decomposition determines the block dimensions of an equivariant
condensate on the single-copy physical carrier (SM Theorem 5).

\textbf{Theorem B.6.2 (Cubic decomposition).} \emph{The six signed cubic
links carry a representation of the proper cubic rotation group \(O\)
that decomposes uniquely as}
\[\mathbf{6} = \mathbf{3} \oplus \mathbf{2} \oplus \mathbf{1}\]
\emph{where \(\mathbf{3}\) is the standard triplet (vector
representation \(T_1\)), \(\mathbf{2}\) is the doublet (representation
\(E\)), and \(\mathbf{1}\) is the singlet (\(A_1\)).}

\emph{Proof.} The cubic rotation group \(O\) has irreducible
representations \(A_1\) (singlet, 1D), \(A_2\) (1D), \(E\) (2D), \(T_1\)
(3D), \(T_2\) (3D). The cubic-character-table decomposition of the
six-dimensional space of internal components requires the natural
geometric structure of the components.

The internal components transform under \(O\) according to their
geometric meaning. In the framework's content, the six components are
organized as: three components transforming as the vector representation
\(T_1\) (one component per spatial axis, \(T_1\) = \(\mathbf{3}\)), two
components transforming as the doublet representation \(E\) (the
``two-fold direction'' structures characteristic of the cubic group,
\(E\) = \(\mathbf{2}\)), and one component transforming as the singlet
\(A_1\) (\(\mathbf{1}\)).

The decomposition \(\mathbf{6}=T_1\oplus E\oplus A_1\) gives exact
geometric block dimensions \((3,2,1)\). The conditional gauge-branch
identifications are - \(\mathbf{3} \rightarrow \mathrm{SU}(3)\) color
(three colors) - \(\mathbf{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{SU}(2)\) weak isospin
(two doublet states) - \(\mathbf{1} \rightarrow \mathrm{U}(1)\)
hypercharge (one singlet)

The representation theorem determines these geometric blocks. The
physical identifications use the carrier, condensate and charged action
stated below. \(\square\)

\textbf{The link to gauge invariance.} The pointwise \(O\)-commutant of
the six-link representation is \(U(1)^3\). Under single-copy H-link and
H-cust, the unitary commutant of the equivariant condensate with
distinct block values is \(U(3)\times U(2)\times U(1)\). Background
independence --- covariance of the dynamics under site-dependent choices
of basis within each eigenspace, the link coupling transforming with
them --- promotes this global commutant to local gauge invariance.
Chapter 5 §5.5 gives the local gauge algebra with A6 and the specified
charged action. The action of the product cover on the specified matter
and Higgs representations has kernel \(\mathbb Z_6\). Physical bundle
and line data remain separate (SM Propositions 14a and 15a).

\textbf{Combined structural result.} Combining B.6.1 and B.6.2 gives the
framework's account of the Standard Model gauge group, conditional on
H-link at the B.6.1 step, unconditional at the representation-theoretic
step (ii) of B.6.2, and conditional on H-cust at the stabilizer step
(iii) (SM Theorem 5):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{(\roman{enumi})}
\item
  The H-link link count with \(m = 1\) on the \(d = 3\) cubic lattice
  fixes \(K = 6\) internal components per site.
\item
  The cubic rotation group's representation theory decomposes the
  six-dimensional internal space as
  \(\mathbf{6} = \mathbf{3} \oplus \mathbf{2} \oplus \mathbf{1}\),
  fixing the block multiplicities at \((3, 2, 1)\).
\item
  With H-cust and distinct condensate block values, the unitary
  stabilizer is \(\mathrm{U}(3)\times\mathrm{U}(2)\times\mathrm{U}(1)\)
  (SM Theorem 5). The subsequent reduction uses the amplitude premise at
  the scope of the observer action and the specified charged
  representations.
\item
  A6 supplies covariance of the link data under the local action.
\item
  Given the chiral family and specified charged action, anomaly
  cancellation (Appendix B.5) gives the hypercharges on the
  nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch up to normalization and the quark-singlet
  interchange.
\item
  Three degenerate sectors follow from the three triplet (\(T_1\))
  staggered tastes related by cubic symmetry; their reading as physical
  fermion generations is under H-spin' (with H-χ' and light-spectrum
  selection likewise flagged).
\end{enumerate}

The physical gauge and matter outputs use the single-copy carrier, the
custodial kinetic premise and charged action, and the physical spin,
chirality and light-spectrum conditions. The supplied Higgs
representation fits the singlet taste.

\hypertarget{b.6b-bravais-lattice-uniqueness-lemma}{%
\subsection{B.6b Bravais-lattice uniqueness
lemma}\label{b.6b-bravais-lattice-uniqueness-lemma}}

\emph{Main-text reference: Chapter 5 §5.5.}

The nearest-neighbor Bravais comparison isolates the simple-cubic link
representation for the stated condensate construction. The physical
selection uses the assumptions of Chapter 5 §5.5.

\textbf{Lemma B.6b.1 (Nearest-neighbor Bravais comparison).} \emph{Among
the fourteen three-dimensional Bravais lattices, simple cubic (\(cP\))
alone has the nearest-neighbor link decomposition
\(A_1\oplus E\oplus T_1\) with block dimensions \((1,2,3)\) in the
stated generic condensate construction.}

\textbf{Proof.}

\emph{Step 1 (3D irreps required).} The stated generic condensate
construction (Chapter 5 §5.5) requires the lattice point group to admit
a three-dimensional irreducible representation for a dimension-three
condensate block. Among the 32 three-dimensional crystallographic point
groups, the dimensions of irreducible representations are bounded as
follows: triclinic (\(C_1, C_i\)) and monoclinic (\(C_2, C_s, C_{2h}\))
groups have all irreps one-dimensional; orthorhombic groups
(\(C_{2v}, D_2, D_{2h}\)) have all irreps one-dimensional; tetragonal,
trigonal, and hexagonal groups have maximum irrep dimension 2; only the
five cubic-system point groups (chiral tetrahedral \(T\) of order 12;
full tetrahedral \(T_d\) and \(T_h\) of order 24; chiral octahedral
\(O\) of order 24; full octahedral \(O_h\) of order 48) admit
three-dimensional irreps. This rules out 27 of 32 point groups and 11 of
14 Bravais lattices: triclinic (\(aP\)), monoclinic (\(mP, mC\)),
orthorhombic (\(oP, oC, oI, oF\)), tetragonal (\(tP, tI\)),
trigonal/rhombohedral (\(hR\)), and hexagonal (\(hP\)) lattices all have
holohedries with maximum irrep dimension at most 2. The
3-dimensional-irrep requirement isolates the cubic system but is not the
tightest constraint, and it is not the binding one: the
\(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) factor requires a \emph{genuine} 2-dimensional
irreducible representation, which the chiral and pyritohedral
tetrahedral groups \(T\) and \(T_h\) --- whose apparent doublet is a
complex-conjugate pair of 1-dimensional irreps with commutant
\(\mathrm{U}(1)^2\) rather than \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) --- do not possess.
Equivalently, the full multiplicity ladder \((3,2,1)\) is the
irreducible-degree set \(\{1,2,3\}\), realized among the finite rotation
groups in \(\mathrm{SO}(3)\) only by \(S_4\cong O\): cyclic and dihedral
groups lack the 3; \(A_4\) lacks a genuine 2; the icosahedral group
\(A_5\) has 3-dimensional irreps but no 2-dimensional one (and carries
unwanted 4- and 5-dimensional irreps). The octahedral group \(O\) is the
unique finite rotation group carrying both a genuine 2- and a
3-dimensional irrep, and the cubic lattice's holohedry \(O_h \supset O\)
supplies both. The binding constraint is therefore the
\(\mathrm{SU}(2)\), not the \(\mathrm{SU}(3)\).

\emph{Step 2 (cubic lattices discriminated by NN decomposition).} The
three cubic Bravais lattices --- simple cubic (\(cP\), six nearest
neighbors), body-centered cubic (\(cI\), eight nearest neighbors),
face-centered cubic (\(cF\), twelve nearest neighbors) --- all have full
octahedral point-group symmetry \(O_h\) and therefore admit
three-dimensional irreps. They are discriminated by the
\emph{decomposition of their nearest-neighbor representations} under the
octahedral group \(O\) (with parity-grading distinctions absorbed into
the choice of \(O\) versus \(O_h\)).

Character-table decomposition of nearest-neighbor permutation
representations gives:
\[\text{cP (6 NN)}: \chi = (6, 0, 2, 2, 0) \Rightarrow A_1 \oplus E \oplus T_1,\]
with block dimensions \((1,2,3)\) and generic unitary condensate
stabilizer \(U(1)\times U(2)\times U(3)\).
\[\text{cI (8 NN)}: \chi = (8, 2, 0, 0, 0) \Rightarrow A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus T_1 \oplus T_2,\]
with block dimensions \((1,1,3,3)\) and generic stabilizer
\(U(1)^2\times U(3)^2\).
\[\text{cF (12 NN)}: \chi = (12, 0, 0, 0, 2) \Rightarrow A_1 \oplus E \oplus T_1 \oplus 2T_2,\]
with a doubled \(T_2\) multiplicity space. The pointwise \(O\)-commutant
acts as \(U(2)\) on this multiplicity space. For a generic equivariant
Hermitian condensate it splits into two eigenspaces of dimension three,
giving stabilizer \(U(1)\times U(2)\times U(3)^3\) before charged-action
reduction.

Among the three cubic nearest-neighbor representations, only \(cP\)
gives the \((1,2,3)\) block pattern of the stated stabilizer
construction.

\emph{Step 3 (the link count excludes BCC alternatives, given H-link).}
A potential ambiguity: BCC's six \emph{next-nearest neighbors} (along
the axial directions \(\pm a\hat{e}_i\)) produce a character identical
to SC's nearest-neighbor character, and would therefore decompose as
\(A_1 \oplus E \oplus T_1\) with the same SM multiplicities. The
framework's nearest-neighbor restriction rules out this alternative ---
BCC's axial directions are next-nearest rather than nearest, and the
nearest-neighbor restriction excludes them.

\emph{Step 4 (Bravais commitment excludes alternatives).} The
framework's substratum commitment to a Bravais lattice with single-atom
basis (Chapter 5 §§5.2-5.3) excludes multi-atom-basis structures (such
as the diamond structure, which would have additional point-group
structure) and quasi-crystalline alternatives. These structures are not
within the lattice class the framework's substratum derivation produces.

The four steps together establish the uniqueness claim. \(\blacksquare\)

\textbf{Computational verification.} The character-table decomposition
in Step 2 admits direct verification: enumerating the action of the
octahedral group \(O\)'s 24 elements on the six nearest-neighbor sites
of simple cubic produces the character \(\chi = (6, 0, 2, 2, 0)\) on the
five conjugacy classes \((E, 8C_3, 3C_2, 6C_4, 6C_2')\). Applying the
orthogonality relation
\(n_\sigma = (1/|G|) \sum_C |C| \chi_\sigma(C)^* \chi(C)\) for the irrep
characters \(\chi_\sigma\) of \(A_1, A_2, E, T_1, T_2\) gives
multiplicities \((1, 0, 1, 1, 0)\), confirming the decomposition
\(A_1 \oplus E \oplus T_1\). Parallel computation for the BCC eight-NN
character \((8, 2, 0, 0, 0)\) gives multiplicities \((1, 1, 0, 1, 1)\),
confirming \(A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus T_1 \oplus T_2\). Parallel
computation for the FCC twelve-NN character \((12, 0, 0, 0, 2)\) gives
multiplicities \((1, 0, 1, 1, 2)\), confirming
\(A_1 \oplus E \oplus T_1 \oplus 2T_2\). The lemma's content is
therefore checkable by direct finite computation; the proof above
formalizes what the computation confirms.

\textbf{Consequences.} The lemma gives the exact nearest-neighbor
representation comparison. Its use to select a physical gauge carrier
requires single-copy H-link, H-cust and the specified charged action.

\hypertarget{b.6c-t_1-generation-assignment-uniqueness-lemma}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{B.6c \(T_1\) generation-assignment
uniqueness
lemma}{B.6c T\_1 generation-assignment uniqueness lemma}}\label{b.6c-t_1-generation-assignment-uniqueness-lemma}}

\emph{Main-text reference: Chapter 6 §6.2.}

The framework's identification of three fermion generations with the
\(T_1\) triplet staggered taste (Chapter 6 §6.2), with the \(A_1\)
singlet taste hosting the composite Higgs, is a load-bearing structural
commitment. This appendix establishes that the assignment is
\emph{uniquely forced} by the framework's other structural commitments
--- it is not one assignment among several alternatives, but the only
one consistent with the substratum's existing constraints.

\textbf{Lemma B.6c.1 (\(T_1\) generation-assignment uniqueness).}
\emph{Given the framework's commitments to (a) simple cubic Bravais
lattice (Lemma B.6b.1), (b) \(K = 2dm = 6\) internal components from the
link count under H-link with \(m=1\) (Chapter 5 §5.4), (c) the
staggered-Dirac reconstruction of spin from Brillouin-zone corner
Gamma-matrix structure (Chapter 6 §6.2), (d) Standard Model anomaly
cancellation (§B.5), and (e) the physical-spin reading of the taste
labels (H-spin', SM §4.7), the assignment of the three fermion
generations to the \(T_1\) triplet (with the \(A_1\) singlet hosting the
composite Higgs) is the unique assignment consistent with these
commitments.}

\textbf{Proof.}

\emph{Step 1 (Available irreps in the 4-taste decomposition).} The
Brillouin-zone corners on a \(d = 3\) simple cubic lattice number
\(2^d = 8\) and pair under the corner-conjugation involution
\(\boldsymbol{\eta} \leftrightarrow \mathbf{1} - \boldsymbol{\eta}\)
into 4 taste pairs (Chapter 6 §6.2). Two corners ---
\(\Gamma = (0, 0, 0)\) and \(R = (\pi, \pi, \pi)\) --- are invariant
under the octahedral rotation group \(O\) and pair into one taste
transforming as \(A_1\) (the trivial 1D irrep). The remaining six
corners pair into three axis-aligned pairs \((X_j, M_j)\) along the
three coordinate directions, transforming under \(O\) as the components
of the \(T_1\) (vector, 3D) irrep through the signed spin-taste matrices
\(\gamma^j\) (the unsigned pair labels alone carry only
\(A_1 \oplus E\)). The 4-taste decomposition under \(O\) is therefore
exactly \(4 = A_1 \oplus T_1\), with no \(A_2\), \(E\), or \(T_2\)
components present. This restricts the available irreps for
matter-content assignments to \(A_1\) and \(T_1\) only.

\emph{Step 2 (Spin-statistics constraint).} The staggered-Dirac
reconstruction (Chapter 6 §6.2) assigns Gamma-matrix structure to each
Brillouin-zone corner. The \(\Gamma\) and \(R\) corners pair with
\(\Gamma\)-matrices \(\Gamma(\mathbf{0}) = I_4\) (scalar) and
\(\Gamma(R) = \gamma^1 \gamma^2 \gamma^3\) (pseudoscalar), both
\(\mathrm{SO}(3)\)-invariant, yielding total angular momentum \(J = 0\)
for the \(A_1\) singlet taste. The \(j\)-th axis-aligned pair
\((X_j, M_j)\) has Gamma-matrices \(\gamma^j\) (vector) and
\(-i\Sigma_j\) (spin generator), yielding \(J = 1/2\) for each component
of the \(T_1\) triplet. The label content (SM Theorem 9) thus assigns
\(J = 0\) labels to \(A_1\) and \(J = 1/2\) labels to \(T_1\); their
physical reading is H-spin' (hypothesis (e)), under which
spin-statistics forces: bosonic (\(J\)-integer) fields must reside in
the \(A_1\) singlet; fermionic (\(J\)-half-integer) fields must reside
in the \(T_1\) triplet. Three fermion generations \emph{cannot} be
hosted by \(A_1\) (which carries \(J = 0\) and would produce bosons);
they must reside in \(T_1\).

\emph{Step 3 (Generation count fixed by \(T_1\) dimension).} The \(T_1\)
irrep has dimension 3 in the standard cubic-group character theory
(Tinkham, \emph{Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics}, Chapter 4). The
three components transform among themselves under cubic rotations as the
three coordinate axes; the cubic group \(O\) acts on them by signed
permutation. Three generations, related by cubic symmetry, therefore
emerge from a single structural commitment (\(T_1\)-housing of
fermions), not from a free parameter. The generation count is not chosen
from a continuum; it is forced by \(\dim(T_1) = 3\).

\emph{Step 4 (Anomaly cancellation requires uniform gauge content).}
Standard Model anomaly cancellation (§B.5) operates
generation-by-generation: each fermion generation must independently
satisfy the anomaly-cancellation equations on \(\mathrm{SU}(3)^3\),
\(\mathrm{SU}(2)^2 \mathrm{U}(1)\), \(\mathrm{U}(1)^3\),
mixed-gauge-gravitational, and global \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-Witten
anomalies. The anomaly-free hypercharge assignment (Appendix B.5)
requires that all three generations carry \emph{identical} gauge
representations, differing only in their Yukawa couplings (i.e., in
their masses). Cubic-group permutation of the three \(T_1\) components
automatically produces three identical copies --- the three components
carry identical gauge content because they are related by symmetry.
Alternative assignments distributing fermions across different irreps
with different gauge content would violate this uniformity requirement.

\emph{Step 5 (Alternatives excluded).} Four alternatives are excluded by
the steps above:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Three generations in \(3 A_1\) (three singlet copies):} requires
  three separate \(A_1\) tastes, which the 4-taste decomposition does
  not provide (Step 1 gives one \(A_1\), not three). Also violates
  spin-statistics (Step 2: \(A_1\) produces \(J = 0\) bosons).
\item
  \emph{Three generations in \(A_1 \oplus E\) (1 + 2 = 3 components):}
  requires \(E\) in the decomposition, which is absent (Step 1: only
  \(A_1 \oplus T_1\)). Also, \(A_1 \oplus E\) is reducible --- cubic
  symmetry does not permute its components, so the three generations
  would not be related by symmetry, violating uniformity.
\item
  \emph{Three generations in \(T_2\):} \(T_2\) is absent from the
  4-taste decomposition (Step 1). Alternative Bravais lattices (BCC,
  FCC) provide \(T_2\) but fail Bravais-uniqueness (Lemma B.6b.1).
\item
  \emph{Generations distributed across multiple irreps with different
  gauge content:} violates uniformity required by anomaly cancellation
  (Step 4).
\end{itemize}

Therefore the unique assignment consistent with the framework's
structural commitments is: \(A_1\) hosts the composite Higgs (bosonic,
\(J = 0\)); \(T_1\) hosts the three fermion generations (\(J = 1/2\),
related by cubic permutation, with identical gauge content).
\(\blacksquare\)

\textbf{Computational verification.} The lemma's content reduces to
finite enumeration in two steps that can be verified directly. First,
the 4-taste decomposition: enumerate the action of \(O\)'s 24 elements
on the 8 Brillouin-zone corners; verify that they form 4 orbits under
corner-conjugation; verify that the orbits decompose as
\(A_1 \oplus T_1\) under \(O\). Second, the spin-statistics step:
enumerate the standard staggered-Dirac Gamma-matrix structure at each
corner; verify that \(\Gamma\) and \(R\) produce \(J = 0\) and the axial
pairs produce \(J = 1/2\). Both verifications are standard exercises in
lattice-fermion representation theory (cf.~Kogut and Susskind 1975;
Sharpe and Patel 1994; Lee and Sharpe 1999).

\textbf{Consequences.} Lemma B.6c.1 fixes the framework's most
consequential matter-content commitment given hypotheses (a)--(e). The
three-generation pattern of the Standard Model, the bosonic character of
the Higgs, the J = 0 versus J = 1/2 separation between Higgs and fermion
sectors, and the uniformity of gauge content across generations are all
forced by the existing substrate commitments (simple cubic lattice,
\(K = 2d\) link count under H-link, staggered-Dirac reconstruction,
anomaly cancellation) together with H-spin'. The framework's matter
content is therefore not freely chosen to match observation --- it is
the unique matter content consistent with the prior structural
commitments. The lemma's specialist-review surface is again the
cubic-group character theory plus the standard staggered-Dirac
reconstruction, both verifiable in independent references.

In combination with Lemma B.6b.1 (Bravais-lattice uniqueness), Lemma
B.6c.1 establishes that the framework's full gauge-and-matter structure
--- simple cubic lattice → cubic group → \(A_1 \oplus T_1\) taste
decomposition → composite Higgs in \(A_1\) + three fermion generations
in \(T_1\) --- is the unique structure consistent with the substratum's
commitments and the Standard Model gauge group.

\hypertarget{b.7-the-lemma-chain-for-emergent-quantum-mechanics}{%
\subsection{B.7 The lemma chain for emergent quantum
mechanics}\label{b.7-the-lemma-chain-for-emergent-quantum-mechanics}}

\emph{Main-text reference: Chapter 1 §§1.5-1.9.}

The framework's characterization theorem --- accessible non-Markovianity
⟺ C1/C3/C4 realization per accessible horizon, the quantum
representation internal and universal
(\(S \iff D \iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\), {[}Main §3.4{]}) --- relies on a
chain of intermediate lemmas. This appendix collects these lemmas with
compact proofs, providing a self-contained reference for the framework's
logical structure.

\textbf{Lemma B.7.1 (Partition relativity).} \emph{The same physical
substratum admits different visible/hidden partitions, with each
partition producing its own emergent description.}

\emph{Proof.} The substratum \((S, \varphi)\) with
\(S = \mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H\) admits alternative
decompositions \(S = \mathcal{C}_{V'} \times \mathcal{C}_{H'}\) for any
reshaping of \(S\) into a product structure. Each such reshaping defines
a different visible/hidden partition with its own visible-sector
emergent dynamics. The emergent dynamics depends on the choice of
partition; the underlying substratum dynamics \(\varphi\) does not.
\(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma B.7.2 (Emergent stochasticity).} \emph{Any deterministic
bijection on a product configuration space produces emergent stochastic
dynamics on the visible sector after tracing over the hidden sector.}

\emph{Proof.} The bijection
\(\varphi: \mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H \to \mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H\)
produces transition probabilities
\(T_{ij} = (1/|\mathcal{C}_H|) \sum_{k} \delta_{x_j, \pi_V(\varphi(x_i, h_k))}\)
on the visible sector. These transition probabilities are stochastic
(non-deterministic) whenever the bijection produces multiple distinct
visible-sector outputs from a single visible-sector input across
different hidden-sector configurations. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma B.7.3 (P-indivisibility from a non-permutation one-step
matrix).} \emph{If the visible one-step matrix \(T = \Gamma(1)\) is not
a permutation and the configuration space is finite, the emergent
stochastic dynamics on the visible sector is P-indivisible at the
recurrence scale.}

\emph{Proof.} The hypothesis is the non-permutation witness on
\(T = \Gamma(1)\), together with finiteness of the configuration space.
It is NOT a consequence of C1: C1 asserts non-zero coupling, which does
not by itself force \(T\) off the permutation set ({[}Main §1.3{]}). C2
and C3 play no part here; they govern \emph{observability}, below. A
column-stochastic matrix that is not a permutation strictly contracts
total-variation distance for some pair of basis states:
\(\mathrm{TV}(Te_i, Te_j) = 1\) exactly when columns \(i\) and \(j\)
have disjoint support, so if \emph{no} basis pair contracted, all
columns would have pairwise-disjoint support and \(T\) would be a
permutation. Hence there is a pair with
\(D(1) := \mathrm{TV}(\Gamma(1)e_i, \Gamma(1)e_j) < 1\). Because
\(\varphi\) is a bijection of a finite set it has finite order
\(\omega\) (the least common multiple of its cycle lengths):
\(\varphi^{\omega} = \mathrm{id}\) \emph{exactly}, so
\(\Gamma(\omega) = \mathbb{1}\) and
\(D(\omega) = \mathrm{TV}(e_i, e_j) = 1\). The trace distance therefore
satisfies \(D(0) = 1\), \(D(1) < 1\), \(D(\omega) = 1\): it decreases
and then recovers. Since every stochastic propagator is a
total-variation contraction, a P-divisible process has monotonically
non-increasing \(D\) for every pair of inputs; the recovery
\(D(\omega) > D(1)\) violates this, so the process is P-indivisible.
\(\blacksquare\)

\emph{Role of C2, C3, and observability.} The recovery above is
guaranteed only at the recurrence time \(\omega\), which can be
astronomically large for a high-capacity hidden sector, so a
non-permutation rooted map and finiteness establish P-indivisibility at
the recurrence scale. On \emph{observable} timescales
\(k\tau_S \ll \tau_B\) the relevant property is conditional memory: C4
(history readback) is the load-bearing condition for it
(\texttt{review4\_probes.py}), with C2 (memory persistence) keeping the
record alive to readback and C3 (sufficient capacity) giving it room;
this is the content of Lemma B.7.4 and Chapter 1 §1.5. This division of
labor follows {[}Main{]}: the recurrence argument uses a non-permutation
rooted map and finiteness, and readback delivers conditional memory on
observable timescales, which does not by itself make the population law
P-indivisible on those windows. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma B.7.4 (Accessible conditional memory from readback).}
\emph{Suppose the visible process has a gap at order \(k\) in the
accessible window, as C4 asserts: two visible histories of length \(k\)
followed by a common present state, each of probability at least
\(p_0\), induce next-step laws at total-variation distance at least
\(\delta\). Then
\(I(X_{<k}; X_{k+1} \mid X_k) \geq p_0\delta^2/\ln 2 > 0\)} (Pinsker;
{[}Main §2.3{]}).

\emph{Status.} The pair-dependent history gap in Lemma B.7.4 certifies
accessible memory. C3 bounds the required capacity. In the coupling-step
model, the persistence form of C2 constrains the realized hidden
conditionals at readback. A slow bath is one realization, and
interpreting that bound as a lower bound on mixing time requires the
mixing hypothesis {[}Main §3.4{]}. The duration and magnitude of a
slow-bath signal depend on the model. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma B.7.5 (Phase locking).} \emph{Assume dimension at least
three, distinct gaps and non-vanishing overlaps for both Hamiltonians
being compared, and, for at least one of them, the triangle-genericity
condition: every relation \(\omega_1 + \omega_2 = \omega_3\) among the
gaps \(\omega_{kl} = E_k - E_l\) of three different pairs of levels is a
triangle identity \(\omega_{kl} + \omega_{lm} = \omega_{km}\). The
emergent effective Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_{\text{eff}}\) on the visible
sector is then determined by the continuous-time transition data
\(\{T_{ij}(t)\}\) up to the lemma's full gauge: an overall energy shift,
the diagonal-unitary rephasing freedom, and the antiunitary conjugation
\(\hat{H} \to -\hat{H}^*\) --- a genuine twofold ambiguity rather than a
convention ({[}Main §3.1{]}).}

\emph{Proof.} The transition data \(\{T_{ij}(t)\}\) determines the
Born-rule probabilities
\(|\langle j|e^{-i\hat{H}_{\text{eff}}t}|i\rangle|^2 = T_{ij}(t)\). The
squared-modulus structure leaves the phase undetermined; specifically,
the transformation \(|i\rangle \to e^{i\theta_i}|i\rangle\) leaves all
\(|U_{ij}|^2\) invariant. This is the basis-convention freedom --- the
choice of phase for each basis state --- which is physically trivial.
The triangle-genericity condition identifies the pair of levels carrying
each frequency, up to a relabelling and a global reflection of the
levels ({[}Main §3.1{]}); this step is not supplied by Fourier
extraction alone, since distinct gaps admit non-congruent spectra with
equal gap sets (scope note to Theorem B.7.5c below). The remaining
alternatives are this rephasing freedom, the energy shift and the
antiunitary conjugation \(\hat{H} \to -\hat{H}^*\) stated above.
\(\square\)

\emph{Scope.} The lemma is stated in its simplest form,
\(T_{ij}(t) = |U_{ij}(t)|^2\) --- the trivial-ancilla case of the
general construction. In the ancilla-marginal form, local generic
rigidity is checked at the certified block structures; general
completeness is open. The visible data constrain the \emph{dilated}
Hamiltonian and configuration projectors, with the energy shift and
diagonal-phase freedoms exactly invisible; the extension, its Fourier
structure, and the constraint analysis of the larger pair-phase gauge
are given in the companion paper ({[}Main §3.4{]}) --- where the
pair-phase gauge reduces to the diagonal one for generic families at
each fixed dimension --- together with the antiunitary conjugate
\(H \to -H^*\), retained there as an intrinsic ambiguity of transition
data.

\textbf{Bohr frequencies and the D-gauge classification.} The proof of
Lemma B.7.5 rests on Theorem B.7.5a and, without the triangle-genericity
condition, on the further results collected here, each stated with its
hypotheses ({[}GR §3.3{]}). Throughout, \(U(t) = e^{-iHt}\) with \(H\)
in frequency units and \(H = V\,\mathrm{diag}(E)\,V^\dagger\) on a
finite configuration space, so that \(V_{ia}\) is the overlap of
configuration \(i\) with eigenvector \(a\), and likewise
\(H' = W\,\mathrm{diag}(E')\,W^\dagger\); the antiunitary reflection
\(-\bar{H}\) is the \(-\hat{H}^*\) of Lemma B.7.5.

\textbf{Theorem B.7.5a (Bohr-frequency completeness).} \emph{Let
\(U(t) = e^{-iHt}\) with non-degenerate eigenvalues and non-vanishing
configuration-basis overlaps. Then the transition probabilities
determine the Bohr-frequency set \(\{E_a - E_b\}\): each return
probability expands as
\(|U_{ii}(t)|^2 = \sum_{a,b} |V_{ia}|^2 |V_{ib}|^2\, e^{-i(E_a - E_b)t}\),
in which every gap value carries a strictly positive coefficient; every
\(|U_{ij}(t)|^2\) is a combination of the same frequencies; and
consequently any \(U'\) of the same form with
\(|U'_{ij}(t)|^2 = |U_{ij}(t)|^2\) for all \(i, j, t\) has
\(\{E'_a - E'_b\} = \{E_a - E_b\}\).}

\emph{Proof.} Expanding
\(U_{ij}(t) = \sum_a V_{ia}\, e^{-iE_a t}\, V_{ja}^*\) gives
\(|U_{ij}(t)|^2 = \sum_{a,b} V_{ia} V_{ja}^* V_{ib}^* V_{jb}\, e^{-i(E_a - E_b)t}\);
at \(i = j\) the coefficients are \(|V_{ia}|^2 |V_{ib}|^2 > 0\), and
grouping terms by frequency value only adds positive quantities ---
degenerate gaps merge coefficients but cannot cancel them. Distinct
characters \(t \mapsto e^{-i\omega t}\) of \((\mathbb{R}, +)\) are
linearly independent (Dedekind), so equality of two probability families
forces equality of the per-frequency coefficients over the union of the
two gap sets, and positivity makes the supports --- the gap sets ---
coincide. \(\square\)

\textbf{The dimensional obstruction.} Theorem B.7.5a is what the gap
equation of §B.4 consumes, and it is less than a reconstruction of
\(H\). The unitary \(U(t)\) is dimensionless, and \(\hbar\) enters only
through \(\hat{H} = i\hbar\,\partial_t U\, U^\dagger\). The transition
probabilities are dimensionless functions of \(t\) and determine
temporal frequencies; converting a frequency to an energy requires the
action scale \(\hbar\) itself, so no amount of transition data fixes it.
The residual ambiguities in passing from frequencies to a Hamiltonian
carry no scale either: diagonal rephasing \(H \mapsto DHD^\dagger\)
moves no modulus, the energy origin \(H \mapsto H + E_0\) contributes
only the global phase \(e^{-iE_0 t}\), the antiunitary reflection
\(H \mapsto -\bar{H}\) satisfies
\(e^{-i(-\bar{H})t} = \overline{e^{-iHt}}\) entrywise and so preserves
every \(|U_{ij}(t)|^2\) exactly, and Theorem B.7.5c below excludes
further ambiguities conditional on its stated classification hypothesis.
The thermal self-consistency of §B.4, Step 4, is therefore the
mathematically obligatory entry point for the dimensionful input.

\textbf{Lemma B.7.5b (Real-to-integer transfer).} \emph{Let \(E, E'\) be
real spectra on \(n\) modes, each with distinct directed gaps ---
\(E_b - E_a = E_d - E_c\) with \(a \neq b\) and \(c \neq d\) only when
\((a, b) = (c, d)\) --- and with equal gap sets. Then \(E'\) is, after
relabeling its modes, a translate \(E + E_0\) of \(E\) or a translate
\(-E + E_0\) of its reflection; or else there are relabelings of the two
spectra and strictly increasing integer rulers \(F, F'\) on \(n\) marks,
each with distinct positive differences, with equal difference sets, and
neither a translate nor a reflection of the other, such that every
integer gap identity \(F'_d - F'_c = F_b - F_a\) with \(a \neq b\) holds
for the relabeled real spectra as well.}

The lemma assumes no classification hypothesis. It is proved in the
framework's Lean formalization (kernel:
\texttt{real\_to\_integer\_surrogate} in
\texttt{OIBridge/TurnpikeScopeTransfer.lean}), and it is the step
through which a classification of integer rulers, such as H-BG below,
applies to real spectra.

\textbf{Theorem B.7.5c (D-gauge completeness, two-branch form).}
\emph{Assume H-BG: every non-congruent pair of strictly ordered integer
rulers with distinct positive differences and equal difference sets has
six marks and, after relabeling, realizes either \(\mu\) or its global
reversal, where \(\mu\) sends each ascending mark pair of
\(\{0,1,4,10,12,17\}\) to the ascending mark pair of
\(\{0,1,8,11,13,17\}\) with the same difference. The orientation is
chosen once for the whole pair. Let \(H,H'\) act on the same finite
configuration space of dimension \(m\ge3\), with distinct nonzero energy
gaps and non-vanishing configuration-basis overlaps for both
Hamiltonians. If \(|U'_{ij}(t)|^2 = |U_{ij}(t)|^2\) for all \(i,j,t\),
then \(H' = DHD^\dagger + E_0\) or \(H' = -D\bar{H}D^\dagger + E_0\),
for a time-independent diagonal unitary \(D\) and a real \(E_0\).}

\emph{Conditional proof.} Equality of the probability families forces
equality of the per-frequency coefficients of
\(|U_{ij}(t)|^2 = \sum_{a,b} V_{ia} V_{ja}^* V_{ib}^* V_{jb}\, e^{-i(E_a-E_b)t}\).
Under the stated overlap and gap hypotheses, the spectra have equal
difference sets and the coefficient matching induces a bijection of
ordered mode pairs preserving directed gaps. A fixed correspondence can
be transferred from real to integer spectra while preserving its gap
identities, strict order, distinct differences and non-congruence (Lemma
B.7.5b): its realization constraints are homogeneous rational-linear
equalities, strict inequalities and inequations, and rational
approximation in the equality subspace followed by denominator clearing
preserves the finite list of strict conditions. H-BG then supplies a
congruent pair or one of the two globally oriented exceptional
correspondences. For congruent spectra, diagonal-line rigidity fixes the
moduli and the phase-coboundary relation fixes the phases, giving
\(W_{i,\tau a}=d_i\beta_a V_{ia}\) with \(d,\beta\) unimodular. The
column phases cancel in the reconstructed Hamiltonian. Reflection
congruence applies this argument to \((\bar V,-E)\) and gives the second
branch. For the positive exceptional correspondence \(\mu\), the
coefficient identities force flat moduli and constrain the phase data to
a graph of maximum clique three, excluding the six orthogonal rows
required by unitarity. For the reversed correspondence, reversing the
source mode pair conjugates its coefficient tensor; applying the same
obstruction to the conjugated source eigenbasis excludes that
orientation as well. Thus the two Hamiltonian branches follow
conditional on H-BG. \(\square\)

\emph{Scope.} The complete comparison of H-BG with the published integer
classification of Bekir and Golomb {[}A. Bekir and S. W. Golomb, IEEE
Trans. Inform. Theory 53 (2007) 2864--2867{]}, including all
normalizations and exceptional orientations, is open. The unsigned
formal premise \texttt{BGIntegerClassification} of the Lean
formalization is false: the strictly ordered rulers \((0,1,4,10,12,17)\)
and \((0,4,6,9,16,17)\) have distinct positive differences and equal
difference sets, are neither translates nor reflections of one another,
and satisfy the reversed exceptional correspondence while admitting no
relabelings with the required positive orientation. The kernel
implication \texttt{twoBranch\_of\_BGClassification} therefore does not
establish reconstruction from the physical hypotheses. The example
contradicts that formal premise, not the published classification.
Bohr-frequency completeness, the real-to-integer transfer, congruent
reconstruction and the positive six-mode obstruction are kernel-proved
independently of it. The exclusion of the reversed orientation and the
assembly of the two branches from H-BG are kernel-proved as well, so
H-BG is the theorem's only unproved premise; under the
triangle-genericity condition of Lemma B.7.5 the two branches follow
without H-BG ({[}Main §3.1{]}). The listed ambiguities are exactly
invisible: \(H+E_0\) contributes only a global phase, while \(-\bar H\)
conjugates the propagator entrywise. The gap condition is used where
coefficient matching induces a bijection of ordered mode pairs: with
degenerate gaps one frequency's coefficient is a sum over several mode
pairs. The \(C_4\) ring of {[}SM{]} Proposition 20 has distinct
eigenvalues, uniform overlaps and degenerate gaps; its conjugate
\(\bar H\) reproduces every \(|U_{ij}(t)|^2\) and conjugates the loop
product \(H_{01}H_{12}H_{23}H_{30}\), which no diagonal conjugation
changes. The ring therefore does not exhibit a failure, without the gap
condition, of the two-branch form conditional on H-BG: \(\bar H\) lies
in the reflection branch, \(\bar H = -D_s\bar H D_s^\dagger\) with
\(D_s = \mathrm{diag}(1,-1,1,-1)\). The raw frequency set alone cannot
distinguish the non-congruent homometric rulers; reconstruction uses
coefficient-labelled frequency data.

\textbf{Corollary B.7.5d (Operational antiunitary invariance).}
\emph{Transposing the preparation, every operation, and the effect
simultaneously --- \(\rho \mapsto \rho^T\),
\(\mathcal{G} \mapsto T \circ \mathcal{G} \circ T\), \(E \mapsto E^T\)
--- preserves every finite circuit probability, for arbitrary operations
and arbitrary finite sequences, hence for every fixed outcome branch of
any adaptive instrument strategy; the transformation carries Kraus
operations to Kraus operations with conjugated operators, preserves the
trace normalization, and on unitary evolution is exactly the branch map
\(H \mapsto -\bar{H}\).}

Enlarging the data from transition probabilities to arbitrary
preparations, instruments, adaptive finite circuits, and effects
therefore cannot remove the second branch: at the purely operational
level the two branches are not two empirically distinguishable theories
but two antiunitarily related reconstructions of the same complete
circuit statistics, and they become physically distinct only once an
oriented structure is fixed ({[}GR §3.3{]}). (kernel:
\texttt{circuit\_invariance}, \texttt{string\_invariance},
\texttt{transposeMap\_kraus}, \texttt{kraus\_normalization},
\texttt{unitary\_channel\_transpose} in
\texttt{OIBridge/AntiunitaryInvariance.lean})

\textbf{Theorem B.7.6 (Characterization theorem).} \emph{For a finite
visible alphabet, the accessible history-memory statement of {[}Main
§3.4{]} uses C1, C3 and a C4 witness at some accessible order \(k\) and
on each specified finite horizon \(K\ge k+1\). The universal finite-law
representation \(S\iff D\iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\) is exact for the supplied
law on that alphabet and horizon. The compressed form uses (T). C2
persistence and its slow-bath implication, the recurrence-scale
divisibility result and phase locking have the separate hypotheses
stated in {[}Main{]}.}
\[\begin{aligned} &\text{Accessible non-Markovianity on } V \\ \iff{}& \exists k\ \forall K \geq k+1:\ \text{embedded observation of } (S, \varphi) \text{ on horizon } K \\ &\text{with C1, C3, C4, readback at } k \end{aligned}\]

\emph{Proof structure.} For a supplied stochastic law on a finite
alphabet and fixed finite horizon, {[}Main §3.4{]} constructs a finite
reversible realization. Its permutation unitary gives the exact
fixed-basis representation. The history-memory equivalence uses C1, C3
and the accessible C4 witness. It has a separate proof from the
recurrence-cycle P-indivisibility of Lemma B.7.3 and the phase-locking
result.

For necessity, the accessible history gap requires C1, C3 and C4 in a
faithful realization. C2 record persistence is treated separately. A
mixing-time bound in the slow-bath formulation uses the quantitative
mixing hypothesis {[}Main §3.4{]}.

The biconditional is the framework's main characterization result.
\(\square\) \textbf{Coherent extension.} The equivalence holds between
the operational, dilated, and fixed-basis descriptions and is exact at
that level; it does not by itself determine a coherent extension of the
fixed-basis theory, and at least one conservative coherent extension
preserves the fixed-basis theory exactly as a quotient while adding
coherent structure not fixed by the equivalence.

\textbf{Scope of the lemma chain.} C1, C3 and C4 govern the accessible
history-memory statement. The exact finite-law theorem applies on the
specified alphabet and horizon whether the law has accessible memory or
is Markov. The coherent extension, C2 persistence and conditional phase
locking each use their own inputs.

\textbf{The framework's full mathematical content.} Combining the
derivations of this appendix:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  B.2 establishes the substratum-to-quantum bridge via Stinespring
  dilation.
\item
  B.3 establishes the period and the Jordan-Chevalley decomposition of
  the ring evolution: spectral invariants are independent of the
  nilpotent part \(N\), and hidden-sector marginalization does not
  remove \(N\) from the visible laws.
\item
  B.4 establishes the gap equation relating \(\hbar\) to the
  discreteness scale through horizon thermodynamics, producing the
  framework's content on gravitational physics.
\item
  B.5 establishes the unique anomaly-free hypercharge assignment on the
  nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch, fixing the framework's content on Standard
  Model matter.
\item
  B.6 establishes the gauge-theoretic derivation from cubic symmetry,
  fixing the framework's content on the SM gauge group structure.
\item
  B.7 establishes the lemma chain for the characterization theorem,
  fixing the framework's foundational claim.
\end{itemize}

The combined derivations constitute the framework's full mathematical
content as a derivation chain from the substratum-level structural
commitments to the Standard Model, the gravitational sector, and the
empirical predictions across the framework's domains. The appendix is
therefore a complete technical reference for readers requiring the
framework's mathematical content at full detail.

\hypertarget{common-objections-and-framework-responses}{%
\section{Common Objections and Framework
Responses}\label{common-objections-and-framework-responses}}

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{c.1-what-this-appendix-develops}{%
\subsection{C.1 What this appendix
develops}\label{c.1-what-this-appendix-develops}}

The framework's content is unusual. It combines a substantial empirical
record (twenty-two classified Standard Model retrodictions --- two
parameter-free structural and five conditional structural --- seven
gravitational-sector entries, seven neutrino-sector entries, and the
prior observation of rescue after Mecp2 reactivation in a mouse model of
Rett syndrome) with structural commitments that overlap with several
distinct programs in foundations of physics. Readers approaching the
framework from different starting points raise different objections; the
framework's content engages each cluster of objections from a single
structural foundation.

This appendix systematically engages the most frequent objections to the
framework's content. The appendix is \emph{not} a defensive document; it
is a reference resource for readers who want to understand how the
framework engages established results in foundations of physics,
established no-go theorems, established interpretive positions, and
established methodological concerns. Each objection is engaged at the
level appropriate to its substance --- technical objections receive
technical responses, methodological objections receive methodological
responses, and meta-objections (about credentials, scope, ambition) are
addressed where they are scientifically substantive.

Twelve clusters of objections occupy the appendix.

Section C.2 engages objections about Bell's theorem and the broader
hidden-variable program: the framework's relationship to local
hidden-variable theories, the Bell branch the framework adopts
(measurement independence retained, ontic parameter independence given
up, operational no-signaling preserved; hidden memory and indivisibility
are not the mechanism), and why the framework is not a
superdeterministic or Bohmian theory. Section C.3 engages the no-go
theorems specifically --- PBR, Frauchiger-Renner, Colbeck-Renner,
Bong-Wiseman --- and identifies which assumptions each makes that the
framework's content satisfies or violates.

Sections C.4-C.6 engage the foundational concerns: the role of the
stochastic-quantum bridge (Barandes route), the necessity direction of
the characterization theorem (whether QM requires embedded observation),
and finiteness (whether the framework's posit A1 is too strong).

Section C.7 engages computational implementability concerns ---
specifically Wolpert's theorem on physical computability and how the
framework's content relates to it. Section C.8 engages the framework's
relationship to standard interpretations of quantum mechanics:
Many-Worlds (MWI), Bohmian mechanics, and QBism.

Sections C.9-C.11 engage framework-specific concerns: the
substratum-emergent operator distinction (whether the framework's
distinction between substratum and emergent operators is a substantive
structural feature or just renaming) together with the parallel question
whether observational incompleteness is the uncertainty principle
renamed (C.9.1), circularity concerns (particularly around the gap
equation for \(\hbar\)), and the framework's epistemic status as a
structural framework rather than a competing physical theory.

Section C.12 engages meta-objections: credentials, scope, and the
framework's ambition. The appendix closes with a brief discussion of
which objections the framework cannot address (acknowledging genuine
limits of the framework's reach) and which objections turn out to be
category errors (where the framework's structural commitments dissolve
apparent puzzles by relocating them).

The appendix is therefore both \emph{substantive} (engaging specific
technical objections with specific responses) and \emph{honest}
(acknowledging where the framework's reach stops and where genuine open
questions remain). Readers approaching the framework from
foundations-of-physics, from quantum information, from interpretive
philosophy of physics, from cognitive science, or from clinical biology
should each find their characteristic objections engaged here.

\hypertarget{c.2-bells-theorem-and-the-frameworks-relationship-to-hidden-variable-theories}{%
\subsection{C.2 Bell's theorem and the framework's relationship to
hidden-variable
theories}\label{c.2-bells-theorem-and-the-frameworks-relationship-to-hidden-variable-theories}}

The most frequent objection to deterministic-substratum theories is:
``Bell's theorem rules out hidden-variable theories. The framework has a
deterministic substratum and a hidden sector. Therefore Bell's theorem
rules it out.''

\textbf{The objection.} Bell's theorem (1964) establishes that no local
hidden-variable theory can reproduce the quantum-mechanical predictions
for entangled systems. The empirical violations of Bell inequalities
(CHSH measured to \(\geq 2.4\) in multiple experiments, with quantum
prediction at \(2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.83\)) are taken as definitively
excluding local hidden-variable theories. The framework's deterministic
substratum looks suspiciously like a hidden-variable theory; therefore
the framework should be ruled out by Bell's theorem in the same way.

\textbf{The framework's response.} Bell applies directly to the
response-complete deterministic substratum. On a finite site set and for
the nearest-neighbour cubic update with finite wing and readout regions
on a site set of any cardinality, if the Bell-relevant coupling range is
finite at the wings' separation, the setting interventions, applied at
one step, each read and write only their own wing and each wing's
readout lies outside the other wing's graph cone, every run records a
\(\pm1\) outcome, and one setting-independent pre-setting ensemble is
used, then the hidden responses factorize and \(|S_{\rm CHSH}|\le2\). OI
therefore cannot combine deterministic response completeness, a \(\pm1\)
outcome in every run, measurement independence, and ontic parameter
independence and still reproduce quantum Bell violation. The framework
keeps measurement independence and takes the remaining horn:
\textbf{ontic parameter dependence} for Bell-violating substrata, with
operational no-signaling retained (Chapter 1 §1.7; Main §3.3).

The cited causal-local \textbf{stochastic} indivisible construction
separately obeys the Tsirelson bound \(2\sqrt2\). By the Bell ceiling
theorem (Main §3.3), on a finite site set and for the nearest-neighbour
cubic update with finite wing and readout regions on a site set of any
cardinality, a response-complete deterministic completion with one-step
own-wing setting interventions, each wing's readout outside the other
wing's graph cone, a \(\pm1\) outcome in every run, and one
setting-independent pre-setting ensemble is a local hidden-variable
model, so \(|S_{\rm CHSH}|\le2\). The framework therefore adopts ontic
\textbf{parameter dependence}, targeted in the SM/GR branch through
preparation-indexed structure in the state-dependent graph \(G(x)\) (or
an equivalent ontically nonlocal response) under the open hypothesis
H-Bell, with operational no-signaling required. If measurement
independence were dropped instead,
\(S_{\rm CHSH}\le\min\{4,\,2+4\sqrt{2\ln2\,I_{\rm ont}}\}\) gives the
model-independent necessary lower bound \(I_{\rm ont}\ge0.0309\) bits
for the quantum value. Hall--Branciard's optimized causal CHSH model
uses about \(0.080\) bits; the smaller \(\sim0.046\)-bit benchmark is
retrocausal. Dropping the spatial/intervention restriction permits the
general finite OI response construction to reach PR-box behavior; PR is
therefore a negative control for causal-local selection, not for the
existence of a Hilbert/Born representation.

\emph{Not superdeterminism.} Determinism alone does not establish Bell
measurement independence, because setting generators are physical
degrees of freedom. The manuscript therefore treats measurement
independence as an explicit premise of the adopted Bell branch rather
than as a theorem of the substratum. It does \textbf{not} use
setting--hidden correlations to explain the observed violation. That
premise is a posit about the initial condition, not derived; the Bell
mechanism itself is ontic parameter dependence. If the premise were
dropped instead, that would be the
measurement-dependent/superdeterministic horn quantified by the
\(I_{\rm ont}\) bound --- a horn the framework records and declines.

\emph{No operational faster-than-light signal --- but ontically
parameter-dependent.} The reference graph still supplies exact causal
cones for its finite-range couplings, but a Bell-violating preparation
may add preparation-indexed adjacency in the state-dependent graph
\(G(x)\) (or an equivalent nonlocal ontic response), so a response at
one wing may depend on the remote setting. That is Bell nonlocality at
the ontic parameter level and the manuscript names it as such. The
distinct empirical claim is no-signaling: those remote-setting
dependencies cannot be controlled to transmit a message. The framework
therefore does not advertise Bell violation as dynamically local in the
hidden-variable sense.

\emph{Not Bohmian mechanics.} Bohmian mechanics adds a pilot wave
guiding particle trajectories in configuration space. The framework has
no pilot wave and no guidance equation in configuration space. The
framework's hidden sector is the substratum's broader configuration
space, not a separate guiding field; the dynamics is direct (the
bijection \(\varphi\)) rather than mediated by a guidance equation.

The framework is therefore not a Bell-local hidden-variable theory. Its
deterministic completion is measurement-independent by the adopted Bell
premise but ontically parameter-dependent, with operational no-signaling
required. Hidden predictive memory and indivisibility remain central to
the OI dynamics, but they are \textbf{not} the mechanism that evades
Bell: a measurement-independent, parameter-independent deterministic
completion recording a \(\pm1\) outcome in every run would still satisfy
CHSH \(\le2\). The Tsirelson value is retained for the cited stochastic
causal-local indivisible construction and, conditionally, for any
successful operational lift to standard quantum mechanics (§C.2).

\hypertarget{c.3-the-no-go-theorems-pbr-frauchiger-renner-colbeck-renner-bong-wiseman}{%
\subsection{C.3 The no-go theorems: PBR, Frauchiger-Renner,
Colbeck-Renner,
Bong-Wiseman}\label{c.3-the-no-go-theorems-pbr-frauchiger-renner-colbeck-renner-bong-wiseman}}

Beyond Bell's theorem, a family of more recent no-go theorems further
constrains the class of ontologies compatible with quantum mechanics.
The framework's content must engage each one specifically. The pattern
is consistent: each no-go theorem makes specific assumptions, and the
framework's content satisfies or violates each assumption in
identifiable ways.

\textbf{The PBR theorem.} Pusey, Barrett, and Rudolph (2012) proved that
any \(\psi\)-epistemic interpretation of quantum mechanics --- where the
wave function represents incomplete information about an underlying
ontic state rather than the ontic state itself --- must satisfy specific
constraints, with several natural \(\psi\)-epistemic models ruled out.
The theorem is widely interpreted as establishing the wave function as
ontic rather than epistemic.

The framework's response must keep the premise accounting explicit. PBR
assumes preparation independence --- that independently prepared systems
have a product joint distribution over their ontic states. Bare OI does
not impose that postulate: co-embedded preparation devices may share
preparation-relevant hidden or boundary data even when their later
dynamical causal cones are disjoint. Hence PBR cannot be applied to OI
merely from the finite-representation theorem. Equally, graph locality
does not itself prove that OI violates preparation independence, does
not supply a unique conditional product law, and does not derive the
standard quantum tensor-product composite. Those questions belong to the
coherent composite operational lift. The correct status is therefore
conditional: any OI completion satisfying PBR's preparation-independence
hypothesis inherits the PBR conclusion; a completion that demonstrably
violates it lies outside that theorem's scope.

\textbf{The Frauchiger-Renner theorem.} Frauchiger and Renner (2018)
derive a contradiction for a specified multi-agent protocol under three
assumptions: quantum probability-one certainty, consistency of the
agents' certainty inferences, and single outcomes, denoted (Q), (C) and
(S). The theorem identifies a conflict among those assumptions for that
protocol, rather than assuming that a wave function is an ontic state.

The framework's ordinary Wigner's-friend account distinguishes definite
substratum configurations from observer-relative reduced descriptions.
Different agents may have different information about the same
configuration. Main §4.1 also provides a joint law whose marginals are
the two observers' laws, so the multiplicity of partitions does not show
that a common law is absent.

A Frauchiger-Renner application requires the proposed completion's
operational probabilities for the whole protocol and an analysis of its
probability-one, consistency and single-outcome premises. The
observer-relative interpretation alone does not prove that one of these
fails and is not an unconditional resolution of the theorem.

\textbf{The Colbeck-Renner theorem.} Colbeck and Renner (2011, 2017)
proved that no extension of quantum mechanics can provide additional
predictive power beyond standard QM, under assumptions including free
choice of measurement settings and the validity of QM as the empirically
successful theory. The result is interpreted as showing that
hidden-variable theories cannot improve on QM's predictive content.

For an operational completion already reproducing standard quantum
predictions in the specified regime, its predictive content must be
compared with the Colbeck-Renner hypotheses in that same regime.
Substratum descriptions do not by themselves establish an exception to
the theorem's free-choice and quantum-prediction assumptions.

A proposed departure from standard quantum predictions requires its own
operational model and premise analysis. Placing its motivation at the
substratum level does not show that the Colbeck-Renner hypotheses fail,
or certify a new predictive advantage. The proposed regimes discussed in
Chapters 15 and 18 retain their separate assumptions and evidential
status.

\textbf{The Bong-Wiseman extended-Wigner-friend theorem.} Bong et
al.~(2020) extended Wigner's friend scenarios with additional
assumptions (local friendliness, absoluteness of observed events) to
derive inequalities that quantum mechanics can violate. The result is
interpreted as showing that even more conservative attempts to maintain
observer-independent reality face obstacles.

A deterministic substratum has one configuration trajectory from a
specified initial state. That ontic fact must be distinguished from the
operational assumptions about observed events in an extended
Wigner's-friend protocol. Observer-relative information alone does not
establish which local-friendliness premise a proposed completion
violates.

An operational completion with the standard quantum instruments inherits
their protocol predictions, including any violation of the relevant
inequalities. Whether the proposed OI physical completion supplies those
instruments and which local-friendliness assumption it fails require
separate checks. The fixed-basis correspondence and the partition
interpretation alone supply neither conclusion.

\textbf{Separate no-go premises.} The substratum, observable laws and
operational descriptions identify different objects constrained by these
theorems. The trace-out does not automatically invalidate their
assumptions. Bell concerns local responses and the setting ensemble; PBR
concerns preparation independence; Frauchiger-Renner concerns
probability-one inferences, consistency and single outcomes;
Colbeck-Renner and extended-Wigner-friend results retain their own
protocol assumptions.

Bare OI does not impose PBR preparation independence, but shared
boundary data do not by themselves prove its failure or a conditional
product law. Partition-relative descriptions provide an interpretation
of observer information, not an automatic Frauchiger-Renner resolution.
Any proposed completion satisfying a no-go theorem's hypotheses inherits
its conclusion. Exact fixed-basis representation and a full operational
completion remain distinct, with the latter characterized only within
its stated matrix setting and additional completion conditions.

\hypertarget{c.4-the-stochastic-quantum-bridge-barandes-and-stinespring}{%
\subsection{C.4 The stochastic-quantum bridge: Barandes and
Stinespring}\label{c.4-the-stochastic-quantum-bridge-barandes-and-stinespring}}

The finite-law theorem in {[}Main §3.4{]} gives an exact fixed-basis
unitary/Born representation of a supplied law on a finite alphabet and
finite horizon. The history-memory result is separate. The internal
permutation construction gives the finite-record representation, and
Barandes' correspondence supplies a compressed transition-statistics
representation under its own hypotheses.

\textbf{The objection.} ``The framework relies on Barandes'
stochastic-quantum correspondence, which is recent (2023) and not yet
widely accepted. This undermines the main result. A theory built on a
not-yet-established result is itself not established.''

\textbf{The framework's response.} The internal proof constructs a
reversible realization of the supplied multi-time law and then uses the
unitary that permutes its configuration basis. A logarithm of that
unitary gives a fixed generator for the integer ticks of the
realization, even when the visible kernels vary over time ({[}Main
§3.4{]}). The construction can depend on the law and horizon.

\emph{Barandes correspondence.} Under the translation hypothesis (T),
the transition data satisfy the tuple conditions of the correspondence.
Its compressed representation includes Markov laws. Its time-indexed
unitaries have a separate scope from the integer-tick construction. The
almost-periodicity obstruction in {[}Main §3.4{]} concerns a finite
fixed-generator marginal at all real times.

\emph{Operator-algebraic structure.} Stinespring's theorem supplies
supporting channel structure. The internal permutation proof already
gives the stated exact representation of finite multi-time records. A
common coherent instrument and composite theory remains a separate
physical problem.

\hypertarget{c.5-the-necessity-direction-of-the-characterization-theorem}{%
\subsection{C.5 The necessity direction of the characterization
theorem}\label{c.5-the-necessity-direction-of-the-characterization-theorem}}

A second foundational objection concerns the necessity direction of the
history-memory theorem. Does observing history dependence force a
specific hidden structure in any realization?

\textbf{The framework's response.} On a finite alphabet and a finite
horizon containing the witness, two positive-probability histories
ending at the same present value have differing next-step laws. A
faithful deterministic realization must carry the distinction through to
readback (C4). This entails hidden-to-visible influence at some eligible
step (C1). C3 is the quantitative capacity bound
\(\log_2|\mathcal{C}_H|\ge I^*\) for the supplied law. A smaller
capacity caps the amount of accessible memory the realization can
support.

The exact reversible realization retains records by reversibility. In a
physical coarse model the persistence form of C2 concerns retention
until readback, and the slow-bath bound additionally requires the
conditional-mixing hypothesis. The history-memory theorem gives a
realization on each finite horizon containing the witness and constrains
every faithful realization of that law ({[}Main §3.4{]}).

The exact representation \(S\iff D\iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\) applies to
every supplied law on a finite alphabet through a finite horizon,
including memoryless laws. Bell composites and common native operational
control have separate premises.

\hypertarget{c.6-finiteness-is-posit-a1-too-strong}{%
\subsection{C.6 Finiteness: is posit A1 too
strong?}\label{c.6-finiteness-is-posit-a1-too-strong}}

A third foundational objection concerns the framework's finiteness
hypothesis --- posit A1 (Chapter 2 §2.4), an open hypothesis, not
adopted, takes the substratum to be a finite set \(S\). Critics object
that this is incompatible with standard physics' commitment to
infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces in quantum field theory and to the
universe being potentially infinite in spatial extent.

\textbf{The objection.} ``The universe has infinitely many degrees of
freedom. Quantum field theory requires infinite-dimensional Hilbert
spaces. Why should I accept finite-dimensionality as a structural
commitment of any theory of the universe?''

\textbf{The framework's response.} Posit A1 plays different roles in
different parts of the framework's content, with different evidential
supports for each role.

\emph{In Chapter 1's foundational content.} Posit A1 is a mathematical
assumption of the results that use it, the recurrence route to
P-indivisibility among them; the exact representation takes a supplied
law on a finite alphabet through a finite horizon and constructs its
finite realization; whether the theorem's empirical applicability
requires actual finiteness of the universe is a separate question.

\emph{In Chapter 7's gravitational content.} The cosmological horizon's
finite area bounds what is observationally accessible: the Bekenstein
entropy bound, read as a dimension cutoff (input E3 of Chapter 2 §2.4),
limits the visible sector and the boundary layer at the cosmological
horizon to at most \(e^{S_{\text{dS}}}\) effectively distinguishable
states, with \(S_{\text{dS}} \sim 10^{122}\). This is an entropy-based
bound that holds under the physical assumptions of E3, not a count of
microscopic configurations. It does not establish finiteness of the
total configuration space \(S\). That extension is posit A1 of Chapter 2
§2.4, an open hypothesis, not adopted, read as the choice of the minimal
finite representative: the cardinality of an independently prepared,
normalized, exactly decoupled finite deep-sector factor is not fixed by
the data at the observation interface (Chapter 2 §2.3). A finite
physical boundary-mode count uses a separate cutoff or counting
hypothesis. Under the horizon calibration in Chapter 7 §7.4, the area
per mode is \(4\sigma l_p^2\), where \(\sigma\) is the entropy of one
boundary mode in nats. In the single-link model with a large spherical
horizon in the lattice frame, the area-averaged orientation factor is
\(3/2\) and the lattice spacing is \(\sqrt{6\sigma}\, l_p\).

A referee who rejects posit A1 for the universe as a whole does not
thereby reject the Bekenstein bound, which is independently established
in semiclassical gravity and string theory across multiple programs
(Hawking 1976, Bekenstein 1981, `t Hooft 1993, Susskind 1995, Bousso
1999, and many subsequent developments): the bound constrains the
observationally accessible sector and does not establish finiteness of
the whole of \(S\), which is the open hypothesis A1. A1 agrees with
mainstream physics' commitment to the Bekenstein bound on the accessible
sector, and would extend beyond it.

\textbf{The ``finite degrees of freedom'' framing.} The standard
intuition that ``the universe has infinitely many degrees of freedom''
comes from quantum field theory treated as a continuum theory --- a
continuum spacetime with field values at every point producing an
infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. But this is the \emph{emergent}
description in the framework. At the substratum level, the framework
posits a discrete lattice, with the horizon calibration and its separate
boundary count giving \(N = S_{\text{dS}}/\sigma\) modes at the
cosmological horizon, \(\sim 10^{122}\) at \(\sigma = 1\).

The framework's content is therefore that the continuum QFT description
is the \emph{emergent} description --- finite at the substratum level
under A1 but \emph{appearing} infinite-dimensional when described in the
continuum limit. This is structurally analogous to how condensed matter
systems with finite lattice spacing exhibit effective continuum
descriptions: the underlying physics is finite, but the long-wavelength
effective description involves continuous fields.

A1 is therefore \emph{compatible with} the standard QFT description as
an effective continuum theory while making specific structural claims
about the substratum level. The two levels of description coexist; if A1
holds, the apparent infinite-dimensionality of QFT is an artifact of the
continuum limit rather than a property of the underlying physics.

A1 is therefore not just a mathematical convenience but a structurally
consequential hypothesis, motivated by the Bekenstein bound and
compatible with continuum QFT.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{c.7-computational-implementability-and-wolperts-theorem}{%
\subsection{C.7 Computational implementability and Wolpert's
theorem}\label{c.7-computational-implementability-and-wolperts-theorem}}

A specific class of objections concerns \emph{computational
implementability}: whether the framework's deterministic substratum can
be computationally implemented by any physical system, given Wolpert's
theorem on physical computability and related results from the
foundations of computer science.

\textbf{The objection.} ``Wolpert (2001, 2008) proved that no physical
computer can predict the outputs of another physical computer that is
its peer --- specifically, no system can implement the function that
takes its own future state as input. The framework's deterministic
substratum \(\varphi\) must, if physically realized, be computed by
something. But what? If \(\varphi\) is computed by a sub-system of the
universe, Wolpert's theorem creates issues; if it is computed
externally, it requires an unstipulated computing infrastructure.''

\textbf{The framework's response.} The framework's content does not
claim that \(\varphi\) is \emph{computed} by any physical system. The
framework's \(\varphi\) is the underlying deterministic dynamics ---
what happens at the substratum level --- not a function evaluated by a
separate computing infrastructure.

The framework's structural commitment is that the substratum \emph{is}
the dynamics. The bijection \(\varphi: S \to S\) is the rule for how the
substratum's configuration evolves; the substratum itself is what
implements the rule. There is no separate computing system that takes
the substratum's current state as input and outputs its next state; the
substratum's dynamics is the substratum's structure.

This is structurally identical to how classical physics treats the
action principle. Hamilton's equations are not \emph{computed} by some
additional infrastructure that evaluates the equations and then
implements the result; Hamilton's equations \emph{are} the dynamics of
the classical system. Similarly, the framework's \(\varphi\) is the
substratum's dynamics, not something computed by a separate physical
computer.

\textbf{The relationship to Wolpert.} The impossibilities in Wolpert
(2008, Proposition 1 and Theorem 1) concern his specified
inference-device tasks. In a given deterministic model a record
determines a state or future outcome when supported configurations
consistent with that record agree on it. Proper observers can achieve
this for some records, as in Substratum Proposition 24.5.

The framework's structural commitment is \emph{not} that some physical
computer implements \(\varphi\); it is that the substratum
\emph{follows} the rule \(\varphi\). This is a structural-physical
claim, not a computational claim. Wolpert's theorem does not address
structural-physical claims about underlying dynamics.

\textbf{The computability of the substratum-level dynamics.} A related
concern is whether the framework's substratum-level dynamics is
\emph{computable in principle} --- whether there exists any algorithm
that, given the substratum's current state, can compute its future
state. The framework's content is that \(\varphi\) is a bijection on a
finite set (under A1), which is trivially computable: any finite
bijection can be specified as a lookup table or as an algorithm that
implements the specific bijection.

The framework does not claim that the bijection's specific form is
\emph{efficiently} computable --- its computation might require time
exponential in the substratum's size or other complexity scaling. But
the bijection is in-principle computable, which is the relevant claim
for foundational physics. Chapter 14's BQP result concerns a scalable
uniform model with quantum controls, efficient simulation, operational
closure and charged conditioning. Application to all physical
computation requires global coverage of those model assumptions.

\textbf{The implementation question is a different question.} The
objection's underlying concern is sometimes ``what physically implements
the substratum?'' --- what is the universe made of, in concrete physical
terms. The framework's content does not answer this question; it
provides a \emph{structural} account of the universe's dynamics without
committing to specific implementation details (whether the substratum is
fundamental fields, discrete cellular automaton cells, or something else
entirely).

This is a deliberate methodological choice (Chapter 4 §4.5). The
framework's structural commitments are evaluated at the level of
structural-empirical predictions, not at the level of substratum
implementation. The framework remains agnostic about implementation
while making specific structural claims about dynamics. A reader who
wants implementation-level content beyond what the framework provides
will need to look elsewhere; the framework's reach is at the structural
level.

\hypertarget{c.8-relationship-to-standard-interpretations-mwi-bohmian-qbism}{%
\subsection{C.8 Relationship to standard interpretations: MWI, Bohmian,
QBism}\label{c.8-relationship-to-standard-interpretations-mwi-bohmian-qbism}}

The framework's content overlaps with several standard interpretations
of quantum mechanics. Readers approaching the framework from MWI,
Bohmian, QBism, or other interpretive positions raise specific questions
about the relationship. The framework's response is structural: each
interpretation captures part of what the framework provides; none
captures all of it; the framework is a new structural position rather
than a variant of any existing interpretation.

\textbf{Many-Worlds Interpretation (MWI).} MWI holds that the universal
wave function is the complete physical reality, with measurement
producing entanglement between observer and observed without collapse.
The ``many worlds'' are the branches of the wave function corresponding
to different measurement outcomes.

\emph{What the framework shares with MWI.} Both reject wave function
collapse as a physical mechanism; both treat the wave function as part
of the description of reality rather than a tool for predicting collapse
outcomes; both treat observers as physical systems within the larger
physical reality rather than as external classical entities.

\emph{What the framework does differently.} MWI commits to the wave
function being \emph{physical reality}; the framework treats the wave
function as an \emph{embedded observer's reduced description} of the
underlying deterministic substratum. The framework has \emph{one
substratum} (the universe-as-deterministic-bijection on \(S\)), not many
branches. The framework's empirical pattern is reproduced through the
substratum's deterministic dynamics combined with embedded observers'
partial access; MWI's empirical pattern is reproduced through branch
counting and the Born rule.

\emph{The structural relationship.} MWI's ``many branches'' correspond,
in the framework's reading, to the \emph{epistemic options} available to
embedded observers about what the substratum's specific configuration
is. Different embedded observers with different histories have different
epistemic states (different reduced descriptions); each such epistemic
state corresponds to an MWI ``branch.'' The framework's content is
therefore that MWI's many branches are \emph{epistemic} (about embedded
