observers' information) rather than \emph{ontic} (about the substratum
having actual multiple realizations).

\textbf{Bohmian mechanics.} Bohmian mechanics adds a pilot wave to
standard QM, with particles having definite trajectories guided by the
wave function. The interpretation reproduces quantum predictions while
preserving definite particle positions at all times.

\emph{What the framework shares with Bohmian.} Both have a deterministic
substratum-level reality (Bohmian: particles with definite trajectories;
framework: substratum bijection \(\varphi\)). Both treat quantum
predictions as statistical statements about the substratum-level
reality. Both are explicitly non-local in some sense (Bohmian: pilot
wave guidance; framework: ontic parameter dependence with operational
no-signaling, §C.2).

\emph{What the framework does differently.} Bohmian mechanics adds a
pilot wave to standard QM as a \emph{separate} ontological element; the
framework has \emph{no pilot wave}. Bohmian particle trajectories are
guided by the wave function; the framework's substratum dynamics is the
bijection \(\varphi\) directly, with no guidance equation. Bohmian
non-locality runs through the pilot wave on configuration space; the
framework's runs through ontic parameter dependence in the hidden sector
(§C.2), its memory effects being temporal.

The framework's reading is therefore that Bohmian mechanics adds an
unnecessary ontological element (the pilot wave) that the framework's
structural content does not require. The framework reproduces Bohmian's
deterministic-substratum and statistical-predictions content without the
pilot wave's structural cost.

\textbf{QBism (Quantum Bayesianism).} QBism interprets the wave function
as a personalist agent's degree of belief about measurement outcomes,
with measurement updating these beliefs via standard Bayesian
conditioning (extended to quantum probabilities). The interpretation
emphasizes the agent-relative character of quantum descriptions.

\emph{What the framework shares with QBism.} Both treat the wave
function as describing an agent's epistemic state rather than directly
describing physical reality. Both emphasize observer-relativity in
quantum descriptions. Both reject the view that the wave function is the
complete physical reality.

\emph{What the framework does differently.} QBism's agent-relative wave
function is \emph{purely epistemic} --- there is no commitment to a
deeper level of physical reality that the wave function is information
about. The framework's wave function is
\emph{epistemic-about-substratum} --- there is a deeper deterministic
level of physical reality (the substratum) that the wave function is
incomplete information about.

QBism therefore lacks the framework's substratum-emergent operator
distinction; the framework provides a structural foundation that QBism's
interpretive content alone does not. The framework's reading is that
QBism captures the \emph{epistemic} character of quantum descriptions
correctly while missing the \emph{structural foundation} of why these
epistemic descriptions take the specific form they do.

\textbf{The framework's position.} The framework is not a variant of any
of these interpretations but a distinct structural position. The
framework's content is closest to MWI in treating the substratum as the
complete physical reality, closest to Bohmian in treating quantum
predictions as statistics over a deterministic substratum, closest to
QBism in treating the wave function as epistemic. But the framework's
distinctive content --- the substratum-emergent operator distinction,
the C1--C4 structural conditions, the specific empirical predictions
across physics and biology --- is not shared by any of the standard
interpretations.

The framework's position is therefore: an interpretive-level structural
framework with substantive empirical content that goes beyond what any
of the standard interpretations provides. Readers approaching from any
of the standard positions will find aspects of their preferred
interpretation in the framework's content while finding the framework's
distinctive content unfamiliar.

\hypertarget{c.9-the-substratum-emergent-operator-distinction-substantive-or-just-renaming}{%
\subsection{C.9 The substratum-emergent operator distinction:
substantive or just
renaming?}\label{c.9-the-substratum-emergent-operator-distinction-substantive-or-just-renaming}}

A specific concern raised by readers familiar with effective field
theory is whether the framework's substratum-emergent operator
distinction is a \emph{substantive} structural feature or just a
\emph{renaming} of the standard fundamental/effective theory
distinction.

\textbf{The objection.} ``Effective field theory already distinguishes
between the fundamental theory (UV completion) and the effective theory
(IR description). Operators in the effective theory can differ from
operators in the fundamental theory through anomaly matching,
integrating-out, and similar mechanisms. The framework's
substratum-emergent operator distinction is just renaming this standard
distinction with new vocabulary. There is no new structural content.''

\textbf{The framework's response.} The framework's substratum-emergent
operator distinction differs from the standard fundamental/effective
distinction in three substantive ways.

\emph{The substratum is not a UV completion.} In effective field theory,
the fundamental theory is the UV completion that produces the effective
theory at lower energies. The relationship is one of energy scale. The
framework's substratum is \emph{not} the UV completion of the emergent
theory; it is the underlying deterministic dynamics with the emergent
theory being a \emph{trace-out} description (the visible sector
projection) rather than a low-energy limit. The relationship is
structural (visible/hidden partition) rather than energy-scale-based.

\emph{Substratum operators include classical bilinears, not just QFT
operators.} Standard effective field theory deals with operators within
a quantum field theory framework --- both fundamental and effective
operators are QFT operators with specific transformation properties. The
framework's substratum operators are \emph{classical bilinears} on the
substratum lattice --- bilinear forms in the substratum's configuration
variables. These have different structural properties than QFT
operators: they are exactly conserved at the substratum level by the
bijection's group properties, with the emergent QFT operators being the
trace-out projections.

This is structurally distinct. Baryon-number conservation, for example,
is exactly conserved by the substratum's bilinear structure (the
bijection respects the bilinear form). At the emergent level, baryon
number is violated by sphalerons in the standard model. The framework's
reading is that the violation is at the emergent level only ---
substratum baryon number is exactly conserved, while emergent baryon
number is approximately conserved with sphaleron-mediated violations.
The two operators (substratum bilinear vs emergent QFT operator) have
different conservation properties.

\emph{Candidate biological comparisons.} The proposed operator analogy
motivates measuring chromatin state and downstream function separately.
Particular reprogramming protocols retain some marks, and bivalent loci
can have poised expression (Chapter 16 §16.10). Tumor methylation
classifiers have benchmarked utility on specified data, and Rett mouse
rescue motivates a comparative therapeutic-window test (Chapters
16--17).

These empirical patterns are not generic effective-field-theory
predictions; they are specific structural predictions of the framework's
substratum-emergent operator distinction. The standard
fundamental/effective distinction does not predict these patterns. The
framework's distinction is therefore \emph{substantively} different from
the standard one, with specific empirical signatures that test the
difference.

\textbf{The methodological asymmetry.} The framework's
substratum-emergent distinction operates \emph{the same way} in
fundamental physics and in biology. The same structural pattern that
organizes baryon-number conservation and anomaly matching in fundamental
physics also organizes iPSC reprogramming residuals, bivalent chromatin
states, and methylation classification in biology. The standard
fundamental/effective distinction does not have this cross-domain reach
--- it is specifically a tool of effective field theory, not a general
structural principle.

The framework's content is therefore that the substratum-emergent
operator distinction is a \emph{general structural principle} with
applications across physics and biology, rather than a domain-specific
tool. This generality is itself substantive content beyond the standard
effective-field-theory distinction.

\hypertarget{c.9.1-observational-incompleteness-and-the-uncertainty-principle-substantive-or-renaming}{%
\subsubsection{C.9.1 Observational incompleteness and the uncertainty
principle: substantive or
renaming?}\label{c.9.1-observational-incompleteness-and-the-uncertainty-principle-substantive-or-renaming}}

\textbf{The objection.} ``Quantum mechanics already says that an
observer cannot know everything about a system: that is Heisenberg's
uncertainty principle. `Observational incompleteness' renames it --- or
revives Heisenberg's original microscope picture, in which observation
disturbs a system that has definite values all along. Either way,
nothing new is being said.''

\textbf{The framework's response.} The two are different statements; the
framework proves an uncertainty-type obstruction and classifies it as
carrying no evidence for the framework; and the sharp form of the
objection points to an open question rather than to a renaming.

\emph{What the uncertainty principle says.} The principle goes back to
Heisenberg (1927). In its standard quantitative forms it is a family of
inequalities in the commutator of two observables: the preparation
relation \(\sigma_A\sigma_B \geq \tfrac{1}{2}|\langle[A,B]\rangle|\)
(Robertson 1929), which limits how sharply a single state can fix two
non-commuting observables, and the error--disturbance relations (Ozawa
2003; Busch, Lahti and Werner 2013), which limit how accurately one
observable can be measured without disturbing another. These are
theorems of the quantum formalism, valid under every interpretation;
they take the formalism as given and say nothing about why it holds. A
single observable can be perfectly sharp: the principle constrains
pairs.

\emph{What observational incompleteness says.} The framework's
incompleteness concerns an observer embedded in a larger finite
deterministic system: the observer's description is a marginal over a
hidden sector it cannot access. Its discriminating content is history
readback (C4): every faithful deterministic completion of the observer's
visible process carries readout-relevant hidden predictive memory that
the observer cannot read. This holds for a single fixed readout --- one
register, recorded over time, with no choice between measurements ---
where the uncertainty principle has nothing to bound. The visible laws
of fixed-readout records are exactly the finite stochastic laws (Main
§3.4), and no uncertainty relation constrains that class.

\emph{Where the uncertainty principle sits in the framework.} The
framework proves a qualitative counterpart of the principle as a theorem
about observation. An instrument that leaves every state unchanged on
average --- a passive instrument --- learns only about the commutative
center of the observable algebra, so complete passive observation fails
whenever the algebra is non-commutative (Main §3.4); this is the
finite-dimensional form of ``no information without disturbance'' (Busch
2009). The framework then classifies the statement as
non-discriminating: it holds in every finite operational theory with two
or more states, whether or not the framework's core conditions hold, and
the framework's formal verification exhibits a theory that satisfies it
and violates the core. Robertson's inequality is in the same position,
since it is a property of density matrices and Hermitian matrices as
such. Neither counts as evidence for the framework.

\emph{The sharp form of the objection.} A stronger critic makes a
different point: the framework does not derive, from embedded
observation, the non-commutative structure that gives the uncertainty
principle its content. That is correct. The relations bind only where
non-commuting observables are operationally available, and the proved
equivalence between stochastic, deterministic and quantum descriptions
concerns readout in one fixed basis, which an ordinary classical
stochastic process also reproduces. The coherent preparations and
non-commuting instruments of standard quantum theory, together with its
composites, form one quantum operational theory under the completion
conditions of the quantum-complete extension OI⁺, none of which embedded
observation supplies on its own; once reversible control is present, the
core clause is logically redundant in that derivation, and the finite
realization theorem realizes non-quantum operational theories as well
(Main §3.4). Whether embedded observation selects the non-commutative
structure is the framework's open selection problem. The framework's
incompleteness accounts for what an embedded observer cannot access; it
does not account for the specific non-commutative form of quantum
uncertainty.

\emph{Heisenberg's microscope and Bell's theorem.} The microscope
picture --- observation disturbing a system with definite values --- is
the picture Bell's theorem constrains: a local model with
setting-independent hidden variables cannot reproduce quantum
correlations. The framework does posit a definite deterministic
substratum, and it states the price (Section C.2): it keeps measurement
independence and takes ontic parameter dependence, with operational
no-signaling. The uncertainty principle carries no commitment of this
kind, so the two positions differ in ontology as well as in content.

\emph{A precedent.} Spekkens' toy theory (Spekkens 2007) shows how far a
bare restriction on knowledge reaches: an epistemic restriction alone
reproduces complementarity, uncertainty-like trade-offs and no-cloning,
but not violations of Bell inequalities. The framework's classification
agrees with this lesson: restricted access does not by itself single out
quantum theory.

\textbf{The relation summarized.} The two are different statements. The
uncertainty-type obstruction is proved and classified as
non-discriminating. Deriving from embedded observation the
non-commutative structure that gives the uncertainty relations their
content is open, as part of the selection problem.

\hypertarget{c.10-circularity-concerns-the-gap-equation-for-hbar}{%
\subsection{\texorpdfstring{C.10 Circularity concerns: the gap equation
for
\(\hbar\)}{C.10 Circularity concerns: the gap equation for \textbackslash hbar}}\label{c.10-circularity-concerns-the-gap-equation-for-hbar}}

A specific technical objection concerns the framework's gap equation in
Chapter 7 §7.3, which relates the Planck constant \(\hbar\) to the
discreteness scale through the cosmological horizon's thermodynamics.
Critics object that the derivation appears circular.

\textbf{The objection.} ``The gap equation equates a classical
temperature to a quantum temperature to derive \(\hbar\). But the
quantum temperature already assumes \(\hbar\) exists. The derivation is
therefore circular --- you are using \(\hbar\) to derive \(\hbar\).''

\textbf{The framework's response.} The logical chain in Chapter 7 §7.3
has four steps that show the derivation is \emph{not} circular.

\emph{Step 1.} Under the canonical measure of Lemma 3 of Chapter 1, the
framework's partition-relativity result proves that the emergent
description is determined by the partition. This is a structural claim
about the framework's setup, not a quantum assumption.

\emph{Step 2.} Step 1's result concerns the transition probabilities,
which determine frequencies, not the action scale: converting a
frequency to an energy requires \(\hbar\) itself (Appendix B.7), so no
value of \(\hbar\) follows from the transition data alone.

\emph{Step 3.} Dimensional analysis on \(c\), \(G\) and \(\epsilon\)
gives \(\hbar = \beta \cdot c^3 \epsilon^2 / G\) with unknown
dimensionless coefficient \(\beta\). This is a consistency check: the
functional form is fixed by the matching of Step 4, which also fixes
\(\beta\).

\emph{Step 4.} The KMS periodicity \(\beta_E = 2\pi c / \kappa\) follows
from Euclidean regularity of the metric at the horizon --- a
\emph{geometric} condition, not a quantum one. The emergent QFT
interprets this periodicity as a temperature
\(T_Q = \hbar \kappa / (2\pi c k_B)\) with \(\hbar\) initially unknown.
Matching \(T_Q\) to the classical temperature
\(T_{\text{cl}} = c^2 \epsilon^2 \kappa / (8\pi G k_B \sigma)\), with
\(\sigma\) the entropy of one boundary mode, fixes
\(\beta = 1/(4\sigma)\).

\textbf{The crucial point.} The KMS periodicity does \emph{not} assume
\(\hbar\). (It does presuppose emergent local boost structure at the
horizon --- a separate, declared dependency, {[}GR §8.5{]} --- which is
a Lorentz-sector condition, not a quantum one.) It assumes the
Wick-rotated metric is smooth at the horizon, which is a condition on
the geometry (the imaginary-time geometry must close smoothly at the
horizon to avoid a conical singularity). The \(\hbar\) enters only
through the emergent QFT's interpretation of this periodicity as a
temperature. The matching is between a \emph{geometric} quantity
(periodicity) and an \emph{emergent} quantity (temperature), not between
two quantities that both assume \(\hbar\).

The structure of the derivation is therefore: - Geometry → KMS
periodicity (no \(\hbar\) used). - Emergent QFT → temperature from KMS
periodicity (with \(\hbar\) as unknown). - Classical-temperature
matching → \(\hbar\) fixed in terms of \(\epsilon\) (conditional on
H-slope, Chapter 7 §7.3).

The \(\hbar\) being ``derived'' enters only in the second step (as an
unknown to be determined), not in the first step (which provides the
geometric input independent of \(\hbar\)). The derivation is therefore
non-circular.

\textbf{The lattice-KMS concern.} A related concern is that the KMS
periodicity assumes a continuous spacetime, while the framework's
substratum is a lattice of spacing \(\sqrt{6\sigma}\, l_p\). The lattice
introduces corrections to the KMS periodicity of order
\((\epsilon\kappa/c^2)^2 \sim 10^{-122}\) at \(\sigma = 1\) --- far
below any observable threshold.

The framework's response: trans-Planckian insensitivity (Jacobson, 't
Hooft, Verlinde, and others) ensures the result is robust against UV
modifications. The continuum KMS periodicity is the dominant
contribution; the lattice corrections are negligible at the relevant
scales. The gap equation is therefore consistent with the lattice
structure rather than requiring strict continuum spacetime.

\hypertarget{c.11-the-frameworks-epistemic-status-as-a-structural-framework}{%
\subsection{C.11 The framework's epistemic status as a structural
framework}\label{c.11-the-frameworks-epistemic-status-as-a-structural-framework}}

A broader objection concerns the framework's epistemic status: whether
it should be evaluated as a \emph{physical theory} competing with the
Standard Model and general relativity, or as a \emph{structural
framework} providing foundations for these theories.

\textbf{The objection.} ``The framework's empirical content is mostly
\emph{retrodictive} --- it explains the Standard Model's parameters and
the gravitational sector's structure after the fact. But a genuine
physical theory should make novel predictions that distinguish it from
competitors. Without such predictions, the framework is not a theory; it
is an interpretation.''

\textbf{The framework's response.} The framework's epistemic status is
intermediate between interpretation and theory. It is a \emph{structural
framework} with substantive empirical content but with different
empirical exposure than a competing physical theory would have.

\emph{What the framework retrodicts.} Twenty-two classified Standard
Model observables (two parameter-free structural and five conditional
structural; the remainder layered, chained or fitted, the gauge
couplings among the fitted), seven gravitational-sector entries
(conditional relations and estimates). The Rett mouse rescue is a prior
observation that motivates a separate therapeutic-window hypothesis.

\emph{What the framework predicts at the present time.} JUNO solar
mixing angle at 0.07\(\sigma\) against the post-JUNO global fit --- a
conditional retrodiction using leading-order Cond 2 and the separate
normalization \(b_{23}=1\). The framework's novel-prediction claims rest
on the forward set (DESI Y5, BTFR at \(z>1\), JUNO design-lifetime
precision on the exact value). (The Bekenstein-Hawking \(1/4\)
coefficient is a consistency relation of the horizon calibration with no
direct empirical test; GW250114 constrains the classical area theorem,
which the framework preserves.)

\emph{What the framework predicts forward.} Specific predictions for the
BEC analogue-gravity experiment (Chapter 15 §15.8) --- the
\(\mathcal{F}(r) = 2r - r^2\) functional form at marginal hidden
capacity (proposed model form; derivation unpackaged). Variant
pathogenicity stratification for reader/writer/eraser genes (Chapter 17
§17.8). These are testable forward predictions that distinguish the
framework's content from current alternatives.

The framework gives an exact fixed-basis representation of supplied
finite records. Common native quantum instruments and coherent evolution
remain open. The local matter and gauge results use their named carrier,
matter-action and chirality hypotheses. The gravitational results give
boundary relations under their horizon assumptions, with native
covariant closure G3 open.

The framework's sector comparisons include the conditional JUNO
retrodiction, the classical area-theorem evidence and the proposed Rett
therapeutic-window test. Each comparison tests the assumptions and
prediction of its own model.

This intermediate status is sometimes uncomfortable. Critics from the
``framework is just interpretation'' camp object that the framework
lacks distinguishing predictions; critics who seek alternative dynamics
ask how the proposed constructions would differ experimentally from
standard physics. The framework's response: it is \emph{intentional}
that the framework operates at the foundational level rather than at the
competing-theory level. The foundational level is where structural
questions are addressed; the framework's empirical content at this level
is substantial.

\hypertarget{c.11.1-is-the-derivation-gerrymandered-the-selector-motivation-audit}{%
\subsubsection{C.11.1 Is the derivation gerrymandered? The
selector-motivation
audit}\label{c.11.1-is-the-derivation-gerrymandered-the-selector-motivation-audit}}

\textbf{The objection.} ``The derivation reaches the Standard Model only
because its axioms and selection principles were chosen, with hindsight,
to land there. The discrete residue --- \(d=3\), \(K=6\), the gauge
group --- is smuggled in through tuned assumptions, so the `derivation'
is a tautological re-encoding of the target rather than a forcing of
it.''

\textbf{The framework's response.} The relevant test applied to each
assumption and selection principle is whether it is motivated
independently of the Standard Model target. On that test the structural
core does not depend on the target. Under H-link \(K=2dm\) follows from
the link count rather than as a selection rule, with \(m=1\) giving
\(K=6\); a different \(K\) corresponds to a different bijection. The
spatial dimension \(d=3\) follows from three filters stated without
reference to the gauge sector (propagating gravity, stable matter,
entropy concordance); renormalizability is not used as a filter, as that
would be circular. The multiplicities \((3,2,1)\) are the decomposition
of the six nearest-neighbor link directions under the cubic point group.
The audit also identifies two inputs that are not derived in this sense
and are recorded as such: the amplitude-scale gauge principle (treated
in the substratum development as an operational input rather than a
theorem) and the identification of the propagation modes with the
gauge-carrying components.

In the quantitative tier the dependence on fitted quantities is larger.
There, \(1/\alpha_0\) is derived, while the leading threshold
coefficient \(A\cdot B\) is a finite-lattice numerical cross-check with
extrapolated values \(\approx 48\)--\(62\) across leading-power models;
the comparison with the fitted product remains inconclusive. The
universal threshold \(\delta_0\) is an empirical input. Comparisons with
candidate threshold identifications, including a group-specific
hypercharge-trace interpretation, must retain the leading-power
dependence of the \(A\cdot B\) calculation; universality of \(\delta_0\)
is a separate structural constraint. The resulting characterization is a
derived structural residue and a coupling-sector retrodiction with a
small number of fits.

\textbf{What remains open.} This audit bears only on whether the residue
is motivated independently of the target. It does not settle the further
question of whether a forced structural residue is \emph{substantively}
non-tautological as opposed to merely entailed, which is recorded as an
open problem (Chapter 19 §19.3.6) and which the framework proposes to
assess by external calibration against the operational reconstruction
theorems of quantum theory rather than by further internal argument.

\hypertarget{c.12-meta-objections-credentials-scope-ambition}{%
\subsection{C.12 Meta-objections: credentials, scope,
ambition}\label{c.12-meta-objections-credentials-scope-ambition}}

The framework attracts meta-objections about its author, its scope, and
its ambition. These are not legitimate scientific objections in
themselves, but they are sometimes raised and warrant brief engagement.

\textbf{Credentials.} ``The author has no formal physics credentials.
The framework should not be taken seriously regardless of its content.''

This is not a scientific objection. Scientific content is evaluated on
its merits, not on the credentials of those who propose it. The
framework's content consists of mathematical proofs, empirical
predictions, and structural derivations --- all evaluable independent of
the author's biography.

However, the underlying concern (familiar standards may not be met by an
outsider) can be addressed substantively. The framework provides
complete proofs in the technical chapters (Chapter 1 for the
characterization theorem; Chapter 7 for the gravitational derivations;
etc.); two derivation routes for key results (Chapter 1 via Barandes
correspondence and Stinespring dilation); and explicit falsifiability
conditions throughout (Chapter 15 §15.8 BEC test; etc.). The standards
the framework meets are \emph{internal scientific standards} (proofs,
predictions, falsifiability), not standards based on author identity.

The author takes responsibility for the framework's scientific content,
including its proofs, derivations, predictions, and supporting
citations.

\textbf{Scope.} ``The framework claims to address fundamental physics
\emph{and} the origin of life \emph{and} the methodological limits of
single-cell bioinformatics. This is too much for a single framework.
Each domain deserves its own framework.''

The framework's response: the claims are \emph{interconnected by a
single mechanism} (C1--C4 structural conditions operating at different
scales). Separating them would obscure the connections --- in
particular, the framework's value comes from being \emph{one} structural
account that produces predictions across multiple domains, not from
being separate accounts for each domain. The unification is the
framework's distinctive content.

This is not a unique pattern. Statistical mechanics in the nineteenth
century similarly addressed thermodynamics, kinetics, transport
phenomena, and other domains with one structural account. The
unification of multiple domains under one structural framework is a
feature, not a bug. The application comparisons use distinct datasets,
tasks and physical mechanisms. Their reported results support the
individual comparisons within their stated scopes.

The framework is structured to allow domain-specific evaluation. Part II
(fundamental physics) is self-contained and can be evaluated
independently. Part III (emergence cascade) builds on Part II but is
independently evaluable. Part IV (applications) builds on Parts II-III
but is also independently evaluable. A reader skeptical of the
framework's overall claim can evaluate Part II alone and engage the
framework's content at that level.

\textbf{Ambition.} ``The framework identifies QM with embedded
observation, dissolves the cosmological constant problem, explains the
dark sector, and provides a unifying account of memory in biology. This
is too ambitious.''

The framework's response: ambition is not a scientific objection. The
relevant questions are: do the derivations work? do the predictions
match empirical data? are the structural commitments coherent? The
framework's content provides specific answers to each: the derivations
are explicit and the proofs are complete; the retrodictions match data
at the precisions classified in Appendix A (JUNO at 0.07\(\sigma\)
against the post-JUNO global fit), and GW250114 is consistent with the
classical area theorem the framework preserves; the structural
commitments are coherent across multiple domains.

A reader who finds the framework's ambition uncomfortable can choose to
engage with subsets of the content. The framework's content is
structured to be evaluable at multiple levels --- at the Chapter-level
(specific empirical predictions), at the Part-level (specific structural
derivations), or at the framework-level (the full structural
commitments). The framework's ambition does not require the reader to
engage with all of it at once.

\hypertarget{c.13-closing-remarks}{%
\subsection{C.13 Closing remarks}\label{c.13-closing-remarks}}

The appendix has engaged twelve clusters of objections to the
framework's content. The pattern across responses is consistent: each
objection is engaged at the level appropriate to its substance, with
specific technical content where the objection is technical, with
specific methodological content where the objection is methodological,
and with specific empirical content where the objection concerns
empirical exposure.

\textbf{What the framework cannot address.} The framework's reach has
genuine limits. The framework does not address:

\emph{The hard problem of consciousness.} Chapter 18 §18.10 explicitly
identifies consciousness as outside the framework's primary scope. The
framework provides structural commitments about the relationship between
observation and physical reality (observation as necessary but not
sufficient for consciousness; structural constraints on physics-based
consciousness theories) but does not derive the \emph{qualitative}
character of conscious experience.

\emph{The initial conditions of the universe.} Chapter 19 §19.3
identifies the cosmological initial state as an open problem. The
framework's content includes the universe's dynamics (\(\varphi\) on
\(S\)) but not the specific initial configuration the universe started
from. Why this initial state rather than another is not addressed by the
framework's structural content.

\emph{The flavor problem.} Chapter 19 §19.3 identifies the detailed
structure of the CKM and PMNS matrices as open. The framework's content
predicts gross structural features (gauge group, generation count, broad
mixing-angle structure) but not the specific values of all twelve Yukawa
couplings.

\emph{The baryon asymmetry.} The framework does not derive the specific
baryon-to-photon ratio (\(n_B / n_\gamma \approx 6 \times 10^{-10}\))
from first principles. This is not a gap awaiting a mechanism: the
framework's relation to baryogenesis is solution-specific (§19.3.3). The
baryon asymmetry is downstream of the flavor-sector CP phases
(\(\delta_{\rm CKM}\), \(\delta_{\rm PMNS}\)), which the framework
treats as solution-specific inputs rather than derived quantities;
\(\eta_B\) inherits that input status. The framework is internally
consistent on this point --- it does not claim to derive \(\eta_B\)
while inputting \(\delta_{\rm CKM}\) --- but it is, by the same token,
incomplete in scope on the baryon asymmetry, and says so.

These are genuine limits of the framework's reach. The framework does
not pretend to address them; they are explicitly identified as open
problems or out-of-scope concerns.

\textbf{What turns out to be a category error.} Several apparent puzzles
in fundamental physics turn out, on the framework's analysis, to be
\emph{category errors} --- problems that arise from confusing levels of
description. The framework recasts these rather than solving them, under
the conditions stated for each.

\emph{The cosmological constant problem.} The ``120-order-of-magnitude
discrepancy'' between QFT vacuum energy and observed cosmological
constant is a category error in the framework's reading (Chapter 7
§7.7), conditional on the open coupling step ({[}GR §6.2{]}; Chapter 19
§19.2.2). The QFT vacuum energy is the \emph{emergent} energy density of
the trace-out; the cosmological constant is the \emph{substratum}
baseline energy density. The two operate at different levels of
description, and their relationship is the framework's specific
information compression ratio rather than a direct equality.

\emph{The measurement problem.} The question ``how does measurement
produce definite outcomes from superpositions'' receives an
observer-relative account (Chapter 1; Chapter 19 §19.2.5): at the
represented fixed-basis level measurement is conditioning and
re-marginalization, while multi-agent protocols require the proposed
completion's operational probabilities and separate premise checks. At
the substratum level, there are no superpositions --- only the
substratum's specific configuration. At the emergent level,
superpositions are reduced descriptions used by embedded observers with
incomplete information. ``Measurement'' is the embedded observer's
interaction with the substratum that updates their reduced description
--- not a physical mechanism producing definite outcomes from a
previously-indefinite physical state.

\emph{The quantum-gravity unification problem.} The standard formulation
(``quantize gravity to unify with QM'') is a category error in the
framework's reading (Chapter 7 and Chapter 18 §18.4). Gravity is
\emph{substratum-level geometry} in the framework, not an emergent-level
field requiring quantization. On the framework's reading QM and GR are
projections of one substratum; the covariant field equations and their
coupling (G3) are open, so this is a framework-level reading rather than
a completed unification (Chapter 19 §19.2.1). The framework does not
``quantize gravity''; it explains why QM and GR are \emph{both} emergent
descriptions of a single substratum-level reality.

These readings are conditional content of the framework. Its reach is
not only retrodictive (explaining established empirical patterns) but
reclassificatory (proposing that some apparent puzzles are category
errors rather than problems requiring solutions, conditionally on the
open steps named above).

\textbf{The framework's epistemic position summarized.} The framework is
a structural framework with substantive empirical content. It engages
standard interpretations of QM, established no-go theorems, established
results in effective field theory, and established methodological
concerns through specific technical responses. Its specific empirical
claims are retrodictions or consistencies with existing data (JUNO,
GW250114, Rett), and its forward predictions can be tested in the future
(BEC, variant pathogenicity). Its structural commitments are coherent
across multiple domains, with the substratum-emergent operator
distinction providing a unifying principle across fundamental physics
and biology.

Where the framework's reach has genuine limits (consciousness, initial
conditions, flavor problem, the baryon asymmetry), the limits are
explicitly identified. Where apparent puzzles are read as category
errors (cosmological constant, measurement problem, quantum-gravity
unification), the readings are conditional content --- on the open
coupling step G3 and the operational completion --- rather than
evasions.

The appendix's value is therefore as a reference resource for readers
approaching the framework from different starting points. Readers
familiar with Bell's theorem and the no-go theorems should find
§§C.2-C.3 directly useful. Readers familiar with effective field theory
should find §§C.9 directly useful. Readers familiar with standard
interpretations should find §C.8 directly useful. Readers concerned
about credentials, scope, or ambition should find §C.12 directly useful.
The appendix is intended to be navigable rather than read straight
through, with each section engaging the specific cluster of concerns
characteristic of one reader audience.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\hypertarget{glossary}{%
\section{Glossary}\label{glossary}}

This glossary defines the framework's distinctive terminology and the
technical vocabulary used throughout the book. Entries are organized
alphabetically. Cross-references to chapter and appendix sections point
to where each concept is most fully developed.

\textbf{Note on convention:} terms in \emph{italics} within definitions
indicate other glossary entries. Where the framework's usage differs
from standard physics or mathematics usage, the difference is noted
explicitly.

\begin{center}\rule{0.5\linewidth}{0.5pt}\end{center}

\textbf{Anomaly cancellation.} A condition in quantum field theory
requiring that the sum of contributions from chiral fermions to certain
triangle diagrams vanishes. In the Standard Model, anomaly cancellation
between fermion generations is a structural consistency requirement that
constrains the allowed hypercharge assignments. The framework derives
the \emph{unique} hypercharge assignment
\((Y_Q, Y_u, Y_d, Y_L, Y_e) = (1/6, 2/3, -1/3, -1/2, -1)\) from the six
anomaly conditions of
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\) on the
nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch, with no free parameters. Developed in Chapter 6
§6.7 and Appendix B §B.5.

\textbf{A1 (Finiteness).} The open hypothesis, not adopted, that the
substratum has a finite total configuration space (Chapter 2 §2.4), as
assumed in the minimal finite representative. Motivated physically by
the Bekenstein bound at the cosmological horizon (an entropy-based
bound, under the physical assumptions of input E3, of at most
\(e^{S_{\text{dS}}}\) effectively distinguishable states of the visible
sector and boundary layer, \(S_{\text{dS}} \sim 10^{122}\)). Discussed
in Chapter 2 §2.4, with defense in Appendix C §C.6.

\textbf{Background independence (A6).} The sixth of the framework's
structural assumptions A1--A6: the substratum dynamics is covariant
under spatially varying internal-index transformations, a site-dependent
transformation being a symmetry provided the coupling data carried on
the links are transformed with it. The content of the assumption is the
covariant interface itself --- the coupling is link-valued data the
transformations act on --- and once that is in place the local
transformation law imposes no further condition on the rule. It is
distinct from the stronger fixed-background condition that the same
transformations leave the dynamics invariant with the coupling held
fixed, which for an invertible coupling forces agreement across every
coupled pair of sites; from the global commutant symmetry, its
specialization to transformations constant across the lattice that leave
the coupling unchanged, from which the local gauge reading proceeds; and
from the state-dependent coupling graph, a separate principle sharing
the name, under which the graph itself evolves with the state. Where the
framework says it has no fixed spacetime background, with spacetime
emergent, that is a third sense of the words and not this assumption.
Developed in Chapter 2 §2.4 and Chapter 5 §5.5.

\textbf{Barandes correspondence.} The mathematical result establishing
that stochastic processes in its own indivisible class correspond
structurally to unitary quantum dynamics under its hypotheses. The class
is a tuple structure --- configuration space, target and conditioning
times, transition maps, prior, random variable --- and divisibility
failure is generic within it rather than definitional, so Markov chains
are included. The framework's link to it is the explicit translation
hypothesis \emph{(T)}: that the framework's per-horizon transition
family instantiates that tuple ({[}Main §3.1{]},
\texttt{tuple\_probes.py}). \emph{P-indivisibility} does not gate the
representation's existence; it determines whether the representation is
nontrivial. This route supplies a compressed transition-statistics
representation. The internal reversible construction and permutation
unitary independently give the exact fixed-basis representation of a
supplied law on a finite alphabet and horizon. A physical operational
instrument algebra requires its own assumptions. Developed in Chapter 1
§1.6 and Appendix B §B.2.

\textbf{Bekenstein-Hawking entropy.} The entropy \(S = A/(4 l_p^2)\)
assigned to a horizon of area \(A\) in units of the Planck length
\(l_p\). The factor \(1/4\) follows from the Hawking temperature and the
first law. In the framework it is the ratio \(2\pi/8\pi\) fixed by the
horizon calibration of Chapter 7 (conditional on H-slope); the mode
count reproduces it for any cell size once the calibration is imposed.
The September 2025 analysis of GW250114, observed on January 14,
supports the classical area theorem from inferred Kerr areas; the
\(1/4\) coefficient has no direct empirical test. Developed in Chapter 7
§7.5.

\textbf{Bell-inequality violations.} Empirical correlations exceeding
bounds derivable from local hidden-variable theories. For a
response-complete deterministic OI completion, measurement independence
plus ontic parameter independence, with a \(\pm1\) outcome in every run,
gives Bell factorization and \(|S_{\rm CHSH}|\le2\). The framework
therefore retains measurement independence but relinquishes
\textbf{ontic parameter independence} for Bell-violating substrata, with
operational no-signaling required. The measurement-dependent alternative
is recorded rather than adopted: the manuscript proves the
model-independent necessary lower bound \(I_{\rm ont}\ge0.0309\) bits
for the quantum CHSH value, while an optimized causal model in
Hall--Branciard uses about \(0.080\) bits (the smaller \(\sim0.046\)-bit
benchmark is retrocausal). Developed in Chapter 1 §1.7 and Appendix C
§C.2.

\textbf{Born rule.} The quantum-mechanical prescription that the
probability of measurement outcome \(i\) on state \(|\psi\rangle\) is
\(|\langle i|\psi\rangle|^2\). Conventionally treated as a postulate of
quantum mechanics. In the framework, at the finite fixed-basis
observable-law layer, the Born form is part of an exact equivalent
representation: \(S\iff D\iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\) ({[}Main §3.4{]}). The
quadratic form is part of the representation dictionary. Its physical
selection independently of that dictionary remains open. What remains is
operational: on a finite carrier, within complex matrix kinematics taken
as given, an operational theory's available instruments on the carrier
and its composites are the standard noncommuting quantum instruments
exactly when the five completion conditions of the
operational-completion characterization ({[}GR §3.3{]}) hold; the
substratum's stated interventions do not supply one of them, full
reversible control; whether an extended OI mechanism can supply it,
which of the others the substratum supplies, and a derivation of that
kinematics are open. The read-write-cycle equilibrium account in Chapter
18 §18.2 is an additional physical mechanism proposal and is not needed
for the finite representation equivalence.

\textbf{BQP (Bounded-error Quantum Polynomial time).} Decision problems
solvable by uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits with error
probability bounded by \(1/3\). Chapter 14 characterizes computation for
observers in a scalable uniform model with quantum preparation, gates
and readout, polynomial time and precision, efficient simulation,
suitable noise assumptions and operational closure with charged
conditioning. Application to all physical computation requires global
coverage of the upper-bound hypotheses.

\textbf{C1 (Coupling).} The hidden-influence condition in the
history-memory characterization. Requires non-trivial coupling between
the \emph{visible} and \emph{hidden sectors} of the \emph{embedded
observer}'s partition: hidden influence on some accessible visible
transition. A non-permutation one-step matrix \(T\) is the cheapest
\emph{sufficient witness} of C1 --- not its definition and not
necessary, since influence can hide at step one and surface later (the
delayed-revival family, {[}Main §3.4{]}). A causal write to the hidden
state is an additional property of particular realizations. Discussed in
Chapter 1 §1.3.

\textbf{C2 (Memory persistence).} A record-persistence condition with a
conditional physical timescale form. The history-memory characterization
uses C1, C3 and C4. Stated in two forms ({[}Main §1.3{]}):
(C2-structural), that a hidden record of visible history persists to the
readback that uses it --- supplied by reversibility in every bijective
realization, so as a condition it bears on coarse-grained descriptions
of the hidden sector; and (C2-slow), \(\tau_S \ll \tau_B\), one
sufficient mechanism, fast conserved dynamics being another
(\texttt{fastbath\_probes.py}). C2 is the persistence half of what C4
operationally needs (the other half is in-window routing), and, in the
coupling-step model of {[}Main §3.4{]}'s physical-memory theorem ---
next visible state determined by the current visible and hidden states,
any hidden map between couplings --- observed conditional memory
\(M_k > 0\) at an accessible order \(k\) forces some realized hidden
conditional at that coupling time to stay at least
\(\varepsilon_{\min}(M_k, n_V)\) from its reference prior \(\pi_H\),
with no mixing hypothesis (the physical-memory theorem, {[}Main
§3.4{]}); under the hidden-sector mixing hypothesis this becomes a lower
bound on bath persistence. The proposed cosmological estimate gives
\(\tau_S / \tau_B \sim 10^{-32}\) for the illustrative laboratory step
if the horizon scale sets the laboratory effective mixing time. When the
coarse-grained hidden sector thermalizes between measurements, C2 fails
in its timescale form and, under the mixing hypothesis, the conditional
memory of the dynamics is bounded in terms of the residue of that mixing
at the coupling time. Discussed in Chapter 1 §1.3.

\textbf{C3 (Hidden-sector capacity).} The second of the framework's
three structural conditions (C1, C3, C4). Requires hidden capacity
sufficient for the process's conditional memory:
\(\log_2 |\mathcal{C}_H| \geq I^*\), the capacity floor --- the
data-processing bound
\(I(X_{<t}; X_{>t} \mid X_t) \leq I(X_{<t}; H_t \mid X_t) \leq \log_2|\mathcal{C}_H|\)
applied to the whole visible future, which holds in every faithful
realization ({[}Main §3.4{]}). \(N_H \gg N_V\) is the comfortable
physical regime, not the condition; for our universe at the cosmological
horizon, \(N_H \sim 10^{122}\). C3 saturation caps accessible memory ---
the theorem-level content. The mechanism proposal hypothesizes that the
marginal-capacity regime is the \emph{restricted quantum-statistical}
regime of partial distinguishability revival, memoryless operational
modeling failing while the transition-statistics layer remains
representable ({[}Main §3.4{]}); all operational-failure readings here
are proposal-level until a selection theorem supplies the implication.
Discussed in Chapter 1 §1.3, with the restricted quantum-statistical
regime in Chapter 15 §15.7 and Chapter 18 §18.3.

\textbf{C4 (History readback).} Two positive-probability histories with
the same current visible state give different next-step laws through the
hidden state. A preloaded hidden selector revealed by the history can
supply this witness. A causal write has the further matched-seed
requirement. For a witnessed history pair, {[}Main §2.3{]} gives a
conditional-memory bound in terms of its probabilities and the
total-variation gap. Discussed in Chapter 1 §1.3.

\textbf{Cabibbo angle.} The CKM mixing parameter
\(\lambda = \sin\theta_C \approx 0.225\) governing
first/second-generation quark mixing in the Standard Model.
Conventionally a fitted empirical parameter. The framework obtains
\(\lambda = 1/(\pi\sqrt{2})\) from a single Brillouin-zone distance on
the substratum lattice, under an identification hypothesis whose
emergent dressing is open (conditional structural), matching observation
at \(0.04\%\). Developed in Chapter 6 §6.5.

\textbf{Cat state (Schrödinger's cat).} A superposition of
macroscopically distinct configurations. In the deterministic model each
full trajectory has one configuration at each step, and the
finite-record theorem gives a fixed-basis representation of its observed
law. In a physical experiment, coherence depends on the preparation and
environmental interaction. Engineered cat states test particular models
of coherence loss or collapse (Chapter 1 §§1.6, 1.11 and Chapter 4
§4.5).

\textbf{CaMKII (Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II).} A
neuronal kinase involved in synaptic plasticity. Its regulatory dynamics
provide a candidate record for a matched-present readback test. The
proposed molecular timescale changes in disease need separate evidence
(Chapter 16 §16.4).

\textbf{Characterization theorem.} The per-horizon characterization of
the memory-bearing sector: an embedded observer's reduced description is
non-Markovian on accessible horizons if and only if, for some accessible
order, every finite accessible horizon extending at least one step
beyond it admits a deterministic realization satisfying \emph{C1},
\emph{C3} and \emph{C4}, with \emph{C4}'s readback at that order;
\emph{C2} lies outside the equivalence, its physical content carried by
the physical-memory theorem (persistence form without a mixing
hypothesis, slow-bath form conditional on it). A fixed-basis unitarily
evolving quantum representation exists for every finite-horizon law ---
internal and universal, by the finite-horizon equivalence
\(S \iff D \iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\) ({[}Main §3.4{]}); the compressed
representation is supplied across the correspondence's class through the
imported stochastic--quantum correspondence, nontrivially where the
dynamics is P-indivisible, under the translation hypothesis \emph{(T)}
--- a separate conditional bridge, not part of the equivalence. Forward
direction (sufficiency): a realization with \emph{C1}, \emph{C3} and
\emph{C4} \(\Longrightarrow\) accessible non-Markovianity, the \emph{C4}
readback gap forcing positive conditional memory. Reverse direction
(necessity): accessible non-Markovianity \(\Longrightarrow\) such a
realization on each accessible witness horizon, by the finite-horizon
process dilation, with \emph{C1}, \emph{C3} and \emph{C4} each necessary
and \emph{C2}'s necessity for physical hidden sectors conditional on the
quantitative mixing hypothesis in its slow-bath (timescale) form and
holding without it in its persistence form. Developed in Chapter 1
§§1.8-1.9, with necessity proofs in Appendix C §C.5.

\textbf{Chk1 (Checkpoint kinase 1).} A serine/threonine kinase
regulating cell-cycle checkpoint responses to DNA damage. The framework
identifies Chk1 as a canonical example of regulatory-domain \emph{memory
asymmetry}: Chk1 inhibitors selectively sensitize tumor cells because
tumor cells rely on non-Markovian checkpoint dynamics that normal cells
with intact G1 checkpoints do not require. Discussed in Chapter 16
§16.3.

\textbf{Chirality (in the framework).} The framework's commitment to
chiral SU(2) electroweak structure rests on the staggered bipartite
structure on the cubic lattice combined with the trace-out operation,
and is conditional on the chirality hypothesis H-χ' (SM §4.8).
Propagates through molecular physics to produce the parity-violating
energy difference (PVED) between mirror-image molecules, predicting
L-amino acids as the slightly more stable enantiomer. Discussed in
Chapter 10 §10.7.

\textbf{Chromatin.} The protein-DNA complex organizing eukaryotic
genomes, including nucleosome positioning, histone modifications
(acetylation, methylation), DNA methylation patterns, and
three-dimensional chromatin architecture. The framework treats chromatin
as the \emph{hidden sector} of the biological \emph{C1--C4} partition
with the transcriptional machinery as visible sector. Developed in
Chapter 16 §16.9.

\textbf{CKM (Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa) matrix.} The unitary mixing
matrix between Standard Model quark mass and weak interaction
eigenstates. Conventionally parameterized by three mixing angles and one
CP-violating phase. The framework obtains the Cabibbo angle
structurally, under an identification hypothesis whose emergent dressing
is open, and provides partial content for the broader CKM structure.
Developed in Chapter 6 §6.5.

\textbf{CHSH inequality.} The Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt formulation of
Bell's inequality, with the Bell-local bound of 2 and the quantum
(Tsirelson) bound of \(2\sqrt{2}\). In the deterministic OI completion,
measurement independence plus parameter independence, with a \(\pm1\)
outcome in every run, gives the bound 2; quantum violation under
measurement independence therefore uses ontic parameter dependence. The
cited stochastic causal-local indivisible construction separately has
the Tsirelson bound. Discussed in Appendix C §C.2.

\textbf{Cosmological constant problem.} The discrepancy of approximately
\(10^{122}\) between quantum field theory's predicted vacuum energy
(\(\sim 10^{113}\) J/m³) and the observed value inferred from cosmic
expansion (\(\sim 6 \times 10^{-10}\) J/m³). The framework proposes to
\emph{dissolve} this problem by identifying the two quantities as
properties of logically distinct descriptions: the quantum vacuum energy
is the emergent QFT's prediction within a partition; the observed
cosmological constant is the gravitational consequence of the
substratum's full content. The descriptive distinction is established;
the dissolution is conditional on the open coupling step. Developed in
Chapter 7 §7.7.

\textbf{Cryptochrome.} A flavoprotein that can participate in
photoinduced radical-pair dynamics. Robin cryptochrome 4 has shown
magnetic sensitivity in vitro. The responsible avian receptor and
mechanism in vivo and its relevant coherence lifetime remain open
(Chapter 13 §13.5).

\textbf{Cubic decomposition.} On the six signed link directions the
cubic group has the multiplicity-free decomposition
\(\mathbf{6}=T_1\oplus E\oplus A_1\) of dimensions \(3,2,1\). The
unitary commutant is \(\mathrm{U}(1)^3\). The distinct-block condensate
stabilizer and specified charged matter action under H-link and H-cust
enter the separate local gauge-algebra result. Developed in Chapter 5
§§5.4--5.6.

\textbf{DSW (Danielson-Satishchandran-Wald) horizon decoherence.} A 2022
result by Danielson, Satishchandran, and Wald proving within standard
QFT in curved spacetime that Killing horizons impose fundamental
decoherence on nearby quantum superpositions, with rate determined by
horizon geometry. External convergence with the framework's
universality-class content. Discussed in Chapter 9 §9.7 and Chapter 15
§15.8.

\textbf{Embedded observer.} The framework's technical term for an
observer that is a proper subsystem of the system it registers ---
coupled to the system, bounded in extent, unable to access the full
state from outside. A detector, a protein interior or a cosmological
horizon qualifies; nothing in the definition requires consciousness. The
central object of the framework's analysis. Defined precisely in Chapter
1 §1.2, characterized by C1--C4 in §1.3.

\textbf{Emergent description.} The reduced description of the visible
sector after marginalizing over (tracing out) the hidden sector. In the
framework, every finite-horizon observable law --- C1--C4 or not ---
admits a fixed-basis unitary quantum representation
(\(S \iff D \iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}\), {[}Main §3.4{]}); systems satisfying
C1--C4 constitute the memory-bearing sector, where hidden predictive
memory is unavoidable in every completion. Developed throughout Chapter
1.

\textbf{Epigenome.} The set of chromatin marks and methylation patterns
that regulate gene expression while remaining heritable across cell
divisions and (partially) generations. The biological instantiation of
the framework's \emph{substratum-emergent operator distinction} at the
molecular scale. Discussed in Chapter 16 §§16.9-16.10.

\textbf{Extended Church-Turing Thesis (ECT).} Conventionally, the
classical efficient-simulation conjecture --- any physically realizable
computation efficiently simulable by a probabilistic classical Turing
machine --- the thesis quantum computing challenges. Its quantum
counterpart, the BQP-form (quantum) ECT, asserts efficient
quantum-simulability of all physical computation. The framework derives
the BQP-form (quantum) ECT as a \emph{conditional theorem} under a
global-coverage premise (every physically realizable computation falling
under Chapter 14 §14.4's operational-closure and efficiency hypotheses):
any computation so covered satisfies the BQP bound. Developed in Chapter
14 §14.6.

\textbf{Fibre-Gram data.} For a coherent lift of a visible law and each
visible output, the Gram matrix of the hidden states into which the lift
sends the visible inputs. Its diagonal is the visible law itself. Two
lifts are related by the two-sided invisible action at one time exactly
when their fibre-Gram data agree up to phases, so the off-diagonal part
modulo phases is exactly what the visible law leaves free at that time.
It is a coordinate on the space of lifts, not a physical quantity, and
no statement is made about what selects its trajectory through time.
Developed in Chapter 1 and §19.3.9.

\textbf{Fine-tuning.} The observation that certain physical parameters
(fine-structure constant, mass ratios, cosmological constant) appear to
occupy narrow ranges supporting chemistry and complexity. The
framework's reading: most chemistry-supporting features are
\emph{structural} (derived from the framework's commitments) rather than
parametric, dissolving the conventional fine-tuning problem. Discussed
in Chapter 10 §10.8.

\textbf{Frauchiger-Renner theorem.} A 2018 multi-agent no-go theorem
deriving a conflict among quantum probability-one certainty, consistency
of agents' certainty inferences and single outcomes for its protocol.
Partition-relative descriptions alone do not resolve that conflict;
applying it to a proposed OI completion requires its operational
probabilities and a separate check of those premises. Discussed in
Appendix C §C.3.

\textbf{Gap equation (for \(\hbar\)).} The thermal self-consistency
condition between the classical horizon temperature
\(T_{cl} = c^2\epsilon^2 \kappa/(8\pi G k_B \sigma)\) and the KMS
temperature \(T_Q = \hbar\kappa/(2\pi c k_B)\) of the emergent QFT,
producing \(\hbar = c^3 \epsilon^2/(4G\sigma)\), with \(\sigma\) the
entropy of one boundary mode. It relates Planck's constant to the
discreteness scale, conditional on H-slope, and fixes only
\(\epsilon/\sqrt{\sigma} = 2\,l_p\): a self-consistency condition, not
an independent determination of the value of \(\hbar\). Developed in
Chapter 7 §7.3 and Appendix B §B.4.

\textbf{Gauge group.} A continuous group of local symmetries under which
the dynamics is invariant. The Standard Model gauge group is
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\).
Conditionally on H-link, the framework derives this gauge group from the
stabilizer of a cubic-equivariant condensate with distinct block values
on the substratum lattice (the coupling matrix itself is scalar); the
stabilizer computation is exact, the physical-carrier identification is
the premise. Developed in Chapter 5.

\textbf{Generation (fermion).} In the Standard Model, the three sets of
fermions with identical gauge-quantum-number assignments but different
masses: \((u, d, e, \nu_e)\), \((c, s, \mu, \nu_\mu)\),
\((t, b, \tau, \nu_\tau)\). The framework derives one singlet plus one
symmetry-related triplet of candidate matter sectors from the staggered
taste structure on the cubic lattice; reading the triplet as three
\emph{physical} generations is conditional on \emph{H-spin'} (SM §4.7),
whose free-kernel and 4D-staggered routes are both settled negative.
Discussed in Chapter 6 §6.2.

\textbf{God's-eye view.} A hypothetical observer coextensive with the
universe, with complete knowledge of all degrees of freedom. The
framework identifies the God's-eye view as the \emph{C3} failure limit
and shows that it is not a limit case of observation but a category
outside it --- observation is partition-relative, and without a
partition, observation does not occur. Discussed in Chapter 1 §1.10.

\textbf{GW250114.} A binary black-hole merger observed on January 14,
2025. The September 10, 2025 LIGO--Virgo--KAGRA paper inferred an
increase in Kerr horizon area, with \(4.4\sigma\) for its fiducial
analysis. This classical area comparison leaves the Bekenstein-Hawking
\(1/4\) entropy coefficient untested. Discussed in Chapter 7 §7.5.

\textbf{Hidden sector.} The portion of the framework's partition that
the embedded observer does not directly access. The framework's four
conditions specify properties of this sector (coupling, slow evolution,
large capacity). For laboratory observers in our universe, the hidden
sector is everything beyond the cosmological horizon plus the
trans-horizon degrees of freedom of any local environment. Defined in
Chapter 1 §1.2.

\textbf{Higgs (in the framework).} The framework treats the Higgs as the
\emph{singlet} (\(A_1\)) taste of the staggered decomposition --- a
\emph{composite scalar} in the framework's account rather than a
fundamental field. The Higgs quartic coupling at the compositeness scale
is exactly zero, with the observed value at low energies generated by
RGE running. Developed in Chapter 6 §6.2.

\textbf{Hsp90.} A molecular chaperone whose role in buffering phenotypic
variation has been studied in evolutionary capacitance. The
matched-present readback and its kinetics remain proposed tests (Chapter
17 §17.9).

\textbf{Hypercharge.} The Standard Model U(1) quantum number of fermion
multiplets, with values
\((Y_Q, Y_u, Y_d, Y_L, Y_e) = (1/6, 2/3, -1/3, -1/2, -1)\).
Conventionally fitted empirical inputs. The framework derives these
values as the unique anomaly-free solution on the nonzero-\(Y_Q\)
branch. Developed in Chapter 6 §6.7 and Appendix B §B.5.

\textbf{Information backflow.} A revival of distinguishability: the
trace distance between the evolved states of two preparations increases
over some interval (the Breuer--Laine--Piilo signature). In a
P-divisible process distinguishability never increases, so backflow
certifies P-indivisibility; a P-indivisible process need not show it. It
is distinct from accessible finite-horizon memory, the conditional
past--future dependence that history readback (C4) supplies on
accessible windows, which does not by itself produce backflow ({[}Main
§2.3{]}). Discussed in Chapter 1 §1.5.

\textbf{Jordan-Chevalley decomposition.} For an invertible operator with
a multiplicative Jordan-Chevalley decomposition,
\(F = F_{ss} \cdot F_u\) has commuting semisimple and unipotent factors,
with \(F_u = I + N\) and \(N\) nilpotent. For the ring wave equation
under the hypotheses of Appendix B §B.3, \(N^2 = 0\) and \(F\) and
\(F_{ss}\) have the same eigenvalues, so spectral invariants are
independent of \(N\); hidden-sector marginalization does not remove
\(N\) from the visible laws. Developed in Appendix B §B.3.

\textbf{JUNO (Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory).} A reactor
neutrino experiment that in November 2025 reported the first
world-leading direct measurement of the solar neutrino mixing angle:
\(\sin^2\theta_{12} = 0.3092 \pm 0.0087\). The flavor-model value
\(1/3 - 1/(4\pi^2) = 0.3080\), with leading-order Cond 2 and the
separate normalization \(b_{23}=1\), matches the direct measurement at
\(0.14\sigma\) and the post-JUNO global fit (\(0.3085 \pm 0.0073\)) at
\(0.07\sigma\) --- a retrodiction; The design-lifetime comparison tests
the stated phenomenological target. Discussed in Chapter 8.

\textbf{Koide relation.} An empirical relation among the three
charged-lepton masses:
\(Q = (m_e + m_\mu + m_\tau)/(\sqrt{m_e} + \sqrt{m_\mu} + \sqrt{m_\tau})^2\).
Observed value \(Q = 0.666664 \pm 0.000005\). The framework predicts
\(Q = 2/3\) from cubic-group quadratic Casimir; the match is better than
\(0.001\%\) (\(0.4\sigma\)). Developed in Chapter 6 §6.6.

\textbf{Markovian.} A process whose next-step conditional law given the
available history depends only on the present state. The exact
fixed-basis representation of a supplied law on a finite alphabet and
horizon includes Markov laws ({[}Main §3.4{]}). Contrasted throughout
Chapter 1.

\textbf{Memory asymmetry.} The framework's unifying therapeutic
principle in medicine: when a disease process depends on non-Markovian
signaling dynamics that the corresponding normal tissue does not depend
on, therapies can target the memory structure rather than the catalytic
function, with the framework predicting wider therapeutic windows.
Developed in Chapter 16 §16.13.

\textbf{MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics).} A phenomenological
framework for galactic rotation curves involving an acceleration scale
of order \(10^{-10}\) m/s². On the stated horizon and heat-input branch,
the framework uses \(a_0=cH/6\) with the factor \(1/6\) imported from
Verlinde. The proposed covariant sourcing remains conditional on G3.
Developed in Chapter 7 §7.9.

\textbf{Non-Markovian.} A stochastic process whose future depends on
past states beyond the present. Accessible history dependence is the
content of a C4 witness. Finite-alphabet and finite-horizon
representability also holds for memoryless laws, and recurrence-scale
P-indivisibility uses a non-permutation rooted map and a finite return
({[}Main §3.4{]}). Physical applications require their own witnesses.
Defined in Chapter 1 §1.5. Three notions are kept apart throughout and
none unconditionally implies another: \emph{accessible finite-horizon
memory} (equivalently conditional past--future dependence in the visible
law) is the framework's own term and is what ``non-Markovian on
accessible horizons'' means here; \emph{stochastic P-indivisibility} is
failure of divisibility of the visible population law and rests on
recurrence together with a non-permutation rooted map, not on C1/C3/C4
alone; \emph{generic quantum non-Markovianity} is an open-system notion
whose content depends on the quantum divisibility or backflow criterion
adopted, and it is not what either of the first two asserts.

\textbf{Operational gluing theorem.} The framework's finite-resolution
operational result ({[}Main §3.4{]}): for a fixed initial state, finite
instrument family \(\mathcal{F}\), horizon \(K\) and grid \(G\), the
exact arithmetic construction requires both the initial state and
instrument data in the working ring, with exact trace comparisons. At
fixed outcome count the adaptive law has grid error \(O(K/G)\), with one
fixed mechanism per instrument, gluing by restriction across overlapping
families, sequential and parallel composition, and a count of reachable
hidden labels. The response-table construction uses supplied real
probabilities. At fixed-point precision the initial rounding error and
the open error bound for the clipped and normalized outcome law are
separate. The theorem establishes finite operational
\textbf{realizability} and, together with the uniform-continuum theorem,
finite-test density. It does not by itself prove that the standard local
quantum instrument category is the unique coherent operational
completion, because the same finite reversible machinery can realize
non-quantum instrument families. Which further conditions select the
quantum instrument category on a finite carrier is stated by the
operational-completion characterization ({[}GR §3.3{]}): five completion
conditions, none supplied by bare finite OI, within complex matrix
kinematics taken as given. Exact arithmetic checks in
\texttt{opglue\_probes.py} cover the stated finite examples.

\textbf{NV (Nitrogen-vacancy) center.} A point defect in diamond where a
nitrogen atom replaces a carbon atom adjacent to a lattice vacancy. The
basis for room-temperature quantum sensing with current sensitivity
limited by the NV electron-spin coherence time. The framework predicts
that backflow-aware sensing protocols exploiting the diamond lattice's
slow nuclear-spin bath recover information Markovian protocols discard;
the resulting sensitivity gain is not quantified. Discussed in Chapter
15 §15.6.

\textbf{Operator distinction (substratum-emergent).} The framework's
structural distinction between operators acting at the substratum level
(with specific conservation properties at the molecular or quantum-field
level) and operators acting at the emergent level (with conservation
properties at the coarse-grained level). The two operators can be
functionally distinct even when they look identical at the emergent
level. Developed in Chapter 6 §6.3 (for fundamental physics) and Chapter
16 §16.10 (for chromatin biology).

\textbf{Page curve.} The time-dependence of black-hole entanglement
entropy: rising during the early evaporation phase, reaching a peak at
the Page time, then falling as the black hole evaporates fully. The
framework obtains a cycle-averaged Page curve on the full product space
of black hole and radiation, under the scrambling condition H-scramble
and the decoupling condition H-decouple (H-scramble fails for every
bijection acting on an initial configuration with the bipartition
aligned to the configuration coordinates, so the Page value needs an
initial superposition over many configurations or a non-aligned
bipartition), with a Page time that, for a mass-independent emission
coefficient, is a fixed fraction of the evaporation time:
\(t_P \approx 0.646\, t_{evap}\) when the radiation's entropy equals the
horizon entropy it carries off, earlier when it carries more. Developed
in Chapter 7 §6.

\textbf{Partition-relativity.} The framework's structural feature that
the same physical substratum admits multiple visible/hidden partitions,
each producing its own emergent description. The emergent description
depends on the partition choice; the underlying substratum does not.
Does not by itself resolve a no-go theorem: the operational
probabilities and each theorem's substantive premises require separate
checks. Developed in Chapter 1 §1.4.

\textbf{P-indivisibility.} Failure of a stochastic transition family to
factor through valid intermediate stochastic maps. In OI, a
non-permutation one-step marginal on a fixed finite reversible system is
a sufficient recurrence witness. More generally, any non-permutation
rooted map forces indivisibility somewhere in the full recurrence cycle:
recurrence returns the rooted visible map to the identity, and a
non-permutation stochastic matrix has no stochastic inverse. A C4
readback gap supplies such a map, and so does every non-deterministic
visible step, including in laws that are Markov on every accessible
window. With a full-support visible prior the indivisibility is
equivalent to memory at some order below the recurrence time, observable
only when that order is accessible. This global result does not imply
accessible short-time P-indivisibility in every window; the two notions
are kept distinct. P-indivisibility is a statement about the visible
population law and is not generic quantum non-Markovianity: inside the
framework's diagonal-preserving realizations it does rule out a
stochastic intermediate map and hence CP-divisibility, but outside that
class the two come apart --- a CP-divisible family with a unitary
intermediate map can induce P-indivisible computational-basis
populations, the intermediate map consuming coherences the population
law never sees ({[}Main §2.3{]}).

\textbf{PMNS (Pontecorvo-Maki-Nakagawa-Sakata) matrix.} The unitary
mixing matrix between Standard Model neutrino mass and flavor
eigenstates. The cubic flavor model gives conditional angle values. Its
solar-angle estimate \(\sin^2\theta_{12} = 1/3 - 1/(4\pi^2)\) uses
leading-order Cond 2 and the separate normalization \(b_{23}=1\). The
value matches the JUNO-era global fit at \(0.07\sigma\), a retrodiction.
Discussed in Chapter 8.

\textbf{Read-write cycle.} In a causal realization of history readback,
varying the visible input at a fixed hidden seed changes the later
hidden state, and the retained difference affects subsequent visible
conditionals. The finite SWAP supplies a write witness. The coin--die
example instead reveals a preloaded selector through the visible
history. The cosmological and laboratory sourcing of a causal cycle
remains open (Chapter 1 §§1.3, 1.5).

\textbf{Reader/writer/eraser pharmacology.} Categorizes molecular
targets by their role in establishing marks, modifying or removing them,
or recognizing their state. Chapter 16 proposes comparing therapeutic
windows for restoration of different molecular functions.

\textbf{Restricted quantum-statistical regime.} The mechanism proposal's
name for partial distinguishability revival on an accessible window,
\(0 < \mathcal{N} < 1\). Here \(\mathcal{N}\) is the revival measure of
Chapter 18 §18.3: the largest increase \(d_t - d_s\), over pairs of
preparations and times \(s < t\) in the window, of their
distinguishability \(d\) (the total variation of the visible population
laws, equivalently the trace distance of the diagonal states) --- the
peak \emph{information backflow} on the window, kept separate from the
cumulative Breuer--Laine--Piilo sum. \(\mathcal{N} > 0\) certifies
P-indivisibility on the window; memory alone does not give
\(\mathcal{N} > 0\) ({[}Main §2.3{]}). The name refers to the quantum
representation at the transition-statistics layer, which every finite
law admits together with a deterministic hidden realization, with the
operational layer not supplied ({[}Main §3.4{]}); it marks a revival
range, neither a partial nor a complete quantum theory and not a
quantum-membership scale. Hypothesized at marginal hidden capacity, with
the proposed model form \(\mathcal{F}(r) = 2r - r^2\), \(r = N_H/N_V\)
(derivation not supplied). Diagnosed by distinguishability-revival
measurements; a multi-time memory test alone does not separate it from
complete revival. Developed in Chapter 13 §13.7, Chapter 15 §§15.7-15.8,
Chapter 18 §18.3.

\textbf{Rett syndrome.} A neurodevelopmental disorder caused by
pathogenic MECP2 variants. Guy et al.~(2007) observed neurological
rescue after reactivating Mecp2 in symptomatic adult mice. Comparative
therapeutic windows and the proposed mechanism require additional
evidence (Chapter 16 §16.12).

\textbf{RNA world.} The hypothesis that early life used RNA for both
information storage and catalysis before DNA and proteins evolved their
specialized roles. RNA's dual role as template and catalyst in a single
molecular species is the hypothesis's chemical support; it is an
empirical hypothesis, not a consequence of C1--C4. Developed in Chapter
11 §11.7.

\textbf{Staggered (fermion structure).} The placement of independent
fermion modes at alternating cubic lattice sites, producing the chiral
structure of the framework's emergent QFT and the multiple-taste
structure that gives rise to the \(1 \oplus 3\) candidate-sector
decomposition (three physical generations only under \emph{H-spin'}).
Developed in Chapter 5 §5.6 and Chapter 6 §6.2.

\textbf{Standard Model.} The current best theory of fundamental particle
physics: a chiral gauge theory with gauge group
\(\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)\), three
fermion generations, one Higgs doublet, and approximately 19 free
parameters. The framework reproduces twenty-two classified observables
--- two parameter-free structural, five conditional structural, the
remainder layered, chained or fitted (Appendix A) --- and the
anomaly-free hypercharges on the nonzero-\(Y_Q\) branch; the gauge group
follows under H-link, whose single-copy premise is not itself derived,
the physical generation reading under H-spin', and the chirality
assignment under H-χ'. Developed in Chapters 5-6.

\textbf{Stinespring dilation.} A 1955 theorem of operator algebra
establishing that any completely-positive trace-preserving map on a
Hilbert space can be realized as a unitary evolution on a larger Hilbert
space with subsequent tracing-out. It provides operator-algebraic
context for dilated channels. The finite-law proof in Main §3.4 directly
constructs a reversible realization and its permutation unitary.
Developed in Chapter 1 §1.6 and Appendix B §B.2.

\textbf{Substratum.} The underlying deterministic system
\((S, \varphi)\), modelled by a bijection on total configurations. Its
total configuration space is finite in the representative specified
under the open posit A1. With a partition and preparation, tracing out
the hidden sector gives a visible law with an exact fixed-basis quantum
representation for finite alphabets and horizons. The substratum is the
framework's primitive ontological commitment, held at the level of the
reconstructed local residue modulo the substratum gauge group rather
than any particular representative (Chapter 3) --- the ``what is really
there'' beneath the emergent quantum-mechanical description. Constructed
concretely in Chapter 2.

\textbf{Substratum-emergent operator distinction.} \emph{See operator
distinction.}

\textbf{Tier 1, Tier 2, Tier 3.} The framework's stratification of
predictions by their robustness across substratum representatives.
\emph{Tier 1}: results that follow from the framework's universality
class (shared across all substrata satisfying the structural
conditions). \emph{Tier 2}: results dependent on broader structural
commitments but not on specific lattice details. \emph{Tier 3}:
solution-specific results dependent on the particular cubic-lattice
realization. Developed in Chapter 9 §§9.3-9.4.

\textbf{TLS (Two-level system).} A candidate microscopic source of
time-correlated noise in superconducting qubits. Device-level
attribution and accessible readback require their own tests (Chapter 15
§15.3).

\textbf{Trace-out.} The mathematical operation of marginalizing over
(summing or integrating out) the hidden-sector degrees of freedom,
producing the reduced description on the visible sector. The framework's
central technical operation. Equivalent to partial trace in quantum
mechanics. Defined throughout Chapter 1.

\textbf{Tsirelson bound.} The maximum CHSH inequality violation
achievable by standard quantum mechanics: \(2\sqrt{2}\). In the
manuscript this value is retained for the cited \textbf{stochastic
causal-local indivisible} construction and for any successful lift to
the standard quantum Bell set. It is not the ceiling of a
measurement-independent, parameter-independent deterministic completion
recording a \(\pm1\) outcome in every run, whose Bell bound is 2. The
deterministic OI branch reaches quantum violation by ontic parameter
dependence; the measurement-dependent alternative is separately
\textbf{bounded and benchmarked} in Chapter 1 §1.7. Discussed in
Appendix C §C.2.

\textbf{U-parity.} The framework's grading structure in the neutrino
sector, distinguishing \(U^+\) and \(U^-\) states in the cubic-group
flavor classification. Produces the framework's distinctive sum rule and
structural relation among the three PMNS mixing angles. Developed in
Chapter 8 §8.4.

\textbf{Universality class.} A set of substrata that share the same
emergent description at the framework's Tier 1 level. The framework's
content: the substratum-to-emergent map is many-to-one, with multiple
bijections producing the same observable physics. Developed in Chapter 9
§9.3.

\textbf{Vibronic coherence.} Coherence involving electronic and
vibrational degrees of freedom. Spectroscopy and dynamical models
constrain these contributions in light-harvesting complexes (Chapter 13
§13.4).

\textbf{Visible sector.} The portion of the framework's partition that
the embedded observer directly accesses. Contrasted with the
\emph{hidden sector}. The visible sector is where measurements occur and
where the emergent description applies. Defined in Chapter 1 §1.2.

\textbf{Wolpert's theorem.} David Wolpert's results (2001, 2008) on
fundamental limits of inference devices embedded in the system they are
trying to predict. A physical analog of Gödel's incompleteness theorem
and Turing's halting problem result --- logical, worst-case, and
unquantified. The framework's partition-induced trace-out is the
mechanism of a \emph{parallel physical} incompleteness, with the
memory-bearing dynamics quantum mechanics represents as the specific
cost; Wolpert's result corroborates the pattern but is not the source of
the framework's derivation. Discussed in Chapter 12 §12.8, Appendix C
§C.7.

\textbf{Yamanaka factors.} The four transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2,
Klf4, c-Myc) whose transient expression reprograms somatic cells to
induced pluripotent stem cells. Particular iPSC protocols retain some
cell-of-origin methylation marks. The extent depends on the protocol and
assay, and the proposed operator analogy motivates comparisons of
chromatin marks and cell function. Discussed in Chapter 16 §16.10.
